papers.title: ConRef: Auditing Reference Reliability in 2D/3D Registration Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Purpose: Accurate 2D/3D registration is crucial for image-guided orthopedic interventions, enabling the alignment of preoperative 3D anatomy with intraoperative X-ray observations for surgical navigation. Public benchmarks have facilitated the development and evaluation of increasingly accurate registration methods. However, as registration errors approach the uncertainty of benchmark reference poses, measured performance may be limited by reference inaccuracies rather than algorithmic errors alone. Methods: We propose Consensus Reference (ConRef), a multi-view framework for auditing reference poses in existing X-ray/computed tomography (CT) registration benchmarks. By jointly exploiting multiple X-ray observations, ConRef estimates an additional reference pose, quantifies its uncertainty, and identifies potential X-ray outliers. We validate the framework using independent anatomical evidence and a newly acquired X-ray/cone-beam CT (CBCT) phantom dataset with bead-based reference poses. Results: On our BeadPhant dataset, ConRef differed from independent bead-based references by 0.08-0.12 mm, while discrepancies with original references reached 2.06 mm on the Femur dataset. It also flagged 22 DeepFluoro X-rays as potential outliers. On Femur F5, reference choice changed the submillimeter success conclusions of the same registrations. Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that reference discrepancies can influence the evaluation of high-accuracy 2D/3D registration methods. By providing an additional, independently validated reference and identifying potential inconsistencies, ConRef enables systematic auditing of existing benchmarks and supports more reliable evaluation of registration error.

papers.intro:
Accurate medical image registration plays a fundamental role in image-guided surgery and surgical navigation by establishing spatial correspondences between images acquired at different stages, across imaging modalities, or in different coordinate systems. These correspondences enable preoperative anatomical information and surgical plans to be aligned with the intraoperative environment, supporting surgical navigation and image-guided interventions Li et al. (2025).

These correspondences enable preoperative anatomical information and surgical plans to be aligned with the intraoperative environment, supporting surgical navigation and image-guided interventions Li et al. (2025).

In orthopedic surgery, procedures such as spinal instrumentation, pelvic fixation, and complex fracture management require accurate localization of bony anatomy Li et al. (2026). Computed tomography (CT) and cone-beam CT (CBCT) provide detailed three-dimensional anatomical information, while intraoperative X-ray imaging provides two-dimensional projections for surgical guidance. Registering these complementary images enables preoperative 3D anatomy to be aligned with intraoperative observations. Developing and evaluating these 2D/3D registration methods requires datasets with reliable reference poses for quantitative evaluation.

Both datasets provide CT volumes, multiple corresponding C-arm X-rays, and reference poses for quantitative evaluation. (2026), evaluated on both datasets. As registration methods become increasingly accurate, the reliability of benchmark reference poses becomes critical for interpreting their reported performance.

Reliable evaluation requires reference poses that are substantially more accurate than the registration methods being assessed Valstar et al. (2005); Zhang et al. (2021). Previous gold-standard datasets for 2D/3D registration have therefore explicitly quantified reference uncertainty Tomaževič et al. (2004); D’Isidoro et al. (2021). In practice, however, reference poses remain subject to sources of uncertainty. DeepFluoro obtained its references through offline image registration followed by visual inspection Grupp et al. (2020), whereas the Femur dataset derived them from a marker of metal spheres mounted on a K-wire Flepp et al. (2025). When reported registration errors approach the millimeter or submillimeter scale, even small discrepancies in reference poses may affect the interpretation of registration error and threshold-based success criteria. Notably, the official XVR evaluation excludes four DeepFluoro X-rays due to questionable ground-truth pose parameters Gopalakrishnan (2026). These observations highlight the importance of assessing reference reliability rather than treating the provided reference poses as unquestionable ground truth.

Although independent ground-truth measurements are often unavailable for existing datasets, their multiple X-ray views provide redundant geometric information that can be exploited to assess reference consistency. By jointly constraining the CT pose across multiple projections, it is possible to estimate an additional reference and examine whether X-rays agree with the resulting consensus. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Consensus Reference (ConRef), a multi-view framework for auditing reference poses in existing 2D/3D registration benchmarks. We further validate the framework using independent anatomical evidence and a newly acquired X-ray/CBCT phantom dataset with bead-based reference poses. Our contributions are: • We propose ConRef, which provides an additional reference for assessing the reliability of existing 2D/3D registration benchmarks and quantifies its uncertainty. • We introduce an X-ray consistency assessment to identify potential X-ray outliers and demonstrate how reference discrepancies can affect the evaluation of registration error. • We provide the open-source framework and BeadPhant, an X-ray/CBCT phantom dataset with independently validated bead-based reference poses at a precision of the order of 0.1 mm.11 1 Code and dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.

papers.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments
papers.abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.

papers.intro:
Agents are increasingly used to modify code, navigate websites, and complete work in terminal environments [28, 55, 37]. An agent combines a large language model (LLM) with a harness, which manages its context, execution flow, and termination. As agents become part of real-world workflows, they still fail on many tasks. Studying these failures can guide improvement: we need to identify where agents fail and understand why. Benchmark scores summarize task success, but the final outcome alone does not explain the cause of a failure. The same outcome can arise for different reasons. For example, a missing report may result from a difficult computation, or simply because the agent stops before saving its result. These failures require different fixes. Improving agents therefore requires not only measuring failures, but also systematically discovering them and diagnosing their causes.

Existing automated evaluation methods often discover LLM failures by generating new questions or selecting informative tests [11, 29, 1]. ProbeLLM [23] goes beyond finding individual errors by explaining incorrect responses and organizing related errors into failure modes. Each mode describes a shared error pattern supported by concrete failure examples. This connects the discovery of individual failures with an account of the patterns shared across them.

These studies help explain observed failures, but leave open how to systematically construct new tasks to discover further failures and organize them into shared modes. We therefore ask: can we build an effective framework that automatically discovers and diagnoses agent failures?

This requires addressing three challenges. (1) Building reliable executable tests. An LLM test can pair a question with a reference answer and a verifier. An agent test also needs a working environment in which actions change the task state, a solvable task, and a checker that evaluates the required outcome. Environment defects or shortcuts accepted by the checker can otherwise give misleading results [3, 45]. (2) Distinguishing task-specific difficulties from recurring agent behavior. A failed trajectory may reflect a difficulty in one task or a behavior that appears in many tasks. Explaining that trajectory alone does not distinguish the two. New tests must change the task context while preserving the condition thought to cause the failure, so that we can check whether the same agent makes the same mistake again. (3) Identifying shared failures across different tasks. Omitting a CSV export after data analysis and a JSON export after a database query can reflect the same error: completing the computation without delivering its output. A failed write can also leave a file missing, but requires a different correction. Diagnosis must distinguish the behaviors behind these similar outcomes.

papers.title: Consensus of Consensus: Decentralized Consensus-Based Optimization
papers.abstract: We propose and analyze a decentralized variant of Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO) for the global minimization of continuous, possibly non-convex functions accessible only through a stochastic, possibly biased, zeroth-order oracle with bounded mean-squared error. The agents are split among $N$ units of an undirected communication network. Each unit evolves its swarm of $M$ agents towards a local tracking variable, which follows the network average of the local consensus points through one round of neighbour-to-neighbour communication via a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, without any central coordinator. We show that, under an explicit condition linking the drift and diffusion parameters to $M$, all agents reach consensus almost surely, at an exponential mean-square rate governed by the spectrum of the mixing matrix. Using a finite-agent quantitative Laplace principle, we prove that, for large $\alpha$ and provided some agent visits a neighbourhood of the global minimizer with sufficient probability, the expected mean-squared distance of the swarm from the minimizer falls below any tolerance within an explicit number of iterations, at a rate that deteriorates for poorly connected networks. We verify this hitting assumption for a simplified dynamics. Experiments on benchmarks up to dimension $d=1000$, with stochastic objectives, and on a federated learning task demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

papers.intro:
Consensus-based optimization (CBO) is a versatile, zero-order metaheuristic for global optimization: an ensemble of interacting agents explores the search space and is driven, through a drift-diffusion dynamics, toward a weighted average of the agents’ positions, the consensus point, computed via a Gibbs-type weighting of the objective function. Since it never requires gradient information, CBO is directly applicable to nonsmooth, nonconvex, and even black-box objectives, while at the same time being amenable to rigorous mean-field and finite-agent analysis, unlike most other metaheuristics of swarm-intelligence type. The model was first introduced by Pinnau, Totzeck, Tse and Martin [34], who proposed the underlying stochastic differential equation and derived its mean-field limit as a nonlocal, degenerate parabolic PDE. The first rigorous proofs that the method actually converges to a global minimizer, under quantitative assumptions on the objective and the initialization, were given by Carrillo, Choi, Totzeck and Tse [8] and, in fully unconditional form with respect to initialization and with agent analysis as well, by Fornasier, Klock and Riedl [16] (see also the independent proof by Ha, Jin and Kim [21]). Since these foundational results, a large body of work has refined the model along several directions: anisotropic, component-wise noise to remove the dimension-dependence of the drift and to reduce computational cost via mini-batching [11], truncated noise [17], jump-diffusion noise [29], memory effects [35], heterogeneous noise combined with random-batch agent interactions [30], noisy/estimated objective evaluations [3], and mechanisms such as a personal-best memory term borrowed from particle swarm optimization [38]. In parallel, CBO has been extended to constrained problems on the sphere and other hypersurfaces [14] and shown to be competitive on high-dimensional machine learning tasks [11, 15], has been connected to consensus-based sampling [10], and has recently been introduced to robotics for global trajectory and policy optimization [37]; we refer to [39] for a broader survey of these developments.

Yet, in order to fully exploit the potential of CBO, in particular on the large-scale, high-dimensional problems arising in modern machine learning, a genuinely parallel and distributed formulation of the algorithm would be crucial. It is a recurring claim in the literature that CBO-type dynamics are “highly parallelizable” or “inherently scalable” [39, 13], and indeed the per-agent updates may typically be distributed across the cores of a GPU or a multi-core machine [37]. However, this common notion of parallelism is architecturally centralized: every agent, regardless of which processor evaluates its update, relies on the very same, globally shared consensus point, so that a central synchronization step is required at every iteration and no genuine network structure or local-only communication is exploited. We recently explored the parallelization of the centralized CBO in the companion paper [4]. A notable departure from a single, globally shared consensus point is given by the kinetic theory-based optimization (KBO) methods of [5], where the mean-field interaction of CBO is replaced by binary interactions between randomly sampled pairs of agents, described by a Boltzmann-type equation. There, however, any pair of agents may interact and the update still involves a collective estimate over the whole population, so that no network structure restricting communication is present. To the best of our knowledge, no distributed formulation of CBO with computational units communicating solely over a network of local connections has appeared in the literature, and, with the possible exception of the federated-learning variants of CBO proposed by García Trillos and collaborators [9, 19, 18], which nonetheless rely on a central server orchestrating the interaction between clients, no convergence proof has been provided for any parallel, decentralized implementation of the method.

In this paper we explore a parallel and distributed formulation of CBO with fully decentralized computation. We assume the NN computational units to be the nodes of a connected, undirected communication network 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}), each holding a local swarm of agents and able to communicate only with its network neighbors. Rather than relying on a single, globally shared consensus point, each node computes its own local consensus point from its own agents and then updates a local estimate of the global consensus by averaging it, through a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, with the estimates held by its neighbors, a mechanism we call consensus of consensus, in the spirit of classical linear gossip and distributed-averaging schemes over networks [40, 33]. Since the network is connected, information about the location of the global minimizer, although initially known only locally and imprecisely at each node, is able to reach every other node; along the dynamics this information is slowly diffused across the network, and, as we prove, global consensus among all agents and all local estimates is asymptotically formed, exactly as in the centralized method, without any node ever having direct access to the whole swarm.

papers.title: Navigating Quantum Education at the University level: Pedagogical Pathways and a Roadmap for Textbook Selection
papers.abstract: Instruction in quantum mechanics (QM) is often categorized by its entry point as 'wave-first' or 'spin-first', yet these labels lack consistent definitions and overlook other established or emerging approaches. Moreover, while capturing broad differences in topic selection and sequencing, this binary framing obscures critical differences in contextualization--how three dimensions (mathematical tools, phenomena and experiments, and theoretical concepts) are framed and connected to support student sensemaking. Research also rarely examines how such pedagogical choices unfold across the undergraduate-to-graduate trajectory. Using textbooks as an analytical lens to map these choices and characterize overarching pathways, encompassing entry points and overall orientations, we comparatively analyze the selection, sequencing, and contextualization of core topics across these 3 dimensions, alongside prefaces and introductions, in 36 university QM textbooks spanning countries and eras. At the topic level, we show that identical topics occupy widely different curricular roles depending on their contextualization. Synthesizing these findings into pathways, we identify three additional entry-point archetypes (labeled path-, qubit-, and axiom-first) and characterize all 5 approaches, showing that most textbooks combine multiple archetypes in their opening chapters. Extending this synthesis beyond entry points, we map textbooks' overall orientations relative to mathematics, experiment and application, and theoretical physics. Interpreting these profiles alongside authors' rationales reveals how educators navigate competing trade-offs among mathematical accessibility, theoretical generality, physical motivation, and modern developments. This study provides a multidimensional framework, substantive examples, and a practical roadmap for textbook selection and curriculum design in QM education.

papers.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
papers.abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.intro:
The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying a model’s inner workings (Olah et al., 2020), encompassing many methods and frameworks (Elhage et al., 2021; Mueller et al., 2026; Ferrando et al., 2024; Sharkey et al., 2025, e.g.). Among these, Causal Abstraction is particularly promising, formally defining notions of equivalence between causal graphs (Beckers and Halpern, 2019). Under this framework, a deep neural network (DNN) is equivalent to a (conceptually simpler) algorithm if they behave similarly under interventions (Geiger et al., 2025b); whenever this is the case, we informally say that the DNN implements the algorithm. Causal Abstraction thus allows us to interpret a DNN in terms of the algorithms it implements.

Causal Abstraction thus allows us to interpret a DNN in terms of the algorithms it implements.

In recent years, however, a number of works have raised potential pitfalls in using mechanistic interpretability approaches, including Causal Abstraction, to draw firm conclusions about a model (e.g., Mueller, 2024; Sutter et al., 2025; Méloux et al., 2025a, inter alia). Most relevant to us are two concerns. First, mechanistic interpretability approaches may be non-identifiable and a DNN might be found to implement many algorithms (Méloux et al., 2025b). Second, Causal Abstraction methods may find interpretability illusions, i.e., interventions that leverage a DNN’s null space to imitate genuine causal behavior (Makelov et al., 2024). As noted by Wu et al. (2024b) in their response to Makelov et al., though, interpretability illusions may not pose an actual obstacle for Causal Abstraction, as it is not inherently problematic for an intervention to leverage a model’s null space.

Concretely, we find parasite features in two tasks, syntactic agreement and two-digit addition, by training interventions with a constrained class of linear alignment maps (which are minimally more expressive than rotation maps). Claims that rest on high intervention accuracy alone should thus be treated with care, with our results further highlighting the importance of sound scientific practice in interpreting the results of mechanistic interpretability experiments. papers.title: Generative Bayesian modelling of radio antenna beams An application to the MeerKAT radio telescope
papers.abstract: Accurate primary beam models are essential for high-fidelity calibration and imaging in radio astronomy. Traditional approaches either lack the ability to represent realistic antenna patterns (analytical models) or become computationally prohibitive to interpolate for wide-bandwidth observations (electromagnetic simulations, direct holographic measurements). We develop a generative beam model that represents both the spatial structure and the frequency variations in the primary beam while remaining tractable for integration into calibration and imaging pipelines, achieving superior accuracy compared to existing parametric models and reducing data storage compared to data-based models. We adopt a non-parametric Bayesian framework grounded in information field theory, implemented using the NIFTy library. The model represents the beam as a base pattern subject to frequency-dependent geometric transformations (scaling and shifting). Performance is validated through posterior predictive checks (chi^2/dof ~ 1) and compared against traditional models (Gaussian, Airy disc, JimBeam, Eidos, electromagnetic simulation). We apply the method to holographic data of the array-averaged MeerKAT Stokes I beam in the L band. The model achieves 400:1 data compression while preserving statistical consistency with holographic measurements, and outperforms existing approaches by more than an order of magnitude in mean squared deviation. Zernike decomposition of the base beam, combined with the geometric transformations, enables efficient beam reconstruction at arbitrary spatial resolution. The 150 kB per-antenna footprint enables memory-slim integration into calibration and imaging software at negligible cost, scales favourably to large arrays and wide bandwidths, and can be readily adapted to other radio telescopes.

papers.intro:
The accurate characterisation of an antenna’s beam is essential for observational studies in radio astronomy. An incorrect beam model can significantly degrade image quality by introducing systematic flux scale distortions that are particularly severe for off-axis sources far from the phase centre. Precise characterisation of the beam sidelobes is especially important in observations that include bright sources outside the target field, as inaccurate sidelobe modelling can lead to spurious flux density contamination and imaging artefacts. Such inaccuracies introduce artefacts that cannot be mitigated by additional temporal or spectral integration.

Such inaccuracies introduce artefacts that cannot be mitigated by additional temporal or spectral integration.

A wide range of beam models has been developed for different types of antennas, ranging from purely theoretical formulations to data-driven approaches that incorporate measurement-based corrections (Silver 1949; Ruze 1966; Harrington 1993; Scott and Ryle 1977; Rahmat-Samii et al. 1980; Olver et al. 1994; Hamaker et al. 1996; Condon and Ransom 2016; Perley and Butler 2017; Iheanetu et al. 2019; Asad et al. 2021; Kern 2025; Wilensky et al. 2025). In recent years, with the advent of increasingly complex radio arrays operating under diverse observing conditions, the need for precise beam modelling has grown substantially. Capturing the detailed behaviour of the antenna beam not only improves calibration efficiency but also enhances image fidelity, thereby enabling more accurate scientific measurements and discoveries.

The objective of this study is to develop a beam model based on a non-parametric Bayesian framework grounded in information field theory (IFT; Enßlin et al. 2009), capable of capturing both the spatial and spectral structure of the beam in a compact and physically meaningful way. This theory provides a theoretical foundation for extending Bayesian inference to continuous fields. Building on this foundation, we employ NIFTy (numerical information field theory; Selig et al. 2013; Arras et al. 2019; Edenhofer et al. 2024), a computational library specifically designed for Bayesian inference in high-dimensional and function-space problems. NIFTy offers tools for estimating statistical properties of complex posterior distributions from noisy and incomplete data and has demonstrated scalability to problems involving half a billion parameters (Edenhofer et al. 2024). By minimising the number of degrees of freedom, the model aims to represent only the physically relevant components and their variations.

In this work, we study the generative Bayesian modelling of the antenna beam of a typical modern radio telescope operating in the mid radio-frequency range (1–10 GHz). We detail the GAMBIT (generative antenna model from Bayesian inference technique) framework, first sketched in Pashapour-Ahmadabadi et al. (2026). These telescopes typically consist of a parabolic primary reflector and can have receiving elements in an on-axis primary focus—as the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) antennas (Hotan et al., 2021) or the planned Deep Synoptic Array (DSA; Hallinan et al. 2019) do — or use an offset Gregorian design, as the MeerKAT (Jonas and MeerKAT Team, 2016) and SKA-Mid (Norris et al., 2015) telescopes do. While ASKAP antennas have the additional complexity of phased array feeds (PAFs), and since DSA, MeerKAT Extension and SKA-Mid are still under construction, we choose MeerKAT for this study due to the availability of high-quality holographic beam measurements across its full operational bandwidth. Holographic measurements characterise the beam by observing a strong, known calibrator source, while scanning the antenna across a grid of pointing offsets, directly mapping the complex beam response across the field of view. Unlike electromagnetic (EM) simulations—which rely on idealised models of antenna reflector and feed geometry, holographic measurements provide a direct, high signal-to-noise, frequency-resolved characterisation of the actual as-built antenna response, capturing real-world imperfections and frequency-dependent effects. We anticipate that lessons learned for MeerKAT antenna beams will be directly applicable to the future characterisation of SKA-Mid antenna beams.

MeerKAT is a radio interferometer comprising 64 offset Gregorian dishes, each with an effective diameter of D=13.5 m, distributed over baselines of up to 8 km in the Northern Cape Province of South Africa (Jonas and MeerKAT Team, 2016). The MeerKAT antenna beam has previously been modelled using several approaches. Among these are full-wave EM simulations (de Villiers et al., 2019; Asad et al., 2021; de Villiers et al., 2021), employing detailed three-dimensional representations of the antenna structure. Although based on the exact physics of Maxwell’s equations, these simulations necessarily rely on idealised as-designed geometries: modelling every structural detail is computationally intractable. As a result, EM simulations do not fully capture the frequency-dependent pointing behaviour (de Villiers and Cotton, 2022), which arises from real-world effects absent from the idealised model. A second efficient approach for beam modelling involves characteristic basis function patterns, which decompose complex beam structures into a small number of representative basis functions. The full beam pattern can then be reconstructed by summing over the dominant ‘eigenbeams,’ resulting in a set of simpler components that capture the essential beam characteristics. This technique enables fast and scalable beam predictions, making it especially suitable for large interferometric arrays like MeerKAT (Maaskant and Ivashina 2012; Mutonkole et al. 2016; de Villiers 2018). An alternative approach characterises the beam using a unique set of Zernike polynomials (von F. Zernike 1934; Born and Wolf 1999), which provide compact mathematical descriptions of the beam’s spatial structure and spectral behaviour.

papers.title: Pharos: Learning to Control Rare Events at Scale
papers.abstract: Rare events drive transformations across physics, chemistry and biology, yet predicting their mechanisms and rates remains a fundamental challenge. Here we introduce Pharos, a framework that learns to make rare transitions accessible while predicting how frequently they occur under physical dynamics. Through stochastic optimal control, Pharos jointly learns the probability of completing a transition and how to steer simulations toward it, allowing sampling and learning to improve one another. Across biomolecular benchmarks, Pharos learns accurate transition probabilities with order-of-magnitude gains in convergence speed over previous algorithms. It transfers across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent while maintaining accurate reaction rate predictions, scales to host-guest binding systems that span millisecond timescales, and enables chemical reaction studies with a computationally demanding machine learning interatomic potential. By combining efficient sampling, quantitative kinetics, and transferability, Pharos opens a route toward foundation models of rare event mechanisms and rates across molecular systems.

papers.intro:
Rare events underlie many important transformations in nature, including protein conformational changes, chemical reactions, and phase transitions[16, 59, 36, 34]. Their rates determine whether these transformations occur on experimentally accessible timescales and how competing processes shape their outcomes. Predicting these rates remains a central challenge because systems can spend exceedingly long periods fluctuating within metastable basins before undergoing a transition[33]. Direct simulations therefore devote most of their computational effort to waiting, with few observations of the events that determine the kinetics. Enhanced sampling has greatly expanded access to transition pathways, but observing how a transformation occurs does not by itself establish how frequently it occurs under the physical dynamics. Rare events underlie many important transformations in nature, including protein conformational changes, chemical reactions, and phase transitions[16, 59, 36, 34]. Their rates determine whether these transformations occur on experimentally accessible timescales and how competing processes shape their outcomes. Predicting these rates remains a central challenge because systems can spend exceedingly long periods fluctuating within metastable basins before undergoing a transition[33]. Direct simulations therefore devote most of their computational effort to waiting, with few observations of the events that determine the kinetics. Enhanced sampling has greatly expanded access to transition pathways, but observing how a transformation occurs does not by itself establish how frequently it occurs under the physical dynamics. Consequently, advances in mechanistic understanding are not always accompanied by quantitative predictions of reaction rates.

A central link between microscopic mechanisms and macroscopic kinetics is the committor function: the probability that a system starting from a given state reaches the product basin before the reactant basin[38]. Widely regarded as the ideal reaction coordinate[13, 4, 3], the committor measures progress toward a transition and identifies configurations equally likely to reach either basin. Within transition path theory, it also enters expressions for reactive probability currents and reaction rates, providing a principled route from molecular configurations to quantitative kinetics [57]. This connection has motivated substantial efforts to learn the committor using molecular simulations and machine learning, including direct trajectory shooting, variational principles, and dynamical self-consistency relations [58, 20, 24, 30, 32, 7, 31, 50, 35].

These approaches share a fundamental difficulty: obtaining informative observations of the reactive region. Unbiased simulations predominantly visit metastable basins, where the outcome is largely determined, while rarely exploring the intervening configurations where commitment to either basin changes. Sampling and committor learning are therefore closely interdependent. An accurate committor can guide simulations toward informative configurations, while those simulations provide the evidence needed to improve its estimate [44, 54, 25]. A common strategy is to embed transition path sampling[12] within an iterative learning loop, using sampled trajectories to refine the committor and the learned committor to guide subsequent sampling [24]. Yet efficiently resolving this interdependence, while retaining access to the underlying reaction rates, remains challenging in complex molecular systems.

Here we introduce Pharos, a highly efficient approach for predicting reaction rates and characterizing transition mechanisms in complex molecular systems. Building on the stochastic optimal control formulation [14], Pharos unifies sampling and committor learning within a single control problem: the committor guides simulations toward reactive configurations, and the resulting trajectories refine both the committor and its associated control, without requiring a separate transition path sampling procedure. Across benchmark biomolecular conformational transitions, Pharos learns accurate committor functions with order-of-magnitude faster convergence. Beyond individual systems, Pharos demonstrates transferability across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent while maintaining accurate reaction rate predictions. Learning on coarse-grained coordinates further extends its reach to larger host–guest binding systems in explicit solvent. These efficiency gains also enable the study of chemical reactions using a computationally demanding machine learning interatomic potential. Together, these results establish Pharos as a basis for a foundation model to predict rare event mechanisms and kinetics across biological and chemical systems.

papers.title: Benchmark Ne-like Transitions of W, Re, Os, Ir, and Bi Measured by High-resolution TES x-ray Spectroscopy with Absolute Energy Calibration
papers.abstract: We present high-resolution measurements of $n=2$-3 transitions in Ne-like tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, and bismuth using a transition-edge sensor (TES) microcalorimeter. These measurements provide new benchmarks for Ne-like ions in the high-$Z$ regime ($Z > 74$), extending previous EBIT studies of the sequence. To achieve sub-eV accuracy, we developed a dedicated x-ray fluorescence source employing well-characterized K-shell emission lines from metallic elements. Our results offer stringent tests for relativistic atomic structure theories and demonstrate the advantage of TES spectroscopy for precision measurements in highly charged ions.

papers.title: A dynamic variational principle on phase space for Wasserstein cubic splines
papers.abstract: Wasserstein cubic splines have been introduced to provide a smooth interpolation in time between prescribed probability measures on $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Their construction for $N$ measures is based on a multi-marginal optimal transport problem on a space of dimension $N\! \cdot \! d$, thus becoming very high-dimensional already for a small number of prescribed measures. We prove that the dimension can be reduced to a fixed number $2d+1$ via a dynamic variational principle on phase space. We also give an example showing that the Monge ansatz, which would also reduce the dimension to a fixed number, fails to capture exact solutions and is in general ill-posed, even for absolutely continuous measures.

papers.title: Action-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
papers.abstract: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.

To forecast the intervened future, we model the action-induced change explicitly as a response relative to the reference future. Paired futures make this response observable, yet predicting it poses three requirements: state dependence, selectivity, and addressability. First, the response should depend on the pre-intervention system state (Figure 1a). Closing the same road at rush hour and late at night can have very different effects. Second, the predicted response should capture changes at affected node–time positions while remaining near zero in quiet regions (Figure 1b). Third, the response should be controllable at individual node–time positions, so that temporal constraints, e.g., no response before onset, can be enforced locally (Figure 1c).

papers.title: On the convergence of greedy algorithms in one-dimensional Wasserstein space
papers.abstract: We study the convergence of the greedy algorithm for approximating a compact set by barycenters in metric spaces, in particular in the space of one-dimensional measures endowed with the 2-Wasserstein distance. To this end, we compare several metric $N$-widths, which measure the best error achievable with $N$-point barycenters, using either classical barycenters having nonnegative weights or signed barycenters, with weights of arbitrary sign summing to one. For the analysis we exploit that quantile functions embed the one-dimensional 2-Wasserstein space isometrically into a convex cone of $L^2(0,1)$, and barycenter sets correspond to nonlinear projections of convex or affine hulls. We prove, both in the algebraic and exponential case, that the convergence rate of the greedy algorithm using signed barycenters matches the one of the metric $N$-width defined with classical barycenters. We provide counterexamples showing that this fails for the other combinations.

papers.title: Active Learning of Flows from Curve Observations using Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: The active learning of real control systems requires informative roll-outs of controls. In this paper, we present a local optimization algorithm that finds the trajectory that most reduces uncertainty about the flow of a control system modeled by a Gaussian process. Therefore, we derive an approximation scheme for the posterior kernel of the Gaussian process after observing it on an entire continuous-time trajectory and establish a Pontryagin-type necessary condition for the optimizer. As the flow is unknown, the actual trajectory can deviate from the planned trajectory. We propose a trajectory planner that searches for the most informative control within a maximal allowed deviation horizon instead of a fixed time horizon. We show by trajectory-wise time rescaling that the underlying optimal control problem is equivalent to a fixed end time optimal control problem. Finally, we study both the fixed end time planner and the fixed maximum deviation planner in a numerical example and compare them with benchmarks.

papers.title: Mechanism Parity for Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous-Driving Perception
papers.abstract: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.

Simulation has become a core pillar of autonomous-driving development, testing, and safety assurance because it enables scalable experimentation over rare, risky, and difficult-to-reproduce traffic situations [1, 2]. Simulation has become a core pillar of autonomous-driving development, testing, and safety assurance because it enables scalable experimentation over rare, risky, and difficult-to-reproduce traffic situations [1, 2]. However, a long-standing question remains unresolved in practical validation workflows: when a real scene and its synthetic counterpart produce similar outputs, did the system under test rely on the same evidence to make that decision?

This question matters because output agreement alone can mask a failure mode that is especially problematic for safety-critical perception: the system can produce a correct or near-correct output for the wrong reason. For example, a steering model may retain the same steering angle across a paired real and synthetic scene while redistributing its reliance from lane boundaries and road texture toward spurious sky artifacts or background structures. Likewise, a segmentation model may preserve mask overlap while shifting its decisiveness from road-aligned evidence toward scene content that does not reliably transfer across domains. Such cases weaken the validity of simulation-based conclusions even when traditional fidelity indicators appear satisfactory [6, 7].

Such cases weaken the validity of simulation-based conclusions even when traditional fidelity indicators appear satisfactory [6, 7].

papers.title: Cannot Wait to Verify: Parallel Drafting to Eliminate Verifier Idle Time in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.

Large Language Models (LLMs) (Minaee et al., 2024) have achieved impressive performance across various tasks (reasoning, generation, decision-making, etc.) largely driven by aggressive scaling in depth and parameter count. This scaling has made autoregressive decoding a primary bottleneck in deployment, as each generated token requires a full forward pass through all transformer layers, enforcing strict token-wise sequential execution. This results in high inference latency, limiting the practicality of large models in latency-sensitive settings (Bajpai and Hanawal, 2025b; Cai et al., 2024).

Numerous approaches have been proposed to mitigate inference latency, including pruning (Vadera and Ameen, 2022), quantization (Gholami et al., 2022), distillation (Xu et al., 2024), and early-exit (Rahmath P et al., 2024) mechanisms. While effective in reducing computation, these methods typically trade accuracy for efficiency by altering model architectures, compressing representations, or terminating computation prematurely. In contrast, decoding-time methods such as speculative decoding (SD) (Hu et al., 2025) achieve acceleration without sacrificing output quality by reducing sequential dependence: a lightweight draft model rapidly generates candidate tokens autoregressively, which are then verified in parallel by a larger, more accurate model.

Despite its success, SD suffers from two fundamental inefficiencies that have received limited attention. First, the drafting stage remains fully autoregressive, forcing the verifier to idle until a batch of draft tokens is produced. This leads to substantial underutilization of compute hardware and limits the achievable speedup (see Figure 1(a)). Second, SD is governed by a trade-off in the drafting stage: a slightly bigger/slower, more accurate draft model improves token acceptance and reduces verification frequency, but incurs higher autoregressive latency during drafting, while a smaller/faster, less accurate drafter lowers per-step drafting cost at the expense of increased rejections and reduced parallel efficiency. Together, these effects make the sequential nature of drafting the dominant bottleneck in SD, impacting the overall system efficiency.

However, frequent rejections limit end-to-end speedup in such methods. Moreover, existing approaches employ static drafting strategies (Leviathan et al., 2023; Elhoushi et al., 2024), allocating a fixed speedup method regardless of input difficulty. These limitations motivate an adaptive drafting mechanism that dynamically balances speed and accuracy, accelerating draft generation for easy inputs while selectively increasing computation for harder cases to maximize acceptance.

Instead of executing transformer layers of the draft model strictly sequentially, our method evaluates multiple layers concurrently by propagating from the most recently available hidden state. A lightweight similarity check continuously monitors divergence in hidden-state space and triggers recomputation only when the proposed hidden state deviates substantially from the true hidden state. When divergence remains small, intermediate layers are effectively skipped by reusing hidden representations, allowing the draft model to advance rapidly with minimal additional computation and approximation error. papers.title: Solar-Conditioned Flow Matching for Multitemporal Aerial Visible-to-Infrared Image Translation
papers.abstract: Aerial visible-to-infrared (V2IR) image translation provides scalable thermal data across the full diurnal cycle. However, existing methods predominantly learn a static mapping within narrow acquisition windows. As the thermal state evolves throughout the day, a single visible image may correspond to multiple plausible IR appearances, making V2IR translation an inherently multitemporal task. This letter proposes solar-conditioned latent flow matching (Solar-Flow), which upgrades aerial V2IR translation from static mapping to multitemporal generation. First, we design three computable physical factors, namely the solar elevation, the thermal phase clock (TPC), and the flight altitude. The TPC counts the elapsed heating and cooling hours on a continuous 24-hour axis anchored at sunrise, so the thermal state stays well defined even at hours without training samples. Second, we inject the condition into every Transformer block of a pretrained flow matching generator through adaptive layer normalization. This design preserves translation fidelity and enables multitemporal generation. Finally, we construct a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering 14 hour groups. Solar-Flow achieves multitemporal generation on this dataset, where a single visible image is translated into plausible IR images at multiple times of day, even at hours that were never seen in training.

papers.intro:
Thermal infrared (IR) imagery is essential for Earth observation because it captures the radiation emitted by the scene itself and remains informative at night and under weak illumination. However, constructing large paired visible-to-IR (V2IR) datasets requires specialized acquisition hardware and pixel-level registration, making aerial V2IR translation an urgent research direction [1, 2]. Image-to-image translation between other sensor pairs such as SAR and optical imagery has also been extensively studied [3, 4], yet these approaches treat the mapping as static and time agnostic, ignoring thermal state evolution. Recent generative approaches such as latent diffusion [5] and ThermalGen [6] produce realistic thermal appearances but remain blind to the underlying thermal state. As a result, one visible input always yields a single fixed IR appearance. PID [7] and IPLD [8] embed thermodynamic decomposition into IR synthesis, yet generation is never conditioned on the thermal state, so each remains a static mapping. Surfaces accumulate heat after sunrise and release it after sunset, so the same scene exhibits different IR appearances at different times of the day. Moreover, existing aerial benchmarks such as AVIID [9] are recorded within short acquisition windows, so this temporally varying behavior cannot be learned. To the best of our knowledge, a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering the full diurnal cycle is still absent. To address these limitations, we propose a multitemporal V2IR framework that shifts the generative objective from static mapping to multitemporal generation. We also construct a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering the full diurnal cycle. Specifically, each frame is paired with three physical factors computed from its timestamp and GPS coordinate alone, namely the solar elevation, the thermal phase clock (TPC), and the flight altitude. The TPC measures the elapsed heating hours during the day and the elapsed cooling hours after sunset within a continuous 24-hour coordinate. This provides a physically meaningful time axis that can be compared across dates. The condition is injected into ThermalGen through adaptive layer normalization. This allows a single visible image to be translated into IR images at any time, including hours unseen in training. To build this dataset, daytime pairs come from synchronized dual-camera videos, and night pairs from georeferenced orthophotos. The main contributions are as follows. 1. We propose solar-conditioned latent flow matching (Solar-Flow), which upgrades aerial V2IR translation from static mapping to multitemporal generation. The physical condition is injected into every Transformer block of a pretrained latent flow matching generator through adaptive layer normalization. This design unifies translation fidelity and multitemporal controllability in a single model. 2. We design a computable physical condition composed of three factors, namely the thermal phase clock (TPC), the solar elevation, and the flight altitude. Anchored at sunrise on a continuous 24-hour axis, the TPC keeps the thermal state well defined even at hours without training samples. The same condition transfers to GAN-based translators, granting them multitemporal control. 3. We construct the first paired aerial V2IR dataset with full diurnal coverage. Daytime pairs are captured by synchronized dual cameras and registered with a calibrated homography, while nighttime pairs are obtained by projecting a georeferenced orthophoto onto each thermal frame.

papers.title: The First Adolescent Super-Earth-Sized Multi-Planet System Around an M Dwarf: TOI-2079
papers.abstract: We identify two planets in close-in orbits around the M-type star TOI-2079 as the first super-Earth-sized planets orbiting a multi-planet M dwarf with a well-determined age of $1$-$2$\,Gyr. The interior planet, TOI-2079 b, has an orbital period of $1.49232359^{+0.00000099}_{-0.00000086}$ d, and the outer planet, TOI-2079 c, has an orbital period of $9.3174523\pm0.0000098$ d. The host star characterization is based on spectroscopic observations, which classify it from an M1.5 to an M3.5 dwarf with an effective temperature of $3695\pm77$ K. Further analysis determined TOI-2079's rotation period to be $17.33^{+0.29}_{-0.28}$ d. Multiple ground-based follow-up observations, combined with a state-of-the-art validation procedure, allow us to rule out possible astrophysical false-positive scenarios and validate the planetary nature of both objects. We find that the inner planet has a radius of $1.320\pm0.050 R_{\oplus}$ and $T_{\rm eq} = 867\pm27$ K, while the outer planet has $R_{\rm p} = 1.671\pm0.051 R_{\oplus}$ and $T_{\rm eq} = 473\pm15$ K.

papers.intro:
Exoplanet discoveries in the past three decades have shown that there is a rich variety of planetary systems within our galaxy, exhibiting diverse physical properties and orbital configurations. Space-based transit surveys, particularly Kepler [10] and TESS [127], have been fundamental to building this picture, with nearly 50005000 confirmed planets discovered through the transit method, corresponding to ∼75%\sim 75\% of the total. Demographic studies have revealed characteristics such as the radius gap, which is an occurrence drop for exoplanets with radii around 1.6​R⊕\rm 1.6~R_{\oplus}, constituting a boundary between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes [39]. The most accepted explanations for this feature involve atmospheric mass loss, either photoevaporation, core-powered mass loss, or both, depending on the age of the system [108, 97]. papers.title: Edge transport mechanisms in small-ELM and type-I ELM regimes at JET using global gyrokinetic simulations
papers.abstract: To explore tokamak operating regimes that combine high energy confinement with edge dynamics relevant for ITER, new regimes with small edge-localized modes (ELMs), referred to as baseline small-ELM (BSE), have been obtained at JET with the Be wall and W divertor. In this work, the edge transport mechanisms in a selected BSE discharge are compared with those in a standard H-mode with type-I ELMs using radially global gyrokinetic simulations with the GENE code. The simulations use experimental input profiles and include kinetic electrons and deuterium ions, electromagnetic (EM) effects, and the radially varying equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. At low toroidal mode number $n$, the type-I ELM pedestal is found to be unstable to kinetic-ballooning modes (KBMs), with radial mode structures covering the full pedestal. In the BSE regime, no KBM branch is found, and the same spectral range is dominated by hybrid ITG--TEM modes. The modifications of the linear modes by finite$-\beta$ effects are discussed in details. In nonlinear simulations of the type-I ELM regime, KBM-driven turbulence produces high transport levels that are resilient to the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. By contrast, in the BSE regime, EM effects moderately increase transport, which is strongly regulated by the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. The two regimes also differ in their radial turbulence organization and in the amplitude and persistence of the zonal shearing rate. These results identify the interplay between EM effects and equilibrium $E\times B$ flow as a key element of edge transport regulation.

papers.intro:
The development of fusion energy based on magnetically confined plasmas relies on the integration of plasma regimes combining high core pressure and energy-confinement time with edge dynamics compatible with the heat- and particle-load tolerances of plasma-facing components (PFCs). High confinement is achieved in tokamak experiments operating in H-mode through the formation of an edge transport barrier and the consequent steepening of the edge pressure profiles, known as the pedestal. Because the pedestal provides the boundary condition for the stiff core profiles, its properties strongly affect the achievable core pressure and fusion performance [1, 2]. The edge dynamics of conventional H-mode plasmas is typically characterized by edge-localized modes (ELMs), which transiently relax the pedestal and expel heat and particles. However, the compatibility of the most common ELMs, the so-called type-I ELMs, with the PFC heat- and particle-load limits is not guaranteed when extrapolated to reactor-scale fusion devices [3, 4].

This issue has motivated the development of ELM-free and small-ELM regimes that preserve high confinement while avoiding large transient pedestal losses. Because these ITER-relevant parameters are rarely achieved in regimes without large type-I ELMs, it is important to understand the physical mechanisms that regulate the BSE edge structure.

Although this framework has successfully described many conventional type-I ELM pedestals, additional physics may be required for regimes whose pedestal structure is not limited by proximity to the P–B boundary [2, 4].

papers.title: Test of gravitational redshift by optical clocks at different latitudes
papers.abstract: General relativity predicts that frequency comparisons between clocks are affected by both gravitational and kinematic time dilation. While the kinematic contribution has been tested with high accuracy, experimental tests of the gravitational redshift remain comparatively less stringent. Here, we measure the frequency shift between two Earth-fixed optical atomic clocks at different potentials and compare it to the redshift predicted by general relativity using independent geodetic measurements. The observed shift agrees with the prediction, testing the gravitational redshift at the $4.6 \times 10^{-5}$ uncertainty level, improving ground-based tests by a factor two. Previous ground-based tests separated the clocks mainly vertically. For clocks at different latitudes, their height difference is governed not only by the gravitational potentials at their locations but also by the centrifugal potentials caused by Earth's rotation. As both contributions can partially cancel, the gravitational contribution can be considerably larger than their height difference suggests. In this work, a separation of the clocks by $4^\circ$ in latitude enhances their sensitivity to a gravitational redshift violation threefold, to the equivalent of an approximately 1200 m difference in height for small latitudinal separation. Our results establish Earth's rotation as a so far unexploited resource for advancing ground-based tests of the gravitational redshift towards the sensitivity of previous space-based experiments.

papers.title: Generalized Markov numbers and plane lattices
papers.abstract: We give new explicit constructions of lattice rules in the two-dimensional square and torus. It is well-known that uniformly distributed lattices (in the sense of low-discrepancy) arise from continued fractions with bounded partial denominators. We demonstrate how integers solutions of the generalized Markov equation $x^2+y^2+z^2 = kxyz-k+3$ give rise to such lattices.

papers.title: Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
papers.abstract: Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.

papers.intro:
Label spaces in 3D medical image segmentation keep growing as datasets are merged and refined. TotalSegmentator [21, 20] delineates 117 structures in CT, MOOSE [19] 125 on the ENHANCE.PET data [6], and whole-body label sets with more than 140 classes exist [13, 23]. Yet both tools split their label space across five or six separately trained networks. The reason is the inference pipeline that the field relies on, implemented in widely used frameworks such as nnU-Net [10] and MONAI [2]. It first resamples each scan to a common working spacing, so that object sizes are consistent across scans. It predicts logits (per-class outputs before softmax) on overlapping windows and blends them with Gaussian weights. It then maps the image-sized logits back to the scanner’s grid and takes the argmax there, which places boundaries as exactly as possible.

papers.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^{3/2}$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
papers.abstract:
Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{\frac{3}{2}-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{\frac{3k}{2}-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size.
  Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.

Pushdown reachability is a standard and well-studied problem in the analysis of recursive programs. A pushdown automaton (PDA) consists of a finite control graph and a stack; each transition changes the control state and pushes a symbol, pops a symbol, or leaves the stack unchanged. Given two control states s,ts,t, the reachability problem asks whether some run starting at ss with an empty stack reaches tt. Reachability with such constraints underlies precise interprocedural dataflow analysis [21] and symbolic verification of pushdown systems [6, 3]; in fact, the problem is quasi-linear-time equivalent (i.e., equivalent up to reductions running in time O⁡(n​logc​n)O(n\log^{c}n) for some cc) to a large number of problems from program analysis [14, 16, 9].

For any fixed stack alphabet, the standard saturation algorithms solve pushdown reachability in cubic time in the number of control states. It is known that this cubic upper bound can be improved by polylogarithmic factors [22, 8, 15]. However, despite decades of research on this problem, no substantially better algorithms are known, i.e., no algorithm running in time O⁡(n3−ϵ)O(n^{3-\epsilon}) for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is known.

Time hierarchy theorems, beginning with Hartmanis and Stearns [13], establish that more computational time allows us to solve strictly more problems. Such unconditional lower bounds are obtained by diagonalization. However, transferring these bounds to a particular algorithmic problem remains difficult and there are very few unconditional lower bounds known for problems in 𝖯\mathsf{P}, or indeed for problems in 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP} or even 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}. papers.title: Longest run for $q$-binary trials
papers.abstract: We investigate the longest-run distribution for binary trials in which the success probability varies geometrically. Exact formulae are derived for the probability mass function and the cumulative distribution function of the length of the longest success run in a sequence of $q$-binary trials, using enumerative combinatorics. The setting covers independent but not necessarily identically distributed zero--one trials whose success probabilities follow a geometric rule, and the classical independent and identically distributed Bernoulli longest-run distribution is recovered in the limit $q\to 1$. A simulation study confirms accurate maximum likelihood estimation of the base success probability and the geometric parameter $q$, a well-calibrated and powerful boundary-corrected likelihood ratio test of the hypothesis that $q=1$, and close agreement between the analytical cumulative distribution function and its empirical counterpart.

papers.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
papers.abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

papers.intro:
Patients with cancer are scanned every few months, and at every scan a radiologist decides whether the disease responds, is stable or progresses. This decision determines whether the treatment is continued, modified or changed. Under the clinical guideline RECIST 1.1 [13], this read means a) finding all lesions in a 3D volume, b) selecting up to five target lesions and measuring them, c) matching each lesion across scans with different fields of view, contrast and anatomy, d) deciding whether a new finding is a new lesion, and e) applying the guideline’s rules. The read is manual and slow, and it varies between readers: two radiologists choose the same target lesions in only 41% of patients [32] and often disagree on the response [27]. Small lesions are easily missed, even by radiologists, whose sensitivity for lung nodules ranges from 51 to 83% [2].

Small lesions are easily missed, even by radiologists, whose sensitivity for lung nodules ranges from 51 to 83% [2].

3D foundation models now solve several of these perception steps zero-shot, one at a time. Text-promptable models detect and segment lesions named in natural language [50], promptable models segment them from a click [23], and registration and longitudinal models find a tumor again in a follow-up scan [63, 30, 49]. None of them, however, performs the whole response assessment. It requires composing these models, catching their failures and making decisions no model is trained for: is a finding a lesion, is it the same lesion months later, is a new finding real, and which lesions should be followed? Learning all of this end to end would need longitudinal annotations at a scale that does not exist, as even recent releases cover a single cancer type [33, 30] or a few dozen patients [48].

LLM agents compose pretrained models without training: they call models as tools and solve compositional visual tasks [19, 60, 71], with medical agents calling specialist models for single images or studies [15, 41, 52, 66]. However, none of these agents assesses response across a patient’s CT scans. The agent chooses the target lesions itself or, if a clinician is available, lets them pick from its best valid sets. At each follow-up, registration carries every lesion into the new scan, where a longitudinal model segments it. papers.title: Star Panoptic Quality: Selectively Evaluating Split and Merged Instances
papers.abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

papers.intro:
In many segmentation problems, the detection and accurate delineation of individual instances are of great importance. Examples include detecting metastases or multiple sclerosis lesions in the medical domain [11], quantifying different cell types in microscopy datasets [16], or detecting individual cars in autonomous driving [5]. PS (PS) unifies the tasks of semantic and instance segmentation, and model performance in this task may be evaluated by PQ (PQ) [10], where each reference segment contributes to the score with equal weight, irrespective of its size. Computing PQ therefore requires instance-level reference labels. Although many semantic segmentation tasks may be viewed as instance segmentation problems, segmentation datasets often lack instance labels due to the additional labor and costs of the annotation process. Practitioners recover instances from semantic maps using methods such as CC (CC) or watershed in order to train and evaluate instance segmentation models on such datasets (Fig. 1). In many datasets, the recovered instances are only approximations, because the assumptions of the recovery method and the dataset’s acquisition method may introduce biases in instance delineation.

In many datasets, the recovered instances are only approximations, because the assumptions of the recovery method and the dataset’s acquisition method may introduce biases in instance delineation.

How a dataset was acquired determines which causes of splits and merges can arise when instances are recovered from semantic maps. Because natural photographs project a 3D scene onto the image plane, objects may occlude one another, in which case the connected components of a semantic map can differ from the true instances: a partially occluded instance can be split into several components (an elephant behind a tree), while adjacent or mutually occluding instances can merge into one (animals in a herd). In volumetric data such as CT or MRI, the split failure due to occlusion does not occur because instances cannot be hidden behind anything. The merge failure, however, remains: touching structures still merge into a single instance, as is the case with adjacent cells in 3D microscopy or tightly packed organs. In all rasterized imagery, limited resolution can merge neighboring instances whenever the gap between them falls below the acquisition’s effective resolution. We speak of OS (OS) when several predicted instances describe a single reference instance, and of US (US) when a single predicted instance describes several reference instances. Depending on the task, dataset acquisition, instance recovery, or downstream requirements, penalization or leniency towards individual failure modes can be required.

PQ matches predictions and references 1:1 (1:1) at a fixed IoU (IoU) threshold of 0.5, the lowest threshold that guarantees a unique matching. This 1:1 matching penalizes correctly predicted instances that were merged or recovered as multiple split fragments in the approximated instance map. Existing alternatives either retain a 1:1 matching [8, 2] or do not measure both failure modes symmetrically [6]. To address these limitations, we present StarPQ (StarPQ), a novel instance segmentation metric that quantifies the occurrence of splits and merges and allows practitioners to penalize or forgive each failure mode individually. StarPQ’s assignment, the star forest, is constructed from the IoL (IoL) rather than the IoU. Unlike an IoU threshold of 0.5, the IoL criterion allows a single segment to be described by multiple segments, and we apply it in both directions, so that a reference can be described by several predictions (a split) and a prediction by several references (a merge). The star forest is a set of stars that share no segments, each consisting of a center segment and one or more leaf segments from the other map. Every matched segment therefore belongs to exactly one star: a clean star with a single leaf, or a split or merge star with several.
