papers.title: Group-III doping of the p-type oxide SnO
papers.abstract: Al-, Ga-, and In-doped tin monoxide (SnO) films were grown by molecular beam epitaxy. Hall measurements reveal acceptor character of all investigated group-III dopants in SnO, which correspond to theoretical calculations and previous experiments for Ga and In, but contradicts theoretical calculations predicting donor character for Al in SnO. Doping concentrations of 10e18-1e22 cm-3 were tested and maximum hole concentrations of 2e19, 3e19, and 1e19 cm-3 with doping efficiencies of 3 percent, 9 percent, and 1 percent were found for Al, Ga, and In, respectively. The observed doping limit in the mid e19 cm-3 aligns with the limits observed in literature for different dopants, hinting to fundamental aspects of the SnO defect chemistry. Due to the unexpected Al acceptor behavior, we hypothesized Al1+ being present instead of Al3+. To stabilize the higher Al3+ oxidation state, another sample series of Al-doped SnO was grown in an oxidizing atmosphere. Despite the oxidizing atmosphere, these samples showed p-type character. A more complex defect chemistry is thus expected to explain the Al acceptor character.

papers.title: Effects of sinusoidal pitch amplitude and phase on power extraction and pitching-energy exchange in a single-blade vertical-axis turbine model
papers.abstract: Sinusoidal blade pitching can improve vertical-axis turbine performance, but whether a blade could follow the same motion passively depends on the energy exchanged through pitching. This study experimentally examines 480 prescribed-pitch conditions using a single-blade model following a circular trajectory in a water channel at four tip-speed ratios (TSRs) from 1.25 to 3.14. The amplitude associated with the highest measured power decreases from 16{\deg} to 12{\deg} and then 8{\deg} as TSR increases, with the corresponding phase shifting from 0 to pi/4. At TSRs of 1.25 and 3.14, the cycle-averaged power coefficient increases from 0.0047 to 0.1037 and from 0.4698 to 0.5948, respectively. Pitching-energy maps show nearly neutral net hydrodynamic pitching work for the highest-performing motions at the two lower TSRs and net energy transfer from the flow to pitching at the two higher TSRs. Virtual damping narrows the positive-energy region, although the higher-TSR best-tested motions retain an energy surplus at nonzero damping. However, net energy transfer from the flow to pitching also occurs for motions with substantial power losses. At the lowest TSR, phase-resolved force measurements and particle image velocimetry link the gain to delayed dynamic-stall-vortex formation and shedding, prolonged favorable loading, and reduced subsequent negative power. At the highest TSR, the flow and loading change locally, with little alteration of the main power-producing event. The joint maps identify performance-enhancing motions with an energetic margin against assumed dissipation, providing candidates for further passive or assisted pitching studies.

papers.intro:
Vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs) operate without continuous alignment with the incoming wind direction [1, 2], but their performance is governed by strongly unsteady blade aerodynamics [3]. During each revolution, the relative flow velocity and effective angle of attack vary with blade azimuth and tip-speed ratio (TSR). These unsteady flow conditions can trigger dynamic stall, during which flow separation and vortex development produce substantial variations in aerodynamic forces and pitching moments [4]. Previous PIV measurements documented the development of dynamic stall [5, 6]. Complementary experiments characterized its competing effects on power production and load fluctuations [7, 8], and showed that much of the aerodynamic work occurs during shear-layer growth and vortex formation [9]. These findings have motivated efforts to regulate the timing and development of separated flow.

Blade pitching offers a direct way to regulate this unsteady response by reshaping the incidence history throughout the turbine cycle. Both intracycle control of rotational velocity [10, 11] and blade pitching [12] modify the effective incidence. However, intracycle speed control changes the blade’s orbital velocity, whereas pitching allows its orientation to be adjusted while maintaining a prescribed constant orbital angular velocity. Previous studies showed that even a fixed pitch offset can redistribute instantaneous blade loading and alter cycle-averaged performance [13]. Prescribed cyclic pitching offers further control over the azimuthal distribution of incidence. Erickson et al. [14] demonstrated improved efficiency and self-starting using mechanically prescribed sinusoidal pitching while examining mean pitch, amplitude, and phase. Benedict et al. [15] combined wind-tunnel experiments with computational analysis and showed that turbine performance depends strongly on pitching amplitude and blade kinematics. Jain and Abhishek further established that favorable sinusoidal pitch amplitudes vary with TSR and operating conditions [16].

More flexible pitch curves have also been optimized by combining computational fluid dynamics with genetic algorithms [21].

These trade-offs have motivated passive variable-pitch concepts, in which the blade motion is driven by the fluid loads rather than by an actuator [24]. Whether a performance-enhancing motion could be sustained in this way depends on the energy exchanged through the pitching degree of freedom. Energy maps address this question using prescribed-motion experiments: the cycle-averaged work done by the fluid on the body is measured over a grid of kinematic parameters, and regions of net positive work identify motions that the flow can sustain against dissipation. This approach has been used to characterize controlled cylinder oscillations [25], prescribed airfoil pitching [26], and related nonlinear and aeroelastic responses [27, 28]. In a vertical-axis turbine, the pitching motion is forced at the rotation frequency, so the map is spanned by pitch amplitude and phase rather than amplitude and frequency. Because turbine power depends on the tangential force whereas pitching energy depends on the pitching moment and pitch rate, motions favorable in one need not be favorable in the other. Mapping both over the same amplitudes and phases, with a virtual torsional damper standing in for friction, shows which motions gain power and also receive enough energy from the flow to cover that loss. The maps give the damping at which each motion is energy-balanced; the pitch inertia and stiffness needed to reach its phase are not determined here.

papers.title: Minkowski Correlation Functions (MCF): Long-range, robust shape descriptors for point patterns
papers.abstract: A morphometric analysis of point patterns using Minkowski functionals is short-sighted, whereas correlation functions do not provide robust, i.e., additive shape descriptors. To combine the advantages of both standard techniques and to overcome their weaknesses, we introduce ring-based Minkowski correlation functions (MCFs) as robust and sensitive descriptors of disordered point patterns. By assigning to each point a spherical shell and quantifying the resulting two-phase morphology via Minkowski functionals, MCFs capture structural information across multiple length scales, remain sensitive at radii where conventional disk-based Minkowski functionals have saturated, and implicitly encode higher-order correlations beyond the pair correlation and structure factor. We present an exact and efficient algorithm for planar patterns extending the established disk-based morphological approach to long ranges. Applications across scales -- active colloids (Quincke rollers), longleaf pine trees, and the Hubble Ultra Deep Field -- demonstrate clear and systematic deviations from homogeneous Poisson references, with distinct responses of covered area, boundary length, and Euler characteristic. The approach combines short computation times, robustness to noise, and straightforward edge handling with clear interpretability as low-dimensional functions of the outer ring radius.

papers.intro:
From astronomical sources in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field to longleaf pine trees and microscopic Quincke rollers, disordered point patterns appear ubiquitously in nature on nearly all length scales. Efficient and sensitive structure characteristics are needed for physical or biological insights, e. g., to explain the mechanism of their formation, as well as for statistical data analysis or model selection. Moreover, these measures should be robust against noise and even with limited statistics they should be able to detect correlations in the point configurations like clustering or local crystallization.

They describe the joint probability densities of finding points in infinitesimal neighborhoods of the positions 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}, normalized by the nn-th power of the intensity. They are, for example, used in materials science [1, 2], in medical image processing [3], and astronomy [4, 5, 6, 7]. Recent extensions of correlation-based summary statistics include local mark correlation functions that resolve spatially varying mark associations in marked point processes [8]. However, the standard pair correlation function is by definition limited to two-point information, and multipoint correlation functions quickly become intractable both analytically and numerically. The brute-force approach to calculate an nn-point correlation function scales with the number of data points NN like 𝒪⁡(Nn)\mathcal{O}(N^{n}). This can be critical for even modest-sized data sets. Although complex algorithms have been developed to improve upon this scaling, they typically still allow only for estimates of the three- or four-point correlation functions [9, 10, 11, 12].

They describe the joint probability densities of finding points in infinitesimal neighborhoods of the positions 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}, normalized by the nn-th power of the intensity. They are, for example, used in materials science [1, 2], in medical image processing [3], and astronomy [4, 5, 6, 7]. Recent extensions of correlation-based summary statistics include local mark correlation functions that resolve spatially varying mark associations in marked point processes [8]. However, the standard pair correlation function is by definition limited to two-point information, and multipoint correlation functions quickly become intractable both analytically and numerically. The brute-force approach to calculate an nn-point correlation function scales with the number of data points NN like 𝒪⁡(Nn)\mathcal{O}(N^{n}). This can be critical for even modest-sized data sets. Although complex algorithms have been developed to improve upon this scaling, they typically still allow only for estimates of the three- or four-point correlation functions [9, 10, 11, 12].

The so-called Minkowski functionals from integral geometry [13, 14, 15] provide a complementary approach, which rectifies the shortcomings of the standard nn-point correlation function like the limitation to low order correlation functions [16]. The central idea is to assign to each point in the point pattern a ball of constant radius rr, see Figs. 1 (a). Thus, the point pattern is turned into a two-phase medium (or black and white image). The latter can be characterized comprehensively, robustly, and efficiently by the Minkowski functionals [17, 18]. The mean values of these Minkowski functionals as a function of the radius rr of the balls define a correlation function that implicitly contains information from nn-point correlation functions of arbitrary order nn [16, 19]. Therefore, they can distinguish different point processes with the same structure factor. Recent work has further established a close connection between germ–grain Minkowski functionals and kk-nearest-neighbour distribution functions, showing that both approaches provide nearly identical constraints on cosmological parameters [20]. Minkowski functionals have already offered insights into astronomy [21, 22, 23, 24, 25], condensed matter physics [26, 27], and biology [19]. In [28], an algorithm is developed for estimating the Minkowski functionals and, more generally, the Minkowski tensors of a broad class of sets from point-cloud representations.

papers.title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs is NP-complete
papers.abstract: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed $k\geq 3$ has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.

papers.intro:
Given a list of linear orders over some set of alternatives, interpreted as preferences of voters, the pairwise majority relation of these orders forms an asymmetric digraph. When the number of voters is odd, this digraph is a tournament. A classic theorem by McGarvey (1953) states that every asymmetric digraph arises in this way, provided sufficiently many voters are available. For digraphs on nn alternatives, the number of voters required is of order Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)\Theta(n/\log n) (Stearns, 1959; Erdős and Moser, 1964). Hence, for every fixed kk, only a restricted class of digraphs can be induced by kk voters. Following Bachmeier et al. (2019), we call a digraph kk-inducible if it is the majority relation of some preference profile with kk voters, and we call the smallest such kk its majority dimension. Inducibility by few voters has been studied in combinatorics (Alon et al., 2006; Milans et al., 2011) and in computational social choice (Brandt et al., 2016).

Inducibility by few voters has been studied in combinatorics (Alon et al., 2006; Milans et al., 2011) and in computational social choice (Brandt et al., 2016).

For one or two voters, inducibility is well understood. A digraph is 11-inducible if and only if it is a transitive tournament. The majority relation of two voters coincides with their Pareto relation, so the 22-inducible digraphs are exactly the partial orders of dimension at most 22, which were characterized by Dushnik and Miller (1941) and can be recognized in polynomial time (Yannakakis, 1982). Three voters are thus the first non-trivial case. Every tournament on at most seven alternatives is 33-inducible (Bachmeier et al., 2019), but there are tournaments on eight alternatives that are not (Shepardson and Tovey, 2009). For five voters, the corresponding threshold has only recently been narrowed down: every tournament on at most 12 alternatives is 55-inducible, but there are tournaments on 22 alternatives that are not (Chindelevitch and Harutyunyan, 2026). Chindelevitch and Harutyunyan (2026) also showed that the quadratic residue tournament on 23 alternatives is not 55-inducible. Bachmeier et al. (2019) characterized 33-inducible tournaments as those whose arc set can be partitioned into a transitive part and an acyclic, transitively reorientable part, but noted that there is no obvious efficient way to check this condition. A more symmetric characterization is the following: a tournament is 33-inducible if and only if its arc set can be partitioned into three sets such that the union of any two of them is acyclic. Equivalently, its arcs can be colored with three colors such that every directed cycle contains arcs of all three colors, or it has three pairwise disjoint feedback arc sets. Recently, there has been some progress on hardness results related to 33-inducible tournaments: Peters (2026) and Madarasi (2026) have shown that computing Kemeny rankings is NP-hard, even when there are only three voters.

The three voters play different roles. A rigid gadget consisting of six anchors and a sequence of separators forces one of the voters to rank the remaining alternatives according to a prescribed ordered partition. This part of the construction works for arbitrary tournaments and ordered partitions. Since the ranking of this voter is essentially fixed, it acts as a predictable tie-breaker on all pairs on which the other two voters disagree. These two voters encode a truth assignment: the value of a variable is determined by which of them ranks all occurrences of the variable before a threshold alternative zz. A clause gadget on seven alternatives can be induced with the third voter following the prescribed order if and only if the three variables of the clause do not all have the same value. For an instance with mm clauses, the resulting tournament has 10​m+710m+7 alternatives. The proof is elementary and self-contained. It only relies on simple properties of three-voter profiles, such as that at most one voter disagrees with each arc and that every voter disagrees with exactly one arc of every directed triangle.

papers.title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
papers.abstract: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.

papers.intro:
Tarski’s fixed point theorem [Tar55] states that all monotone functions over a complete lattice have a greatest and least fixed point, and so in particular, they possess at least one fixed point. In this paper we study the computational complexity of finding a fixed point in a lattice defined by an integer grid. A function f:{0,1,…,n}d→{0,1,…,n}df:\{0,1,\dots,n\}^{d}\rightarrow\{0,1,\dots,n\}^{d} is monotone if x≤yx\leq y implies that f⁡(x)≤f⁡(y)f(x)\leq f(y), where ≤\leq denotes the coordinate-wise ordering over the grid. We are interested in the following computational problem called 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski}: given the function ff represented as a Boolean circuit, find a point xx such that x=f⁡(x)x=f(x), or two points xx and yy that witness a violation of the monotonicity of ff.

[EPRY20] showed that 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} is equivalent to finding a pure Nash equilibrium in a supermodular game. They also showed that the problems of solving parity games, mean-payoff games and Condon’s simple stochastic games reduce to finding a Tarski fixed point. An efficient algorithm for 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} would therefore have consequences for several longstanding open problems.

We prove our result by providing a sub-exponential-time reduction from the 𝖴𝖤𝖮𝖯𝖫\mathsf{UEOPL} problem to 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski}, which produces a sub-exponentially sized 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} instance. We show that if an algorithm could solve a 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} instance of size MM in time MO⁡((log⁡M)1−ε)M^{O((\log M)^{1-\varepsilon})} for some ε>0\varepsilon>0, then applying it to our reduced instance would give an algorithm that falsifies the weak ETH for 𝖴𝖤𝖮𝖯𝖫\mathsf{UEOPL}.

This means that we can show hardness for 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} by making use of existing works that have established hardness of 𝗋𝖲𝖵𝖫\mathsf{rSVL} from a variety of different cryptographic hardness assumptions. Our strongest 𝖳𝖺𝗋𝗌𝗄𝗂\mathsf{Tarski} lower bound is obtained from the work of Ephraim et al. papers.title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

papers.intro:
Proteins, DNA and RNA form the basic building blocks of life, performing functions from oxygen transport and muscle contraction to storing and processing genetic information. Their activities combine three recurring processes: (i) conformational changes, which alter a molecule’s three-dimensional arrangement; (ii) binding and dissociation, which assemble complexes and capture or release ligands; and (iii) chemical reactions, which transform substrates or act as molecular switches. These processes are often coupled. In haemoglobin for example, oxygen binding shifts the conformational equilibrium from the low-affinity tense (T) state toward the high-affinity relaxed (R) state. This coupling supports cooperative oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading at the lower oxygen partial pressures in tissues [1]. In adenylate kinase, the catalytic cycle connects nucleotide binding, domain closure, phosphoryl transfer and reopening for product release [2]. These molecular activities form interconnected pathways that underpin cellular function. A scalable means of understanding molecular function and its disruption in disease could transform drug-target selection, clarify mechanisms of action, and improve predictions of drug efficacy and safety.

Next-generation sequencing has made molecular sequences broadly accessible [3], while AlphaFold, RoseTTAFold and their all-atom extensions have transformed the prediction of molecular structures and complexes [4, 5, 6, 7]. A predicted structure alone, however, does not specify which conformations are populated, how rapidly they interconvert, or how ligand binding changes these properties. Understanding function therefore requires information about structural ensembles and their dynamics.

Biophysical experiments can reveal many aspects of biomolecular function, but usually suffer from either low throughput or low resolution. E.g., cryo-electron microscopy can resolve different conformational states, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy measures structural fluctuations and exchange processes [8, 9], but both are expensive and require lengthy sample preparation, data collection and data analysis. A broad range of biophysical techniques probe biomolecular shape, dynamics and interactions, including fluorescence and infrared spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry [10, 11, 12, 13]. Cell-free expression, miniaturization and cDNA display expand the scale of functional characterization, enabling high-throughput measurements of biochemical activity and protein stability [14, 15]. Even when scaled up, these approaches measure low-dimensional observables rather than directly resolving the full atomistic conformational ensemble.

Atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) describes the detailed time-resolved evolution of biomolecular structure subject to a chosen force field. Its predictive power is limited by the accuracy of the interaction potential, but especially by the computational cost of adequate sampling. Folding, conformational rearrangements and association can involve rare barrier crossings, requiring extensive simulation timescales, as illustrated by simulations of protein folding and protein–protein association [16, 17]. Specialized hardware and enhanced sampling algorithms extend the accessible timescales, but the computational burden of exploring complex conformational landscapes still remains high [16, 17, 18]. Machine-learned coarse-grained models reduce this burden by learning effective interactions for fewer degrees of freedom [19, 20]. Recent transferable models reproduce structural and thermodynamic properties of atomistic simulations while achieving orders-of-magnitude computational savings on benchmark proteins [20]. Yet extending this accuracy across small molecules, recovering atomistic detail and calibrating kinetics remain challenging.

Generative models learn to directly sample a target distribution rather than resolving every intervening simulation step. Boltzmann generators sample distributions defined by known energy functions [21] but have limited capability to scale to large systems. DiG, AlphaFlow and BioEmu learn molecular ensembles from data [22, 23, 24], but are coarse-grained single-protein models. Timewarp, MDGen and implicit transfer operators extend this approach to time-separated configurations or trajectory segments [25, 26, 27], but neither of these are biomolecular foundation models that can generalize over a wide range of complex structures.

Here we introduce BioEmu2, which unifies three modes in one atomistic framework: (1) structure prediction, with accuracy comparable to current open-weight biomolecular folding models [28, 29, 30, 31] on FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses [32, 33]. (2) approximate room-temperature equilibrium sampling reproducing free energy surfaces of extensive MD simulations within 1 kcal/mol free energy error and covering the major minima; (3) time propagation, which allows structures to be propagated an arbitrary time lag τ\tau in the future, to emulate long-timescale MD trajectories and predict kinetics of conformational changes and binding. BioEmu2 supports multicomponent systems containing proteins, DNA, RNA, modified residues, ligands and ions at heavy-atom resolution. Context parallelism enables inference on systems with over 5000 residues. Contact conditioning and inference-time steering provide control over structure generation. Enhanced sampling improves coverage of rare states, and valid reweighting can recover statistics of the learned base ensemble. Several capabilities remain experimental, particularly slow kinetics, and require larger high-quality experimental datasets and further validation. By accelerating many MD-style sampling tasks by orders of magnitude, BioEmu2 enables rapid iteration toward scalable emulation of biomolecular dynamics and function.

papers.title: Predicting HCN, HCO$^{+}$, multi-transition CO, and dust emission of star-forming galaxies
papers.abstract: We present an analytical model of a turbulent clumpy star-forming disk that reproduces the spatially resolved observations for 6 molecular lines and 3 continuum bands at 250-700~GHz in the central 30~pc of the Circinus Galaxy. Using the properties of the stellar disk as input, and when matched to the line and continuum emission, the model yields the Toomre $Q$ parameter, mass accretion rate $\dot{M}$, metallicity $Z$, and cosmic ray ionization rate $\zeta_{CR}$. These in turn are used to infer the gas properties (surface density, velocity dispersion, and radial velocity) as well as the star formation rate. Our main findings from the model include a low CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor that varies with radius in the range $\alpha_{\rm CO}=0.5$--1.5 $M_{\odot}$pc$^{-2}/({\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1})$, close to the canonical value for such environments. It shows that CO(3-2) is a poor tracer of the gas mass surface density $\Sigma_{{\rm H}_2}$ on these small scales, which is better represented by molecules such as HCO$^+$(3-2) with higher critical density. The steep relation between $\Sigma_{{\rm H}_2}$ and star formation rate surface density $\dot{\Sigma}_*$ is typical of compact starburst systems, and the star formation rate (10~$M_{\odot}$kpc$^{-2}$yr$^{-1}$ averaged over the disk) is high enough to drive a wind. Despite this, and in contrast to typical large scale galactic disks, the energy injection rate into the ISM is dominated by gas inflow through the disk rather than the supernova rate. As such, the decreasing inflow rate at smaller radii could be caused by a wind, or indicate a recent increase of the mass inflow from larger scales. We suggest that such variations in the inflow rate could be associated with the nested spiral structures which have been observed in Circinus.

papers.intro:
Supermassive Black Holes (SMBH) can grow through black hole merging or gas accretion. Theoretical studies and observations suggest that major mergers are the dominant process leading to SMBH growth (Menci et al. 2014, Hopkins et al. 2014, Gatti et al. 2015) for SMBH masses higher than 10810^{8} M⊙. SMBHs with masses lower than 10710^{7} M⊙ located in disk galaxies mainly grow through secular processes (spirals and bars), which lead to gas inflows (Hopkins et al. 2014, Davies et al. 2015, Rosario et al. 2018). For a review on the growth of SMBH, see Storchi-Bergmann & Schnorr-Müller (2019) and Alexander et al. (2025). With the advent of the Atacama Large Millimetric Array (ALMA), the mapping of gas flows on parsec scales is now possible (Alonso-Herrero et al., 2018; Alonso-Herrero et al., 2019; Impellizzeri et al., 2019; Tristram et al., 2022; Goesaert et al., 2025; Oakes et al., 2025).

For a review on the growth of SMBH, see Storchi-Bergmann & Schnorr-Müller (2019) and Alexander et al. (2025). With the advent of the Atacama Large Millimetric Array (ALMA), the mapping of gas flows on parsec scales is now possible (Alonso-Herrero et al., 2018; Alonso-Herrero et al., 2019; Impellizzeri et al., 2019; Tristram et al., 2022; Goesaert et al., 2025; Oakes et al., 2025).

At kpc-scales a galactic bar can efficiently transfer angular momentum within the disk, allowing gas to move inwards. Since gas and stars are not aligned, stellar bars exert a torque on the gas, except at resonances, where the gas configuration falls back into symmetry with the bar. The infalling gas forms a ring at the Inner Lindblad Resonance (ILR; see e.g., Knapen et al. 2006) located at galactic radii of a few hundred pcs to a kpc (Comerón et al., 2010). Between corotation and ILR, the gas spiral arms exert negative torques, and gas is driven inwards, increasing the depth of the potential well. The vertical resonance with the bar develops a peanut-shape bulge, weakening the bar. This can trigger the decoupling of a secondary bar, an embedded nuclear bar, rotating faster than the primary bar (e.g. Buta and Combes, 1996). However, high resolution hydrodynamical simulations of gas flows in barred galaxies have shown that a secondary bar can prevent rather than enhance further inflow because it ends well inside its corotation radius (Maciejewski & Sparke, 2000; Maciejewski et al., 2002). The large scale bar may instead drive a circumnuclear spiral which can drive gas to smaller scales (Maciejewski, 2004a; Maciejewski, 2004b). Martini et al. (2003a) showed that circumnuclear dust structures span a range of morphologies - spiral, chaotic, or absent - in both barred and unbarred galaxies, but found no cases with secondary bars. Notably, grand design circumnuclear spirals were found almost exclusively in barred galaxies (Martini et al. 2003b; see also Davies et al. 2014), supporting the theoretical understanding that these can bring the gas down to 10–100 pc scales. Multiscale simulations (Hopkins & Quataert, 2010; Hopkins et al., 2024) show that one can expect such structures to be repeated on smaller scales in a nested hierarchy, with the details depending either on the initial cosmological environment, or on a variety of galaxy properties such as prominence of the bulge, mass of the black hole, and gas fraction. In this context, it is no surprise that disks and their associated structures are observed on a variety of increasingly smaller spatial scales.

High-resolution ALMA observations of the central ∼100\sim 100 pc regions of disk galaxies reveal distinct circumnuclear structures that regulate nuclear fueling. For example, Combes et al. (2019) identified resonant gas rings on a 100100 pc scale within seven active spiral galaxies, which serve as reservoirs feeding the nucleus, occasionally displaying inner trailing spirals and decoupled circumnuclear disks (see also Audibert et al. 2021) with radii of 66–3030 pc and masses of ∼107\sim 10^{7} M⊙. Similarly, Garcia-Burillo et al. (2021) resolved dusty molecular disks around the AGN of ten nearby Seyfert galaxies via 870​μ870\penalty\ \mum continuum and CO line emissions. These disks are characterized by a median diameter of ∼40\sim 40 pc, a median molecular gas mass of ∼6×105\sim 6\times 10^{5} M⊙, and an orientation perpendicular to the AGN wind axes. The gas masses are uncertain because of the unknown CO-to-H2 conversion factor, especially for higher-transition CO lines.

The Circinus galaxy hosts the nearest type 2 Seyfert active galactic nucleus (AGN) at a distance of 4.24.2 Mpc (0.1′′=20.1^{\prime\prime}=2 pc; Tully et al. 2009). Because it is so near, spiral structures have been observed to exist on several distinct scales in the central regions. They extend across radii from several kpc down to ∼2\sim 2 pc over three or four hierarchical levels, and are all oriented in the same direction with trailing arms.

Recent APEX and ALMA multi-scale molecular line observations of the Circinus galaxy revealed a complex, hierarchical structure. At the kiloparsec scale, Lasrado et al. (2025) identified a molecular gas bar characterized by an X-shaped position-velocity diagram indicative of a weak bar potential, while Zschaechner et al. (2016) mapped a symmetric main disk with extended spiral arms alongside an inner bar structure (∼200\sim 200 pc) and a significant molecular outflow (0.350.35–12.312.3 M⊙yr-1) originating from the central gas disk (R≤80R\leq 80 pc). Probing closer to the nucleus, Izumi et al. (2018) resolved this nuclear environment into gas arms and a circumnuclear disk (CND; 7474 pc ×\times 3434 pc) with a molecular mass of MH2∼3×106M_{\rm H_{2}}\sim 3\times 10^{6} M⊙, which Tristram et al. (2022) further characterized as a geometrically thin, rotation-dominated structure harboring a compact, unresolved torus (∼<4\lower 2.15277pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}4 pc) traced by high-density molecular emission. At the highest angular resolution (0.250.25 pc), Goesaert et al. (2025) demonstrated that the CND hosts molecular and dusty spiral arms that channel gas inward toward the torus at a feeding rate of 0.30.3–7.57.5 M⊙yr-1 via a non-axisymmetric potential; because this inflow drastically exceeds the supermassive black hole accretion rate of ∼<0.01\lower 2.15277pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}0.01 M⊙yr-1, the majority of this transported mass is ultimately expelled in a multi-phase outflow before reaching the accretion disk.

papers.title: WISDOM Project -- XXIX. Catalogue of CO observations of nearby galaxies and the CO Tully-Fisher relation
papers.abstract: We present Tully-Fisher relations (TFRs) that use carbon monoxide (CO) as the kinematic tracer and Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) $W1$-band and Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) $K_\text{s}$-band magnitudes as tracers of stellar luminosity. CO data were obtained using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array for the mm-Wave Interferometric Survey of Dark Object Masses (WISDOM) project for a sample of $102$ galaxies located at redshifts $z \lesssim 0.03$, with $81$ detections. The best-fitting reverse $W1$-band and $K_\text{s}$-band CO TFRs are $M_{W1}=(-7.18\pm0.93)\left[\log\left(\frac{W_{50}/\sin i}{\text{km~s}^{-1}}\right)-2.6\right]+(-24.04\pm0.13)$ and $M_{K_\text{s}}=(-5.95\pm0.62)\left[\log\left(\frac{W_{50}/\sin i}{\text{km~s}^{-1}}\right)-2.6\right]+(-24.01\pm0.10)$, respectively, where $W_{50}$ is the velocity width of each integrated CO spectrum at $50\%$ of its maximum, $i$ is the galaxy inclination and $M$ is the galaxy absolute magnitude. Our results are in excellent agreement with those of Tiley et al. (2016b), and together they constitute a robust local benchmark for the CO TFR. We however measure a shallower slope and a smaller zero-point offset compared to the relation of Tully & Pierce (2000). Due to the morphological diversity of our sample, we construct separate late-type and early-type galaxy (ETG) CO TFRs, finding that ETGs are $1.40\pm0.39$~mag fainter at $W1$ band and $0.89\pm0.28$~mag fainter at $K_\text{s}$ band at a given velocity width. We also generate and include a comprehensive catalogue of WISDOM CO data products for use in future molecular gas studies.

papers.intro:
Scaling relations between the luminosity (or mass) and kinematics of galaxies are central to our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution. Among these, the Tully-Fisher relation (TFR; Tully and Fisher 1977) remains one of the most fundamental, linking a galaxy’s luminosity and rotational velocity. As the former traces the stellar mass of a galaxy while the latter traces its enclosed dynamical mass, the relation provides insights into the distribution of both baryons and dark matter within galaxies (Zwaan et al., 1995; McGaugh and de Blok, 1998; McGaugh et al., 2000, e.g.), it constrains stellar mass-to-light ratios (M/LM/L; e.g. Bell and de Jong 2001) and it serves as a test of galaxy formation and cosmological models (van den Bosch, 2000; Yang et al., 2003; Trachternach et al., 2009; McGaugh, 2012; Ponomareva et al., 2017, e.g.). In addition, the TFR can be used as a distance indicator, extending the cosmic distance ladder beyond the local Universe (Pierce and Tully, 1988; Sakai et al., 2000; Springob et al., 2007; Lelli et al., 2016, e.g.). Indeed, by comparing the absolute magnitude of a galaxy expected from the TFR with its observed apparent magnitude, the distance to the galaxy can be estimated independently of its redshift.

Scaling relations between the luminosity (or mass) and kinematics of galaxies are central to our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution. Among these, the Tully-Fisher relation (TFR; Tully and Fisher 1977) remains one of the most fundamental, linking a galaxy’s luminosity and rotational velocity. As the former traces the stellar mass of a galaxy while the latter traces its enclosed dynamical mass, the relation provides insights into the distribution of both baryons and dark matter within galaxies (Zwaan et al., 1995; McGaugh and de Blok, 1998; McGaugh et al., 2000, e.g.), it constrains stellar mass-to-light ratios (M/LM/L; e.g. Bell and de Jong 2001) and it serves as a test of galaxy formation and cosmological models (van den Bosch, 2000; Yang et al., 2003; Trachternach et al., 2009; McGaugh, 2012; Ponomareva et al., 2017, e.g.). In addition, the TFR can be used as a distance indicator, extending the cosmic distance ladder beyond the local Universe (Pierce and Tully, 1988; Sakai et al., 2000; Springob et al., 2007; Lelli et al., 2016, e.g.). Indeed, by comparing the absolute magnitude of a galaxy expected from the TFR with its observed apparent magnitude, the distance to the galaxy can be estimated independently of its redshift.

Traditionally, the TFR has been derived for late-type, gas-rich galaxies using emission from the hyperfine transition of atomic hydrogen (H i) at 2121 cm (Tully and Pierce, 2000; Verheijen, 2001; Meyer et al., 2008; Ponomareva et al., 2021, e.g.). However, direct H i detections of individual galaxies within large-area untargeted surveys are rare beyond the nearby Universe (Giovanelli et al., 2005; Serra et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2021; de Blok et al., 2024, e.g.). Recently, targeted deep observations have yielded eleven detections at redshifts 0.25<z<0.3840.25<z<0.384 (Jarvis et al., 2025), a single detection at z=0.376z=0.376 (Fernández et al. 2016; although this result has recently been called into question by Heywood et al. 2024) and six detections at 0.38<z<0.50.38<z<0.5 (Xi et al., 2024). In exceptional cases H i can be detected at z≈0.7z\approx 0.7, but only through the use of strong gravitational lensing (Lawrie et al., 2025). A previously claimed strongly lensed H i detection at z≈1.3z\approx 1.3 (Chakraborty and Roy, 2022) was subsequently challenged by Deane et al. (2024), highlighting the difficulty of H i detections at such redshifts. H i is also problematic when attempting to probe the TFR of early-type galaxies (ETGs). Indeed, extended atomic gas is less frequent in ETGs (Young et al., 2014; Young et al., 2018, e.g.), and when present it is often kinematically disturbed (Williams et al., 2010; Serra et al., 2012, e.g.), preventing reliable determinations of rotational velocities and therefore undermining the construction of reliable TFRs. When extended regularly rotating H i discs are present, ETG TFRs can be defined, but samples remain small (den Heijer et al., 2015, e.g.).

Thus, the use of carbon monoxide (CO) as an alternative kinematic tracer in TFR studies has grown considerably in recent years (Davis et al., 2011b; Davis et al., 2015; Tiley et al., 2016a; Topal et al., 2018, e.g.). CO is observed across the full Hubble sequence, with large surveys mapping CO in a substantial fraction of nearby spirals [e.g. Berkeley-Illinois-Maryland Association Survey of Nearby Galaxies (BIMA SONG), Helfer et al. 2003; Extragalactic Database for Galaxy Evolution and Calar Alto Legacy Integral Field Area Survey (EDGE-CALIFA), Utomo et al. 2017; Extended CO Legacy Database for GASS (xCOLD GASS), Saintonge et al. 2017; CO Multi-line Imaging of Nearby Galaxies (COMING), Sorai et al. 2019] and targeted studies demonstrating routine CO detections in ≈20%\approx 20\% of ETGs (e.g. ATLAS3D, Young et al. 2011; MASSIVE, Ma et al. 2014 and Davis et al. 2019; KILOGAS, Davis et al. in prep.). These studies collectively demonstrate that CO TFRs yield slopes, zero-points and scatters consistent with those of the classical relations, thus providing a robust alternative to H i for rotation-based scaling relations.

papers.title: Characterisation of B-type stars in four young Galactic open clusters. II. Photometric variability with TESS and identification of pulsating stars
papers.abstract: Pulsations and binarity are important properties of massive stars and influence their structure and evolution. Young open clusters are ideal laboratories to study massive stars, since they are mostly coeval and chemically homogeneous. We analyse 82 B-type stars in the Galactic open clusters $h$ and $\chi$ Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, and NGC 1960, which have ages between 15 and 30 Myr. We extract light curves using both simple aperture photometry and a point-spread-function-based method that minimises contamination from crowded fields in full-frame images from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. We successfully extract light curves for 63 stars. The majority have photometric variability caused by pulsations, showing how pulsations are a common property of young B-type stars in clusters. We classify stars into different pulsator types based on their spectral type and frequency spectrum. The most common pulsator class are beta Cephei stars, with 29 stars in total, and we discover pulsation modes in almost all stars with a spectral type of B2 or earlier. All Be stars show pulsations, which supports the consensus of the ubiquity of pulsations in these stars. Finally, we confirm that the majority of early B-type stars are in binary systems, except for two pulsating Be stars and a star with rotational modulation. This indicates that pulsations do not significantly bias the spectroscopic detection of short-period binaries, except for Be stars where the spectroscopic radial velocity variability threshold should be higher than the typical value of 20 km s$^{-1}$.

papers.intro:
In recent years, our understanding of the physical processes that govern stellar structure and evolution has largely improved (see Kippenhahn et al., 2013, for a monograph). However, we still lack a sufficient understanding to predict the end products of single-star evolution. This is because of the variety of physical processes in their lives, from strong stellar winds, high rotation rates that influence the internal mixing, and potentially magnetic fields (Langer, 2012). For example, large theoretical uncertainties for mixing exist in stellar evolution models, both due to rotation and other instabilities related to convective boundaries, which play a crucial role in the mass of the helium core, the main-sequence lifetime, and subsequent evolution (Talon et al., 1997; Johnston, 2021). Moreover, most massive stars are born in binary or multiple systems and eventually interact with at least one companion (Sana et al., 2012; Sana et al., 2013; de Mink et al., 2014; Offner et al., 2023; Frost et al., 2024; Bordier et al., 2024). These interactions, such as mass transfer and tides, introduce additional complications and can even lead to mergers (see Marchant and Bodensteiner, 2024; Schneider, 2025, for recent reviews).

Asteroseismology is a powerful tool that allows us to constrain the structure of stars across the Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram using stellar pulsations (Aerts et al., 2010). For example, the asteroseismic analysis of massive stars has allowed us to estimate their interior rotation and mixing profiles (Aerts et al., 2003; Dupret et al., 2004; Burssens et al., 2023; Vanlaer et al., 2025; Fritzewski et al., 2025), and even constrain their interior magnetic fields (Lecoanet et al., 2022; Vandersnickt et al., 2025, e.g.). Modern space telescopes, such as MOST (Walker et al., 2003), CoRoT (Auvergne et al., 2009), BRITE (Weiss et al., 2014), Kepler/K2 (Borucki et al., 2010; Howell et al., 2014), and the ongoing TESS mission (Ricker et al., 2015) have shown that almost all massive stars in the Galaxy pulsate (Balona et al., 2011; Burssens et al., 2020; Thomson-Paressant et al., 2026, e.g.). Moreover, a large fraction of massive stars in the low-metallicity Large and Small Magellanic Clouds exhibit photometric variability that probes their mass and age (Bowman et al., 2019; Bowman et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024). Massive stars are intrinsically rare compared to low-mass stars, and these space missions have provided the first high-precision, long-duration time-series data for a large sample of massive stars suitable for ensemble asteroseismology (see Bowman, 2020, for a review). For massive stars in binary systems, which can be subject to mass transfer, mergers, and tidal forces, asteroseismology is more complicated but provides valuable constraints on binary evolution theory (see Southworth and Bowman, 2026, for a review).

Pulsations are typically characterised by their dominant restoring force. Gravity modes have buoyancy as the restoring force, while pressure modes have the pressure gradient as their main restoring force. In massive stars, pulsations can be excited by different mechanisms, including a heat-engine mechanism operating in local opacity bumps (κ\kappa mechanism) near the stellar surface (Dziembowski and Pamiatnykh, 1993; Dziembowski et al., 1993; Miglio et al., 2007), stochastically excited gravity waves (see Bowman, 2023, for a review) and tides in close binary systems (Southworth and Bowman, 2026). It is sometimes difficult to identify the pulsation excitation mechanism from observations alone, since this requires non-adiabatic pulsation models (e.g. Townsend and Teitler 2013). However, since the κ\kappa mechanism excites coherent pulsation modes with long lifetimes and turbulent convection typically excites damped modes with short lifetimes, it is usually possible to distinguish between the two cases.

However, since the κ\kappa mechanism excites coherent pulsation modes with long lifetimes and turbulent convection typically excites damped modes with short lifetimes, it is usually possible to distinguish between the two cases.

Among stars of spectral types O and B, there are three main pulsator types: slowly pulsating B-type stars (SPB), β\beta Cephei stars, and stochastic low-frequency (SLF) variables. These are separated because of distinctions in their excitation mechanism and/or instability regions in the HR diagram. SPB stars have spectral types between B3 and B9 and typically have high-radial order gravity modes excited by the κ\kappa mechanism (Dziembowski et al., 1993; Pápics et al., 2017; Szewczuk and Daszyńska-Daszkiewicz, 2018; Szewczuk et al., 2021; Pedersen et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2022). At higher masses, the β\beta Cep stars have birth masses approximately between 8 and 30 M⊙ and typically show low-radial order pressure and gravity modes (Dziembowski and Pamiatnykh, 1993; Stankov and Handler, 2005; Burssens et al., 2023; Fritzewski et al., 2025). The pulsation periods of SPB and β\beta Cep stars are of order several hours to a few days. It is also possible to have so-called “hybrid” pulsators (Handler, 2009), which are stars that show characteristics of different pulsator classifications. Historically, this has been used to refer to stars with characteristics of both SPB and β\beta Cep stars and located in the overlapping instability regions of the HR diagram.

At higher masses, the β\beta Cep stars have birth masses approximately between 8 and 30 M⊙ and typically show low-radial order pressure and gravity modes (Dziembowski and Pamiatnykh, 1993; Stankov and Handler, 2005; Burssens et al., 2023; Fritzewski et al., 2025). The pulsation periods of SPB and β\beta Cep stars are of order several hours to a few days. It is also possible to have so-called “hybrid” pulsators (Handler, 2009), which are stars that show characteristics of different pulsator classifications. Historically, this has been used to refer to stars with characteristics of both SPB and β\beta Cep stars and located in the overlapping instability regions of the HR diagram.

Another relevant group of pulsators among early-type stars are Be stars. Space-based photometry has demonstrated that non-radial pulsations are almost ubiquitous among Be stars (Rivinius et al., 2003; Semaan et al., 2018; Labadie-Bartz et al., 2022). Both the light curves and the frequency spectra of pulsating Be stars are usually characterised by similar properties (Bradley et al., 2015; Kurtz et al., 2015, e.g. complex beating patterns and frequency groups;). On longer time scales of months to years, Be stars experience epochs of brightening or fading, which are likely attributed to the dissipation or growth of an equatorial decretion disc created by mass ejections (Rivinius et al., 2013; Rivinius et al., 2016; Semaan et al., 2018; Labadie-Bartz et al., 2025; Nova et al., 2025). Spectroscopically, classical Be stars are characterised by rapid rotation as well as emission lines in their spectra caused by the presence of the equatorial decretion disc (Rivinius et al., 2013; Rivinius and Klement, 2026). The formation of a Be star, specifically if it was born as a single fast rotator or if it is a binary interaction product, is still debated in the literature (Hastings et al., 2020; Bodensteiner et al., 2020b).

papers.title: The Time Domain Telescope: A Global Spectroscopic Array
papers.abstract: The Time Domain Telescope (TDT) is an initiative in the context of the ESO Expanding Horizons program. The TDT project aims for a global telescope array for spectroscopic time-resolved and time-critical observations in the optical-near-infrared, with a core at the European Southern Observatory and partners around the world. The TDT core consists of 100 unit telescopes of 2-meter diameter each that are fully Adaptive Optics-assisted in the blue, to deliver an enclosed energy of >=80% within 0.12" at 400nm. The unit telescopes are coupled to a set of spectrographs covering spectral resolutions R=10^3 - 10^5 over the wavelength range 0.35 - 1.8 micrometer. The combination of extreme adaptive optics with near-read-noise-free detectors will allow the TDT to reach unprecedented depths and/or high cadence. When all 100 units target a single object a depth of 25 mag can be reached in 30 minutes at a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 per spectral resolution element at a spectral resolution of R=5000. With this the TDT will spectroscopically match the imaging depth of the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Euclid and Roman spacecrafts, the expected brightness of electromagnetic counterparts discovered by the LISA space mission, as well as by the next-generation gravitational wave detectors. The science of the TDT covers a large part of astronomy, and ranges from the outer Solar System, to stellar and binary systems to extragalactic transients and the growth of supermassive black holes, all the way back to the expansion history of the Universe. The TDT is transformational, unique and highly complementary to the current and near-future ESO facilities, in particular by providing the possibility for time-resolved spectroscopic observations well below the brightness of the optical night sky.

papers.title: Nearly pristine gas and hard ionizing radiation one billion years after the Big Bang
papers.abstract: The first stars formed out of light elements (H, He, and Li leftover from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis) and began the chemical enrichment of the Universe. Identifying this first-generation population of stars, known as Population III, and understanding their properties is one of the most ambitious goals of modern extragalactic astrophysics. We report the detection of He and H emission lines and extremely low Oxygen abundance in AMORE6, a strongly magnified galaxy at redshift z = 5.725, i.e. approximately one billion years after the Big Bang, with deep James Webb Space Telescope spectroscopy. He II lambda1640 and lambda4686 emission lines are detected at 16.7 sigma and 4.0 sigma significance, respectively. The observed He II-to-Hbeta ratios are consistent with predictions for extreme ionizing radiation fields and the low chemical compositions typical of Population III stars. Oxygen abundance of the interstellar medium is estimated to be 8 x 10^-4 solar from weak [OIII]lambda4363 and lambda5008 lines, consistent with an almost pristine environment, perhaps enriched by the Pop III stars themselves. Although we cannot exclude alternative sources of hard ionizing radiation, such as accreting black holes, these observations offer the first view of the extremely low metallicity environment where the Universe's first stars are predicted to be born. The data show that such pockets of pristine gas still exist one billion years after the Big Bang and that they are dominated by very massive stars.

papers.title: Magnetic vector potentials and helicity in periodic domains
papers.abstract: For a magnetic field in three-dimensional Euclidean space, we argue about the existence of a magnetic vector potential in a finite cuboid with periodic boundary conditions. We first argue in physical terms by representing periodic domains as tori and show that in some cases, the generating electric current is unphysical. We then represent magnetic fields and vector potentials as differential 2 and 1-forms. For a given magnetic field we ask the question whether a corresponding vector potential exists. Singly periodic domains are shown to always allow for a vector potential. For doubly periodic domains it only exists if the net magnetic flux through the non-periodic dimension vanishes, while for triply periodic domains the net flux must vanish in all directions. This has implications for the definition of magnetic helicity in periodic domains. We show that periodic domains together with a mean magnetic flux lead to contradicting results about the value of the magnetic helicity and we show in a few thought experiments fundamental contradictions to the interpretation as the linking of magnetic field lines. For the helicity we can even construct magnetic fields in periodic domains for which the magnetic helicity exists, but the calculations of the magnetic helicity do not lead to meaningful results due to the gauge freedom. With that we conclude that in presence of a mean magnetic field the calculated magnetic helicity cannot be interpreted geometrically in a straightforward way. However, using the winding gauge we can recover the geometric interpretation of the helicity as the flux averaged magnetic field line winding. Finally, for the solar relevant non-periodic domain with finite point-wise flux and zero integrated flux, using an appropriate gauge transformation the magnetic helicity can be shown to vanish. The winding helicity, however, would lead to a non-vanishing value here.

papers.intro:
Magnetic fields are used in a vast number of scientific areas. They appear in particle physics, plasma physics, geology, astrophysics, biology, atomic physics, fusion science, electric engineering and many more. For modeling the dynamics of such physical systems it is more often than not necessary to solve partial differential equations numerically. papers.title: NormFlowSDE: Normalizing Flows for Amortized Bayesian State Estimation
papers.abstract: Bayesian state estimators, such as Kalman filters, estimate states from noisy observations based on dynamical models. However, obtaining accurate models can be challenging when the system involves effects that are difficult to model faithfully, such as friction, impacts, and deformation in contact-rich manipulation. Uncertainty in system parameters, inputs, and disturbances, together with simplified noise models, can further introduce simulation-to-reality mismatch and degrade estimation accuracy. These limitations motivate learning a distribution over state trajectories conditioned on observations and controls without explicitly specifying the underlying physical models. We introduce NormFlowSDE, an amortized Bayesian state estimator that learns a distribution over state trajectories by combining neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows. Its key design choice is to utilize the capability of normalizing flows to learn stochastic behavior of variables, while leveraging the continuous-time dynamics of SDEs to model the evolution of states over time. Once trained, the model draws state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization. In addition, we connect NormFlowSDE to stochastic continuous-time dynamics by proving weak convergence of a mean-centered, drift-corrected inference scheme to an It\^o diffusion under stated assumptions. Finally, we benchmark NormFlowSDE against direct estimators and learned particle filters based on normalizing flows on partially observed dynamical systems, including simulated systems and real-world robot datasets. The results show that NormFlowSDE attains the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty intervals on both robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest particle filter on every dataset.

Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for estimating unknown quantities from noisy observations. Conditional normalizing flows provide a way towards amortized Bayesian inference, which means making Bayesian parameter identification reusable across datasets (Radev, 2021). Trained on simulated parameter–observation pairs, BayesFlow (Radev et al., 2022) combines a learned summary of the observations with an invertible transformation to approximate the parameter posterior. Once fitted, the model produces posterior samples for new observations without repeating parameter optimization. This amortization makes expressive Bayesian inference practical for repeated identification tasks. Its success motivates the question studied here: how can conditional normalizing flows be combined with temporal dynamics to infer evolving states and their uncertainty?

Latent SDEs (Li et al., 2020) represent time series through an underlying stochastic process and learn its dynamics through variational inference, coupling a generative SDE with an approximate posterior process. When the observation model uses a Gaussian decoder with learned variance, it can inherit a decoder variance-collapse problem. The estimated variance may approach zero, which makes training highly sensitive to small reconstruction errors and destabilizes optimization (Takahashi et al., 2018; Rybkin et al., 2021). In addition, every increment of the posterior process is Gaussian given the current state, so a non-Gaussian conditional distribution of the next state can only arise through the nonlinearity of drift and diffusion over several steps.

In addition, we implement NormFlowSDE as a transition model in a particle filter. Both implementations are thoroughly benchmarked. First, NormFlowSDE as a direct amortized filter is compared with latent Neural Stochastic Flow (latent NSF), latent SDE, and a neural SDE trained with the signature-kernel score (SigKer SDE). Second, NormFlowSDE in a particle filter is compared with three NF-based methods: an NF-based differentiable particle filter (NF-DPF), Neural Stochastic Flow (NSF), and a flow-matching-based SDE (FlowSDE). The benchmark methods are described in detail in Section 2.

Several other works use generative methods to model stochastic processes directly. The continuous-time flow process (CTFP) (Deng et al., 2020) maps a Wiener process through a time-indexed invertible transformation, which gives the observed process tractable finite-dimensional likelihoods. Continuous latent process flows (Deng et al., 2021) apply such a transformation to a latent process driven by an SDE. The GP-VAE (Fortuin et al., 2020) combines Gaussian-process priors with deep encoders, and neural processes learn distributions over functions (Garnelo et al., 2018). Diffusion and flow-matching models have also been applied directly to time series. TSDiff (Kollovieh et al., 2023) trains an unconditional diffusion model over whole windows and obtains forecasts by guiding it toward the observed past at sampling time. TSFlow (Kollovieh et al., 2025) uses conditional flow matching with Gaussian-process priors to generate and forecast series. Stochastic process diffusion generates whole series as continuous functions (Biloš et al., 2023). All of these models target the distribution of the entire time series and do not model a process in physical time. They therefore provide neither a transition model for a recursive filter nor a causal state estimator comparable with the methods in our work, and we do not include them in the benchmark.

papers.title: A Lightweight Method for Validating Simulated LiDAR Configurations Based on Point Density over Distance
papers.abstract: Simulated LiDAR sensors play a crucial role in validating autonomous systems, yet achieving signal-level realism remains challenging due to simplified sensor models and limited configurability in common simulation environments. This paper presents a lightweight, platform-agnostic method to assess one observable aspect of LiDAR simulation fidelity: the range-dependent point density on annotated objects. The method uses only 3D bounding boxes and point clouds and does not require semantic labels, detailed maps, simulator internals, or perception models. To quantify agreement between real and simulated range-dependent point distributions, we formulate the Density Similarity Score (DSS), a bounded similarity representation derived from the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) over discretized distance bins. The method is evaluated against a real-world LiDAR using three CARLA configurations of varying complexity. Results show that naive parameter matching based on sensor datasheets leads to systematic point-density deviations, particularly in the near field, while a custom configuration using the sensor's non-uniform vertical beam angles achieves the highest similarity in the evaluated scenario (DSS: 0.559--0.709). The proposed approach is intended as an early-stage, signal-level consistency check for identifying gross mismatches in simulated LiDAR configurations. It should be interpreted as a complementary validation step rather than a complete measure of simulation quality or downstream perception performance.

Simulation plays an increasingly vital role in the development and validation of autonomous systems [1]. It enables scalable, repeatable, and cost-efficient testing under controlled conditions [2], particularly important when working with safety-critical functions such as object detection, tracking, or collision avoidance. Among the most commonly used sensors in autonomous vehicles, LiDAR stands out for its ability to provide high-resolution 3D representations of the environment [3].

To enable realistic evaluation of perception systems, simulation environments must offer sensor models that closely approximate real-world behavior. The approach focuses on analyzing point density within object bounding boxes as a function of distance, yielding density-over-distance profiles that can be compared between real and simulated data without requiring semantic segmentation, detailed maps, simulator internals, or trained perception models. papers.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
