papers.intro: Hydroclimatic extremes at both ends of the spectrum, floods and landslides on the one hand and water scarcity and drought on the other, have severe impacts on human societies and are projected to intensify in a warmer climate (IPCC, 2023; IFRC, 2021; Athanase et al., 2024b; Klimiuk et al., 2025). These extremes are scale-dependent: sub-hourly convective bursts that cause flash floods and urban drainage failures, and multi-day persistent rain that causes fluvial floods and soil saturation, arise from fundamentally different mechanisms and act on vastly different spatial and temporal scales (Breugem et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016). Global Climate Models (GCMs), the primary tool for projecting climate change under warming, operate at ≈10\approx 10–150150 km resolution and often do not resolve the catchment- and urban-scale rainfall processes at which impacts materialize. Unresolved orography, coastlines, and convective processes are known to be a primary bias source in both mean climate and extremes (Dawson and Palmer, 2015; Stevens and Bony, 2013; Davini et al., 2017). Dynamical downscaling with regional climate models (RCMs) narrows this scale gap by integrating a physics-based limited-area model under GCM boundary conditions. At convection-permitting resolution this measurably improves the representation of sub-daily precipitation extremes (Giorgi, 2019; Prein et al., 2015; Hundhausen et al., 2025). This improved fidelity comes at high computational costs, limiting the exploration of different physics parametrization, warming scenarios and ensemble sizes needed to sample internal climate variability. Addressing these limitations motivates the development of cheap, data-driven emulators that learn the GCM→\rightarrowRCM mapping, as currently benchmarked by initiatives such as CORDEX-ML-Bench (Rampal et al., 2026). The development of such emulators is, however, particularly challenging for precipitation, which is characterized by an intermittent, zero-inflated and heavy-tailed distribution. Generative models have proven to be particularly effective in addressing this challenge: unlike deterministic regressors, which tend to underestimate extremes, they sample from the conditional distribution of the high-resolution fields and thereby represent uncertainty and tail behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of an RCM (Leinonen et al., 2021; Harris et al., 2022; Glawion et al., 2025). With their stable, non-adversarial training and better representation of extremes, diffusion models have emerged as a leading approach, outperforming GANs and deterministic baselines in recent benchmarking (Rampal et al., 2026). This has fueled a growing interest in generative-ensemble approaches, including residual/corrective diffusion (Mardani et al., 2025) and diffusion and flow-matching emulators (Wetherell, 2026; Addison et al., 2026; Aich et al., 2026; Perkins et al., 2026). However, these recent efforts to advance generative AI downscaling have mostly assessed skill per timestep only, treating each generated field as an independent snapshot. Yet atmospheric processes and especially precipitation-relevant phenomena like fronts, mesoscale convective systems, or persistent stratiform rain, are spatiotemporal objects whose impact is governed by duration and accumulation, rather than single-timestep values. Hydrological and soil-moisture models integrate forcing over time and are sensitive to this structure regardless of per-timestep accuracy. Generating each timestep independently of its predecessor, conditioned only on the concurrent GCM state (referred to as per-timestep independent, PTI, generation hereafter), is trivial to parallelize, but offers no guarantee of coherent trajectories: generated sequences may be merely independently plausible snapshots rather than physically consistent in time. The standard route to temporal consistency in sequence modeling is autoregressive (AR) conditioning, where each generated state feeds back as input to generate the next (Price et al., 2025; Lam et al., 2023; Brandstetter et al., 2022). This closed loop exposes the model to exposure bias: training relies on ground-truth previous states, whereas inference can only rely on the model’s own, imperfect predictions, so that small deviations may compound over the rollout (Bengio et al., 2015; Ranzato et al., 2016). In practice, this can lead to error accumulation and progressive degradation of generated trajectories over long rollouts, potentially manifesting as a loss of sharpness and small-scale variability (Bonavita, 2024; Couairon et al., 2026). PTI generation sidesteps this feedback-related risk entirely, but forgoes the coherence that AR conditioning is designed to provide, resulting in a coherence–diversity trade-off between temporally coherent trajectories and preserved ensemble spread. Existing work has addressed temporal consistency in generative downscaling in three ways. The first enforces it through the training objective: EnScale (Schillinger et al., 2026) is, to our knowledge, one of the few generative RCM emulation frameworks to explicitly target temporally consistent multivariate output, using a proper scoring rule. The second imposes it at inference, e.g. through discriminator-based guidance of a pretrained, temporally unconditioned diffusion model (Hess et al., 2025). The third generates multiple timesteps jointly (Glawion et al., 2025; Srivastava et al., 2024; Bassetti et al., 2024; Schmidt et al., 2025), which is memory-intensive for long sequences at high resolution and requires stitching across generated blocks. Outside climate emulation, related approaches have been explored to achieve temporally consistent predictions in generative sequence models. In Ho et al. (2022), the outputs of preceding cascade stages are noise-augmented before being passed to subsequent super-resolution models, with the noise level explicitly provided to the network. Blattmann et al. (2023) similarly corrupt a conditioning image at randomly sampled noise levels, but generate video frames jointly rather than autoregressively. More directly related to autoregressive generation, Chen et al. (2024) train a causal sequence model on independently noise-corrupted frames, explicitly providing their noise levels to the network. At inference, slightly noisy previous frames can be used to stabilize long autoregressive rollouts. Related input perturbations have also been explored to improve the robustness of autoregressive idealized physics simulators (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020). However, the setting of these approaches differs fundamentally from autoregressive GCM→\rightarrowRCM emulation. In video generation, forecasting, and PDE surrogates, the preceding state is observed at initialization and provides the dominant predictive signal. In RCM emulation, by contrast, the concurrent GCM state is the primary predictor, while the preceding high-resolution state carries only secondary, short-range persistence information. Moreover, no observed high-resolution initial state is available at rollout start. To our knowledge, noise-conditioned AR generation has not yet been investigated for RCM emulation. It therefore remains open whether this strategy can produce stable rollouts in this setting, and whether the conditioning noise level can serve as an inference-time control of the coherence–diversity trade-off. We address this gap by adopting noise-augmentated AR conditioning for GCM→\rightarrowRCM emulation, using a single trained diffusion model with a parameterized transition between AR and PTI generation at inference time. This is motivated by the complementary benefits of each regime: coherence on the one hand, and parallel sampling and generating initial frames without prior high-resolution states on the other. During training, the model is conditioned on a previous high-resolution state corrupted at a randomly sampled noise level that is not provided to the network. The model therefore learns to weigh the previous state against the concurrent GCM state by its information content. At inference, a single noise level τ\tau applied to the previous prediction interpolates continuously between the two regimes. Rollouts are initialized from the model’s own PTI sample, so no observed high-resolution initial state or spin-up is required. Because the scheme only modifies the conditioning input and training procedure, it can be readily integrated into other conditional diffusion frameworks for sequential data generation. As a reference, we additionally train a conventional teacher-forcing baseline on uncorrupted previous states. We demonstrate the approach by emulating hourly, European-domain simulations in which the ICON-CLM regional climate model (≈12\approx 12 km) downscales an AWI-CM1 global simulation (≈1∘\approx 1^{\circ}) spectrally nudged toward ERA5. Both datasets are regridded to a common 0.25∘0.25^{\circ} grid, and we focus on precipitation and 2-meter temperature, evaluating the emulation on a held-out six-month period (July–December 2021). While this setup is not convection-permitting, the training scheme makes no assumption about spatial or temporal resolution. Our study is guided by three questions. First (feasibility and control), can AR conditioning produce temporally coherent rollouts when the concurrent GCM state, rather than the previous state, is the primary predictor and no observed high-resolution initial state is available, and can a single trained model provide continuous inference-time control over the coherence–diversity trade-off, interpolating between AR and PTI generation without retraining? Second (rollout robustness), does coherence come at the characteristic cost of exposure bias, i.e. error accumulation, smoothing, or reduced or miscalibrated ensemble spread? Third (downstream relevance), how does the presence or absence of temporal consistency affect relevant statistics from hourly extremes to multi-day accumulations?

papers.title: Searching for substellar companion candidates with Gaia IV. New planetary-mass companions found in debris disks
papers.abstract:
When spatially resolved, debris disks often exhibit structures (gaps, rings, and spirals) that may indicate the presence of unseen planetary-mass companions. However, such planets have not been detected in most cases. Gaia opens a new mass-separation parameter space for detecting unseen planets. A tool named GaiaPMEX has been developed to detect and characterize companions to stars. It is based on two binarity indicators derived from DR3: the Gaia astrometric signature and, when the sources were also observed by Hipparcos, the Gaia-Hipparcos proper motion anomaly.
  We used GaiaPMEX on 94 stars hosting resolved debris disks to search for companions. When companions were identified, we combined GaiaPMEX results with high-contrast imaging and radial velocity data to further constrain their mass and orbital properties.
  We found stellar or substellar companions around five targets (HD 54341, HD 146897, HD 206893, HD 107146, and HD 106906) and indications (2 sigma) for companions around three additional targets (BD+45 598, TWA 7, and HD 120326). The companion to the 150 Myr star HD 107146, which harbors a ring-like dust disk, is found to be a 2-6 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting between 2-10 au. A massive 3-20 Jupiter-mass companion is found 3-10 au from the close binary HD 106906, which already hosts a remote planet orbiting at more than 700 au, and an edge-on disk. The tentative companions to TWA 7 and HD 120326 are planetary-mass companions at 1-3 au. Both stars host a multiple-ring system. We finally provide meaningful upper limits on the possible presence of companions in the range of 0-100 au around a few emblematic stars (49 Cet, AU Mic, beta Pic, and epsilon Eri) and stars hosting well-defined ring-like structures.

papers.intro:
Debris disks are valuable tracers of planetary formation. Most are found around stars in young (10-150 Myr) nearby associations, but a few have also been resolved around more mature stars with ages of up to 5 Gyr. The young stars trace phases when giant planets have formed and terrestrial planets may be forming (for a detailed introduction, see Matrà et al. (2025), hereafter Ma25). In many instances, the disks appear to be highly structured, with warps, gaps, inner voids, and rings. These structures are often interpreted as indirect signatures of planets (Pearce et al. 2024). However, it has been shown that alternative mechanisms might exist that do not involve planets (Lyra & Kuchner 2013) (examples of such features were reported in Ma25). To date, definite evidence of planets shaping disks is limited to two systems, however: β\beta Pictoris (Mouillet et al. 1997; Augereau et al. 2001; Lagrange et al. 2009b; Lagrange et al. 2010), and TWA7 (Lagrange et al. 2025b). In some cases, such as HR 8799, planets and disk rings are observed (Booth et al. 2016; Faramaz et al. 2021; Boccaletti et al. 2024), but they are not directly linked. It is therefore crucial to search for planets within these disks that might account for the observed structures.

The identification of low-mass companions in disks has mostly relied on ground-based high-contrast imaging (HCI) so far. The number of detected planets remains limited because the achievable contrasts only allow us to detect young, massive (≥\geq 3MJM_{J}) giants that in most cases orbit at separations of 10 au or more from the central stars. Such massive planets are rare, as demonstrated by surveys of hundreds of stars that are part of young, nearby moving groups (Nielsen et al. 2019; Vigan et al. 2021). However, lighter planets, such as the Saturn-mass planet TWA 7b, are now detectable with JWST (Lagrange et al. 2025b; Crotts et al. 2025). Short-period planets have also been found in the AU Mic system with transit photometry (Plavchan et al. 2020; Wittrock et al. 2023).

papers.title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
papers.abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.

papers.intro:
Sub-4-bit quantization, below 4 bits per weight (BPW) on average, allows a mobile device to hold a larger LLM. Larger LLMs can better support on-device AI use cases involving personal data such as contacts, photos, calendar events, and messages. Two levers can improve accuracy under a sub-4-bit budget. The first is a better datatype, such as the perfectly symmetric 2-bit grid (Liu et al., 2025) or 3-bit weights. The second is mixed precision (MP), which assigns more bits to sensitive weights and fewer bits to the rest. With these additional format choices, MP can further improve accuracy at a given BPW.

However, on mobile NPUs, the most accurate sub-4-bit configurations save memory, but their decode time may not be as fast as their bytes promise. This is because the matrix unit of a mobile NPU admits only a few datatypes directly in hardware. We call these datatypes native. In contrast, non-native datatypes require converting the weights on the vector unit before the matrix unit execution. For example, a straightforward approach expands perfectly symmetric 2-bit and 3-bit weights to native 4-bit values on the vector unit before matrix-unit execution. A GPU could hide such conversion with a powerful general computing capability (Frantar et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025), but on a mobile NPU, one vector-unit thread delivers two to three orders of magnitude less throughput than the matrix unit (Hao et al., 2026). MP faces a constraint driven by the matrix unit as well. Each matrix unit tile uses one datatype, so mixing bitwidths within a tile breaks the native layout.

Existing approaches do not fulfill both requirements at once. llama.cpp converts the weights on the vector unit before every multiplication (The ggml authors, 2023). MP methods assign bitwidths per layer (Dong et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2026), per channel (Zheng et al., 2026), or per salient group (Huang et al., 2024). Per-layer assignment keeps each tile in one bitwidth but ignores the sensitivity variation within a layer. The finer two may assign different bitwidths within a tile.

papers.title: On the factorization of Dirac hypergraphs
papers.abstract: A celebrated result from the 70s due to Baranyai states that the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices decomposes into perfect matchings if $k\mid n$. We prove a minimum degree version of this result. Note that a necessary condition for a $k$-uniform hypergraph $G$ on $n$ vertices to admit a decomposition into perfect matchings is that $G$ is vertex-regular and $k\mid n$. We show that, if this is satisfied and, in addition, $G$ has minimum $(k-1)$-degree at least $(\frac{1}{2}+o(1))n$, then it indeed decomposes into perfect matchings. The constant $1/2$ is optimal, as below this threshold, $G$ might not even contain a single perfect matching. This settles a conjecture of Glock, K\"uhn and Osthus from 2021.

papers.intro:
A folklore construction shows that the edges of every complete graph of even order can be partitioned into 11-factors, yielding a so-called 11-factorization. An important class of structures in design theory, 11-factorizations have significant theoretical importance and arise naturally in various scheduling problems, most notably in the organization of round-robin tournaments (see, e.g., [5]). In this paper, we consider 11-factorizations of dense hypergraphs.

Given a positive integer kk, a kk-uniform hypergraph, or kk-graph for short, is a hypergraph whose edges all have size kk. Given two hypergraphs FF and GG, an FF-decomposition of GG is a collection ℱ\mathcal{F} of subgraphs of GG, each isomorphic to FF, such that every edge of GG is contained in exactly one of the hypergraphs in ℱ\mathcal{F}. Graph and hypergraph decomposition problems involve determining necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypergraph GG to have an FF-decomposition. These problems have a long history in combinatorics: for example, Kirkman [14] proved in 1847 that the complete graph KnK_{n} has a K3K_{3}-decomposition if and only if n≡1,3(mod6)n\equiv 1,3\pmod{6}, and Walecki’s theorem from 1892 states that for all odd nn, KnK_{n} has a decomposition into Hamilton cycles. See, e.g., [9] for a survey on graph and hypergraph decomposition problems.

papers.title: Fully Automated Discovery of Phase Diagrams Using Agentic Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Classifying phases of matter and mapping out phase diagrams are central problems in physics. Recently, machine learning techniques have emerged as promising tools for phase classification, ranging from supervised learning to various unsupervised methods. However, these techniques provide limited qualitative insight into the discovered phases, typically work only for specific system classes, and do not by themselves efficiently map out the phase diagram. Autonomously constructing the phase diagram of a general system purely from measurements, without prior knowledge of the system, while also yielding qualitative understanding of the phases, remains an open task. In this work, we introduce Phasonaut, a two-agent framework that leverages the tool-use capabilities and broad knowledge of large language models (LLMs) to drive an active learning loop that constructs phase diagrams of physical systems and provides interpretations of the discovered phases. Starting from scratch, it iteratively selects and performs measurements, analyzes the resulting data, and segments the parameter domain into the phases it discovers. Phasonaut recovers the phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin systems to substantial precision. In the future, this framework could enable rapid exploration of systems with unknown phase diagrams, including in autonomously driven experiments.

papers.intro:
Throughout physics, determining the different phases of a system is a central challenge. Phase diagrams provide a qualitative understanding of a system’s behavior by compressing its many possible configurations into a small number of regimes with similar properties. In doing so, they reveal how microscopic interactions give rise to emergent macroscopic phenomena, and which microscopic details are relevant for them. They can also guide the search for materials with desired properties and applications. However, identifying phases typically requires both broad physical intuition and system-specific considerations, for example to choose suitable order parameters. As a result, mapping phase diagrams remains largely a manual process.

Phase diagrams provide a qualitative understanding of a system’s behavior by compressing its many possible configurations into a small number of regimes with similar properties. In doing so, they reveal how microscopic interactions give rise to emergent macroscopic phenomena, and which microscopic details are relevant for them. They can also guide the search for materials with desired properties and applications. However, identifying phases typically requires both broad physical intuition and system-specific considerations, for example to choose suitable order parameters. As a result, mapping phase diagrams remains largely a manual process.

Over the past decade, machine-learning approaches have emerged as a promising route toward automatically distinguishing phases [1]. When phase-labeled data is available, neural networks are able to recognize phases from previously unseen simulated [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] or experimental [7, 8] data after supervised training. However, often no such labeled data is available, and unsupervised approaches have to be employed. These include principal component analyses [9, 10, 11], clustering and manifold learning [12, 13], autoencoders [11, 10], anomaly detection [14, 15, 16], confusion-based methods [17, 18, 19, 20], and network-prediction analyses [21, 22, 23, 24]. These methods have successfully been applied to both conventional symmetry-breaking transitions associated with local order parameters, and topological ones where order is inherently non-local. However, each of these tools typically performs well only on certain system classes. Moreover, they do not provide qualitative understanding of the phases, i.e., they do not yield order parameters associated with the transitions on their own. Different approaches try to tackle this problem [25, 26, 27, 28], e.g., by analyzing weights or activations of a trained neural network [29, 30, 31]. Human input and analysis are still crucial for operating these methods and understanding their results.

To automatically find different phases present in a system without labeled data, the search can be steered by gradient descent through a differentiable ground-state solver [32], but this requires a differentiable simulation. To instead locate entire phase boundaries, confusion-based methods can be combined with segmentation algorithms from computer vision [33]. However, this can only separate two distinct regions, instead of autonomously mapping out the full diagram, and relies on manually choosing reasonable initial conditions. Often, gathering data is the most expensive part of mapping out a phase diagram. If experimental data can be phase-labeled, active learning methods lower the cost by adaptively choosing the most informative measurements. For example, Bayesian active learning efficiently locates phase boundaries [34, 35, 36]. However, these techniques either ignore physical reasoning or rely on physical constraints hand-coded for specific systems in advance.

We show that Phasonaut recovers a selection of phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin lattice models with substantial accuracy, and further discuss the application of our framework to a yet unexplored model. We demonstrate that boosting Phasonaut’s performance is possible by leveraging its separation into two agents, as well as by making use of self-criticism abilities of modern LLMs [52, 47]. Additionally, we show that the active learning strategies employed by Phasonaut surpass naive grid searches. This work opens the way towards fully autonomous phase-diagram explorations of unknown systems, including programmatically controlled real experiments.

papers.title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
papers.abstract: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

papers.intro:
A dynamical generative model starts with samples from a simple probability distribution and moves them toward a distribution represented by data. When the data consist of finitely many points, this task has a geometric aspect: trajectories must approach those points. It also has a probabilistic aspect: the points must receive the appropriate proportions of samples. Understanding how these two aspects interact can guide both the analysis of generative dynamics and the construction of their learning targets.

Flow matching learns a velocity field from prescribed paths connecting source and data samples. For linear interpolation, each training pair traces a straight segment, although trajectories of the corresponding marginal velocity can curve [12, 15]. Score-based diffusion provides another dynamical description: Gaussian noise smooths the data distribution, and the score, its logarithmic gradient, defines a probability flow toward decreasing noise [8, 21, 22, 9]. For independent Gaussian and empirical samples, an exact change of space and time relates these two flows [25, Propositions 2.1-2.2]. The final stage of flow matching can therefore be studied through the geometry of Gaussian-smoothed finite data as the noise vanishes.

papers.title: Beyond the Ground State: Assessing the Machine-Learned Skala Functional in {\Delta}SCF Calculations of Molecular Excitation Energies
papers.abstract: We assess the transferability of the machine-learned Skala exchange-correlation (XC) functional beyond ground-state energetics using molecular vertical excitation energies and singlet-triplet gaps calculated with the $\Delta$-self-consistent-field ($\Delta$SCF) approach. We compare Skala with PBE, r$^2$SCAN, and PBE0 on subsets covering small-molecule excitations (QUEST1), inverted singlet-triplet gaps (ST-gap), and intramolecular charge-transfer excitations (QUEST6). Both spin-unrestricted Kohn-Sham (UKS) and restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) formalisms are considered. On QUEST1, Skala achieves the lowest mean absolute errors (MAEs) for singlet and triplet excitation energies with both formalisms, although PBE0 and r$^2$SCAN provide more accurate singlet-triplet gaps through error cancellation. For ST-gap, Skala yields the lowest gap MAEs with both UKS and ROKS. Evaluating the mixed-spin and triplet energy components on the same orbitals optimized for the ROKS open-shell singlet yields negative splittings for seven of eight ST-gap molecules with Skala. Separate triplet optimization increases the gaps, but six remain negative. All three conventional functionals give positive common-orbital splittings and optimized gaps for all eight molecules. For QUEST6, treated with UKS only, Skala yields more accurate singlet excitation energies than PBE and r$^2$SCAN but remains less accurate than PBE0. Across QUEST1 and ST-gap, Skala yields lower MAEs with UKS than ROKS. Overall, these results support Skala's transferability to molecular excited states while highlighting its dependence on the excitation class and open-shell treatment.

papers.intro:
Density-functional theory (DFT) [18, 23, 36], within the Kohn–Sham (KS) [23] or generalized KS (GKS) [46] framework, is widely used for electronic structure calculations in chemistry, physics, and materials science owing to its favorable balance between computational cost and accuracy. The accuracy of both KS and GKS methods, however, depends on the quality of the approximation for the exchange–correlation (XC) functional. The development of more accurate XC energy functionals has therefore been a central goal of DFT research. A major strategy toward this goal has been the systematic incorporation of increasingly sophisticated ingredients into XC approximations, as illustrated by Jacob’s ladder [39, 40]. The first rung corresponds to the local-density approximation (LDA), which depends only on the electron density n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}). Generalized gradient approximations (GGAs) on the second rung additionally incorporate the density gradient ∇n​(𝐫)\nabla n(\mathbf{r}), while meta-GGAs on the third rung introduce further ingredients, such as the kinetic-energy density τ⁡(𝐫)\tau(\mathbf{r}), the density Laplacian ∇2n​(𝐫)\nabla^{2}n(\mathbf{r}), or both [50]. The fourth rung incorporates exact exchange, an explicitly nonlocal functional of the occupied orbitals, which can be treated using either a nonlocal Fock-type exchange operator or a local multiplicative potential obtained through the optimized effective potential method [27]. The fifth rung additionally introduces dependence on unoccupied orbitals and their energies through the correlation energy [43, 14]. Density-functional theory (DFT) [18, 23, 36], within the Kohn–Sham (KS) [23] or generalized KS (GKS) [46] framework, is widely used for electronic structure calculations in chemistry, physics, and materials science owing to its favorable balance between computational cost and accuracy. The accuracy of both KS and GKS methods, however, depends on the quality of the approximation for the exchange–correlation (XC) functional. The development of more accurate XC energy functionals has therefore been a central goal of DFT research. Conventional XC functionals have often been developed using physically motivated functional forms guided by exact constraints, as exemplified by PBE [37] and SCAN [48]. Machine learning (ML) offers a complementary strategy, employing highly flexible functional representations whose parameters are optimized using reference data [5, 20, 4, 12]. This flexibility opens up new possibilities for XC functional design, particularly in how established electronic-structure ingredients can be combined. Skala [33], a recently developed machine-learned XC functional, illustrates one such possibility. Unlike conventional approaches that introduce nonlocal XC dependence through explicit orbital expressions, such as exact exchange, Skala learns this dependence by combining semilocal meta-GGA ingredients evaluated at different spatial points. Trained primarily on extensive and diverse high-accuracy ground-state quantum-chemical data, Skala achieves accuracy competitive with hybrid functionals for main-group energetics while retaining the favorable computational scaling of semilocal DFT.

The transferability of machine-learned XC functionals beyond their original training domains requires careful evaluation, as illustrated by SCF convergence difficulties reported for DM21 in transition-metal systems [22, 58]. Although Skala was developed primarily for ground-state molecular energetics [33], recent applications have demonstrated its transferability to periodic solids, including molecular-crystal lattice energies and electronic band gaps, without retraining [42]. Beyond its application to periodic solids, state-specific SCF calculations of molecular excited states [44] offer a distinct test of Skala’s transferability. Since excited-state solutions were not explicitly targeted during training [33], the accuracy of excitation energies obtained from differences between ground- and excited-state total energies provides a quantitative assessment of Skala’s ability to describe electronically excited states in terms of their energies relative to the ground state.

To perform this assessment, we employ state-specific orbital-optimized DFT for excited states, with excitation energies evaluated using the Δ\Delta-self-consistent-field (Δ\DeltaSCF) approach [16, 44]. In this approach, excited states are targeted starting from non-Aufbau orbital occupations [13, 2], with the ground- and excited-state orbitals optimized in separate SCF calculations at a common nuclear geometry. For single-electron excitations from closed-shell systems, the resulting configurations contain two singly occupied orbitals that can couple to form singlet or triplet states. For open-shell singlets, a single-determinant description generally leads to spin-symmetry breaking and significant spin contamination, which can be addressed using spin purification or spin-adapted approaches [59, 9]. Unlike linear-response time-dependent density-functional theory (LR-TDDFT) [35, 53], which determines excitation energies from the response of a ground-state reference, the Δ\DeltaSCF approach allows state-specific orbital relaxation. Such relaxation can be particularly beneficial for excitations involving substantial redistribution of the electron density, including charge-transfer states [47].

papers.title: A Vision-Based Framework for Manual Assembly Verification and Adaptive Operator Assistance
papers.abstract: Manual assembly remains difficult to monitor because operator actions, components, and task progress must be interpreted together. This paper presents a modular framework based on a single overhead red-green-blue (RGB) camera, combining object detection, hand-motion tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, task-specific pose classification, and configurable visual guidance. The system was evaluated during pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under three assistance conditions: full, mid, and no guidance. Mixed-effects analysis identified an association between assistance condition and a composite measure of motion quality, with lower estimated scores under mid and no guidance relative to full guidance. However, the condition-by-trial interaction was not statistically significant, and the estimated differences in learning trajectories remain descriptive. No condition differences were detected in completion time or failed-stage counts. The study demonstrates the integration of visual perception, procedural verification, and configurable operator feedback in a single-camera workflow. Selecting assistance according to operator expertise remains a design objective for future investigation.

Human-centered manufacturing requires monitoring that relates operator actions to parts, workspace locations, and procedural state, rather than recognizing objects or movements in isolation (European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2024). For manual assembly, a system must infer whether an interaction is occurring, determine which component is involved and whether its task-relevant orientation is acceptable, and evaluate the action in the context of the prescribed sequence. These inferences are difficult under occlusion, visually similar parts, and reflective surfaces.

Prior work addresses components of this problem, including object and action recognition, trajectory-based verification, and procedural monitoring (Aganian et al. 2023; Kawase and Hashimoto 2019; Zhang et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2024). The engineering question addressed here is how to connect visual evidence to explicit procedural reasoning and operator-facing feedback in a single-camera RGB system. The contribution is an integrated, replaceable pipeline: learned perception provides detections, hand landmarks, and task-specific orientation classes; region-based interaction logic and two finite-state machines use these outputs to verify manipulations and assembly stages; and a configurable interface presents one of three guidance levels. The work does not introduce a new general-purpose detection or pose-estimation algorithm.

papers.title: Adaptive obstacle deposition drives dynamical localization in chase-and-escape dynamics
papers.abstract: Most pursuit--evasion models assume a fixed environment, although defensive actions can leave persistent structures that affect subsequent encounters. We study a two-dimensional lattice model in which threatened escapers deposit permanent obstacles, coupling capture kinetics to the geometry explored by their pursuers. Increasing the deposition probability enhances escaper survival and strongly suppresses chaser transport. For dilute chasers, the mean-squared-displacement exponent decreases from values near unity towards zero, trajectories contract to a few lattice spacings and the localized fraction rises sharply. The localization response becomes weaker as chaser abundance increases. Time-resolved obstacle densities support a kinetic explanation: rapid capture depletes obstacle-producing escapers before a comparably confining environment can develop. At intermediate parameters, broad or bimodal distributions of trajectory radii and MSD exponents reveal simultaneous mobile and localized subpopulations. Thus deposition redistributes trajectories between distinct dynamical behaviors, producing heterogeneity beyond a uniform slowdown. We summarize the coupled survival and transport response in an empirical map of mobile, heterogeneous and trapping-dominated regimes, interpreted as finite-time crossovers. These results identify the lifetime of the obstacle-producing population as a key control of adaptive localization: a stronger instantaneous pursuit pressure can weaken confinement by shortening the period over which the environment is modified.

papers.intro:
Pursuit–evasion dynamics constitute a broad class of non-equilibrium processes in which one population attempts to approach, intercept or capture another population that simultaneously tries to avoid contact. Despite the apparent simplicity of this definition, local pursuit and escape rules can generate collective structures, coordinated strategies and non-trivial capture statistics that cannot be inferred directly from single-agent motion [25, 2, 24, 33]. Extensions of the group chase-and-escape model have further shown that heterogeneity in chaser activity can improve capture [28, 42]. Such models provide a useful bridge between individual-level decisions and population-level outcomes because they preserve the directional asymmetry between chasers and escapers while remaining sufficiently minimal for systematic statistical analysis.

Defensive responses that leave persistent structures in the environment are common in nature. Members of the family Holothuriidae eject Cuvierian tubules when disturbed; the tubules elongate, adhere to nearby objects and can entangle a predator while the sea cucumber withdraws [18, 12]. Their regeneration is slow, so repeated threats progressively deplete this defence [44]. At a very different scale, protozoan grazing can stimulate microcolony formation and thickening of the exopolymeric matrix in bacterial biofilms, so that the medium through which a grazer moves is itself altered by predation pressure [29, 49]. These examples motivate a general ingredient that is rarely included in minimal pursuit models: a local response to threat that persists after the encounter and constrains subsequent motion.

From the perspective of statistical physics, chase-and-escape systems belong to the broader family of active and driven many-body systems. Their microscopic rules violate detailed balance: chasers bias their motion towards targets, escapers bias their motion away from threats, and the resulting probability currents persist even in statistically stationary states. Persistence, exclusion, local crowding and interaction-induced correlations are known to generate anomalous transport and large dynamical fluctuations in active systems [46, 4, 7, 14, 43]. Activity can also generate compact configurations through self-organized geometric constraints, as illustrated by chirality-induced self-wrapping in active polymers [9]. Pursuit introduces an additional source of non-equilibrium organization because the preferred direction of motion is continually updated by the evolving relative positions of the two populations. Capture efficiency is therefore controlled not only by the mobility of isolated agents, but also by how collective motion reshapes the set of accessible trajectories.

The physical environment is central to this problem. Walls, obstacles and bottlenecks constrain available paths and modify both the frequency and the geometry of encounters. This sensitivity appears across very different contexts. Immune and invasive cells migrate through dense, heterogeneous tissues whose architecture channels or impedes motion [19, 41, 31, 30]. Predator–prey encounters depend on habitat fragmentation, connectivity and barriers [20, 11]. Robotic pursuit and autonomous navigation require simultaneous target tracking, collision avoidance and path planning in obstacle-filled domains [35, 27, 26, 52, 1], while aerial predators also alter pursuit trajectories to negotiate obstacles [8]. Boundaries and congestion similarly affect escape routes and evacuation efficiency in pedestrian systems [22, 48].

Most theoretical treatments separate agent dynamics from environmental structure: the environment is generated first and then held fixed while the agents move through it. In lattice chase-and-escape models, fixed obstacles reduce accessible area, create detours and can divide the domain into weakly connected regions [40, 38]. Active particles in heterogeneous media exhibit related subdiffusion, intermittent displacements and trapping [10, 4, 5]. These studies establish that geometric disorder can strongly affect transport and capture, but they do not address the converse coupling in which pursuit itself generates the disorder that subsequently controls the dynamics.

This distinction between externally imposed and self-generated structure is important. In a quenched environment the obstacle field is statistically independent of the trajectories. In an adaptive environment, by contrast, obstacles are created at locations and times selected by the dynamics. The resulting disorder is correlated with threat events, escape routes and local population densities. The broader relevance of spatial correlations in disorder is illustrated by elastic networks, where correlated disorder modifies the packing fraction at the onset of rigidity [15]. A trail left behind an escaper may close a corridor, redirect a chaser or combine with earlier deposits to form a local cage. Conversely, rapid capture terminates further modification of the environment. Geometry is therefore both an outcome of the pursuit and a feedback mechanism acting on its subsequent evolution.

When variables evolving on a network or substrate also alter that substrate, new time scales, heterogeneous states and sharp crossovers can emerge that are absent under fixed connectivity [17]. Related ideas have recently been explored for transport on adjustable networks, where the substrate responds to the moving particles [34]. Chase-and-escape dynamics provides a particularly transparent realization because environmental modification directly affects both the survival of the agents that create the structure and the transport of the agents pursuing them.

papers.title: CoGITAtion: Collaborative Gaze-based Interpretable Task-adaptive Representation for Privacy-sensitive Applications
papers.abstract: Gaze-based analysis provides rich behavioural information for privacy-sensitive applications, but deployment is challenged by heterogeneous, scarce, and distributed data. We present CoGITAtion (Collaborative Gaze-based Interpretable Task-Adaptive Representation), a framework for privacy-preserving inference over vertically distributed gaze data. CoGITAtion transforms variable-length gaze recordings into compact, interpretable gaze-transition graphs and descriptors computed locally by each data owner. Task-adaptive models accommodate heterogeneous and missing feature blocks through task and availability gating, avoiding unnecessary private computation. Results show that shared components capture patterns that generalise across tasks, while task-specific components provide capacity without increasing model size. Public availability gating further reduces encrypted computation by removing branches determined by publicly known task and owner availability without altering predictions. Overall, CoGITAtion enables gaze model reuse, efficient privacy-preserving deployment, and robust inference under incomplete owner availability while retaining interpretable gaze representations.

papers.intro:
Gaze behaviour provides rich information about human attention, perception, and behaviour (Vertegaal and others, 2003; Bulling and Gellersen, 2010). This information may also be used in sensitive application domains, including the assessment of neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions, mental-health-related analysis, or software development with proprietary and confidential code (Elfares et al., 2025a; Al Madi et al., 2026). Unlike conventional approaches that depend on verbal responses, questionnaires, or structured observations, gaze-based analysis can provide behavioural measurements directly from how individuals visually interact with stimuli (Iwauchi et al., 2023).

Unlike conventional approaches that depend on verbal responses, questionnaires, or structured observations, gaze-based analysis can provide behavioural measurements directly from how individuals visually interact with stimuli (Iwauchi et al., 2023).

Despite its potential, the adoption of gaze-based analysis in sensitive applications remains limited. One fundamental challenge is the heterogeneity, scarcity, and distributed ownership of gaze data (Elfares et al., 2023; Holmqvist et al., 2012). There is no universally established representation or acquisition protocol, and gaze recordings can differ substantially across eye trackers, experimental protocols, stimuli, interfaces, and behavioural tasks. Even within the same application domain, the same condition may be assessed using different paradigms, while programming-related gaze behaviour may depend on the particular code, interface, or development environment being inspected (Elfares et al., 2025a; Al Madi et al., 2021). These discrepancies hinder the integration of heterogeneous datasets and limit the effectiveness of models that assume a homogeneous input space. Moreover, gaze data are often scarce and distributed across multiple data owners, such as hospitals, research institutions, and other organisations, which may hold complementary feature sets for the same individuals, a.k.a. vertically distributed data. For instance, different owners may possess gaze statistics, pupil measurements, or task-specific behavioural information. Privacy regulations, consent constraints, and institutional data-sharing policies further restrict the centralisation and aggregation of such data for model training (European Parliament, ; European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024).

A second challenge is interpretability. Many high-performing gaze-analysis approaches learn directly from images, raw scanpaths, or other high-dimensional representations. Although such models can capture complex behavioural patterns, their predictions may be difficult to relate to observable gaze behaviour. This is particularly problematic in sensitive or regulated settings, where understanding why a model produces a particular prediction can be as important as predictive performance itself (Kumar et al., 2020). A representation based on interpretable behavioural descriptors can instead provide a direct connection between model inputs and measurable properties of visual exploration, such as revisits, regressions, dwell concentration, transition structure, and reading behaviour.

However, it introduces substantial computational and communication overhead. However, it introduces substantial computational and communication overhead. Efficient private inference therefore requires not only an appropriate predictive model but also a representation and computational structure tailored to encrypted execution.

To address these challenges, we present CoGITAtion – Collaborative Gaze-based Interpretable Task-Adaptive Representation. The core idea of this novel gaze representation is to enable moving computationally expensive, data-dependent gaze processing to the data owners, and provide the privacy-preserving model with a compact fixed-dimensional representation. Each gaze recording is locally transformed into a directed, weighted gaze-transition graph describing transitions between spatial or task-specific regions. From this graph, CoGITAtion extracts descriptors capturing complementary aspects of visual exploration, including spatial coverage and density, self-loops and revisits, hubs and attractors, reciprocal and cyclic transitions, transition and dwell entropy, and text-reading behaviour. The resulting owner block is then used for private inference rather than the original variable-length gaze sequence.

Overall, CoGITAtion provides an important deployment advantage; it enables a unified model to operate across multiple tasks and heterogeneous owner configurations, reducing the need for separate models, compilations, and cryptographic configurations.

We evaluate CoGITAtion across heterogeneous privacy-sensitive applications: neurodevelopmental, medical, and programming datasets (Duan et al., 2019; Cilia et al., 2022; Song et al., 2025; Wainstein et al., 2017; Rojas-Líbano et al., 2019; Bednarik et al., 2020; Elfares et al., 2025b). Our results show that explicitly separating task-independent and task-specific structure allows shared components to capture reusable patterns across tasks, while task-specific components provide additional capacity only where needed. Gating further improves deployment efficiency. Because task identity and owner availability are known before private inference, corresponding branches can be removed at compile time without changing the model output. This provides a lossless reduction in private computation when task or owner availability is heterogeneous. Thus, CoGITAtion allows model reuse, simpler deployment, and robustness to missing data owners11 1 Note that privacy-preserving computation does not compensate for poor-quality data. Since CoGITAtion is a statistical learning framework, acquisition artefacts, weak labels, missing data, gaze drift, and other measurement errors can directly affect model performance (Section 5). We therefore recommend performing data-quality assessment before applying privacy-preserving computation..

papers.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.

papers.intro:
Perspective taking is the mental and emotional ability to step outside one’s own frame of reference and understand a situation from another person’s point of view. Its visual form is visual perspective taking: The task of determining whether another person can see an object (Level 1) or how the visual scene looks from their position (Level 2) [13, 40, 42, 50]. Humans rely on this ability during collaboration [51], for example when handing over an object, when referring to an object only visible to the collaborator, or when avoiding obstruction of another person’s view or motion. Consequently, robots collaborating with humans were argued to require similar abilities [57, 5, 25, 12]. Prior work reduced visual perspective taking to estimating symbolic or geometric states [57, 5, 29], reconstructing the visual scene from another viewpoint [25, 12], or answering spatial questions [30, 15]. We explore the significantly more challenging task of visually synthesising what the collaborator actually sees.

In this work we study generative visual perspective taking between two human collaborators: Given the posed egocentric video of one person, the ego person, with access to earlier frames of the same recording, a scene point cloud, and the camera trajectory of the other person, the collaborator, the task is to generate the egocentric video that the collaborator sees at any point in time. While pretrained video diffusion models provide strong priors over scene appearance and human motion, they cannot directly relate two views separated by large viewpoint changes. Our key insight is that collaboration takes place in a shared workspace: its static 3D geometry, together with the collaborator’s camera trajectory, determines which surfaces the collaborator sees and where, while the ego person’s observations provide appearance cues that the video prior can build on for many of these surfaces. We thus propose Ego2Ego– a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that ground video generation in this shared geometry and visual memory. First, to handle extreme viewpoint shifts and dynamic occlusions, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into a scene coordinate map for every view, so that the same 3D point receives the same value across views and serves as a shared spatial reference. Second, to relate two independently moving cameras, relative geometric attention extends single-trajectory ray-aligned attention [82] to align tokens between the ego person’s and the collaborator’s views, pairing token-wise ray-frame transforms with shared temporal encodings. Third, to handle sparse visual overlap, the ego person’s visual memory selects earlier ego-person frames that best cover the collaborator’s view, recovering regions outside the current clip.

papers.title: NGC 1300: A rich reservoir of ultraluminous X-ray sources
papers.abstract: We present the first systematic multi-epoch study of the X-ray source population of the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1300, using 12 archival Chandra observations spanning more than 15 years and archival Swift/XRT monitoring. Within the optical extent of the galaxy, we identify 42 X-ray sources, including six ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) and 13 ULX candidates. The candidates have measured luminosities below $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, but their upper uncertainty bounds reach or exceed this threshold in at least one epoch. We examine source luminosities, long-term variability, broad-band spectral properties, and epoch-resolved X-ray luminosity functions (XLFs). Ten sources meet our transient criterion, seven have a variability significance of $S_{\rm var}\geq3$, and four meet both criteria. X32 is a highly variable ULX with a peak X-ray luminosity of $1.5\times10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$, more than 715 times the non-detection upper limit. The hardness-intensity diagrams show diverse spectral behavior among the luminous sources, with no common hardness-luminosity evolution. X32 remains predominantly hard despite its large luminosity variations, and its X-ray colors are consistent with the empirical high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) region of the color-color diagram. The cumulative XLFs above $10^{38}$ erg s$^{-1}$ have slopes of $\beta\simeq0.6$ to $1.0$, with evidence for a broken power law in only a few epochs. The number of off-nuclear sources reaching $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ ranges from zero to four per epoch. Long-term source variability thus strongly shapes the bright end of the XLF and makes the observed ULX census of NGC 1300 strongly epoch dependent. Multi-epoch monitoring is essential for establishing representative ULX populations in nearby galaxies.

papers.intro:
NGC 1300 is a nearby, strongly barred spiral galaxy of morphological type SB(s)bc (Sandage and Tammann, 1981), characterized by a prominent stellar bar connected to two well-defined spiral arms. We adopt a distance of 20.7 Mpc, following Maeda et al. (2020b), corresponding to a physical scale of 100​pc​arcsec−1100\penalty\ {\rm pc\penalty\ arcsec^{-1}}. This distance is based on a systemic velocity of 1511​km​s−11511\penalty\ {\rm km\penalty\ s^{-1}}, corrected for the Virgo Cluster, Great Attractor, and Shapley concentration, and H0=73​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=73\penalty\ {\rm km\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ Mpc^{-1}}. The galaxy has an inclination of 50.2∘50.2^{\circ} (England, 1989). NGC 1300 is actively forming stars, with a global star-formation rate (SFR) of 1.4​M⊙​yr−11.4\penalty\ M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr^{-1}} when rescaled to the distance adopted here, and has a stellar mass of log⁡(M⋆/M⊙)≃10.6\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\simeq 10.6 (Leroy et al., 2021). Its prominent bar, spiral arms, and bar-end regions contain markedly different molecular-gas and star-forming environments (Maeda et al., 2020b; Maeda et al., 2020a). Spatially resolved stellar-population analysis further indicates sub-solar metallicity across much of NGC 1300, with mean [M/H][{\rm M/H}] values of −0.22-0.22 dex in the disk and −0.18-0.18 dex in the nuclear ring, compared with approximately solar metallicity in the nucleus (Rosado-Belza et al., 2020). These spatially distinct environments make NGC 1300 a useful system for investigating whether variations in local star-forming conditions are reflected in the properties and distribution of its compact X-ray source population.

The molecular gas and star-forming environments of NGC 1300 have been studied extensively through CO observations. Single-dish CO12​(1CLOSE{}^{12}{\rm CO}(1–OPEN0)0) observations revealed substantial molecular gas in both the bar and spiral arms, despite the lack of prominent H ii regions along much of the bar (Maeda et al., 2018). High-resolution ALMA observations subsequently identified 233 giant molecular clouds (GMCs) in the bar, spiral arms, and bar-end regions, with no strong systematic differences in their sizes, velocity dispersions, molecular masses, or virial parameters (Maeda et al., 2020b). Despite these similarities in GMC properties, star formation is strongly suppressed in the bar. The molecular-gas star-formation efficiency is 0.060.06–0.16​Gyr−10.16\penalty\ {\rm Gyr^{-1}} in the bar, compared with 0.230.23–0.96​Gyr−10.96\penalty\ {\rm Gyr^{-1}} in the spiral arms and bar-end regions, while the diffuse molecular-gas fraction reaches 0.740.74–0.910.91 in the bar (Maeda et al., 2020a). Hydrodynamical simulations tailored to NGC 1300 suggest that the elongated gas motions induced by the strong bar increase cloud–cloud collision velocities and may contribute to the suppression of massive star formation (Fujimoto et al., 2020). The resulting contrast between the relatively quiescent bar and the more actively star-forming spiral arms and bar-end regions is particularly relevant to its X-ray source population, because high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) are generally associated with recent star formation, whereas low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) more closely trace the older stellar population (Fabbiano, 2006).

X-ray binaries (XRBs) constitute a substantial fraction of the resolved X-ray source populations of nearby galaxies. The numbers and integrated X-ray luminosities of HMXBs scale with the recent SFR, whereas LMXBs predominantly trace stellar mass (Gilfanov, 2004; Fabbiano, 2006; Mineo et al., 2012; Lehmer et al., 2019). The X-ray luminosity function (XLF) is therefore commonly used to characterize resolved XRB populations and their dependence on the stellar content and star-formation activity of the host galaxy. In star-forming galaxies, HMXBs dominate the luminous end of the XLF, which extends into the ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) regime (Grimm et al., 2003; Mineo et al., 2012). ULXs are non-nuclear X-ray sources that reach LX≥1039​erg​s−1L_{\rm X}\geq 10^{39}\penalty\ {\rm erg\penalty\ s^{-1}} and include neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes accreting at high or super-Eddington rates (Bachetti et al., 2014; Kaaret et al., 2017; Fabrika et al., 2021). Their observed luminosities can vary by several orders of magnitude, and individual sources may reach across the conventional ULX threshold only during their brightest states. Repeated observations have revealed transient ULXs that were either undetected or observed at substantially lower luminosities in earlier epochs, including systems in NGC 5907, NGC 7090, NGC 55, and NGC 4254 (Pintore et al., 2018; Earnshaw et al., 2020; Walton et al., 2021; Robba et al., 2022; Allak, 2023). ULX censuses based on single-epoch observations may not capture sources that attain ultraluminous luminosities only intermittently. Multi-epoch X-ray observations are required to sample the luminosity range of individual sources, identify transient systems, and determine how strongly variable sources affect both the observed ULX census and the bright end of the XLF.

papers.title: Comparing weakly interacting and free quantum dynamics locally
papers.abstract: Lieb-Robinson bounds (LRBs) have become a standard tool for perturbative results in quantum many-body physics, including gap stability and many-body adiabatic theory. Here, we use LRBs to locally approximate weakly interacting many-body dynamics with one-body dynamics on large, perturbative time scales. This allows us to use one-body transport results to establish the expected many-body transport behavior on finite time scales in the following two illustrative settings: (i) We prove quantum diffusion, as quantified by a certain operator spreading diagnostic, in weakly interacting and weakly disordered Fermi systems in dimensions $D\geq2$ on large finite time scales based on the non-interacting diffusion result of Black, Drogin, and Hern\'andez [arXiv:2506.06468]. (ii) We show for Fermi-Hubbard models with initially low spin-down density, that all local multi-time spin-up correlation functions are approximated by their free counterparts. In particular, we obtain an OTOC (out-of-time-ordered correlator) counterpart to the patterns of short-time entanglement related to lattice path counts observed numerically by Bippus et al. [Phys. Rev. B 113, 035152 (2026)].

papers.title: Quantum Dobrushin comparison and locality of fermionic equilibrium states
papers.abstract: We prove a quantum analogue of Dobrushin's comparison theorem for lattice fermions. As in the classical case, it is a tool for proving uniqueness of equilibrium states, decay of correlations, and stability of local expectations under distant perturbations. We apply it to fermions with weak many-body interactions added to a quadratic Hamiltonian, allowing pairing, spatial inhomogeneity and long-range interactions. If the quadratic Hamiltonian is gapped, there is a coupling strength below which the thermal equilibrium (KMS) state is unique at every positive temperature and its correlations decay uniformly in the temperature. Its local expectations converge to those of the unique gapped ground state exponentially fast in the inverse temperature. In the same regime, local perturbations perturb locally in a strong sense (strong LPPL): every equilibrium state of a system with a distant defect is locally close to the equilibrium state without the defect, however strong or extended the defect is. The same holds for finite-volume Gibbs states with arbitrary even boundary terms. Without a gap, uniqueness, decay of correlations and strong LPPL hold at each positive temperature for interactions below a coupling strength that depends on the temperature. At high temperature, they hold for general interactions.

papers.intro:
How Hamiltonians determine equilibrium states is a central question in statistical mechanics of classical and quantum many-body systems. For systems on an infinite lattice, two closely related problems are whether a given Hamiltonian determines a unique equilibrium state at a prescribed temperature and how local changes in the Hamiltonian affect local expectations and correlations. For classical lattice systems, Dobrushin’s comparison theorem answers both questions by controlling differences between conditional distributions [28, 33]. An influence matrix measures how changing the spin at one site affects the conditional distribution at another site. Under a contraction condition, its resolvent bounds the resulting differences between Gibbs measures. Uniqueness, decay of correlations, and estimates on the effect of perturbations and boundary conditions follow from the same comparison principle.

papers.title: PepDeTech: Anonymous Occupancy Monitoring on a Battery-Powered 2.3k-Zone dToF LiDAR Node with On-Chip Processing and Bluetooth LE Reporting
papers.abstract: As populations grow, society is increasingly required to shift towards systems of shared resources, which allow space, energy and time to be optimised. Facilitating this transition depends on data: how many people are present, when and where. From such information, schedules can be organised more efficiently and resources allocated where they matter. At the same time, privacy concerns and energy consumption limit deployment: cameras are frequently unacceptable, while simpler sensors miss people and cannot provide the full picture. This paper presents PepDeTech, a compact, battery-powered occupancy node that combines a 54 x 42-zone direct Time-of-Flight (dToF) Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) (VL53L9CX) with a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) System on Chip (SoC). Three deterministic algorithms, background subtraction, motion history and a track lifecycle, run on-chip and count the people simultaneously, providing real-time occupancy monitoring. No trained model is involved, and setup takes less than a minute. Over three scenarios, background subtraction reaches a per-frame +-1-person accuracy of 83.6 % (mean absolute error (MAE) 0.70 persons), tested with up to five people present. At a 30 s interval the node draws only 3.1 mW, lasting 60 d on a 1200 mA h cell. Several weeks of deployment on a single charge make the node usable as a survey instrument for facility management: a room can be characterised for a measurement campaign without cabling, network provisioning or a camera, and the resulting occupancy record is what ventilation, lighting, cleaning and space-allocation decisions are argued from, ultimately resulting in more efficient resource allocation.
papers.intro:
Optimising resource allocation in facility management increasingly calls for decisions justified by data rather than by assumption: when to light, heat and cool a space, and how many desks, chairs and meeting rooms are needed. Studies show that lighting and HVAC (HVAC) dominate the energy use of commercial buildings and are usually operated on schedules or for an assumed maximum occupancy [1, 2]. Feeding the actual number of occupants into the control loop has saved 25 %25\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of HVAC energy in a deployment [3] and up to 45 %45\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in simulation [2]. Occupancy has been sensed with PIR (PIR), CO2, radio signals [4], cameras, thermal arrays and depth sensors [1], each with a trade-off: PIR sensors are responsive only to motion [5], environmental sensors react within minutes, and cameras raise privacy concerns [2]. Thermal arrays and depth sensors avoid identifiable images, but the reported systems rely on models trained on labelled data, which reach at most 82.7 %82.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} balanced accuracy [6], or are mains-powered, mounted at doorways and processed on a single-board computer or server [7, 2, 8]. Low-power applications have combined acceleration data with a single-zone ToF (ToF) sensor [9], which leaves a gap between counting the exact number of people and keeping energy consumption low.

papers.title: Improved perimeter bounds for Hausdorff approximation by convex polygons
papers.abstract: We investigate how closely a convex polygon with at most n vertices can approximate a plane convex body of given perimeter. For free approximation in the Euclidean Hausdorff metric we improve Popov's bound for every $n \geq 3$. We also improve his inscribed bound for every $n \geq 3$ and his circumscribed bound for $n = 3$. The common step is to join successive boundary contacts of the body and estimate the perimeter lost in passing to their convex hull.

papers.intro:
Fix an integer n≥3n\geq 3. Among plane convex bodies of perimeter one, how large can the error of a best approximating nn-gon be? The answer depends on whether the polygon is freely placed, must lie in the body, or must contain it. Popov studied all three versions. He conjectured that the regular (n+1)(n+1)-gon is extremal, and obtained upper bounds with the correct leading terms as n→∞n\to\infty [8, 9]. The fixed-nn questions are recorded as Problems 2, 3 and 4, respectively, in Brass, Moser and Pach [3, §11.5, p. 468]. Here we improve Popov’s finite-nn bounds by using the geometry of the points where the approximation error is attained.

papers.title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
papers.abstract: The number formats that accelerators execute natively are fixed at fabrication, yet large language model (LLM) checkpoints are released with MXFP4 weights in the Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023. FPGAs adopt new formats through bitstreams. However, to the best of our knowledge, no deployed FPGA LLM accelerator executes MXFP4 weights alongside BF16 products. We characterize the decoding of MXFP4 checkpoints, whose layers alternate between MXFP4$\times$BF16 products and BF16$\times$BF16 products of attention and BF16 layers. With a BF16 KV cache, BF16$\times$BF16 products take 56%-77% of the datapath time, during which a separate MXFP4 unit idles. We present Cruella, whose unified dot-product unit (UDPU) executes both product types on one DSP array and reduction pipeline. First, per-group pre-alignment keeps this pipeline at the BF16 width and changes perplexity by at most 0.7%. Second, pre-adder packing places two signed MXFP4$\times$BF16 products in one DSP48E2 multiplier with an exact correction. On an Alveo U55C, the UDPU needs 23% fewer DSP slices and 36% fewer LUTs than separate MXFP4 and BF16 units of equal throughput. On this board, MXFP4 weights speed up decoding by 1.15$\times$-1.87$\times$ over BF16 weights, and an NVIDIA A40 GPU decodes faster but spends 0.92$\times$-2.01$\times$ the board's energy per token.

papers.intro:
The number formats that an accelerator executes natively are fixed when it is fabricated, yet those of large language model (LLM) inference (Grattafiori et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2025) now change within the service life of deployed hardware. LLM inference has moved from the FP16 of the 2020 A100 GPU to FP8 in 2022 and to the 4-bit Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023 (Choquette et al., 2021; Micikevicius et al., 2022; Darvish Rouhani et al., 2023a). MXFP4 has become a production format, because open-weight LLMs from the 20B-parameter GPT-OSS (OpenAI, 2025) to the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI, 2026) release most of their weights in MXFP4. The key insight is that the two modes differ only in operand structure, because both compute a mantissa product per element pair followed by an aligned sum. Therefore, each mode keeps its own product stage that prepares the operands and forms the products on the unified DSP array, while the reduction pipeline is common to both modes.

papers.title: Modelling scintillation in Fast Radio Bursts
papers.abstract:
Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are bright, ms-duration, extragalactic radio transients. Propagation through inhomogeneities in the ionised medium produces scintillation, observed as frequency-dependent intensity variations in their spectra, with bright patches, called scintles. The characteristic scintillation bandwidth probes scattering material along the line of sight. Measuring this scale can be challenging when the observing bandwidth of the burst spectra contains a few scintles. We study the uncertainties associated with recovering $
u_s$ from frequency autocorrelation functions (ACFs) under finite-bandwidth conditions. We examine the recovery of $
u_s$ from individual ACFs and investigate if averaging multiple independent ACFs provides a more robust measurement. Using simulations, we reproduce observational conditions to investigate the modelling of scintillation in ACFs and the associated measurement uncertainties. We use these simulations to test the finite scintle error (FSE) prescription and assess its applicability to real observations. We test the resulting modelling framework on Effelsberg Ultra Broad Band receiver observations of the repeating FRB 20240114A. As the number of scintles decreases, individual ACFs develop fluctuations that deviate from the expected Lorentzian profile. This results in increased scatter in the recovered $
u_s$ and a less reliable FSE prescription. Averaging multiple independent ACFs mitigates these effects and improves the recovery of $
u_s$ in the low-scintle regime. Our results provide a framework for ACF modelling and uncertainty estimation in FRBs. For individual bursts, the FSE is effective with sufficient scintles; we find $\eta = 0.055$ more suitable for FRB analysis and update the FSE accordingly. For repeaters, averaging multiple ACFs and bootstrap resampling improve the recovery and uncertainty estimation of $
u_s$.

papers.intro:
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are energetic, millisecond-duration radio transients. Since their first discovery (Lorimer et al. 2007), thousands of FRBs continue to be detected in large-scale radio surveys (e.g. CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. (2026)). These sources are of particular interest due to their extragalactic origin, the coherent nature of their emission, and the still-uncertain physical mechanism responsible for their production (Petroff et al. 2019). Among the proposed progenitor models, magnetars currently represent the most promising candidates. This interpretation is supported by the detection of FRB-like radio bursts associated with Galactic magnetars SGR 1935+2154 (CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. 2019; Bochenek et al. 2020) and later 1E 1547.0-5408 (Lower et al. 2026). Observational campaigns have successfully localised several FRBs to their host galaxies (e.g. Bannister et al. (2019)), extending to cosmological distances (Caleb et al. 2025).

FRBs are commonly classified into repeating and apparently non-repeating (one-off) sources. The discovery of repeated bursts from FRB 20121102A (Spitler et al. 2016) established the existence of a repeating FRB class, suggesting that the observed diversity of FRB activity may arise from different progenitor channels. Beyond their origin, FRBs serve as powerful cosmic probes of the intervening baryonic matter, allowing constraints on the ionised, magnetised, and turbulent plasma along lines of sight (Walters et al. 2018; Macquart et al. 2020).

They then pass through the Milky Way’s halo and ISM before they reach the detector via the interplanetary medium of the Solar System (Macquart and Koay 2013; Ocker et al. 2021). Small-scale inhomogeneities in the plasma density act as scattering screens, inducing multipath propagation that leads to temporal broadening, angular broadening, and interference patterns in the signal, known as diffractive scintillation (Rickett 1990; Lorimer and Kramer 2004). Studying scintillation in FRBs provides a unique view on both the emission mechanism and the local plasma environment.
