papers.title: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
papers.abstract: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Synthetic Defects for Anomaly Detection in Industrial Small Load Carriers
papers.abstract: Recent industrial anomaly detection methods use procedural noise to generate synthetic training defects. Their effectiveness in real-world settings and the impact of different noise generation methods have not been sufficiently investigated. We evaluate the effectiveness of training using synthetic defects for both supervised and unsupervised methods, the impact of different noise generation methods, and the differences in detection performance between benchmark datasets and a real-world small load carrier (SLC) dataset. Trained on synthetic defects only, a supervised classifier reaches 0.65 AUROC on real SLC defects, while three unsupervised methods using the same kind of noise (Perlin) reach 0.87--0.90. Except for SuperSimpleNet, which fails with the foreground-confined fractal Brownian motion (fBm) recipe, models trained with the custom recipe or with nine other noise types do not differ reliably from those trained with Perlin noise. Finally, results with synthetic defects on benchmark datasets do not carry over to the SLC dataset, possibly because the synthetic defects differ too much from the real ones (a larger angle in feature space). These results call for caution when training models on synthetic defect images.

However, [8, 9] reported a gap between benchmark performance and real-world industrial applications. Several factors set the SLC dataset apart. As SLCs are reused, wear and discolouration occur even on OK ones. Diverse defect types and a changing environment during operation can also widen the gap. This study investigates the effectiveness of synthetic defects generated from ten noise types and blending methods, as labels for a supervised classifier and as a training signal for unsupervised methods, on benchmark datasets and the SLC dataset.

papers.title: Linear and Quadratic Penalties for Cardinality Constraints in Unconstrained Binary Optimization
papers.abstract: We study penalty strategies for converting constrained binary optimization problems to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) form on the example of the sparsest $k$-subgraph problem. We adopt an augmented Lagrangian approach involving a linear penalty in addition to the commonly used quadratic one, and show the benefits of this approach. From the constraint structure, we derive sufficient bounds on the penalty coefficients. We conduct extensive experiments comparing combinations of our different penalty strategies with a wide range of classical and quantum QUBO solvers. Our experiments show that to obtain a good-quality solution, the right penalty strategy is almost as important as the quality of the QUBO solver, and iterative approaches appear to be the most efficient. We discuss the mechanisms that lead to a degradation of the solution quality due to large quadratic penalties.

Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) [39] has attracted renewed research interest because of its relevance in quantum computing. Being equivalent to the Ising problem, QUBO is the native input format of quantum annealers [28, 10] such as D-Wave [27], and it can also serve as the input of algorithms for gate-based quantum computers, such as QAOA [15, 2]. QUBO is also equivalent to Max-Cut, for which many good classical heuristics are available [13]. Being equivalent to the Ising problem, QUBO is the native input format of quantum annealers [28, 10] such as D-Wave [27], and it can also serve as the input of algorithms for gate-based quantum computers, such as QAOA [15, 2]. Many real-world applications, however, lead to constrained problems. To use the above solvers, such a problem has to be transformed to QUBO form, most commonly by quadratic penalties: the square of the violation of an equality constraint, multiplied by a large enough number, is added to the objective [36, 17]. The appropriate choice of the large enough multiplier is often not trivial.

Lasserre [34] and Gusmeroli and Wiegele [24] derived general penalty bounds for linearly constrained quadratic binary programs with integer coefficients. The penalties obtained in this way guarantee optimality, but they can be hard to calculate and are often too big in practice. Hence, it is worth taking into account the structure of the constraints in the actual problem. For the one-hot encodings of permutation constraints, for instance, Ayodele [1] derives closed-form static penalties from single-flip changes of the QUBO, which outperform global bounds on Fujitsu’s Digital Annealer. These bounds, however, are not provably tight.

Several empirical approaches tune the penalties for specific problem classes in the quantum setting, by the cross-entropy method [43], by machine-learning regression [44], or by characterizing the penalties of multi-knapsack variants under QAOA and quantum annealing [21]. These and most other applied contributions in the quantum realm are specific to quantum solvers, and typically address small problems because of the limited size of the available hardware. Quintero et al. [42] study QUBO formulations of the maximum kk-colorable subgraph problem in detail. Building on the known formulations of the max-clique and stable set problems, they introduce linear-based and nonlinear QUBO reformulations and, exploiting the properties of the constraints, analyze the optimal choice of the penalty parameters. They show the benefits of a well-chosen encoding and penalty values through the time dependence of the energy gap during annealing, the embedding properties, and the time-to-solution on different D-Wave processors. Vyskočil and Djidjev [46] consider a cardinality constraint whose squared penalty makes the problem graph complete, so that its minor embedding requires a number of physical qubits quadratic in nn. They replace it by a sparse Ising program assembled from small unit-cell gadgets, maximizing the gap between feasible and infeasible assignments under the coefficient range of the hardware. How the objective and the constraint share this range is left open.

[4] derive a closed-form estimate of the multipliers for bin packing, similar in spirit to our sufficiency bounds but heuristic rather than provably tight, and Liu and Moraglio [35] search for the penalty coefficients iteratively in a multi-constraint setting with an empirical sensitivity heuristic.

papers.title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.

papers.intro:
Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) is a fine-grained natural language processing (NLP) task that aims to extract detailed sentiment information from text [29]. ABSA includes several sentiment elements, e.g. aspect term (aa), aspect category (cc), and sentiment polarity (pp). For example, in the review “I did enjoy the soup”, the elements are “soup”, “food quality”, “positive”, respectively. Implicit aspect terms, like in “Delicious!” are often denoted as “null”. Target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) [21] simultaneously extracts all three sentiment elements. In contrast, related subtasks like aspect term extraction target aspect terms alone, whereas E2E-ABSA [10] extracts target terms alongside sentiment polarities.

While mainstream ABSA research primarily focuses on English, real-world applications require robust multilingual capabilities [24, 9]. However, annotated ABSA resources in non-English languages are scarce, and manual dataset creation is costly and labour-intensive. A common solution is cross-lingual ABSA, where a model is fine-tuned on a high-resource language (e.g. English) and evaluated on target languages. Nevertheless, syntactic shifts and semantic divergence across language families often degrade cross-lingual transfer performance. To mitigate these disparities, prior work relies on machine translation pipelines [28] or cross-lingual data augmentation [17]. Furthermore, most multilingual ABSA literature focuses on simplified sub-tasks (e.g. ATE or E2E-ABSA), leaving full TASD tuple prediction under-explored in non-English contexts [14].

An alternative paradigm that eliminates task-specific fine-tuning is the deployment of large language models (LLMs). Trained on massive multilingual corpora, instruction-tuned LLMs exhibit strong zero-shot capabilities across diverse NLP benchmarks. However, in complex ABSA tasks, zero-shot LLMs frequently underperform smaller, task-specific fine-tuned models – largely due to the strict multi-variable constraints required by tuple extraction. Moreover, existing LLM evaluations in ABSA focus predominantly on English [15, 27]. Multilingual evaluations remain sparse and frequently rely on legacy LLM architectures [16, 25], trailing behind the rapid evolution of modern open-weight models. Furthermore, the comparative efficacy of dense models against sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures – which route tokens dynamically to a subset of specialized expert subnetworks rather than utilizing all parameters per token to reduce inference compute – remains largely unexplored under zero-shot multilingual constraints. While advanced prompting paradigms like chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning [22] improve complex multi-step reasoning, their efficacy in zero-shot cross-lingual TASD remains minimally studied and often yields inconsistent gains over direct prompting.

In this work, we address these research gaps by presenting a systematic empirical benchmark of modern open-weight LLMs on cross-lingual TASD across three domains and 12 languages, evaluating four distinct prompting paradigms. Our main contributions are: 1) We perform an extensive empirical investigation of zero-shot TASD across 12 languages and three evaluation domains (hotel, laptop, restaurant), evaluating compound sentiment extraction across diverse language families. 2) We systematically evaluate seven modern open-weight instruction-tuned models – spanning dense and MoE architectures up to 35B parameters – across four prompting paradigms (monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine). 3) We demonstrate that dense models systematically outperform MoE models of comparable or larger total scale, attributing this to higher active per-token parameter capacity required for simultaneous multilingual alignment and strict target extraction. 4) We quantitatively trace intermediate pipeline behaviour, showing that initial aspect extraction establishes an unrecoverable recall ceiling, while multi-step decomposition underperforms direct prompting and iterative refinement yields net-negative trade-offs on smaller models without matching monolithic extraction on larger architectures. 5) We conduct fine-grained error and generation overhead analyses identifying recall bottlenecks, schema ambiguity, and token inefficiencies in zero-shot TASD.

papers.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
papers.abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.

papers.intro:
Investigating an instrumentation anomaly in a complex industrial system requires engineers to establish what a measurement represents and how its behaviour relates to the operating conditions of the plant. Numerical readings provide the starting point but diagnosis requires a much broader body of knowledge. Earlier tests and measurements, maintenance records, previous investigation reports, and technical specifications are just some of the pivotal information sources that guide the reasoning process (Kang et al. (2026)). Much of the work then consists of gathering this evidence across several applications and determining how it relates to the anomaly under investigation. In legacy plants that have operated for several decades, this task involves information accumulated through successive equipment modifications and changes in monitoring systems. The resulting layered architecture reflects decades of incremental modernisation that have supported continued operation while making troubleshooting increasingly demanding. Personnel know-how in dealing with these issues is hence an essential part of the plant’s engineering knowledge. Recent energy crises and concerns over security of supply have renewed interest in extending the operating lives of existing nuclear power plants, with several countries reconsidering planned closures (International Energy Agency (2022)). Longer operation increases the importance of transferring accumulated experience to the personnel who will maintain and operate these plants in the coming decades. It is no coincidence that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has identified the preservation and transfer of such knowledge as a continuing concern for nuclear operating organisations (International Atomic Energy Agency (2006)).

The growing use of large language models in engineering is changing how personnel interact with technical information. An engineer can express a question in the language used to discuss a problem with a colleague, while an assistant retrieves the records and performs the operations required to address it. This capability is particularly relevant to diagnostic work, where a question often crosses the boundaries between monitoring data, maintenance history, and technical documentation. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a technical basis for this interaction by supplying an LLM with material retrieved from external sources. Responses can therefore incorporate information maintained independently of model training (Lewis et al. (2020)). Tools using agents extend this approach by selecting operations and using the returned results to guide subsequent steps (Yao et al. (2023)). The investigation can hence develop as evidence is obtained, with each result informing the next task.

Industrial maintenance research has begun to examine these capabilities in settings where operational data and engineering records are maintained in different forms. For instance, MindRAG combines multimodal retrieval with LLM-based agents to support condition-monitoring workflows using measurements, annotations, and maintenance work orders (Löwenmark et al. (2025)). MAKG introduces collaborative agents and knowledge-graph retrieval for equipment-maintenance questions (Lin et al. (2026)). These studies show how the organisation of evidence and the design of the agent workflow influence the assistance provided. The idea of recreating a team of specialists through agents has found fertile ground in many applications, and strategies based on this paradigm are indeed flourishing. In this sense, orchestrated multi-agent architectures organise an investigation around specialised agents whose work is directed by a coordinator. The coordinator interprets the request, assigns tasks, and uses the returned results to guide further work. Magentic-One provides a general implementation of this approach, with an orchestrator responsible for planning, tracking progress, and recovering from unsuccessful steps (Fourney et al. (2024)). In industrial maintenance, Farahani et al. use an LLM planner to coordinate specialised agents across data preparation, analysis, and maintenance recommendation (Farahani et al. (2026)). Gong et al. examine how diagnostic questions can be routed according to their complexity, involving several agents in deliberation when further reasoning is required (Gong et al. (2026)). Schall addresses the integration of monitoring agents into process automation through an orchestrator and a separate validation layer grounded in plant documentation (Schall (2026)).

papers.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking

papers.title: Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse
papers.abstract: Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.

papers.intro:
Honeybee (Apis mellifera) colonies can experience abrupt declines in fitness and may collapse [1, 2], with potentially relevant consequences for biodiversity, agriculture, and food security [3, 4]; in particular, colony losses associated with infestations of the ectoparasitic mite Varroa destructor and the Deformed wing virus, which can make colonies collapse within one or two years [5], are regarded as the biggest threat for the apicultural industry and the major cause of honeybee colony collapse [6]. Anticipating such transitions to collapse could therefore provide valuable opportunities for earlier intervention. The advent of affordable methods to assess features (such as temperature), that can be more or less related to the health status of a honeybee colony [7, 8], opened up new perspectives in this respect. However, an actionable warning must appear sufficiently before collapse and be reliably measurable and interpretable; alerting for an impending collapse using observational data is thus particularly challenging as ecological systems are subject to multiple interacting stressors, environmental variability and seasonal changes.

Early warning signals (EWS) based on Critical Slowing Down (CSD) have been proposed as a model-independent approach to anticipate abrupt regime shifts (RS; see Fig. 1 for an overview) in diverse natural systems [9]. CSD describes the progressive slowing of recovery from perturbations as a system approaches certain critical transitions through points of no return (“tipping points”) [10, 11, 12]. As recovery becomes slower, present dynamics become more correlated with its past and fluctuations persist for longer and accumulate [13], leading to characteristic increases in lag-1 autocorrelation and variance [12, 14]. Increases in other statistical indicators, including skewness, kurtosis, spectral properties and entropy, have also been proposed as EWS [15, 16, 17, 18]. Contrary to typical ecological analysis, that focuses on identifying system-specific stressors such as chemical, parasites and pathogens [19, 20, 5], EWS analysis looks at systems’ variables, parameters and noise [21] and seeks generic statistical patterns that signal proximity to the tipping point. These signals are attractive because they can potentially be extracted from observational time series without requiring a detailed mechanistic model [9]; they do not explain the underlying mechanisms, but aim to give decision-makers time to intervene and prevent undesirable outcomes [22, 23].

Early warning signals (EWS) based on Critical Slowing Down (CSD) have been proposed as a model-independent approach to anticipate abrupt regime shifts (RS; see Fig. 1 for an overview) in diverse natural systems [9]. CSD describes the progressive slowing of recovery from perturbations as a system approaches certain critical transitions through points of no return (“tipping points”) [10, 11, 12]. As recovery becomes slower, present dynamics become more correlated with its past and fluctuations persist for longer and accumulate [13], leading to characteristic increases in lag-1 autocorrelation and variance [12, 14]. Increases in other statistical indicators, including skewness, kurtosis, spectral properties and entropy, have also been proposed as EWS [15, 16, 17, 18]. Contrary to typical ecological analysis, that focuses on identifying system-specific stressors such as chemical, parasites and pathogens [19, 20, 5], EWS analysis looks at systems’ variables, parameters and noise [21] and seeks generic statistical patterns that signal proximity to the tipping point. These signals are attractive because they can potentially be extracted from observational time series without requiring a detailed mechanistic model [9]; they do not explain the underlying mechanisms, but aim to give decision-makers time to intervene and prevent undesirable outcomes [22, 23].

The applicability of such indicators to real natural systems, however, has shown mixed success [25, 29, 30, 31, 32] and is conditional to several factors. First, CSD is expected only for certain types of transitions [18, 24]: those involving mildly perturbed dynamics and slow and gradual parameter changes near low-dimensional bifurcation points ([12], see also Fig. 1). Sudden shocks, rapid parameter changes, or stochastic effects, such as multiplicative or correlated noise, may not yield CSD or display uninterpretable warning signals [33, 34, 35, 36, 37]; nonlinearities and high system dimensionality can also make early detection more challenging [38, 39]. Second, the relevant state variable, or a sufficiently informative proxy, must be observable with adequate temporal resolution and precision. Finite and irregular sampling, measurement noise, seasonal forcing or temporally correlated environmental fluctuations can obscure or mimic the statistical signatures of CSD [29, 40, 41, 42]. Warnings also must be detected within meaningful time frames: in ecology, EWS must emerge before predictable changes such as seasonal or cyclic event, rather than occurring at any point in the future [43]. Third, even when an indicator increases as theoretically expected, this does not necessarily imply useful prediction: similar changes may occur in systems that do not subsequently undergo a transition, generating false warnings [44, 45, 46]. Thus, the presence of a theoretically expected EWS and its practical predictive value are distinct questions. These considerations motivate a distinction between three requirements for applying EWS to ecological monitoring. Dynamical plausibility asks whether the biological system can exhibit a transition for which EWS are theoretically expected; detectability asks whether the relevant dynamical signatures can be recovered from available measurements given their sampling frequency, noise structure, temporal extent and relationship to the underlying state; predictive utility asks whether observing such a signal provides sufficiently specific and timely information about a subsequent transition, beyond what is provided by ordinary changes in system state or environmental conditions. This distinction is important because an indicator can increase as theoretically expected near a transition without necessarily providing sufficiently specific or timely information that the system will undergo that transition [23, 47, 48].

The applicability of such indicators to real natural systems, however, has shown mixed success [25, 29, 30, 31, 32] and is conditional to several factors. First, CSD is expected only for certain types of transitions [18, 24]: those involving mildly perturbed dynamics and slow and gradual parameter changes near low-dimensional bifurcation points ([12], see also Fig. 1). Sudden shocks, rapid parameter changes, or stochastic effects, such as multiplicative or correlated noise, may not yield CSD or display uninterpretable warning signals [33, 34, 35, 36, 37]; nonlinearities and high system dimensionality can also make early detection more challenging [38, 39]. Second, the relevant state variable, or a sufficiently informative proxy, must be observable with adequate temporal resolution and precision. Finite and irregular sampling, measurement noise, seasonal forcing or temporally correlated environmental fluctuations can obscure or mimic the statistical signatures of CSD [29, 40, 41, 42]. Warnings also must be detected within meaningful time frames: in ecology, EWS must emerge before predictable changes such as seasonal or cyclic event, rather than occurring at any point in the future [43]. Third, even when an indicator increases as theoretically expected, this does not necessarily imply useful prediction: similar changes may occur in systems that do not subsequently undergo a transition, generating false warnings [44, 45, 46]. Thus, the presence of a theoretically expected EWS and its practical predictive value are distinct questions. These considerations motivate a distinction between three requirements for applying EWS to ecological monitoring. Dynamical plausibility asks whether the biological system can exhibit a transition for which EWS are theoretically expected; detectability asks whether the relevant dynamical signatures can be recovered from available measurements given their sampling frequency, noise structure, temporal extent and relationship to the underlying state; predictive utility asks whether observing such a signal provides sufficiently specific and timely information about a subsequent transition, beyond what is provided by ordinary changes in system state or environmental conditions. This distinction is important because an indicator can increase as theoretically expected near a transition without necessarily providing sufficiently specific or timely information that the system will undergo that transition [23, 47, 48].

These issues are particularly relevant to honeybee colonies. CSD-based EWS, estimated from frequently sampled time-series of hive temperature, have recently been proposed as a means of assessing colony condition and identifying those potentially at risk of collapse [8]. However, it remains unclear whether the dynamical conditions required for EWS are present across relevant levels of honeybee organization, how the structure of the underlying transition affects the expected signals, and whether the available temperature measurements provide sufficient temporal and statistical information to detect them reliably and with sufficient lead time. In addition, honeybee colonies undergo seasonal changes, and internal temperature may reflect several interacting processes rather than a single measure of colony fitness. Consequently, increases in variance, in autocorrelation or in other typical CSD indicators extracted from hive temperature cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence of an approaching collapse and must be backed up by theoretical interpretation.

papers.title: Recurrent sets and Lyapunov functions: from topological dynamics to weak KAM theory
papers.abstract: The aim of this survey is to clarify the intimate relations between Lyapunov functions and chain recurrent sets. The study of this subject comes from a seminal paper by Conley and has had recent advances by the so-called Weak KAM Theory for homeomorphisms. We provide a survey of the state of the art, presenting recent improvements and connections with the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Finally, in order to illustrate the distinctions between recurrent sets in a non-trivial case as well as their dependence on a parameter, we discuss a compartmental model from mathematical epidemiology and a fast-slow version of a prey-predator model with Allee effect.

One of the basic problems in the qualitative study of a dynamical system is to distinguish recurrent motions from those trajectories which move irreversibly towards simpler asymptotic states. Lyapunov functions provide a natural tool for this purpose: they are non-increasing along trajectories and therefore identify the regions where the dynamics has a preferred direction. Recurrence, on the other hand, describes the possibility for a trajectory to return, exactly or approximately, to a previously visited state. Understanding the relation between these two viewpoints is the main theme of this survey.

Lyapunov functions provide a natural tool for this purpose: they are non-increasing along trajectories and therefore identify the regions where the dynamics has a preferred direction. Recurrence, on the other hand, describes the possibility for a trajectory to return, exactly or approximately, to a previously visited state. Understanding the relation between these two viewpoints is the main theme of this survey.

A fundamental contribution to this problem is due to C.C. Conley. His Fundamental Theorem of Dynamical Systems shows that every continuous flow admits a complete Lyapunov function [14, 13]. This function is constant on the chain recurrent part of the dynamics and strictly decreases along all other trajectories. It therefore decomposes the phase space into two qualitatively different regions: a recurrent region and a gradient-like region. Equivalently, the neutral set of the Lyapunov function, namely the set where no strict decrease occurs, coincides with the chain recurrent set. This point of view gives chain recurrence a distinguished role in topological dynamics and provides a global decomposition which does not depend on the particular metric chosen on the compact phase space.

The resulting strong chain recurrent set may be strictly smaller than the chain recurrent set and, unlike the latter, may depend on the metric. These notions therefore provide increasingly refined ways of separating recurrent behaviour from gradient-like dynamics.

papers.title: Conformally flat Mercator equation and conserved quantities of conformal circles
papers.abstract: We study properties of solutions of the conformal Mercator equation on the conformal sphere. We focus on conformal circles and give two different approaches of finding their conserved quantities from conformal Killing vector fields - variational and tractorial. We find a direct relation between the two sets of quantities.

papers.intro:
Conformal circles are the most degenerate examples of conformal curves on the conformal sphere. There are various approaches to study these curves. Tractor calculus [2, 12] is a well-established theory to study conformal curves by means of conformal curvatures and an invariant tractor Frenet-like frame. Then conformal circles are those curves for which all conformal curvatures degenerate. Other examples of such curves are loxodromes [6], which can be viewed as having the first conformal curvature constant and all other curvatures vanishing [13, 14]. We introduce these invariants and tractors in Sections 2.3 and 2.4.

Tractor calculus [2, 12] is a well-established theory to study conformal curves by means of conformal curvatures and an invariant tractor Frenet-like frame. Then conformal circles are those curves for which all conformal curvatures degenerate. Other examples of such curves are loxodromes [6], which can be viewed as having the first conformal curvature constant and all other curvatures vanishing [13, 14]. We introduce these invariants and tractors in Sections 2.3 and 2.4.

The most traditional approach to studying conformal curves is to view them as solutions to suitable conformally invariant ODEs [1, 6, 5]. For example, conformal circles are defined as solutions of a third-order ODE [16, 1, 15]. In this respect, it is natural to ask whether the equation for a class of conformal curves is variational, and to focus on conserved quantities of the solutions. For conformal circles, it was proved in [10] that the conformal circle equation in any dimension greater than 33 is not variational in the classical sense. However, if one goes beyond the classical variation, there exists in any dimension a variational formulation for the conformal circle equation [1, Section 3], associated with a conformally invariant 33rd order Lagrangian [5].

This conformally invariant Lagrangian leads to examples of variational conserved quantities of conformal circles in the conformally flat case. It is due to the work of [11], where the 44th order Euler-Lagrange equation under classical variation of the Lagrangian was considered. The equation, called the conformal Mercator equation, admits conformal circles as solutions in the conformally flat case [5, Section 5]. Therefore the conserved quantities along solutions of the conformal Mercator equation, found using Noether’s theorem, in [11, Section 3], are examples of conserved quantities along conformal circles that come from variational method. The quantities, which are constructed from generators of conformal symmetries of the Lagrangian, i.e. conformal Killing vector fields, are reviewed in Section 2.2. In addition, we study properties of solutions of the conformal Mercator equation and present a characterization of solutions in terms of tractor quantities in Section 2.5.

Our main result, given in Section 4.1, is the identification of the two sets of conserved quantities, which shows that the conserved quantities from tractors are variational.

papers.title: $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Grid-Forming Control in DC Microgrids
papers.abstract: The growing share of DC-based generation, storage and loads has increased interest in DC microgrids. As a result, DC-bus voltage regulation and stability have become active research topics, with considerable effort directed at improving the transient performance of conventional droop control. Although numerous variants of droop algorithms have been proposed, many rely on increasingly complex control structures with multiple tuning parameters and measurements, thereby increasing the commissioning burden. Moreover, stable interaction with the surrounding microgrid is not guaranteed by design. To address these issues, this paper develops a passivity-constrained $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ synthesis method for the DC-bus voltage controller. The proposed $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ controller emulates the desired grid-forming behavior of the converter by minimizing the $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ error norm between device-level performance indices and their desired values, while additionally enforcing passivity during the optimization. The novel $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ control scheme is benchmarked in the frequency domain against representative droop-based and virtual-DC-machine algorithms from the literature, while experiments on a four-converter DC microgrid corroborate the frequency-domain analysis and validate the practical applicability of the algorithm.
papers.intro:
The rapid growth of distributed energy resources and energy storage systems has increased interest in DC microgrids, since many of these resources operate inherently on DC or are interfaced through DC conversion stages [1]. By eliminating unnecessary AC/DC and DC/AC conversion stages, DC microgrids can reduce conversion losses, converter count, and overall system cost [2, 3]. Moreover, unlike AC microgrids, DC microgrids do not require reactive power management, frequency regulation, or AC synchronization, thus simplifying the overall control architecture [4]. In DC microgrids, the primary grid-forming objective is DC-bus voltage regulation, which plays a role analogous to frequency regulation in AC systems [5].

Moreover, unlike AC microgrids, DC microgrids do not require reactive power management, frequency regulation, or AC synchronization, thus simplifying the overall control architecture [4]. In DC microgrids, the primary grid-forming objective is DC-bus voltage regulation, which plays a role analogous to frequency regulation in AC systems [5].

To regulate DC-bus voltage within prescribed limits while enabling decentralized load sharing, droop control has become a widely adopted solution for parallel source converters, as it allows coordination without communication among units [6, 7]. In this context, two droop-control variants are commonly considered in DC microgrids literature [8, 9, 10]: voltage–current (V–I) droop and current–voltage (I–V) droop. In V–I droop, the measured output current is used to generate the converter voltage reference, whereas in I–V droop, the measured output voltage is used to compute the current reference. More generally, these two signal mappings define the V–I and I–V control architectures, with a proportional droop gain as their conventional realization. The former employs a dual-loop control implementation and therefore requires an additional current measurement, whereas the latter uses a single-loop implementation, thus reducing commissioning effort since only the DC-bus voltage measurement is needed. Nevertheless, neither structure is uniformly superior, and both variants have been extensively studied with the aim of improving their transient performance [11].

Nevertheless, neither structure is uniformly superior, and both variants have been extensively studied with the aim of improving their transient performance [11].

Recent enhancements to conventional droop control can be broadly grouped into three categories: virtual-inertia emulation [12, 13, 14], machine-analogous control [15, 16, 17], and output-impedance shaping [18, 19, 20]. The first augments the droop loop with virtual energy-storage dynamics to enhance the inertial response beyond that provided by the physical DC-link capacitor, whereas the second, inspired by the virtual synchronous machine concept for AC-grid converters [21], reproduces the electromechanical behavior of a DC machine to the same end. Both introduce additional tuning parameters and remain constrained by the converter control bandwidth. Furthermore, machine-analogous control requires a voltage-restoration controller constrained by the emulated machine dynamics. In contrast, output-impedance shaping modifies the converter dynamics directly to obtain resistive-capacitive impedance characteristics that improve both power sharing and transient disturbance rejection. Although effective, output-impedance shaping techniques rely on a first-order droop transfer function imposed by the adopted control structure rather than being freely selectable, which could limit impedance matching in certain cases. Moreover, the physical interaction of the converter with the surrounding network remains nontrivial due to the lack of guaranteed output-impedance passivity [22].

These limitations motivate a design procedure in which the desired converter behavior is specified rather than approached through iterative parameter tuning. For this purpose, ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} synthesis is well suited [23], since competing design objectives are expressed as frequency-domain weighting functions. The synthesis then yields a controller that minimizes the worst-case gain from the disturbance inputs to the weighted performance outputs over the entire frequency range. Moreover, structured and fixed-order formulations [24, 25] allow the controller complexity to be fixed a priori, ensuring the resulting scheme remains implementable and interpretable, while additional stability requirements can be imposed as constraints during synthesis rather than verified a posteriori. In AC systems, these features have motivated extensive use of ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} synthesis for grid-following [26, 27, 28], grid-forming [29], and arbitrary [30] converter control strategies. In DC microgrids, by contrast, its use has remained sparse.

In DC microgrids, by contrast, its use has remained sparse.

Most reported ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} designs in DC microgrids address the dual-active-bridge converter [31, 32, 33, 34], in which mixed-sensitivity weightings tune the loop that controls the phase-shift ratio to handle parameter uncertainty and input- and output-voltage disturbances, rather than to shape the behavior at the converter terminals. Among the few works that address the overall control design of DC microgrid converters using the ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} norm, [35] synthesizes a robust voltage controller for a point-of-load buck converter through the ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} loop-shaping design procedure, combined with a virtual capacitor and conductance that emulate inertia. The synthesis, however, concerns a load-side unit and targets robust stabilization under parametric load uncertainty, thus neglecting the output impedance as a design variable, and the results remain limited to simulation. Conversely, [36] focuses on source-side converters, applying non-smooth ℋ∞\mathcal{H}_{\infty} optimization to tune a fixed-structure droop controller such that the shaped output impedance allows the converter output capacitance to be reduced, and validates the design experimentally on buck- and boost-type half-bridge converters. Although effective, the method is formulated for the V–I control architecture, and thus inherits the need for the additional current measurement and the dual-loop implementation discussed above. Moreover, it treats the output capacitance as a free design variable, whereas in practice this quantity is typically fixed in advance by the converter configuration and its ratings. The relevant question is therefore not how to choose the capacitance, but what terminal behavior can be achieved with a given capacitance. Finally, since only magnitude requirements are imposed on the output impedance, the passivity of the resulting converter behavior is left unaddressed.

papers.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
papers.abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

papers.intro:
Symbolic control methods compute, from a model of a system and a task description, a controller that carries out the task by construction (Belta et al., 2017). This guarantee has a price: the task must be stated in a formal language, such as a temporal logic. Consider a mobile robot that receives the instruction “Visit street 5 while ensuring you never enter parking lot 2”. In linear temporal logic (LTL), it reads “◇​street_5∧□​¬parking_lot_2\Diamond\,\texttt{street\_5}\;\wedge\;\Box\,\neg\,\texttt{parking\_lot\_2}”, where the atomic propositions street_5 and parking_lot_2 hold when the robot is at the corresponding location. Writing such formulas takes expertise that most users do not have and is, together with scalability, one of the two main bottlenecks in applying formal methods (Rozier, 2016). This makes automatic translation of natural language (NL) into a formal language important.

This makes automatic translation of natural language (NL) into a formal language important.

Many recent translators from natural to formal language rely on the most powerful language models available, from Codex to GPT-5, Claude Opus, and the latest Gemini models (Cosler et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Sundarsingh et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Bayat et al., 2026; Newcomb and Ochoa, 2026). Such translators have outperformed earlier translation methods on shared benchmarks (Pan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) and are therefore considered the state of the art (Appendix A provides a literature review). Most of these models are proprietary and behind an API, or too large to be run on a single computer, and only a minority of translators run entirely on local, open-weight models. On a robot, however, the translator must run onboard. New instructions may arrive during operation and require translating and replanning in real time, with limited compute and energy resources, and often without access to the cloud, e.g., for security or reliability reasons (Kehoe et al., 2015; Firoozi et al., 2025).

We ask whether such generative models are needed at all for physical AI applications. Indeed, translators can identify a formula by asking a model a few simple questions; for the running example, four questions suffice (Figure 1). The two “yes” answers select the operators ◇\Diamond (eventually) and □¬\Box\neg (never), and the two choices fill them with street_5 and parking_lot_2. Recently, general-purpose frontier classifiers were introduced with TypeSafe’s model Jev (Almeida, 2026). These recent models read unstructured text together with a question and return a probability for each of its possible answers, instead of generating text. These System-One models are particularly cheap and fast: they answer a question in a single forward pass instead of one per generated token, and the open-weight model Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) has 421 million parameters, orders of magnitude fewer than state-of-the-art LLMs and small enough to run locally on a robot.

We introduce the first family of translators from NL into LTL built on a System-One model rather than on a generative language model. Its questions are designed for each system’s fragment of possible requirements and atomic propositions, so the same architecture serves different control systems (Section 3). By construction, its number of forward passes per instruction is bounded in advance, and every output is a well-formed formula; generative models lack both properties. We compare our translators with 20 off-the-shelf and 5 fine-tuned local language models on three benchmarks, including a new Mine Rover benchmark, measuring accuracy, runtime, and energy consumption on a laptop and a Raspberry Pi 5 (Section 4); to our knowledge, no prior study of translation into temporal logic measures energy. papers.title: Overview and recent progress on the classical Bernoulli free boundary problem
papers.abstract: This survey gives an overview of the Bernoulli or one-phase free boundary problem, with emphasis on recent progress.
papers.intro:
Free boundary problems are variational or PDE models in which part of the boundary of the relevant domain is unknown and must be determined together with the solution. In contrast to boundary value problems posed in a fixed region, here the geometry of the interface is an additional unknown, and the equations typically couple bulk behavior to boundary conditions on the a priori unknown set. This coupling is a natural way to encode “phase” separation: one phase is described by a PDE in an open set, while the complement is constrained by an obstacle/contact condition, and the interface between them is the free boundary.

In contrast to boundary value problems posed in a fixed region, here the geometry of the interface is an additional unknown, and the equations typically couple bulk behavior to boundary conditions on the a priori unknown set. This coupling is a natural way to encode “phase” separation: one phase is described by a PDE in an open set, while the complement is constrained by an obstacle/contact condition, and the interface between them is the free boundary.

In recent years, one of the main drivers of development in the theory of nonlinear elliptic PDE has been its connection with physical models involving phase transitions. This line of study has been of particular mathematical interest because of the interdisciplinarity of its techniques, and because, while it was originally nurtured by theories developed in other areas, the flow of information has by now become genuinely bi-directional. Free boundary problems are a paradigmatic example of such a connection: at the intersection of Geometric Analysis and Partial Differential Equations, their study fully benefits from techniques coming from both areas. Furthermore, especially in the last few years, we have seen how some of the insights obtained in the free boundary setting can be translated back to the aforementioned contexts. For instance, recent proofs of one-dimensional symmetry for bounded stable solutions of the classical Allen–Cahn equation in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} build on ideas developed in the free-boundary setting [16, 53].

The one-phase Alt–Caffarelli free boundary problem is a prototypical model for a variety of interface phenomena. It arises in idealized fluid-mechanical regimes (notably jet flows and cavitational flow), in combustion-related models such as flame propagation, and electrostatics [7, 11, 57, 51, 60]. It also appears naturally in optimal design and shape optimization, where free boundaries encode the geometry selected by competing bulk and boundary effects [1, 49, 50]. From a mathematical point of view, the variational formulation was introduced by Alt and Caffarelli in [1], and the subsequent works of Caffarelli and collaborators developed a far-reaching regularity and structure theory for minimizers and related solution classes [12, 14, 13, 9]. These contributions are among the results recognized by Caffarelli’s Wolf Prize (2012) and Abel Prize (2023). The subject remains very active, with many recent developments in analysis and geometry of free boundaries [22, 45, 26, 31, 20, 29, 36, 27, 55]; see also the monographs [10, 62].

Historically, the problem was motivated by questions from fluid mechanics [1]. In that setting, the Bernoulli condition models interfaces in idealized flow regimes; even in simplified configurations, the geometry of the interface can be remarkably subtle. A classical manifestation of this flexibility is the existence of nontrivial critical points with intricate geometry related to vortex arrays and “hollow vortex” configurations [4]. The one-phase framework also appears in other evolution and combustion models through quasi-static limits or associated free boundaries; for instance, free boundary problems arise naturally in flame propagation models [11].

A different but closely related source is the theory of overdetermined elliptic problems. Prescribing both Dirichlet and Neumann-type boundary data typically forces rigidity (Serrin-type phenomena, where under appropriate assumptions the domain must be a ball), but relaxing the hypotheses (e.g. allowing unbounded or periodic domains, or adopting weaker notions of solution) leads to rich families of “exceptional” domains and reconnects directly with one-phase free boundaries; see, for example, [42, 61, 54] and the references therein.

papers.title: Little Red Dots at Cosmic Noon: Spectroscopy Reveals Declining Abundance but a Non-Evolving Luminosity Function Shape
papers.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are an extremely abundant population of red, compact, broad-line objects primarily found in the early universe. At $5<z<8$, they are at least 10 times more abundant than UV-selected quasars. Yet, how this population evolves towards lower redshift is unclear. In this work, we present our search for LRDs at cosmic noon ($2\lesssim z\lesssim 4$) in nearly 20 deg$^2$ of the Deep/UltraDeep fields of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Combining multiwavelength wide-field imaging surveys from 0.3 to 4.5 $\mu$m, we identify 266 photometric LRD candidates. With spectroscopic follow-up from Keck/NIRES, VLT/X-shooter, and Magellan/FIRE on 24 candidates, we identify a sample of four LRDs with broad H$\alpha$ emission. With the purity of the photometric sample calibrated by spectroscopy, we estimate the number density of LRDs to be approximately $6.8\times10^{-7}$ cMpc$^{-3}$ at $2.10<z<2.55$---this is nearly a factor of 35 decrease from their flat number density evolution at $4\lesssim z\lesssim8$ estimated from JWST spectroscopic surveys. The knee of the LRD optical luminosity function also remains consistently at $M_{5500}\approx-22$ mag across $2<z<5$, below that of quasars. We further speculate that only the abundance of LRDs, but not the shape of their optical luminosity function, evolves with redshift, and the Roman Space Telescope will be able to test this decisively with a substantially larger sample of low-redshift LRDs.

papers.intro:
Little red dots (LRDs; Matthee et al. 48) are arguably one of the most surprising discoveries of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in the early universe. They exhibit compact morphology (re≲200​pcr_{\mathrm{e}}\lesssim 200\,\mathrm{pc}) and a characteristic V-shaped spectral energy distribution (SEDs) consisting of a faint, blue UV component and an extremely red optical continuum [31, 3, 29, 34]. They often show Balmer emission lines broadened to ∼\sim2000 km​s−1\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} [18] suggesting active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. However, they do not resemble typical type-1 AGN in many ways. No strong X-ray emission has been detected in LRDs [4, 79]. Despite their red optical color, they also lack thermal emission from the typical AGN dusty torus in the near-infrared or from obscured star formation activity in the far-infrared [63, 76]. Variability has only been tentatively detected in strongly lensed and multiply imaged LRDs on a 100 year-timescale [81]. Furthermore, some LRDs also show Balmer breaks that are much stronger than what stellar populations alone could produce [17, 35, 15, 44, 69, 52]. This motivates a class of models where the central engine of LRDs is enshrouded in an envelope of dense gas, whose photosphere emits like a blackbody with Teff∼3000T_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim 3000–7000 K resulting in the intrinsic redness and the ubiquitous, strong Balmer break of LRDs [22, 40]. Models of supermassive stars have also been proposed to explain these spectral features given their similarity to stellar objects [13, 42, 53]. Yet, so far, no model has been able to consistently explain the unique combination of features observed in LRDs.

In addition to their peculiar SED shape, the demographics of LRDs is also puzzling. At z≳4z\gtrsim 4, they are at least 10 times more abundant than UV-selected quasars if extrapolating the quasar luminosity function to LRD luminosity—a result that has been consistently confirmed [18, 31, 3, 29]. At z≳4z\gtrsim 4, they also exhibit a sharp luminosity cutoff at M5100​Å∼−23M_{\mathrm{5100\,\AA}}\sim-23 (or L5100​Å∼1044.5​erg​s−1L_{\mathrm{5100\,\AA}}\sim 10^{44.5}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}), which may suggest an upper bound in black hole mass at MBH∼107​M⊙M_{\mathrm{BH}}\sim 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} [45]. However, at cosmic noon, measurements of LRD abundances are more uncertain. On one hand, early LRD searches with JWST photometry found a disappearance of LRDs from z∼5z\sim 5 to z∼2z\sim 2 [29]. Yet, these JWST searches lack robust optical wavelength coverage (although F814W imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope was used). That coverage is required to select for the blue UV continuum of LRDs, an essential component of their V-shaped SEDs; thus, selection effects could account for this disappearance. The abundance measurements of LRDs at cosmic noon estimated using these JWST spectroscopic samples often show differences of up to 1 dex, partially due to small-number statistics.

papers.title: MambaSplit: Severity-Robust and Inference-Efficient Semantic Unmixing of Fluorescence Microscopy Image Data
papers.abstract: The number of structures fluorescence microscopy can image in one sample is limited by how few fluorophores can be separated without significant spectral overlap. Semantic unmixing circumvents this limit by imaging two structures in one fluorescent channel and computationally separating the superimposed image into one image per structure. Because pixels rarely identify their structure, unmixing requires both local and long-range spatial context. The relative brightness of the two structures is unknown and can be very uneven, so predictions must remain accurate across mixing severities, from balanced mixtures to ones where a structure is barely visible. Existing methods either process small image patches or add context through auxiliary pathways that slow inference on large images. Unmixing is difficult because single pixels do not give away which structures contributed to the measured intensity. Instead, this must be decided by the surrounding image content. How much context is needed to make the best prediction is unknown a priori, but larger context has been shown to help [4]. At the same time, the predicted channels must preserve thin filaments, sharp boundaries and other fine detail. Unmixing therefore requires both local and long-range spatial context, on microscopy images that are often many megapixels in size.

papers.title: Little Red Dots at Cosmic Noon: Spectroscopic Identification and Broad-Line Properties
papers.abstract: We present Keck/NIRES, VLT/X-shooter, and Magellan/FIRE spectroscopic follow-up observations of photometrically selected Little Red Dot (LRD) candidates targeting H$\alpha$ at $2<z<3$. The apparent decline of LRDs at cosmic noon raises the question whether they retain the spectra of the high-redshift population. From a parent sample of 266 unresolved sources with V-shaped broadband SEDs, identified in 19.9\,deg$^2$ of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program Deep/UltraDeep fields, we observe 24 and confirm broad H$\alpha$ in 6. The remaining 18 candidates show no broad H$\alpha$. Four have Ly$\alpha$ redshifts, which place H$\alpha$ outside our coverage for two. The other 14 have only photometric redshifts, so their H$\alpha$ coverage is uncertain; they may have incorrect photometric redshifts, broad H$\alpha$ fainter than $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}\approx3\times10^{42}$ erg s$^{-1}$, or not be LRDs. All six broad H$\alpha$ lines are best fit by exponential profiles, with FWHM $\approx 950$--$2150$ km s$^{-1}$. Three show Balmer absorption, all show Balmer decrements above Case B ($H\alpha/H\beta \approx 8$--$34$, though H$\beta$ is not detected), and four have V-shaped SEDs consistent with JWST-selected LRD samples. Archival \textit{JWST}/NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec spectroscopy independently confirm one source as an LRD. One of the six is X-ray detected at a luminosity typical of ordinary AGN and is better described as a broad-line AGN. Only one of seven dust-reddened F2M quasars and two of 38 heavily reddened quasars at $2<z<3$ meet typical JWST V-shape criteria. Four of the six sources with broad H$\alpha$ ($67$\%) resemble JWST-selected LRDs, showing that ground-based photometric selection and spectroscopy can identify LRDs.

papers.intro:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of compact, red objects that went previously undetected, now known as Little Red Dots (LRDs; 56, 71, 50). They are often unresolved in JWST imaging (re≈50r_{e}\approx 50–300300 pc: 51, 27) and display a characteristic “V”-shaped spectral energy distribution (SED) which is blue in the rest-frame UV and red in the rest-frame optical [51, e.g.,]. They are found predominantly at 4<z<84<z<8 [3, 50] where they outnumber comparably luminous UV-selected quasars by at least 1 dex [51, e.g.,] and may account for at least a few percent of galaxies at comparable redshift and stellar mass [78].

Most LRDs show broad Balmer emission [31, 16, 84], with widths and luminosities exceeding what star formation can plausibly produce [71, 41, 17], suggesting active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. However, LRDs are undetected in the deepest Chandra exposures [99, 69, 82], and show little to no variability [54, 101, 63]. Their Balmer lines frequently show absorption, with non-Gaussian profiles (Lorentzian, exponential) and wings [47, 53, 84, 67, 72], alongside Balmer decrements far above expectation from Case B recombination [23, 41, 93] that cannot be explained by standard dust extinction, although even that has been challenged [76]. Together these signatures have been interpreted as an accretion source embedded in dense gas [41, 17, 75], a configuration rare among typical AGN. Whether that gas fully encloses the source, or is seen only along high-inclination sightlines, remains open [68, 6].

Although they are extremely abundant at high redshift, LRDs seem to disappear towards later cosmic epochs [50]. Yet, how fast this abundance decline occurs is similarly contested [24, 49, 64, 65]. The redshift evolution of LRDs can give clues to the conditions under which LRDs form, and it needs to be pinned down to identify physical drivers that distinguish LRDs from typical AGN. Cosmic noon provides a useful test of the connection between LRDs and the broader accreting black hole population. Ordinary quasar activity is abundant at this epoch, whereas LRDs are quite rare. Determining whether cosmic-noon candidates exhibit the characteristic spectral properties of JWST-selected LRDs will reveal whether the physical conditions giving rise to these properties persist at later cosmic epochs. These sources are also accessible to ground-based facilities: at 2<z<32<z<3, Hα\alpha falls in the near-infrared, and wide-field imaging samples the V-shaped SED over areas far larger than current JWST surveys. Follow-up ground-based spectroscopy can reach greater resolution than JWST offers, resolving emission-line profiles and recovering Balmer absorption that is readily missed at low resolution [21, 94]. Comparisons with dust-reddened quasars, whose continuum colors sometimes overlap those of LRDs [29, 90], can assess contamination and test whether the populations share similar spectral properties and physical conditions.

papers.title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator
papers.abstract:
To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline.
  We release the complete code and datasets: https://github.com/tum-ai/toumaii-gen and https://huggingface.co/collections/tum-ai/toumaii-generated-datasets

papers.intro:
Enterprise AI is shifting from language models used as passive answer generators to agents that autonomously execute multi-step tasks on existing business systems [2, 12]. To connect to these systems, agents rely on tool-calls to interact with developer tools, query databases, or read and process documents. Reliable tool use requires models to produce schema-conformant arguments and correct function names, and to maintain context across multiple interaction turns. Benchmarks such as the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [15] and τ2\tau^{2}-bench [3] probe these increasingly complex scenarios, which are especially challenging for the small language models favoured in enterprise settings for cost, latency, and local deployment. The importance of reliable tool-calling has sparked broad interest in tool-calling training data: large corpora of tool-call demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) [14], and models trained on them, are now available. Gorilla [16] targets API hallucination, ToolLLM [18] covers real multi-step endpoints, APIGen [11] adds execution-level verification, xLAM [23] and Hammer [9] train function-calling model families on such corpora, ToolACE [10] increases API diversity, and Toucan [22] grounds trajectories in live MCP servers.

papers.title: 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection via Visual Alignment and Generative Captions
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals. These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

papers.intro:
Accurate 3D object detection is foundational for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving. Current state-of-the-art 3D detectors, which rely on LiDAR point clouds [1, 2] and multi-view images [3, 4], have achieved remarkable performance on challenging benchmarks [5, 6]. However, these methods are fundamentally limited: they can only identify and localize objects that belong to a pre-defined set of categories seen during training. In real-world environments, systems constantly encounter novel objects and long-tail concepts, rendering closed-set detectors unreliable. When a closed-set detector fails to identify a novel obstacle such as debris or an unconventional vehicle, it poses a direct threat to downstream motion planning and collision avoidance systems.

Accurate 3D object detection is foundational for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving. Current state-of-the-art 3D detectors, which rely on LiDAR point clouds [1, 2] and multi-view images [3, 4], have achieved remarkable performance on challenging benchmarks [5, 6]. However, these methods are fundamentally limited: they can only identify and localize objects that belong to a pre-defined set of categories seen during training. In real-world environments, systems constantly encounter novel objects and long-tail concepts, rendering closed-set detectors unreliable. When a closed-set detector fails to identify a novel obstacle such as debris or an unconventional vehicle, it poses a direct threat to downstream motion planning and collision avoidance systems.

The emerging field of open-vocabulary 3D object detection addresses this limitation by aiming to detect arbitrary objects described by natural language. To achieve this open-set capability, prevailing approaches typically rely on knowledge distillation from large-scale pre-trained 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [7]. These methods transfer the VLM’s rich semantic features to the 3D detector, either by projecting 2D features to 3D points/voxels for alignment [8], or by using 2D open-vocabulary detections [9, 10] as pseudo-labels for 3D localization [11, 12]. This enables the 3D model to predict an embedding vector that can be compared against arbitrary text queries (e.g., object names) at inference time.

papers.title: Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions
papers.abstract: The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

papers.title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
papers.abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $\Theta(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.
