Observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST; Gardner et al. (2023)) have discovered a considerable population of SMBHs at 5≲z≲115\lesssim z\lesssim 11 (Schneider et al. 2023; Natarajan et al. 2024; Eilers et al. 2023; Harikane 2025), as well as young massive clusters (YMCs) that could eventually form IMBHs through runaway collisions (Schleicher et al. 2026). The presence of such SMBHs challenges the light seed scenario, since Pop III remnants would require sustained super-Eddington accretion to grow to these masses (Kiyuna 2026). In contrast, heavy seeds can reach SMBH masses through Eddington-limited accretion (Jeon et al. 2025; Silk et al. 2024). Recent observations of extremely red, point-like objects, known as little red dots (LRDs), may help elucidate the origins of early SMBHs, as they could represent an intermediate population between seeds and the observed SMBHs (Vaida and Farber 2026). Observations of LRDs span a redshift range of 3≲z≲103\lesssim z\lesssim 10. LRDs were initially identified as extremely red galaxies (Endsley et al. 2023; Labbé et al. 2023). There is no consensus on their nature. Evidence supporting an AGN interpretation includes the detection of high-ionization coronal lines, such as [FeX], and broad Hα\alpha emission (Kocevski et al. 2023; Furtak et al. 2024). Although many LRDs are radio and X-ray quiet, this could be expected from super-Eddington accretion models, where thick discs suppress high-energy emission (Secunda et al. 2026). From a stellar interpretation, LRDs are thought to be dusty, intensely star-forming galaxies (Escala et al. 2025; Kritos and Silk 2026; Rantala 2026). If this is the case, these objects would be among the densest stellar systems ever observed, with core densities as high as ∼108​M⊙\sim 10^{8}\penalty\ M_{\odot} pc-3, largely exceeding the threshold for runaway collisions, and may include tidal disruption events (TDEs) in some models (Bellovary 2025).

papers.title: Hints of planet formation in progress around DR Tau from observations with LBT SHARK-NIR and SHARK-VIS
papers.abstract: Protoplanetary disks are the primary sites of planet formation. However, the direct imaging of protoplanets still embedded within their parental disks remains a significant challenge, with only a small number of confirmed detections to date and several candidates awaiting verification. We search for embedded planets in the protoplanetary disk of the young star DRTau by targeting accretion signatures from forming sub-stellar objects. Using narrow-band imaging, we observe both visible Halpha and near-infrared Paschen-beta (Pabeta) emission to identify actively accreting companions. To this end, we performed high-contrast observations of DRTau using the SHARK-VIS (0.40-0.95 micron) and SHARK-NIR (0.96-1.70 micron) imagers at the LBT. The study uses a combination of narrow-band filters to isolate accretion signatures and broad-band filters for multi-wavelength characterization in both the visible and near-infrared. Our observations recover the primary disk structures previously identified in the literature, albeit at low signal-to-noise (S/N). We identify two compact features with S/N between 6 and 13 in both narrow- and broad-band filters. The first, an elongated structure, matches previous SPHERE detections, while the second, more compact feature, is now confirmed despite its low S/N in earlier datasets. A comparison over a seven-year baseline confirms the stability of both structures. Their observed orbital motion is consistent with Keplerian rotation, potentially suggesting the presence of an undetected planetary-mass companion (few MJup) at the location of the second feature. However, our analysis does not confirm Halpha or Pabeta emission originating from localized accretion. Instead, we conclude that the observed flux is likely stellar light reflected by dust at these locations and discuss alternative mechanisms that could account for such detections.

papers.intro:
Protoplanetary disks surrounding stars with ages up to a few Myr are considered the natal environment for planets (Chen et al. 2012; Marshall et al. 2014, see e.g.,). Observations in the visible, in the near-infrared (NIR), in the mid-infrared (MIR) and at millimeter wavelengths have allowed the detection of different types of sub-structures in the protoplanetary disks including gaps and rings (Feldt et al. 2017; Fedele et al. 2018; Isella et al. 2018; Leiendecker et al. 2022; Miley et al. 2024; Lovell et al. 2025, e.g.,), cavities (Avenhaus et al. 2017; van der Plas et al. 2017a; van der Plas et al. 2017b; Norfolk et al. 2021, e.g.,), and spirals (Boccaletti et al. 2020; Brown-Sevilla et al. 2021; Mesa et al. 2022; Ginski et al. 2025, e.g.,). More than one single mechanism can be implied in the formation and the evolution of such structures and, moreover, structures in different disks can be explained with different mechanism. However, one of the most accepted scenario to explain such structures is that they are caused by the interactions between the disk and unseen companions embedded in the disk itself. papers.title: Boundary gradient asymptotics for superquadratic viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equations via optimal control
papers.abstract:
We study the boundary behavior of the maximal solution of \[
  -\Delta u + |\nabla u|^{p} + \lambda u = f \] on arbitrary bounded $C^{2}$ domains, where $p > 2$ and $\lambda > 0$. For bounded state-dependent terms $f$, we resolve a conjecture of Lasry and Lions by establishing sharp boundary gradient asymptotics without geometric restrictions on the domain. Previously, such asymptotics were established only for certain classes of domains with additional restrictions on $p$ and $f$. We also extend the analysis to state-dependent terms that may be singular near the boundary and obtain sharp boundary profiles and gradient asymptotics.
  Our approach relies on stochastic optimal control and boundary blow-up analysis. Dynamic programming estimates and comparisons of near-optimal trajectories establish tangential invariance of boundary blow-up limits, leading to the identification of one-dimensional profiles and the asymptotic formulas. For the associated state-constrained control problem, we establish sharp asymptotics for the minimizing feedback and deduce its admissibility and optimality, with corresponding results for the ergodic problem.

papers.title: Federated KPI Aggregation with Local Privacy Constraints and Coordinated OLAP Roll-Ups
papers.abstract: Cross-organizational KPI analysis can require aggregated results from independently administered data warehouses without centralizing detailed records. To limit disclosure from small local groups, a site can require a minimum number of contributing records before releasing a KPI value for a group. If each site applies this rule independently, different local contributions may be suppressed and the combined KPI can become incomplete. This paper investigates whether OLAP granularity can be coordinated before local query results are released so that all sites satisfy their local minimum-cohort rules and contribute at the same analytical level. The proposed method selects the least-generalized common roll-up accepted by every site. Site agents coordinate current capabilities and approved local execution across independently administered sites, with privacy checks and aggregate computation remaining deterministic local functions. In a four-site prototype, coordinated roll-up retained all contributions and reproduced the corresponding centralized result, compared with 78.3% retained under independent suppression. A capability-change experiment showed fewer candidate checks and replies and no unsupported requests when current site-agent state was used. The results demonstrate the feasibility of federated KPI aggregation under local privacy constraints through coordinated granularity selection and agent-based coordination.

papers.title: SciPIC-lite: A flexible Halo Occupation Distribution pipeline aimed at clustering observables
papers.abstract: The Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework provides a flexible approach to modelling the galaxy--halo connection in cosmological simulations, encoding the statistical relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter haloes. We present SciPIC-lite, a new public Python library for fast, flexible, and user-friendly HOD modelling, designed to populate dark matter haloes extracted from cosmological simulations with galaxies and to provide a comprehensive suite of tools for their subsequent analysis. The library is built around a modular and extensible codebase that incorporates the full breadth of the HOD framework, from the core occupation functions to a wide range of physically motivated extensions, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of galaxy clustering applications. We validate and characterise the performance of SciPIC-lite by developing a pipeline to fit the two-point correlation functions of H$\alpha$-selected galaxies from the Flagship~2 simulation across multiple redshift bins. To this end, we populate AbacusSummit dark matter haloes with galaxies according to a variety of HOD parametrisations. We assess the robustness of the fits with respect to the choice of HOD parametrisation and the inclusion of physically motivated extensions, including assembly bias, velocity bias, conformity, and halo profile rescaling. The best-fit models are found to be remarkably robust across different HOD parametrisations and fitting configurations, with reduced $\chi^2$ values clustering tightly around a common value regardless of the model adopted. We exploit these results to generate new AbacusSummit-based galaxy mocks that accurately reproduce the clustering properties of the Flagship~2 H$\alpha$ galaxy population.

papers.intro:
The construction of realistic galaxy mock catalogues from high-resolution cosmological simulations plays a central role in the study of galaxy clustering and the large-scale structure of the Universe. Such mocks are indispensable for testing the range of scales over which theoretical models remain valid (Maus et al., 2025b; Maus et al., 2025a; Nishimichi et al., 2020; Brieden et al., 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Pezzotta et al., 2024; Euclid Collaboration: Pardede et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Guidi et al., 2026), and for gaining deeper insight into the physical processes that govern galaxy formation and evolution (Contreras et al., 2026; Jiménez et al., 2019; Hadzhiyska et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2026). In addition, they provide a controlled framework for quantifying systematic and modelling uncertainties (Euclid Collaboration: Monaco et al., 2026), validating analysis pipelines, and generating reliable covariance matrices for large-scale structure observables (Euclid Collaboration: Monaco et al., 2025; Lippich et al., 2019; Blot et al., 2019).

The construction of realistic galaxy mock catalogues from high-resolution cosmological simulations plays a central role in the study of galaxy clustering and the large-scale structure of the Universe. Such mocks are indispensable for testing the range of scales over which theoretical models remain valid (Maus et al., 2025b; Maus et al., 2025a; Nishimichi et al., 2020; Brieden et al., 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Pezzotta et al., 2024; Euclid Collaboration: Pardede et al., 2026; Euclid Collaboration: Guidi et al., 2026), and for gaining deeper insight into the physical processes that govern galaxy formation and evolution (Contreras et al., 2026; Jiménez et al., 2019; Hadzhiyska et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2026). In addition, they provide a controlled framework for quantifying systematic and modelling uncertainties (Euclid Collaboration: Monaco et al., 2026), validating analysis pipelines, and generating reliable covariance matrices for large-scale structure observables (Euclid Collaboration: Monaco et al., 2025; Lippich et al., 2019; Blot et al., 2019).

A key ingredient of this process is the so-called galaxy-halo connection, i.e. the relationship between the properties of dark matter haloes and the galaxies that they host. There exist several approaches to studying the galaxy-halo connection (Wechsler and Tinker, 2018, see e.g.); the simplest of these, referred to as Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework, consists of placing galaxies directly into dark matter haloes following empirical relations (Peacock and Smith, 2000; Berlind and Weinberg, 2002; Berlind et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2005, e.g.). In its standard form, the HOD framework populates each halo with a number of galaxies drawn from an occupation function that depends solely on halo mass. Extensions of the basic model can reproduce effects predicted by more detailed approaches, such as sub-halo abundance matching (Conroy et al., 2006; Contreras et al., 2022, e.g.), semi-analytic models (Croton et al., 2016; Behroozi et al., 2019, SAM; e.g.) and hydrodynamical simulations. These include assembly bias, i.e. a dependence of galaxy occupation on halo properties beyond mass, such as formation history, concentration or environment (Chaves-Montero et al., 2016, e.g.). Another example is galactic conformity, i.e. correlated properties between central and satellite galaxies (Yuan et al., 2025; Hadzhiyska et al., 2023b, e.g.). A further one is velocity bias, i.e. a difference between galaxy velocities and those of the underlying dark matter (Guo et al., 2015, e.g.).

A key ingredient of this process is the so-called galaxy-halo connection, i.e. the relationship between the properties of dark matter haloes and the galaxies that they host. There exist several approaches to studying the galaxy-halo connection (Wechsler and Tinker, 2018, see e.g.); the simplest of these, referred to as Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework, consists of placing galaxies directly into dark matter haloes following empirical relations (Peacock and Smith, 2000; Berlind and Weinberg, 2002; Berlind et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2005, e.g.). In its standard form, the HOD framework populates each halo with a number of galaxies drawn from an occupation function that depends solely on halo mass. Extensions of the basic model can reproduce effects predicted by more detailed approaches, such as sub-halo abundance matching (Conroy et al., 2006; Contreras et al., 2022, e.g.), semi-analytic models (Croton et al., 2016; Behroozi et al., 2019, SAM; e.g.) and hydrodynamical simulations. These include assembly bias, i.e. a dependence of galaxy occupation on halo properties beyond mass, such as formation history, concentration or environment (Chaves-Montero et al., 2016, e.g.). Another example is galactic conformity, i.e. correlated properties between central and satellite galaxies (Yuan et al., 2025; Hadzhiyska et al., 2023b, e.g.). A further one is velocity bias, i.e. a difference between galaxy velocities and those of the underlying dark matter (Guo et al., 2015, e.g.).

In the last two decades, the HOD framework has been widely used to characterise the galaxy-halo connection observed by different surveys, from 2dF (Magliocchetti and Porciani, 2003) and SDSS (Zehavi et al., 2011) to VIPERS (de la Torre et al., 2013) and DESI (Rocher et al., 2023b; Yuan et al., 2024). Accurately modelling the HOD of a survey population is crucial for the scientific exploitation of its data: a detailed understanding of the galaxy sample is required to build realistic mock catalogues, which are essential to estimate the statistical and systematic error budgets. Moreover, it can provide informative priors on large-scale models, which can tighten the resulting cosmological constraints (Zhang et al., 2025). The characterisation is usually performed by populating dark matter haloes from high-resolution cosmological simulations and fitting the resulting summary statistics, typically two-point correlation functions (2PCF), to the observed data. Each evaluation of the model is computationally expensive, so that fast methods to populate haloes are required, within pipelines flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of models.

In this work, we present SciPIC-lite, a newly developed Python library designed for the fast and flexible modelling of galaxy populations through the HOD framework, with a particular focus on galaxy clustering applications. SciPIC-lite is inspired by SciPIC (Carretero et al., 2017; Euclid Collaboration: Gonzalez et al., 2026), and inherits its core philosophy while offering a significantly more flexible implementation. SciPIC was the code employed to generate the Flagship 2 galaxy mock (Euclid Collaboration: Castander et al., 2025), designed to provide a realistic representation of the galaxy population expected from the Euclid survey (Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al., 2025). SciPIC-lite supports a wide variety of HOD parametrisations for both central and satellite galaxies, making it suitable in principle for any galaxy population. It also natively includes several physically motivated extensions of the standard HOD paradigm. Being primarily designed for galaxy clustering applications, SciPIC-lite implements a comprehensive set of functions to measure and model the key statistical quantities involved in such analyses, including halo and galaxy mass functions, 2PCFs and power spectra. The library is designed with extensibility in mind: support for a broad range of galaxy populations is built-in, and new user-defined HOD functions can be integrated into the existing pipeline, making SciPIC-lite a versatile tool for the wider galaxy clustering community. SciPIC-lite will be made publicly available upon publication of this work11 1 https://github.com/GabrieleParimbelli/scipiclite. The code is accompanied by worked examples and a suite of notebooks illustrating how to generate simple HOD-based galaxy mocks and set up minimisation pipelines.

A widely used alternative is AbacusHOD (Yuan et al., 2022a), a highly optimised HOD framework developed for the AbacusSummit simulations (Maksimova et al., 2021). While efficient, it is mostly tailored to the Abacus code data products, which limits its portability to other NN-body simulations. Moreover, implementing new occupation functions requires modifying the source code, and, at the time of writing, light-cone outputs are not supported. In contrast, SciPIC-lite is designed to be simulation-agnostic: it operates on generic halo catalogues, allows user-defined HOD shapes and satellite profiles without modifying the code, and supports both snapshots and light cones, making it a flexible and portable tool for a broad range of applications.

papers.title: A periodic Ambrosetti-Prodi problem with sign-changing nonlinearities
papers.abstract: We study the periodic solutions of the second-order equation \begin{equation*} u''+f(t,u)=s, \end{equation*} where $s\in\mathbb{R}$ is a parameter and $f$ is periodic in the time variable and satisfies the one-sided sublinear growth condition \begin{equation*} f(t,x)\geq a(t)|x|^p+b(t), \qquad 0<p<1, \end{equation*} for some $a,b\in L^1([0,T])$ with $\int_0^T a(t)\,\mathrm{d}t>0$. We establish an Ambrosetti--Prodi type theorem: there exists a threshold $s_0\in\mathbb{R}$ such that the equation has zero periodic solutions for $s<s_0$, at least one for $s=s_0$, and at least two for $s>s_0$. The main novelty of our result is the removal of the non-negativity assumption on the weight $a$, which is replaced by the weaker requirement of a positive mean value, thus allowing for sign-changing nonlinearities.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
papers.abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

Each pixel of an event camera fires independently the moment its brightness changes, producing a sparse stream with microsecond temporal resolution and high dynamic range that is well suited to depth estimation in high-speed and low-light regimes [5]. In this setting, scene structure and camera motion are coupled prediction problems: each event must be assigned a depth, and the continuous camera motion that carries the same 3D point across the sensor must be known at each event’s own timestamp.

In this setting, scene structure and camera motion are coupled prediction problems: each event must be assigned a depth, and the continuous camera motion that carries the same 3D point across the sensor must be known at each event’s own timestamp.

The difficulty is that event streams are irregular in time and sparse in space, whereas dense metric depth is usually available only at image timestamps. Assigning the same endpoint depth map to every event ignores the fact that the camera and the visible geometry evolve within the interval. Most learning pipelines respond to this mismatch by converting events into event frames, voxel grids, or recurrent frame surrogates before estimating geometry [6, 18, 12, 7, 13]. This suits standard backbones but discards the fine-grained timing that is the main advantage of event sensing.

We instead derive supervision from the geometry of the measurements themselves. A predicted depth and the camera motion together allow each event to be back-projected at its own timestamp and transported to a common instant. If both are correct, events generated by the same edge arrive at the same place with consistent timestamps. If either is wrong, the events smear across the image. Sharpness after motion compensation is therefore a measure of geometric quality that requires no depth label.

Our method (Figure 1) learns per-event depth from motion-compensated event alignment using a local-global event-state encoder trained by dual-anchor alignment losses. A selective state-space model captures temporal context across the time-ordered events of each window, and a multi-scale local branch captures image-plane neighbourhoods. An occlusion-aware renderer then combines the per-event depths into a target-time map while preserving event-time geometry and gradients to the contributing depths. It anchors each pixel on its most recent observations and combines samples through smooth weights, allowing the rendered map to enter the training objective. A camera-motion head predicts each window’s motion, which is also estimated by aligning its events under the predicted depths.

papers.title: From Pilots to Position: Experimental Near-Field Localization for ISAC
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables wireless systems to reuse communication signals for environmental sensing, potentially reducing the need for dedicated sensing resources. However, the achievable localization accuracy of communication-centric waveforms under practical hardware constraints remains an important challenge. In this paper, we experimentally investigate near-field target localization using OFDM pilot signals in a distributed communication system. We consider both coherent and noncoherent localization approaches, exploiting multistatic propagation delays and time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) information extracted from pilot-based channel estimates. A hardware setup comprising two transmitters and four receivers was developed and configured to operate at 3.4 GHz with 198 MHz occupied bandwidth to evaluate localization performance under realistic propagation and synchronization conditions. Experimental results across 16 static target positions demonstrate mean localization errors of 19.8 cm and 18.8 cm for coherent backprojection and noncoherent delay-TDOA fusion, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of occupied bandwidth on localization accuracy of the two proposed algorithms. These findings provide experimental insights into the capabilities and practical limitations of OFDM pilot-based sensing, supporting resource-efficient localization in future ISAC systems.

papers.intro:
Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is emerging as a key capability of future wireless networks, enabling communication infrastructure to provide environmental awareness alongside conventional data transmission. By sharing spectrum, hardware, and signal resources, ISAC offers the potential to support sensing functionalities without deploying dedicated radar systems [1]. Among its applications, passive target localization is particularly attractive for indoor automation, robotics, and intelligent wireless environments, where the positions of objects without active communication capabilities need to be determined. In particular, known pilot symbols allow the extraction of channel frequency responses (CFRs), from which target-induced propagation changes can be exploited for localization. This creates opportunities to extend the functionality of communication signals toward environmental sensing [1]. Despite this potential, accurate near-field indoor localization using communication waveforms remains challenging due to their finite bandwidth and practical hardware constraints, where target reflections often overlap with direct-path components and environmental multipath. Nevertheless, spatially separated transmitters and receivers observe different bistatic propagation paths, providing complementary geometric constraints on the target position. By combining these spatial observations, localization can exploit information beyond the delay resolution of any individual link. Therefore, understanding how frequency-domain information and spatial diversity jointly contribute to localization performance is essential for practical ISAC system design [2].

Recent research has extensively investigated the theoretical foundations of near-field sensing and localization. Near-field ISAC frameworks have explored joint distance and angle estimation through Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) analysis and beamforming optimization [3], while cooperative and multistatic localization schemes using 5G NR OFDM signals and communication preambles have further explored TDOA, spatial backprojection, and fusion of measurements across multiple access points, with performance primarily assessed through numerical simulations [4, 5]. Experimental ISAC prototypes have also demonstrated promising localization capabilities under different hardware and signal configurations. Near-field coherent sensing using an OFDM massive-MIMO communication testbed has achieved centimeter-level localization accuracy despite an occupied bandwidth of only 18 MHz, highlighting the substantial spatial information provided by large antenna arrays [2, 6]. More recently, a bistatic MIMO-OFDM prototype operating at 28 GHz with 1.92 GHz bandwidth has demonstrated real-time target localization and tracking [7]. Meanwhile, hardware measurements have shown that phase inconsistencies across OFDM channels and antennas can severely degrade localization accuracy, motivating dedicated calibration procedures for coherent processing [8]. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the feasibility of OFDM-based sensing, but also highlight the dependence of localization performance on available bandwidth, spatial aperture, and hardware coherence. Comparatively less experimental evidence is available on the accuracy achievable with a small number of distributed sensing channels and moderate occupied bandwidth.

papers.title: Transition processes of camphor particle motion in a three-chamber system
papers.abstract: The motion of a camphor particle in a chamber with three circular regions was investigated through experiments and numerical simulations. Transitions between circular regions were analyzed as discrete stochastic processes. Experiments revealed the probabilistic transition of the camphor particle between regions, suggesting a tendency for the particle to undergo transitions in the same direction when transitions occur after a short dwell time. Numerical simulations using a stochastic mathematical model, where the geometry of the experimental system was incorporated through the boundary conditions, reproduced the tendency of transition of the camphor particle between three regions.

papers.intro:
In non-equilibrium systems, particles can continuously move while gaining and dissipating energy; this behavior is known as self-propelled motion [42, 49, 39, 3]. Self-propelled motion has attracted interest because it is one of the fundamental characteristics of living organisms [27, 21, 48, 1]. However, studying self-propelled motion in biological systems from a physical perspective is challenging due to environmental fluctuations, inter-individual variability, and the complexity of underlying physiological processes. To address these challenges, physico-chemical systems such as Janus particles [50] and active droplets [28, 29] have been widely adopted, as they are less complex and more controllable than living organisms, and the mechanisms of their self-propelled motion can be described by mathematical models constructed based on physics and chemistry.

Achieving control over self-propelled motion may lead to a wide range of applications, such as cargo transport [2, 45, 47], in vivo drug delivery [41], artificial motors [15] and logic gates [12]. Among the various methods for controlling self-propelled motion, the use of boundary geometry provides one potential approach, as self-propelled motion is generally influenced by the boundary shape [52, 8, 37]. For instance, in biological systems, cells migrate through narrow spaces formed by surrounding tissue and the extracellular matrix [7, 40, 11]. As a simplified system for studying self-propelled motion in confined geometries, a two-state system consisting of two regions connected by a narrow bridge has been proposed [6, 10, 5, 51, 43]. This system serves as a model for migration under confined environments encountered by cells in physiological settings, where they migrate through narrow channels or constrictions. While the two-state system provides an important minimal framework, extending the system to three states can reveal behaviors that do not appear in the two-state system. That is to say, in a three-state system, a particle can select the direction of the transition between regions, allowing for several possible transition modes: transition to the other two regions with an equal probability, transition with a biased probability, or back-and-forth transition between two regions. This system provides a simple example of a system with several possible transition modes.

As a model of physico-chemical self-propulsion, we have investigated the motion of a camphor particle in confined geometries [37, 25, 26, 22]. Nakata and coauthors investigated a camphor scraping moving between two connected chambers and revealed that its residence in each chamber generates an asymmetric camphor concentration field, which induces its motion toward the other chamber through a surface tension gradient [33]. Motivated by this study, we consider a three-state system using a camphor particle. This approach offers a simple model system that is easy to realize both in experiments and in numerical simulations. A camphor particle on a water surface is a well-known example of a self-propelled particle interacting through a concentration field [36, 34, 30] as a model system for autodiffusiophoretic motion, which is commonly observed in living organisms [31, 4]. When a camphor particle is placed on water, camphor molecules dissolve from the particle into the surrounding fluid, reducing the surface tension. Fluctuations induce spontaneous symmetry breaking [13, 25, 26], which generates a surface tension gradient that drives the particle. papers.title: From data pencils to image representations of continuous-time LTI systems
papers.abstract: The continuous-time fundamental lemma describes the set of all trajectories of a linear time-invariant system by a Gramian matrix built from measured input--output data and their derivatives. The jet of a trajectory is represented as the Gramian applied to a nonunique parameter satisfying a differential-algebraic equation. We determine the complete Kronecker structure of the associated data pencil for multiple-input multiple-output systems. This enables the construction of a polynomial image representation of the input--output behavior directly from the data. The resulting image matrix has column degrees equal to the controllability indices, and its latent variable is free and serves as a flat output of the system. The computation relies on an orthogonal staircase reduction followed by basis reconstruction using polynomial kernels. We also propose a structure-preserving preconditioning of the Gramian to improve its condition number and facilitate rank decisions in the reduction. We illustrate our approach on a chain of mass-spring-damper systems.

papers.intro:
Data-driven control aims to design controllers directly from measured trajectories, without first identifying a model. For controllable discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, the fundamental lemma of Willems et al. [30] states that, under persistency of excitation, finite-length trajectories are spanned by the columns of a data Hankel matrix. This result underlies data-driven prediction and control [5, 2, 6]; see also the review papers [13, 7].

Many physical systems are naturally modeled in continuous time. Sampling turns them into discrete-time systems, but the resulting model depends on the sampling period and ignores the intersample behavior. This has motivated several continuous-time versions of the fundamental lemma. In [12, 11], the data and their time shifts form a time-varying Hankel matrix, and trajectories are generated by a time-varying parameter vector that solves a differential equation. The approach in [12] requires state measurements, whereas [11] uses input–output data together with their derivatives. In [19], persistency of excitation is defined via the input and its derivatives, and it is shown to guarantee identifiability. The fundamental lemma in [20] is based on Chebyshev polynomial expansions of a trajectory and its derivatives. Linear combinations of the resulting coefficient sequences generate the Chebyshev coefficients of every trajectory. In practice, the expansions are truncated, so the resulting trajectories are approximate. The approach in [21] builds a Gramian matrix from the input–output data and their derivatives. This yields an exact characterization, in which the parameter generating a trajectory satisfies a differential-algebraic equation (DAE). All these approaches need derivatives of the measured signals, either explicitly or through a polynomial expansion. The approach in [18] uses algebraic differentiators to estimate the required derivatives from measured data. In contrast, [31] employs modulating functions, transferring differentiation to known test functions and thereby avoiding differentiation of the measured signals. Related continuous-time developments concern informativity based on linear functionals [17], derivative-free input–state formulations [29], and extensions of the Gramian approach to LPV systems [23]. Applications include optimal, predictive, and iterative learning control [21, 24, 32, 4].

papers.title: Data Informativity for Robust Feedback Rectification of Switched Linear Systems
papers.abstract: Feedback rectification is a method for switched linear systems that constructs a mode-dependent state feedback such that the closed-loop subsystems share a common eigenvector basis. If the assigned eigenvalues lie inside the unit disk, this yields a common quadratic Lyapunov function and guarantees exponential stability under arbitrary switching. In this paper, we study robust feedback rectification from input-state data affected by bounded disturbances. Using the concept of data informativity, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for approximate feedback rectification without requiring full row-rank of the collected input-state data. If the rectification error is smaller than the stability margin of the prescribed eigenvalues, we obtain global exponential stability under arbitrary switching in the disturbance-free case, and practical global asymptotic stability under bounded disturbances. The approach is illustrated by a mass-spring-damper chain with varying stiffness, where prescribed poles are assigned in every mode from data that do not determine the system matrices uniquely.

papers.intro:
Switched linear systems describe processes whose dynamics change between a finite number of operating modes, e.g., power converters [1], aero-engine control [2], and precision motion systems [3]. Since switching between stable subsystems may lead to instability, their stability analysis is more subtle than for a single linear system [4, 5, 6]. Stability can be recovered by restricting the switching signal, e.g., by average dwell-time conditions [7], or, under arbitrary switching, certified by a common quadratic Lyapunov function (CQLF). A CQLF is sufficient but not necessary; more general certificates use multiple or nonquadratic Lyapunov functions [8, 5].

Switched linear systems describe processes whose dynamics change between a finite number of operating modes, e.g., power converters [1], aero-engine control [2], and precision motion systems [3]. Since switching between stable subsystems may lead to instability, their stability analysis is more subtle than for a single linear system [4, 5, 6]. Stability can be recovered by restricting the switching signal, e.g., by average dwell-time conditions [7], or, under arbitrary switching, certified by a common quadratic Lyapunov function (CQLF). A CQLF is sufficient but not necessary; more general certificates use multiple or nonquadratic Lyapunov functions [8, 5].

Controller design for such systems has to reconcile two goals. Stability under arbitrary switching is typically enforced by searching for feedback gains together with a CQLF, e.g., by LMI-based synthesis [9] or H∞H_{\infty} control [10]. In contrast, placing stable poles in every mode separately gives no guarantee under switching. The closed-loop matrices have different eigenvectors, and switching between them can cause large transient amplification or even instability. Performance of each mode, on the other hand, is naturally specified by closed-loop poles. The CQLF-based methods above certify stability, but at best confine the closed-loop eigenvalues to a region, so the damping of each mode is bounded rather than prescribed. Both goals are partially addressed by constructive designs for single-input systems [11], eigenvalue assignment with simultaneous triangularization [12, 13], and predictive control [14, 15].

Feedback rectification [16, 17] achieves both goals simultaneously. It builds on eigenstructure assignment: Moore’s classical result [18] characterizes the closed-loop eigenvectors compatible with prescribed distinct eigenvalues and thereby identifies the design freedom beyond pole placement; see [19, 20] for extensions. Feedback rectification uses this freedom to choose mode-dependent gains such that all closed-loop matrices have the prescribed eigenvalues and a common eigenvector basis. In these coordinates, every closed-loop matrix is normal and has the prescribed poles as eigenvalues. Consequently, the norm in these coordinates defines a CQLF whose decay rate is set by the designer. No separate Lyapunov search is required, and this norm decreases monotonically without transient amplification. The same eigenstructure-based approach has been used for monotone tracking and non-overshooting output shaping [21]. Model-based rectification, however, requires the subsystem matrices and intersections of particular subspaces given by Moore’s result [17, 16].

Robust designs therefore impose their requirements on the entire compatible model set, using tools from semidefinite programming such as the matrix SS-lemma [24]. This extends the data-driven counterpart of exact feedback rectification from noise-free data [29] to disturbed data.

papers.title: Bayesian Quantum Thermometry of Ultracold Gases with Non-Equilibrium Single-Atom Probes
papers.abstract: Precise thermometry is essential for experiments with ultracold quantum gases, but conventional techniques such as time-of-flight thermometry are destructive and lose sensitivity at low atomic densities. Quantum probes provide an alternative route by encoding temperature information in accessible internal degrees of freedom. Here, we implement Bayesian thermometry with non-equilibrium spin-based single-atom probes immersed in an ultracold atomic bath. Temperature-dependent spin-exchange collisions map the bath temperature onto the internal spin populations of the probe atoms. Measurements of these populations are then used to iteratively update a Bayesian temperature estimate. We connect the information gained at different measurement settings to the underlying spin dynamics, identifying intersections of temperature-dependent population trajectories as a source of thermometric ambiguity. Using the expected information gain to optimize measurement settings, we experimentally compare unoptimized, a priori optimized, and adaptively optimized protocols. Both optimized protocols accelerate convergence, with the adaptive protocol reducing the average number of measurements required to reach a prescribed precision by a factor of 2.5 compared with the unoptimized protocol. In the many-measurement regime, we further characterize the protocols through their asymptotic error scaling and the accumulation of Fisher information, while testing consistency with the expected Cram\'er-Rao bound (ECRB) and the Bernstein-von Mises theorem. These results connect the microscopic dynamics of a quantum probe to efficient measurement design and establish Bayesian spin thermometry as a practical approach for ultracold-gas experiments.

papers.intro:
Temperature is a key parameter for characterizing and controlling ultracold quantum gases. In most setups, the standard approach for determining the temperature is time-of-flight thermometry, where the gas is released from the trap and its expansion is imaged after a period of free evolution. While highly successful, this method is destructive and becomes increasingly challenging for small samples, low atomic densities, or scenarios requiring repeated measurements on the same system. These limitations motivate non-invasive measurement schemes based on quantum probes [34].

Quantum probes are highly controllable quantum systems that can be coupled to a sample to infer its temperature and other physical properties. By preparing and monitoring the probe’s state, information about the sample can be extracted either at thermal equilibrium or during transient non-equilibrium dynamics [34]. Experimentally, single-atom probes have been realized to estimate the temperature [13], magnetic fields [38, 48], and bath density [2, 49] of ultracold gases, while single-qubit probes have also been implemented in superconducting circuits [30]. In parallel, theoretical efforts have established the fundamental precision limits of quantum probes both in equilibrium [15, 43, 25, 1, 57] and non-equilibrium regimes [23, 33, 53], together with novel thermometry schemes based on coherent dynamics [35, 36, 4, 58, 9, 14, 3, 7, 54, 12, 56] and strong probe-sample coupling [16, 22, 32, 63, 42, 26, 29, 62, 45, 3, 61].

To date, most advances in quantum thermometry have focused on the frequentist approach to address local estimation and the limit of large data. However, when experimental data are scarce, or in global estimation, a Bayesian approach is better suited [37]. This has motivated the development of Bayesian thermometry protocols and precision limits [46, 11, 24, 31, 47, 8, 10, 6]. Bayesian estimation has recently begun to move from theory into cold-atom experiments, where it has been used to speed up release–recapture thermometry of few trapped atoms in tweezers [21] and to improve atom-number measurements [40]. Here, we bring Bayesian thermometry to a probe with rich internal dynamics: single-atom spin probes immersed in an ultracold bath [13, 38], where temperature is encoded in multilevel, non-equilibrium spin dynamics.

Our system uses individually measured 133Cs atoms with quantized spin states as probes, which are coupled to a thermal 87Rb cloud via elastic and inelastic collisions [50]. Temperature is inferred from the non-equilibrium spin dynamics of the 133Cs atoms induced by inelastic spin-exchange collisions [13, 38]. Since the optimal choice of measurement parameters, namely the interaction time and the measured spin state, depends on the unknown temperature, the problem can benefit highly from adaptive protocols, which the Bayesian approach enables straightforwardly. Using the Bayesian mean information gain per measurement as an optimization criterion, we design and compare three distinct measurement protocols that differ in their degree of optimization: an unoptimized protocol, an a priori optimized protocol, and a greedy adaptive protocol. Of these schemes, the greedy adaptive protocol makes the most direct use of the Bayesian framework, as it incorporates a feedback loop, as sketched in Fig. 1(a). While the adaptive scheme achieves the highest performance, reducing the number of measurements required to reach a pre-set precision by a factor of 2.5, our results highlight a key trade-off between measurement sensitivity and experimental overhead. We also investigate the asymptotic limit of many measurements. Remarkably, our estimation protocols, in all three scenarios, closely follow the expected Cramér-Rao bound (ECRB). Moreover, the posterior distribution is consistent with the Bernstein-von Mises theorem, which states that its variance is inversely proportional to the accumulated Fisher information. Ultimately, this work establishes Bayesian single-atom spin thermometry as a versatile, high-precision tool for ultracold gas experiments, especially when data acquisition is constrained or costly.

papers.title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
papers.abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.

Overview. In this work we study the size blow-up that might occur when rewriting an existential-positive first-order query into a logically equivalent one that has a bounded number of variables. Existential-positive queries (EP\mathrm{EP}) are those first-order queries that only use existential quantification (∃\exists), conjunction (∧\land), and disjunction (∨\lor)–so, those that disallow negation and universal quantification. This query language has been studied intensively in database theory and constraint satisfaction (Chen, 2014; Chen and Mengel, 2016; Chen and Mengel, 2017). It can be alternatively described by the fragment of relational algebra that uses Select, Project, Join, and Union (SPJU), which is in turn semantically equivalent to the class of unions of conjunctive queries (UCQ).

papers.title: On the loss landscape of the linear neural network: beyond critical points
papers.abstract: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. The present article introduces an intermediate structure, termed the critical thalweg, which encompasses all critical points and exhibits key geometric properties. Beyond providing a geometric proof of Baldi \& Hornik's results using simpler assumptions than the existing literature, this framework offers a global view of the loss landscape that can be easily visualized in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss continues to decrease to its global minimum.

papers.title: LingSante-Pulse: Unified Physiological Pretraining through Random-Feature Prediction and Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.abstract: Clinical monitoring and wearable devices capture complementary physiological signals, but their partially overlapping modality coverage makes within-signal information and cross-modal relationships difficult to exploit jointly. We introduce LingSante-Pulse, a unified, general-purpose and flexible physiological representation framework that learns from these heterogeneous recordings. A shared, signal-conditioned encoder processes each physical channel independently and supports different numbers and combinations of signals for multimodal assessment and single-sensor inference. Pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP) and masked waveform reconstruction jointly learn physiological relationships and preserve informative within-signal structure. Across 38 general physiological task configurations spanning PPG, ECG, EEG and EMG, the frozen encoder achieves the best dataset-balanced mean rank in each domain. In sleep assessment, multimodal staging on the HMC dataset and EEG-only staging on the Sleep-EDF dataset reach Macro-F1 scores of 0.7784 and 0.7941, respectively, while single-lead ECG apnea screening achieves an AUROC of 0.9183. Controlled experiments show that function prediction and waveform reconstruction provide complementary supervision for retaining temporal and rhythmic information. Representations learned under continually refreshed random supervision generalize to unseen teacher realizations, and correct auxiliary modality correspondence improves respiration-only representations. These results demonstrate that a single encoder can learn reusable physiological features across signal types, prediction targets and sensor configurations from partially overlapping recordings.
papers.intro:
Clinical monitoring and wearable devices are accumulating physiological data at increasing scale. Recent foundation-model studies have used up to 40 million hours of minute-level wearable measurements and over 585,000 hours of polysomnography (PSG) recordings [1, 2]. These recordings provide complementary observations of human physiology, in which neural, cardiovascular, respiratory and neuromuscular processes interact across time scales. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural rhythms and transient events, electrocardiography (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity, photoplethysmography (PPG) measures peripheral blood-volume changes, and electromyography (EMG) reflects muscle activation. Each signal reveals a different aspect of physiological state, while relationships among signals provide information about interactions among physiological systems. Learning from both individual signals and their relationships is therefore an important goal for physiological representation learning. Figure 1 summarizes the main downstream results.

Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural rhythms and transient events, electrocardiography (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity, photoplethysmography (PPG) measures peripheral blood-volume changes, and electromyography (EMG) reflects muscle activation. Each signal reveals a different aspect of physiological state, while relationships among signals provide information about interactions among physiological systems. Learning from both individual signals and their relationships is therefore an important goal for physiological representation learning. Figure 1 summarizes the main downstream results.

These complementary observations are distributed across recording settings with different sensor configurations. For example, PSG captures synchronized neural, cardiac, respiratory, and muscular signals, whereas a wrist wearable may provide PPG and movement measurements. Physiological datasets therefore contain partially overlapping collections of modalities, and downstream applications range from multimodal assessment to single-sensor monitoring. Alongside modality-specific foundation models that learn transferable features within individual signal domains [3, 4, 5, 6], researchers have developed multimodal physiological models that learn relationships among synchronized signals [2, 7, 8]. These approaches motivate exploiting both the information within individual signals and the relationships across modalities.

These approaches motivate exploiting both the information within individual signals and the relationships across modalities.

Cross-modal learning offers two complementary benefits. First, when multiple modalities are available, their complementary information can improve physiological assessment through joint modeling of signals and their relationships. Second, during pretraining, a related modality can provide additional supervision that improves representations for subsequent single-modality inference. For example, AnyPPG [3] demonstrates the value of ECG-guided pretraining for learning transferable PPG representations, drawing on the physiological coupling between cardiac electrical activity and peripheral hemodynamics. This motivates extending cross-modal learning across partially overlapping recordings, using shared modalities to connect supervision across data sources. A target signal could then benefit from a broader set of physiological observations, including recordings in which that signal is absent.

Our goal is to build a general-purpose framework for multimodal physiological representation learning with a single shared encoder. First, by learning from signals and their relationships across data sources, the encoder should match or surpass modality-specific foundation models when given a single modality, such as dedicated EEG models on EEG-only tasks. Second, the framework should learn cross-modal relationships within a unified architecture that accommodates different numbers and combinations of channels and can incorporate new signal types during pretraining. Third, it should support applications ranging from full PSG to single-sensor monitoring and remain useful when entire modalities are unavailable or individual recordings contain gaps.

Two challenges arise from this goal. First, how can cross-modal relationships be learned across datasets that record different subsets of signals? Each dataset supplies direct evidence for the relationships among its observed channels. Shared signals must connect these relationships so that supervision from different recordings contributes to a common representation space. Second, how can cross-modal learning preserve the distinctive information within each signal? Related physiological events produce different observations across modalities, while individual signals contain patterns such as QRS morphology in ECG and transient spindles in EEG. Pretraining must capture cross-modal relationships while retaining these signal-specific structures. Enforcing invariance between temporal crops can further suppress event timing or amplitude context relevant to downstream prediction.

papers.title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.

Fine-tuning a pre-trained model for each task yields one expert per task, each a full copy of the weights or an adapter on top of them. Storing and serving many experts is costly, especially for large language models. Model merging combines the experts into a single multi-task model without joint training (Wortsman et al., 2022; Ilharco et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026). Most methods operate on task vectors, the differences between each expert and the shared pre-trained weights (Ilharco et al., 2023).

papers.title: Seeing Is Not Steering: Where Verifiable Reasoning Can Enter an End-to-End Driving Planner
papers.abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.

A driving planner, however, is judged by the path it drives, not by what a VLM says. A fact may be correct and still be ignored, while a trajectory may improve for reasons unrelated to that fact. We therefore ask whether the facts stated by a VLM actually influence a planner’s decisions, and whether that influence improves driving.

papers.title: Off-diagonal long-range order and $p$-wave pairing in one dimension from critical density fluctuations
papers.abstract: A central theme in the theory of unconventional superconductivity is that Cooper pairing can be mediated by bosonic collective modes other than lattice vibrations. However, collective fluctuations in reduced dimensions can also have a destabilizing effect on superconductivity, by suppressing long-range order or by destroying Fermi-liquid quasiparticles in the normal state. In this work, we study a one-dimensional (1D) model of spinless fermions with local interactions that exhibits a continuous quantum phase transition from a Luttinger liquid to a phase-separated state. Combining field-theoretic arguments with numerical exact diagonalization and matrix-product-state methods, we find that the quantum critical point exhibits two-particle off-diagonal long-range order and $p$-wave pairing. Our work shows that critical density fluctuations at a phase-separation instability can act as pairing glue for unconventional superconductivity in 1D, overcoming the disordering effect of phase fluctuations and the absence of long-lived fermionic quasiparticles in the normal state.

papers.intro:
While conventional ss-wave superconductivity is generally believed to arise from attractive effective interactions between electrons mediated by phonons [1], the nature of the pairing mechanism for unconventional (e.g., pp-wave or dd-wave) superconductors remains a largely open question. By analogy with the phonon mechanism of Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, a broad class of theories ascribe the formation of unconventional Cooper pairs to fermion interactions mediated by other bosonic collective modes, for example, ferromagnetic spin fluctuations in pp-wave superfluid 3He [2, 3, 4] and antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations [5, 6, 7] in dd-wave superconductors.

While conventional ss-wave superconductivity is generally believed to arise from attractive effective interactions between electrons mediated by phonons [1], the nature of the pairing mechanism for unconventional (e.g., pp-wave or dd-wave) superconductors remains a largely open question. By analogy with the phonon mechanism of Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, a broad class of theories ascribe the formation of unconventional Cooper pairs to fermion interactions mediated by other bosonic collective modes, for example, ferromagnetic spin fluctuations in pp-wave superfluid 3He [2, 3, 4] and antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations [5, 6, 7] in dd-wave superconductors.

An interesting scenario in which soft bosonic collective modes naturally arise is the vicinity of a symmetry-breaking quantum critical point (QCP). At a QCP, long-wavelength fluctuations of the order parameter become gapless and can mediate interactions between electrons. Recent theoretical proposals along this line include pairing mediated by quantum-critical fluctuations of loop-current order [8], ferroelectricity [9, 10, 11], and nematicity [12, 13]. However, quantum-critical fluctuations can also result in a non-Fermi liquid and destroy the coherent fermionic quasiparticles in the normal state, an effect which competes with the Cooper instability [14]. This effect is exacerbated in lower dimensions, and is particularly acute in one spatial dimension (1D), where interacting electrons generally form a Luttinger liquid [15] without coherent fermionic excitations. Furthermore, the hallmark of superconductivity, two-particle off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) [16], is naively forbidden in 1D even at zero temperature due to the Mermin-Wagner theorem [17, 18, 19]. Indeed, because of the disordering effect of long-wavelength fluctuations of the U⁡(1)U(1) phase of the superconducting order parameter, pairing correlations decay algebraically at long distances, suppressing true ODLRO in favor of quasi-ODLRO.

In this work, we study a 1D lattice model of spinless fermions with local interactions that exhibits pp-wave pairing and true two-particle ODLRO at a QCP in its phase diagram. The QCP describes a continuous quantum phase transition from a Luttinger liquid to a phase-separated (PS) state with a spontaneously broken ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} particle-hole symmetry. The order parameter for this transition corresponds to the uniform (zero-momentum) component of the fermion number/charge density relative to half filling, and critical fluctuations of this order parameter are key to the existence of superconducting ODLRO in this model. Conceptually, number and phase are canonically conjugate quantum-mechanical variables which do not mutually commute, thus strong density fluctuations at a QCP are naturally expected to lead to reduced fluctuations of the superconducting (Josephson) phase. More quantitatively, using bosonization techniques, we derive an effective field theory for the PS transition and show that it is equivalent to a previously studied field theory describing Ising ferromagnetic transitions in spin chains [20, 21, 22, 23, 24] and 1D spinful itinerant electron systems [25, 26, 27]. Importantly, Ref. [20] recently argued that this field theory exhibits spontaneous breaking of the continuous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry associated with XY spin rotations around the Ising axis. In our work, the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry corresponds instead to the conservation of fermion number, and its spontaneous breaking at the phase-separation QCP is associated with pp-wave superconductivity. To verify the field theory predictions, we study the model numerically using exact diagonalization (ED) as well as matrix-product state (MPS) methods and confirm the existence of both the phase-separation QCP and true pp-wave ODLRO at this QCP.

papers.title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

As shown in Figure (a), existing approaches often focus on full observation histories [35] or text descriptions [5, 34]. Full observation histories are complete yet redundant, thus falling short when facing long-horizon tasks [38, 37]. Text captures abstract events, yet can omit visual details, or cannot fully describe certain information (e.g., “move the cube back to where it was”). As a first step, we propose VMBench, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks that require visual moment memory. Its key design principle is to make successful manipulation depend on remembering precise visual information. Different from existing benchmarks [7, 10, 5, 22], our benchmark emphasizes tasks that cannot be well addressed by concise text memory. Specifically, these tasks require remembering exact positions and visual patterns, rather than only object identities or task progress. Concise text summaries may omit these details, as illustrated in Figure (b). We organize the tasks around spatial locations, visual appearances, and appearance-location bindings. For example, returning a cube to its original position requires remembering exactly where it was, rather than just knowing that it was moved. Across these tasks, the key visual moment is only visible across a short period of time and the model has to capture such moments for successful task completion. Together, these tasks provide a testbed for studying how robots memorize precise visual information for manipulation tasks.

We annotate this span as a temporal segment. We aim for the memorizer to select a keyframe in the segment as early as possible. Also, if it misses an earlier frame, it should still try to capture the later frame in the same segment. During inference, the executor predicts actions from the selected keyframes together with the current observation. Details are provided in Section 4.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Using Hadamard-Encoded Multipulse and 4D Denoising on a 256-Channel System with a 1024-element Matrix Array: A Feasibility Study in Human Kidney Transplants
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional ultrasound localization microscopy (3D ULM) enables volumetric visualization of microvasculature beyond the acoustic diffraction limit, but its clinical translation remains limited by long acquisition times, low microbubble (MB) signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and insufficient MB contrast, particularly on ultrasound systems with a limited number of acquisition channels. In this study, we developed an in-human 3D ULM framework for a 256-channel research ultrasound system equipped with a 1024-element matrix array. The framework combines diverging-wave Hadamard-encoded multipulse (HEM) transmission to enhance MB SNR with denoising strategy combining MB enhancement and four-dimensional non-local means filtering to improve MB contrast. The framework was implemented on a research ultrasound platform and evaluated in phantom experiments and four in vivo human kidney transplants. In phantom experiments, HEM improved the MB contrast ratio around 2 dB, while the proposed denoising strategy enhanced in vivo MB contrast by up to around 9 dB. 3D ULM reconstruction achieved a spatial resolution of approximately 84 um, as estimated by Fourier shell correlation. The number of reconstructed microvascular voxels increased exponentially with acquisition duration, reaching approximately 74% of the estimated saturated vessel density using 3000 volumes (~12 s). The subject with the highest histopathological injury exhibited quantitatively reduced microvascular vessel density, flow velocities, and mean perfusion index. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables high-quality volumetric super-resolution imaging and quantitative characterization of renal microvasculature using a 256-channel ultrasound system, providing a practical step toward the clinical translation of in vivo 3D ULM.

papers.title: Nutrient limitation drives Turing instabilities in cross-feeding microbial communities
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by metabolic interactions, often in the form of cross-feeding in which microbes exchange metabolites via diffusion through the environment. We show here that the diffusion of cross-fed metabolites generically leads to a Turing instability in resource-poor environments, driven by the feedback between local metabolite availability and cell growth. A coarse-grained model of community biomass identifies the few dimensionless parameters that control the instability, most notably the ratio of environmental energy supply to cellular maintenance costs. We find that the detailed topology of the metabolic interaction network can be coarse-grained into a single effective parameter to quantitatively characterise the instability. Beyond the onset of the instability, the community forms compact aggregates whose merger is prevented by a competition for shared resources. Overall, our results demonstrate how spatial structure can arise as an inevitable consequence of metabolic interactions in a microbial community.

papers.intro:
A central interest in the study of ecology is to understand how large, complex ecosystems remain stable in the face of small (and not so small) perturbations. Since at least the work of Robert May in the 1970s [30], such questions have been addressed by analysing the stability of ‘typical’ solutions to an underlying complex dynamical system, applying methods from random matrix theory and the physics of disordered systems. Consequently, we understand how many properties of well-mixed ecosystems – species diversity [7, 4, 40], resource abundance [1, 28], and the reciprocity of interactions [5] – determine their stability to perturbations in biomass, the invasion of new species, or the depletion of a food source.

Consequently, we understand how many properties of well-mixed ecosystems – species diversity [7, 4, 40], resource abundance [1, 28], and the reciprocity of interactions [5] – determine their stability to perturbations in biomass, the invasion of new species, or the depletion of a food source.

Less understood, however, is how perturbations to the spatial distribution of ecosystem constituents, rather than their net mass, affect their stability. Many ecosystems, from biofilms to forests, reside in spatially extended environments, in which organisms interact locally with neighbours and resources [45, 10, 25, 19, 2]. While in some cases the spatial organization of community members might be imposed by environmental gradients [38, 14] or a range expansion of the population [32, 6], in others it may emerge as a self-organised phenomenon in which species dispersal or the abiotic diffusion of resources destabilises the well-mixed state [39, 23, 18, 29]. These spatial instabilities are known as Turing instabilities [43], and they can lead to patterned steady states that differ qualitatively and quantitatively from the initial well-mixed state [35, 2].

These spatial instabilities are known as Turing instabilities [43], and they can lead to patterned steady states that differ qualitatively and quantitatively from the initial well-mixed state [35, 2].

While the mathematical conditions for a Turing instability are well understood in the abstract, it remains uncertain how common they are in different classes of ecosystems [16, 17]. A standard criterion is that the different components of the system have sufficiently different rates of diffusion or dispersal. Recent work has shown, for instance, that a trophically structured model of predators and prey will exhibit a Turing instability when the dispersal rate of prey differs from that of their predators [3]. Establishing such broad, qualitative heuristics can be valuable in the study of such complex systems, as they indicate when insights gained from a well-mixed treatment are expected to hold, and when a more complex, spatial analysis might be required.

Here we determine the conditions under which a large class of microbial ecosystems undergo a Turing instability. We focus on ecosystems with metabolic cross-feeding between species, an interaction argued theoretically and empirically to underpin the diversity of microbial communities from soils to the human gut [12, 15, 13, 9, 46]. In these systems, the difference in diffusion coefficients necessary for a Turing instability arises naturally between the micron-sized microbes and the nanometre-scale metabolites they exchange. We focus on communities governed by reactive dynamics that represent a thermodynamically-consistent metabolism, with a well-defined energy supply and cellular maintenance costs. Under these constraints, we find that Turing instabilities arise only in resource-poor environments, through a positive feedback between metabolite diffusion and cell growth. Leveraging a coarse-grained model, we identify the few dimensionless parameters that control the onset of the instability. Finally, we go beyond the onset of instability and characterise community biomass and composition in the spatially-patterned state.

papers.title: Regular quadratic lattices are rare over real quadratic fields
papers.abstract: We show that a positive definite regular quadratic lattice of rank at least 4 over a totally real number field contains a regular sublattice that represents precisely the totally positive integers lying in an ideal. Under the generalized Riemann hypothesis and a conjecture on class numbers, it follows that, for each $m$, real quadratic fields admitting a positive definite regular lattice of some rank between 4 and $m$ have density 0. Unconditionally, only finitely many real quadratic fields of narrow class number 1 admit a positive definite regular lattice of some rank between 4 and 7.

papers.intro:
A positive definite integral quadratic form over ℤ\mathbb{Z} is regular if it represents every positive integer that is represented by its genus, i.e., every positive integer that it represents over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} for every prime pp. Thus a regular form represents all positive integers except those excluded by congruence conditions. Every universal form, i.e., every quadratic form that represents all positive integers, is regular.

Regular forms were introduced by Dickson [Di] in 1927, who also determined those of the type x2+a​y2+b​z2x^{2}+ay^{2}+bz^{2}. Jones and Pall [Jo, JP] then completed the classification of regular diagonal ternary forms a​x2+b​y2+c​z2ax^{2}+by^{2}+cz^{2}. Watson [Wa1] proved that there are only finitely many equivalence classes of primitive positive definite regular ternary forms by bounding their discriminants. Jagy–Kaplansky–Schiemann [JKS] produced a list of 913913 candidates for regular ternary forms and proved the regularity of all but 2222 of them. Of these 2222 forms, 88 were proved to be regular by Oh [Oh2] and 1414 by Lemke Oliver [LO] under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. In rank at least 44, however, the analogous finiteness statement fails, since Earnest [Ea1] constructed infinitely many regular quaternary forms.
