From now on, we will use the geometric language of quadratic lattices. Watson’s proof of his finiteness theorem used transformations that replace a lattice by a sublattice whose discriminant becomes smaller after rescaling [Wa1, Wa2]. These transformations preserve regularity and do not increase the class number, and by applying them repeatedly, one can reduce every regular ternary lattice to one of bounded discriminant. papers.title: Trust What Repeats: Capped World-Model Policy Gradients for Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.

papers.intro:
A general motion tracker turns a library of human motion into a single policy that a humanoid can run: given the next frames of a reference, the policy outputs joint targets that make the robot follow it. Such trackers are the low-level layer under teleoperation, motion generation and learned skills, and their quality is set by how many motions they follow without falling and by how long they take to train. With model-free reinforcement learning the second number is large: trackers for libraries of a hundred hours and more are trained for days on many GPUs [1, 2, 3].

papers.title: Prediction and characterisation of cation topology of pentanary high-entropy alloy (MoWNbTaV)S$_2$
papers.abstract:
High-entropy transition-metal dichalcogenides offer properties tuned by composition, yet two basic questions remain open: which arrangement of the metals forms under synthesis conditions, and how it can be recognised in experiment. Density functional theory (DFT) cannot sample the vast space of possible arrangements, and the ground-state energies usually employed to screen them do not take into account the temperatures at which these materials are made. This work solves both issues for the pentanary (MoWNbTaV)S\textsubscript{2} monolayer with a Gaussian approximation potential trained on DFT data by iterative learning. Gibbs free energy calculations reveal that vibrational entropy reshapes the stability ranking, while five selected configurations retain their trigonal-prismatic framework during nanosecond molecular dynamics up to \qty{1300}{\kelvin}. Raman and infrared spectra combine parent-monolayer signatures with disorder-activated modes, providing fingerprints for experimental identification. %
The predicted lattice parameter follows Vegard's law and agrees within \qty{0.8}{\percent} with X{-}ray diffraction on a sputtered alloy film, which identifies the solid solution but not the arrangement of its metals: distinguishing between arrangements requires the vibrational fingerprints. The potential and its development workflow enable further atomistic simulations and offer a transferable approach to screening related two-dimensional high-entropy materials.

papers.intro:
The past two decades have witnessed a fundamental shift in material design, moving from the long-held “one principal element” philosophy towards the exploration of vast multidimensional compositional spaces. A prime exemplar of this new paradigm is the class of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), first introduced in 2004 [1, 2]. By combining five or more principal elements in nearly equimolar ratios, HEAs leverage configurational entropy to overcome the enthalpy of mixing, thereby stabilizing single‑phase solid solutions, rather than intermetallic compounds or phase-separated mixtures. This entropic stabilization effect has unlocked an extraordinary range of mechanically robust, thermally stable, and corrosion-resistant materials. Importantly, the HEA concept has transcended its original metallic alloy domain, finding a successful extension to oxides [3], carbides [4, 5], borides [6], nitrides [7, 8], and most recently, to two-dimensional (2D) layered materials [9, 10, 11].

Among 2D materials, transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), MX2 with M a group IV, V, or VI transition metal and X = S, Se, or Te, are especially versatile. Prototypical members such as MoS2 and WS2 exhibit remarkable optoelectronic properties [12], including direct bandgaps in the monolayer limit (∼\sim1.8 eV for MoS2 [13]), strong excitonic effects [14], valley polarization [15], and high carrier mobilities [16]. These features drove their use in nanoelectronics [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23] and in electrocatalysis for hydrogen evolution [24, 25, 26, 27] and CO2 reduction [28, 29]. Yet the small chemical palette of binary TMDCs limits their properties. Mixing several transition metals on a shared cation sublattice opens a far larger design space, in which local bonding, and therefore electronic and catalytic behavior, can be tuned by composition and by atomic arrangement.

Yet the small chemical palette of binary TMDCs limits their properties. Mixing several transition metals on a shared cation sublattice opens a far larger design space, in which local bonding, and therefore electronic and catalytic behavior, can be tuned by composition and by atomic arrangement.

Despite their promise, understanding the stability of high-entropy TMDCs remains challenging because chemical disorder generates numerous possible atomic arrangements with different local environments. Even at identical overall compositions, variations in atomic coordination, bond strengths, and lattice distortions can significantly influence structural energetics and vibrational behavior. The relative thermodynamical stability of individual atomic configurations depends on their Gibbs free-energy contributions, whereas configurational entropy plays a major role at elevated temperatures. Consequently, configurations favored at low temperatures may not necessarily remain thermodynamically preferred at higher temperatures. Entropy-assisted stabilization has been predicted for multicomponent disulfides [30], and compositionally complex TMDCs have been synthesized [26, 28, 31, 32]. Mapping the configurational landscape and its temperature dependence, however, requires extensive sampling, reliable lattice dynamics, and finite-temperature simulations, a combination that is prohibitively expensive with density functional theory (DFT) alone.

Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) address this bottleneck by learning the potential-energy surface from first-principles data, delivering near-DFT accuracy at a small fraction of the cost [33, 34, 35]. Among the various MLIP frameworks [33, 34, 35], the Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) [36, 37, 38] is a particularly powerful approach. GAP provides a rigorous Bayesian framework for uncertainty quantification, employs a sparse Gaussian process to balance accuracy and computational cost, and has been successfully applied to diverse systems ranging from elemental metals [39, 40] and alloys [41] to high-entropy alloys [42, 43, 44], liquids [45], and MXenes [46]. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study reported a GAP force field specifically developed for multi-cationic 2D TMDC HEAs, particularly for the (MoWNbTaV)S2 system. Existing MLIP studies on 2D HEAs [47, 48, 49, 50, 51] either focused on fine-tuning universal potentials (e.g., CHGNet [52], MACE [53], MatterSim [54]) or employed other MLIP architectures, such as neural network potentials [55, 56]. Although these efforts are valuable, universal potentials often lack the specialized accuracy required for subtle energy differences (e.g., mixing energies and defect formation energies) in a specific HEA composition, and fine-tuning can inadvertently compromise transferability.

papers.title: Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). Most fairness benchmarks evaluate demographic discrimination under a single reasoning objective, and none we know of tests whether a model treats the same item differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the extent to which a model's differentiation between matched candidates depends on whether it is asked to predict or to decide, and measure it with the Normative--Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB): 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, each posed under both framings, and three metrics, Normative Engagement Rate (NER), Normative Leakage Rate (NLR), and Normative--Descriptive Separation (NDS). Across six LLMs, NDS separates 13 of 15 model pairs, against 7 for BBQ accuracy and none for BOLD, although these counts also reflect each benchmark's sample size. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 separate the framings most strongly (average NDS $= +0.55$ and $+0.52$, with overlapping confidence intervals), whereas GPT-5.5's average NDS is negative ($-0.14$) under the single-pick instruction and near zero ($+0.02$) without it. In a simplified prompt template, removing single trigger words never changes the sign of a model's average NDS but can shift it by up to 0.46 and reorder models. Reversing candidate order reveals a further effect: when forced to choose between identical candidates, all six models favor whichever is listed first, and once order is averaged out their demographic-aligned lean is toward the marginalized candidate. Describing disparities and prescribing them are separable behaviors that differ across models.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, including hiring, education, healthcare, criminal justice, and public services Qiu et al. (2024); Li et al. (2023); Chu et al. (2025); Gaebler et al. (2024). As these systems move beyond information retrieval toward decision support that directly affects individuals Tamkin et al. (2023), alignment is no longer only about producing truthful, harmless, or unbiased outputs; it also requires selecting the appropriate reasoning strategy for the user’s objective. The same factual information may be appropriate when describing Benthall and Haynes (2019) the world yet inappropriate when recommending actions that affect individuals Bommasani et al. (2026); Bowen III et al. (2024). Whether a model recognizes and adapts to this distinction, on the same item, is a behavioral property of alignment that existing evaluations leave untested. Figure 1 illustrates both behaviors on a matched pair: given two identically qualified candidates, Claude Opus 4.6 shifts its verdict between the “who is likely” and “who should” framings, whereas GPT-5.5 returns an equal verdict under both.

papers.title: Accountable AI Delegation in Banking: Identity, Commitment Controls, Decision Evidence and Recovery
papers.abstract: An AI-assisted payment can pass assessment and lose release authority before commitment. We specify a banking delegation contract that checks current authority, the shared payment cap and the capacity of eligible instruments to cover losses. It books the new payment and its recovery demands and writes the outcome record in the same atomic transition. A paired example identifies the authorised mandate, applied rule and selection inputs a reviewer needs to assess mandate conformance. We show that, under fixed resource inputs, the transition preserves the payment cap and recovery feasibility when commitments and effective withdrawals are ordered against the same authoritative state. Reversing a transmitted priority changes the selected route in 4 of 32 distinct behavioural combinations, represented by 96 of 576 labelled contexts. The executor follows the transmitted rule in all of them. Reusing earlier state admits 23 releases in 123 histories blocked by the reference. Pooling recovery capacity admits 69 infeasible configurations in a grid of 576. Both current-state implementations agree with the reference in all 144 commitment histories and 624 concurrent schedules. The retention test recovers five specified outcome fields from each of 47 complete records. Fifteen survey responses informed requirements for resolving holds and handling uncertain delivery. An insurance example illustrates referral after an adverse coverage finding.

papers.title: How communities help epidemics persist
papers.abstract:
Empirical studies show that communities such as households and workplaces strongly influence how an infection spreads and how long it persists in a population. To understand this effect, we study the contact process (SIS epidemic model) on random intersection graphs and their local weak limit. In the contact process, infected vertices recover with rate $1$ and transmit the infection to each of their neighbours with rate $\lambda$. The random intersection graph is defined on a finite population; each individual belongs to a random number of communities (captured by a membership distribution), and each community has a random size (captured by a community size distribution). Communities are all taken to be complete graphs. The local weak limit of the random intersection graph, called the branching community tree, has complete graphs arranged in a tree structure.
  Letting $M$ have the membership distribution and $K$ have the community size distribution, we prove that if either $\mathbb E[e^{cM}]=\infty$ for all $c > 0$ or $\mathbb E[e^{cK\log K}] = \infty$ for all $c > 0$, then for all $\lambda > 0$, the infection on the finite graph survives for exponentially long with high probability, and on the local limit graph, it survives forever with positive probability. On the other hand, if for some $c > 0$ both $\mathbb E[e^{cM}]<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[e^{K\log(cK)}]<\infty$ hold, then the process with small $\lambda$ dies out in the local limit graph. We compare these findings with known results on the behaviour of the contact process on a "community-free" random graph with similar degree distributions, to highlight the impact of communities.

papers.title: Annular Terahertz Near-Field of a Breathing Charged Vortex
papers.abstract: We study the radial electric field around a singly quantized vortex in a charged BCS superconductor, when the Higgs amplitude mode is driven by a uniform terahertz (THz) electromagnetic pulse. In a local-density approximation the pairing gap vanishes on the vortex axis at all times, so the particle density on the axis cannot oscillate, whereas the curvature of the density profile around the axis does. Starting from the electrostatic-lens formalism of our previous work, we show that this converts the electrically neutral Higgs oscillation into an alternating radial electric field that vanishes on the axis. When the electrostatic screening length is much shorter than the vortex core, we obtain the field in closed form: it has a ring-shaped profile, with a maximum at a distance of the order of the coherence length from the axis, and the Higgs drive modulates it by a fraction $2\eta$, where $\eta$ is the relative oscillation of the gap. For niobium nitride and $\eta=0.1$ the static field of the vortex is about $140$~V/m and its modulation about $30$~V/m, independently of the carrier density and of the dielectric constant. We also discuss how the thermodynamic factor entering the field changes toward the BCS-BEC crossover.

papers.intro:
Superconductors are characterized by a complex pairing order parameter [1]. Its phase fluctuations give rise to the Goldstone mode, while its amplitude fluctuations give rise to the Higgs mode [2, 3], which has been observed in THz experiments on conventional superconductors such as NbN [4, 5]. In a type-II superconductor a magnetic field penetrates in the form of quantized vortices [6, 7]: these are topological defects around which the phase of the order parameter winds by 2​π2\pi and the pairing gap vanishes on the axis, recovering its bulk value over a coherence length [8]. A vortex core is also depleted of charge carriers and can therefore be electrically charged [9]. A basic question is then how the Higgs mode, which is electrically neutral in a homogeneous system, can couple to electromagnetic fields. This question is central in THz spectroscopy, particularly in spatially inhomogeneous geometries where density gradients break translational invariance [10].

papers.title: The GAPS programme at TNG. LXXXIII. Orbital refinement and atmospheric investigation of TOI-1518 b (BD+66 1610 b)
papers.abstract: TOI-1518 b (BD+66 1610 b) is a highly irradiated ultra-hot Jupiter on a strongly misaligned orbit, a benchmark target for atmospheric and dynamical studies. We comprehensively characterise the TOI-1518 system by refining its orbital and physical parameters, and by investigating the chemical composition of the planetary atmosphere through transmission spectroscopy. We employed a joint Bayesian framework combining TESS photometry, HARPS-N high-resolution spectroscopy, and least-squares deconvolution profiles to break stellar geometrical degeneracies. We then applied single-line and cross-correlation function (CCF) transmission spectroscopy across theoretical templates. By anchoring the stellar projected rotational velocity ($v \sin i_\star \approx 79.7$ km s$^{-1}$), we confirmed the nearly polar orbit ($\lambda \approx 238^\circ$) and the theoretically predicted nodal precession ($\mathrm{d}i/\mathrm{d}t \approx 0.15^\circ$ yr$^{-1}$). We revealed an atmospheric Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) effect and a bulk atmospheric blue-shift of $\approx -7.0$ km s$^{-1}$. Through transmission spectroscopy, we detected H I, C I, Na I, Ca I, Sc II, Ti II, V II, Cr I, Fe I, Fe II, Ni I, Sr II, Y II, Eu II, and W I. This marks the first detection of H I, C I, Sc II, V II, Sr II, Y II, Eu II, and W I in this planet, and the first ever detection of Eu II and W I in an exoplanetary atmosphere. Inconsistencies in the Na I doublet shifts suggest likely stellar contamination. Furthermore, time-resolved CCF analysis revealed morning-to-evening limb asymmetries for species like Mg I and Ba I, hinting at night-side cold traps. The atmosphere of TOI-1518 b exhibits a rich chemical inventory shaped by intense irradiation and bulk circulation. Our results emphasize the necessity of simultaneously modelling stellar line morphology and planetary tracks to accurately interpret atmospheric signals under strong RM effects.

papers.intro:
One of the primary objectives of exoplanetary research for the upcoming decade is the atmospheric characterisation of terrestrial planets, with the ultimate goal of identifying potential biosignatures (Fujii et al. 2018). High-resolution transmission spectroscopy (HRTS) has emerged as one of the most promising techniques with the potential to achieve this milestone. By resolving individual spectral lines, HRTS allows for the unambiguous identification of molecular and atomic species. It leverages the distinct Doppler shift of the moving planet to effectively disentangle the planetary signal from the dominant, relatively static stellar and telluric spectra, typically employing the cross-correlation function (CCF) technique (Snellen et al. 2010; Brogi et al. 2012, e.g.,). While the application of these advanced techniques to progressively cooler and smaller planets is of immense scientific interest and offers groundbreaking potential, pushing these limits requires extreme precision and a robust understanding of instrumental and astrophysical systematics. Therefore, to rigorously verify and corroborate current analysis frameworks and to develop novel methodologies, targets that provide high signal to noise ratio (S/N) observable features are essential. In this context, ultra-hot Jupiters (UHJs) serve not only as ideal astrophysical benchmarks (Hoeijmakers et al. 2018, e.g.,), but also as profoundly compelling targets in their own right. Their extreme temperatures significantly expand the atmospheric pressure scale height, boosting the amplitude and detectability of spectral features. Furthermore, by preventing the condensation of obscuring clouds and hazes, UHJs offer an unhindered view of their atmospheric bulk composition. Characterizing this pristine chemical inventory is intrinsically crucial, as it provides fundamental clues regarding the formation mechanisms and early dynamical evolution of gas giant planets. Defined by equilibrium temperatures exceeding 2000 K (Fortney et al. 2008), UHJs are characterised by extreme environments in which most molecules are thermally dissociated. Consequently, their upper atmosphere hosts vaporised metals, both neutral and ionised (Casasayas-Barris et al. 2017; Hoeijmakers et al. 2019, e.g.,). These metals, along with the high-temperature molecules containing them, are recognised as strong sources of opacity in the optical and near-ultraviolet regions (Fortney et al. 2008; Lothringer et al. 2018). The absorption of intense stellar irradiation by these species is predicted to be the primary driver for the formation of strong thermal inversions (stratospheres) often exhibited by UHJs (Hubeny et al. 2003; Haynes et al. 2015, e.g.,). Nevertheless, the exact chemical species responsible for these inversions remain a subject of active debate (Fortney et al. 2008; Lothringer et al. 2022), necessitating precise observational constraints. Furthermore, in these extreme regimes, intense UV irradiation can drive the upper atmosphere out of local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE), significantly altering the level populations of atomic species and complicating the interpretation of line strengths (Fossati et al. 2021).

Beyond the detection of important species, HRTS serves as a vital means of probing the complex dynamics of UHJ atmospheres. The analysis of high-resolution line profiles allows for the characterisation of atmospheric kinematics, including day-to-night side winds and equatorial jets (D’Arpa et al. 2024; Borsa et al. 2021a; Casasayas-Barris et al. 2019), and provides insights into extended atmospheres and potential escape mechanisms (Borsa et al. 2021b). However, applying HRTS to UHJs often involves navigating significant astrophysical challenges. The planetary transit across a rotating stellar disk creates a well-known spectral distortion referred to as the Doppler shadow, or the Rossiter-McLaughlin (RM) effect (Collier Cameron et al. 2010). While this phenomenon occurs in all rotating systems, it becomes particularly challenging for UHJs, which frequently orbit early-type, fast-rotating hosts. In these extreme regimes, the highly broadened Doppler shadow often strongly overlaps with the planetary track in velocity space, making the disentanglement of atmospheric absorption from stellar surface variations a critical task. However, this signal is not solely a source of contamination. In this work, rather than treating the RM effect merely as a nuisance, we exploit it as a valuable resource to independently refine the orbital parameters of the system.

While its F0-type host star implies a significantly softer UV irradiation environment compared to the A0-type host of the archetypal UHJ KELT-9 b, which inherently drives different photochemical and ionization balances, the comparable temperature makes it an ideal candidate for a strictly analogous application of single-line and cross-correlation analyses. Furthermore, the system parameters result in a remarkably large atmospheric scale height (H≈609H\approx 609 km, corresponding to ∼0.48%\sim 0.48\% of the planetary radius) and a transmission spectroscopy metric (TSM) of 352. papers.title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
papers.abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.

papers.intro:
Preventing the harmful effects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems has become a major concern, especially in high risk domains such as recruitment, education, credit scoring and insurance, where automated decision systems directly affect persons’ rights and access to opportunities (Stazi, 2025; Deshpande, 2024). The European Union AI Act (European Union, 2024) addresses this issue by imposing detailed obligations on providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems (European Union, 2024). Yet, a persistent challenge remains: how to practically implement these abstract legal provisions during AI systems’ design, deployment, monitoring, and assessment (Duke and Giudici, 2025).

Preventing the harmful effects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems has become a major concern, especially in high risk domains such as recruitment, education, credit scoring and insurance, where automated decision systems directly affect persons’ rights and access to opportunities (Stazi, 2025; Deshpande, 2024). The European Union AI Act (European Union, 2024) addresses this issue by imposing detailed obligations on providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems (European Union, 2024). Yet, a persistent challenge remains: how to practically implement these abstract legal provisions during AI systems’ design, deployment, monitoring, and assessment (Duke and Giudici, 2025).

This paper addresses this challenge through collaborative work between academic researchers and key stakeholders from a partner banking institution, namely its AI software developer and compliance teams. It proposes a toolkit, namely High Risk - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (HR-RAI), intended to facilitate the development of an abstract legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment system. This system integrates third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models at multiple critical stages of the pipeline, without the need for additional training or fine-tuning. Applications used in the recruitment context are included among the high-risk sectors listed in Annex III(4)(a), as explicitly referenced by Article 6(2). Under Article 8, providers of AI systems are required to ensure compliance with the techno-normative requirements set forth in Section 2, with the aim of ensuring, in accordance with the precautionary principle (Garnett and Parsons, 2017), an adequate level of product safety to protect the health and fundamental rights of persons. The pipeline examined in this work presents heightened compliance challenges due to its reliance on GPAI components characterized by multiple levels of opacity. These range from corporate or institutional secrecy in the case of closed models to algorithmic inaccessibility, even for open-source models (Buttaboni and Floridi, 2026). As such, the scenario serves as a stress test for the difficulties that providers may encounter when gathering evidence to demonstrate compliance, with a particular focus whenever closed components are integrated. The choice underlying this study reflects prevailing industry practices shaped on one hand by market and financial pressures to adopt the latest available technologies, on the other by benchmark studies showing that proprietary models continue to outperform open-source alternatives in terms of performance, user experience, access to state-of-the-art capabilities (Cottier et al., 2024), and perceived reliability (Huang et al., 2024).

The proposed toolkit supports the evaluation of high-risk recruitment AI systems against the requirements of the AI Act, translating the legal obligations set out in Chapter III, Section 2 of the Act into a structured checklist of techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. These questions are intended to stimulate critical reflection on the adequacy of an AI system’s design, development and deployment. In doing so, the toolkit serves a dual function: first, to assist in the systematic collection of evidence necessary for compliance verification; and second, to encourage responsible practices among AI designers and developers (Bignami et al., 2025). In this way, the toolkit not only facilitates compliance assessment but also promotes the integration of ethical and legal considerations throughout the AI development lifecycle, thereby advancing the implementation of transparent and legal-by-design AI systems.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 sets out the legal framework governing high-risk AI systems under the AI Act, focusing in particular on Articles 9–15 and Annex IV, and reviews prior efforts in putting legal requirements into practice, including existing tools aimed to facilitate legal-by-design development. Section 3 introduces the application domain by outlining AI-assisted screening techniques in recruitment and the key stages of state-of-the-art technical screening pipelines, situating the regulatory analysis within a concrete deployment context. Section 4 presents the core contribution of the paper, namely the HR-RAI toolkit. It details the checklist of techno-normative requirements and guiding questions that translate Articles 9–15 and Annex IV into actionable legal-by-design questions, and, in Section 4.1, presents a simplified example of how the toolkit can be used in practice by providers. In Section 4.2, we also discuss informational gaps along the AI value chain, highlighting how operational compliance is shaped by structural asymmetries when downstream providers integrate third-party GPAI models. Finally, Section 5 concludes by summarising the contribution, outlining the main limitations, and indicating directions for future work, including empirical and quantitative evaluation.

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
papers.abstract: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

papers.intro:
Minimum sum-of-squares clustering (MSSC) is a fundamental problem in data analysis that has attracted extensive research in mathematical optimization and computer science. Given a set of observations and a prescribed number of clusters, MSSC seeks a partition that minimizes the sum of squared Euclidean distances from each observation to the centroid of its cluster. Classical kk-means procedures approach this problem by alternating assignment and centroid updates [MacQueen, 1967, Hartigan and Wong, 1979, Lloyd, 1982]. Although computationally efficient, these procedures depend on initialization and provide no guarantee of global optimality.

Clustering is typically formulated as an unsupervised learning task, but applications often provide partial information about the desired partition. Pairwise must-link (ML) and cannot-link (CL) constraints offer a simple way to incorporate this knowledge: an ML constraint requires two observations to belong to the same cluster, whereas a CL constraint requires them to belong to different clusters. Because these relations do not require complete class labels, they are among the most widely studied forms of supervision in constrained clustering [González-Almagro et al., 2025]. MSSC is NP-hard even without pairwise constraints [Aloise et al., 2009, Mahajan et al., 2012]. Heuristic methods can quickly produce feasible solutions to problem (1), but their objective values provide only upper bounds on the global optimum. Certifying how close these solutions are to optimality also requires strong lower bounds. Exact methods provide such bounds, but their computational cost limits their applicability to large instances. Obtaining tight optimality certificates at this scale therefore remains challenging.

[2027] proposed a decomposition approach that partitions the dataset into smaller, tractable subsets and sums the optimal values of the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a valid lower bound for the original problem. An auxiliary optimization problem guides the decomposition by constructing internally heterogeneous subsets, called anticlusters, that reproduce the geometric structure of the full dataset. Extending this approach to pairwise-constrained MSSC is not immediate since geometric representativeness alone is insufficient in this case: the decomposition must also preserve the pairwise constraints. Indeed, if the points involved in a pairwise constraint are assigned to different anticlusters, that constraint is neglected. Although the resulting decomposition can still provide a valid lower bound, omitting constraints enlarges the subproblem feasible regions and can weaken the bound.

An auxiliary optimization problem guides the decomposition by constructing internally heterogeneous subsets, called anticlusters, that reproduce the geometric structure of the full dataset. Extending this approach to pairwise-constrained MSSC is not immediate since geometric representativeness alone is insufficient in this case: the decomposition must also preserve the pairwise constraints. Indeed, if the points involved in a pairwise constraint are assigned to different anticlusters, that constraint is neglected. Although the resulting decomposition can still provide a valid lower bound, omitting constraints enlarges the subproblem feasible regions and can weaken the bound.

In this paper, we develop a decomposition framework for computing strong lower bounds and certified optimality gaps for MSSC with pairwise constraints. We show that the optimality gap is given by the sum of two terms: the first arises from decomposing the original problem into independent subproblems, whereas the second results from using the available subproblem lower bounds in place of their exact optimal values. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP). CAP represents the pairwise constraints through an undirected graph and assigns each connected component to a single anticluster, ensuring that every constraint is retained in exactly one induced subproblem. Its objective promotes geometric representativeness relative to a feasible reference clustering, while cardinality constraints control subproblem sizes. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program (MISOCP) and develop a variable neighborhood search (VNS) heuristic to construct high-quality feasible partitions. Valid lower bounds for the induced clustering subproblems are then computed using a specialized exact solver. We evaluate the framework on synthetic and real-world constrained instances with up to 4,1774{,}177 observations. The experiments examine the trade-off between decomposition quality and subproblem tractability, compare VNS with direct MISOCP optimization, and assess the effect of preserving CL constraints. Extensive experiments show that the proposed framework achieves a mean optimality gap below 1%1\%, with mean total running times below 1010 minutes, providing near-optimality guarantees for feasible solutions to large-scale constrained MSSC.

papers.title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
papers.abstract:
Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed.
  Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

papers.intro:
Coding-agent benchmarks give an AI agent programming tasks and score whether it solves them. They are the main way to measure and compare the capabilities of coding agents. Researchers use the scores to track progress and to direct further work, and companies use them to decide which model to deploy. The tasks ask the agent to write code, produce files, or change an environment. A benchmark is useful only if its scores reflect how well the agent completes these tasks. If the agent can alter the grading process or obtain protected evaluation information, such as the expected answers, it may receive credit for work it has not done. In DeepSWE’s abs-stepped-slices task, for example, the agent must extend a small scripting language so that "abcdef"[::2] returns "ace". The tests hold the expected value "ace", and the agent is not meant to see them. An agent that reads them anyway can hard-code the value without implementing the feature. In another case, an agent replaces a download utility in a Terminal-Bench task. The test setup later calls this utility, and it installs a modified test runner. That runner reports success whether or not the task was solved [1]. We therefore treat benchmarking agents as adversarial measurement [2]. The agent being measured can tamper with the infrastructure that measures it.

papers.title: Mammalian gonadal development: origins, specification and differentiation of ovary and testis cell lineages
papers.abstract: Testicular and ovarian development requires the coordinated formation and assembly of multiple cell types that enable these organs to fulfill their roles in sexual differentiation, reproduction, and endocrine function. A defining feature of gonadal development is that both testes and ovaries arise from a common bipotential primordium, the genital ridge, composed of multipotent progenitors. In this Review, we synthesize current knowledge on the origin, specification, differentiation, and function of the major fetal gonadal somatic lineages, drawing primarily on mouse and human studies. We describe how the adrenogonadal primordium (AGP) gives rise to the gonadal primordium (GP), how coelomic epithelium-derived progenitors generate the supporting, steroidogenic/stromal, and supporting-like cell lineages, and how these progenitors become progressively fate-restricted. We highlight recent evidence for early lineage priming within spatially organized domains of the coelomic epithelium. We further examine the molecular pathways and cellular processes governing sex-specific differentiation of these lineages and discuss remaining gaps in our understanding of how bipotential gonads differentiate into testes or ovaries, and their implication for human health.

papers.title: Sharp Last-Iterate Bounds for the Stochastic subGradient Method
papers.abstract: We determine the worst-case expected optimization error of the last iterate of constant-stepsize projected Stochastic subGradient Method on convex Lipschitz objectives. The upper and lower bounds match up to universal constants for every stepsize, horizon, dimension, and conditional noise moment of order $p\in[1,\infty]$. With bounded noise and a fixed positive bound on the initial distance to a minimizer, the best constant stepsize gives worst-case error after $n$ iterates of order $1/\sqrt n$ on the line and $\sqrt{\log n/(n\log\log n)}$ in every fixed dimension at least two.

papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Ultra-Low-Bit Inference on LLM Accelerators
papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ) enables ultra-low-bit compression of large language models (LLMs) by encoding groups of values as compact codebook indexes. However, reconstructing these values for computation requires frequent codebook lookups, which conflict with the dataflows of conventional LLM accelerators and limit the performance gains from VQ compression. Consequently, prior work has resorted to VQ-specific accelerator designs, which either incur substantial additional hardware overhead or support only a limited range of inference scenarios. In this work, we argue that existing systolic-array-based LLM accelerators already possess the essential hardware resources for efficient VQ inference, but lack the mechanisms to effectively exploit them. To bridge this gap, we present VQACC, an architectural enhancement that jointly redesigns the existing operand buffer's access logic and data mapping to reuse its storage and port resources for codebook lookups, seamlessly integrating dequantization into the normal operand-addressing dataflow. Evaluation shows that VQACC achieves a 2.63$\times$ speedup over the EVA baseline, with additional hardware occupying only 0.17\% of the compute array's area.

papers.intro:
The success of large language models (LLMs) in language understanding and generation places increasing demands on hardware memory capacity and bandwidth [14, 37, 18, 22]. LLM inference stores large model weights and key–value (KV) caches that retain information from previously processed tokens. KV caches grow with context length and the number of concurrent requests, and both weights and KV caches must be accessed repeatedly during token generation. Quantization represents these data with fewer bits, reducing transfers and allowing larger models and longer contexts within a given memory budget [23, 9, 11, 12, 13].

Vector quantization (VQ) extends this opportunity to ultra-low-bit inference with 4-bit or lower precision per value. Unlike commonly used element-wise quantization, which compresses each value independently, VQ jointly represents a group of values as a vector. It learns a shared codebook of representative vectors and replaces each original vector with the low-bit index of its closest representative (Fig. 1(a)). The index thus encodes the pattern across multiple elements, exploiting their correlations to preserve information that independent quantization loses. For LLMs, VQ can achieve higher accuracy than element-wise quantization at an effective precision of 4-bit per value, or retain comparable accuracy at 2-bit [8, 30, 34], and some methods even achieve 1-bit compression [2]. Element-wise quantization, in contrast, is commonly limited to 4-bit by substantial accuracy loss at lower bit widths [19, 15, 20]. This improved accuracy–compression tradeoff makes VQ attractive for ultra-low-bit LLM inference.

As Fig. 1(b) shows, VQ introduces dequantization before LLM matrix computations, retrieving vectors from codebooks using their indexes. Commercial accelerators handle these frequent lookups poorly, which erodes the expected speedup from VQ: some VQ operators even run slower than their FP16 counterparts [23, 7]. Specialized accelerators for VQ-based LLMs address this problem at the cost of additional hardware or limited applicability. Vortex builds a custom dequantization pipeline with units such as additional codebook buffers and lookup staging buffers, which incurs expensive hardware overhead [27]. EVA bypasses conventional dequantization through a mathematical transformation, but supports VQ only for model weights, with benefits concentrated in small-batch LLM decoding [7].

papers.title: Show Me the Answer: Visual Grounding on Dashboards
papers.abstract: Natural language interaction has become an increasingly important paradigm for accessing complex visual information systems. In visual data analytics environments, such as dashboards, a key capability is to ground user queries to specific visual elements, enabling systems to identify the visual evidence relevant to the query. However, existing visual grounding research has primarily focused on natural images, while grounding in dashboards remains underexplored due to their complex multi-chart layouts and fine-grained visual elements. In this paper, we study the task of Visual Grounding on Dashboards (VGD): Given a dashboard screenshot and a natural language query, the goal is to localize the visual element corresponding to the query using a bounding box. We propose VGD-Net, a two-stage grounding framework that reflects how users typically locate information in dashboards, by first performing query-aware chart retrieval and then fine-grained in-chart grounding. To systematically evaluate VGD-Net's performance on this task, we construct VGD-Bench, a benchmark specifically designed for VGD, covering three complementary settings: chart retrieval, in-chart grounding, and overall VGD. Experimental results show that our two-stage VGD-Net outperforms strong multimodal baselines on the VGD task, achieving a mean IoU of 57.06 and a success rate of 66.82, while also delivering superior performance over existing methods in both stages of chart retrieval and in-chart grounding. These results highlight the value of stage decomposition for reliable and interpretable VGD, and its potential to support query-driven visual analysis.

A fundamental task in such environments is to locate elements relevant to analysis (e.g., locating the highest bar in a chart). By achieving VGD, we aim to improve the overall visual data analysis from three aspects. First, VGD improves interpretability by providing explicit visual references for predicted answers. Grounding relevant visual elements establishes clear correspondence between textual queries and structured visual information, making model outputs more transparent and trustworthy [52]. Second, it can further facilitate semantic alignment, as prior work [57, 41] suggests that grounding relevant elements could improve the performance of reasoning tasks by enabling models to focus on the correct visual evidence. Finally, VGD also enhances accessibility by enabling more flexible interaction processes in interactive visual analytics environments. By supporting flexible natural language inputs, users can directly express their analytical intent for efficient information localization, which in turn facilitates downstream interactions such as selection and filtering [35], and further supports diverse multi-user collaborative scenarios with mixed input modalities.

While visual grounding (VG) has been extensively studied in natural images [46], dashboards differ fundamentally in their visual and structural characteristics, making VGD non-trivial. Dashboards are structured collections of charts and visual elements with explicit spatial relationships. Multiple charts of the same type and style often co-exist and are arranged in a regular layout across the dashboard, while visual elements within each chart (e.g., bars) can appear highly similar. Existing VG methods fail to exploit this structured layout while handling visual similarity across charts and elements. In addition, VGD is driven by analysis-oriented queries that refer to chart content rather than isolated objects, further increasing the difficulty of VGD [4].

When human users locate visual elements in a visual information system, they naturally exploit the underlying hierarchical structure [40, 15]: first identifying the relevant chart and then focusing on visual elements within it. Inspired by this strategy, we propose VGD-Net, a two-stage framework that decomposes VGD into chart retrieval and in-chart grounding, enabling structured and query-driven reasoning over dashboards. To align linguistic semantics with this decomposition, VGD-Net reformulates each user query into stage-specific sub-queries [18], namely a chart-retrieval query and an in-chart grounding query, which capture different levels of intent and inform the grounding process. In Stage I, VGD-Net performs query-aware chart retrieval by detecting candidate charts and ranking them based on their relevance to the chart-level query, effectively narrowing down the search space. In Stage II, conditioned on the selected chart, VGD-Net employs multi-level cross-modal features to localize the fine-grained query element.

papers.title: The Complexity of Fair and Stable Data Exchange
papers.abstract: Data exchange is a fundamental challenge for Web applications such as recommender systems, personalized search, and fraud detection, where combining data across participants can improve predictions. Sustaining such collaboration requires fair returns for contributions and protection against groups leaving for a more beneficial exchange. These requirements are captured by reciprocity, which equates each participant's received utility with its credited contribution to others, and core stability, which rules out any coalition exchanging its own data to make every member strictly better off. Akrami et al. prove that such exchanges exist under broad assumptions, but leave efficient computation open. Two fundamental cases are submodular utilities, capturing diminishing returns from overlapping datasets, and supermodular utilities, capturing complementarities. We settle the approximate computation of reciprocal and core-stable exchanges in both cases, establishing a computational separation under Shapley sharing. For cross-monotone shares, which include Shapley shares under monotone submodular utilities, we give a circulation algorithm that computes an exactly core-stable, $\epsilon$-reciprocal exchange in time poly$(n,1/\epsilon,L)$ given efficient access to approximate shares, where $n$ is the number of participants and $L$ bounds how fast each donor's credit changes with its own contribution. This yields an FPTAS when $L$ is polynomially bounded. In contrast, finding an $\epsilon$-reciprocal, $\epsilon$-core-stable exchange is PPAD-hard for monotone lattice-supermodular utilities, even at inverse-polynomial accuracy, with constant $L$ and exact polynomial-time evaluation of Shapley shares. Thus overlapping information permits efficient fair and stable exchange, while complementarities create a computational barrier even when contribution credits are easy to evaluate.

papers.intro:
Data fuels modern AI and machine learning: access to large, informative datasets has enabled advances in statistical learning and Web applications [HNP09]. Much of this data is distributed across organizations, making exchanges of useful data valuable to participants with different learning tasks. Yet a data-exchange platform cannot rely on the benefits of collaboration alone. Data holders expect a return commensurate with their contributions [OEC19], and lack of reciprocity has been documented as a barrier to sharing public-health data [vPE+14]. We study data exchange without monetary transfers, where each agent’s utility depends on the data it receives from others. Following Bhaskara et al. [BGI+24] and Akrami et al. [ACGM25], we require an exchange to satisfy reciprocity: each agent’s received utility equals the credit it earns through its contributions to others. Reciprocity alone permits the trivial outcome in which no data is shared. We therefore also require core stability: no coalition can strictly improve every member’s utility by exchanging its own data internally. Such a deviating exchange need not itself satisfy reciprocity.

papers.title: Length and Sequence-Dependent Dipolar and Electronic Properties of $\alpha$-helical Polypeptides
papers.abstract: Helical polypeptides combine the chemical tunability of synthetic macromolecules with the highly ordered backbone architecture of natural proteins. Here, density-functional tight-binding calculations are used to determine how chain length and sequence chemistry govern the dipolar and electronic properties of three $\alpha$-helical polypeptide families: polyalanine [AAAAA]$_n$, leucine-modified [AAAAL]$_n$, and cysteine-capped, lysine-containing C[AAAAK]$_n$. Increasing chain length produces systematic shifts and splitting of the molecular orbital levels together with an approximately additive increase in the molecular dipole. Analysis of the C[AAAAK]$_3$ helix shows that aligned backbone carbonyl groups provide the dominant contribution to the macro dipole, whose growing electrostatic potential is consistent with an intrinsic Stark-like contribution to the length-dependent orbital-energy evolution. Side-chain and terminal modifications introduce localized perturbations to frontier electronic states while preserving this global backbone-driven trend. Residue-resolved frontier levels additionally form a staircase-like energy landscape along the helical scaffold: individual peptide units retain large local HOMO-LUMO gaps of approximately 5 eV, whereas spatially proximate hydrogen-bonded residues exhibit smaller inter-residue energy separations. Application of external electrostatic fields modifies the frontier-level separation in a direction-dependent manner and induces structural distortions predominantly near the flexible termini, while the helical core remains comparatively robust. By establishing these fundamental sequence-structure-property relationships, this work provides a foundational blueprint for the rational design of peptide-based biomacromolecules tailored for next-generation bio-electronic interfaces, biosensors, and artificial electron-transfer systems.

papers.intro:
α\alpha-helical peptides have emerged as versatile building blocks for biological and biomimetic functional materials because they combine a structurally persistent hydrogen-bonded scaffold with sequence-level chemical programmability and sensitivity to their molecular environment [1, 2]. Their ordered architectures support functions ranging from molecular recognition and self-assembly to charge transfer, molecular electronics, and field-responsive behavior [3, 4, 5, 6]. This combination of structural resilience and chemical adaptability makes the α\alpha-helix an attractive platform for constructing sequence-defined functional materials. First described by Pauling, Corey, and Branson in 1951, the α\alpha-helix is also distinguished by a collective electrostatic property: the vectorial alignment of individual peptide-bond dipoles, each on the order of 3–4 D, generates a substantial macrodipole along the helical axis [7, 8, 9]. High-resolution crystallographic analyses further indicate that peptide bonds within α\alpha-helices display a subtly enhanced enol-like character compared with those in β\beta-strands, providing a more detailed picture of peptide-bond electronic structure within the helical environment [10]. The resulting collective dipole gives rise to a substantial internal electric field that influences protein function, including active-site electrostatics, ligand binding, and the p​KapK_{a} shifts of terminal residues [8, 11].

papers.title: Vanishing bond-percolation threshold implies vanishing contact-process threshold
papers.abstract: We show that for any infinite, locally finite and connected graph $G$ and $p\in(0,1/2]$ the survival probability of the contact process with infection rate $\lambda\ge20p$ is at least $3/4$ times the bond percolation probability with retention probability $p$. In particular, $\lambda_c(G)\le20\,p_c(G)$ whenever $p_c(G)<1/2$, and $p_c(G)=0$ implies $\lambda_c(G)=0$. The proof uses a submartingale built from percolation clusters on finite balls. We contrast this with the SIR epidemic, in which every vertex is infected at most once, and for which there are graphs with $p_c(G)=0$ on which the SIR epidemic dies out almost surely for every infection rate.

papers.title: Pure Orbitronics: Hall Responses and Torques by Orbital Exchange in Spinless Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides
papers.abstract: Recent studies have identified orbital exchange fields as a novel mechanism for controlling electronic and magnetic phenomena through the orbital degree of freedom. In contrast to conventional spin exchange fields, orbital exchange fields couple directly to orbital angular momentum and can emerge from purely orbital interactions or dynamically through couplings to chiral excitations such as phonons and magnons. Motivated by these developments, we investigate the transport and torque responses generated by orbital exchange fields in two-dimensional materials. Using monolayer H-phase MoS$_2$ as a prototypical transition-metal dichalcogenide, we introduce a Zeeman-like orbital exchange field that breaks time-reversal symmetry in orbital space while leaving the spin degree of freedom inactive. We demonstrate that this perturbation induces a sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity even in the absence of spin magnetism and spin--orbit coupling driven mechanisms. Simultaneously, the orbital Hall response remains robust in the weak-field regime and undergoes substantial reconstruction at larger exchange strengths due to pronounced band modifications. In addition, we show that currents can generate sizable current-induced orbital torques on the orbital magnetization. Our results establish orbital exchange fields as an effective route toward Hall transport and nonequilibrium torque phenomena driven purely by orbital physics, opening new perspectives for orbitronics and orbitally engineered quantum functionalities.

papers.title: MoHA: Model-Conditioned Harness Adaptation for Long-Video Agents
papers.abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.

papers.intro:
Long-video understanding remains challenging not only because videos contain far more visual content than can be processed densely, but also because useful evidence is sparse and unevenly distributed over time. Recent methods therefore increasingly move beyond processing a fixed video representation and instead actively decide what evidence to acquire and how to acquire it. Some methods adaptively select frames or regions during reasoning (He et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026), while external video agents use retrieval, memory, navigation, and perceptual tools to inspect videos on demand (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b; Yin et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). As a result, long-video performance increasingly depends not only on the underlying models, but also on the execution harness that coordinates reasoning, evidence acquisition, and perception.

Existing agentic long-video systems typically pair a model stack with a prescribed execution pipeline that specifies the planner’s reasoning support, the routing of perceptual requests, and the processing of video evidence. Recent work has shown that the computation surrounding frozen models can itself be optimized (Zhang et al., 2026). However, improving a harness for one model stack does not establish whether the resulting design is equally well suited to others. A natural alternative is to expose all available capabilities to every stack, but this still leaves the harness model-agnostic and does not account for which forms of reasoning support or perception each stack can use effectively. Planners may differ in how effectively they search for, retain, integrate, and verify evidence, while observers may differ in which perceptual requests they handle reliably and which execution configurations they benefit from. These differences motivate adapting the harness not only to the task, but also to the reasoning and perceptual capabilities of the models it hosts (see Figure 1).

papers.title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
papers.abstract: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. Consequently, fingerprint distances alone provide an incomplete basis for model identity, and identification typically relies on a classifier trained jointly on fingerprints from many checkpoints. We propose DistDNA, which represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions and compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). The model under examination is assigned to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints, collected at several decoding settings, lie nearest to its own, without training a classifier. We show that finite sampling adds variance-dependent terms to the expected squared fingerprint distance, with these terms decreasing as $O(1/R)$ for equal response counts, where $R$ is the number of responses per prompt. Experiments across 115 model checkpoint entries demonstrate that DistDNA improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by 10.36%.

papers.title: Operative Representation of Quasi-Arithmetic Means, Complex Branch Structure, and Covariant Commutator Defects in Iterated Logarithmic Operation Hierarchies
papers.abstract: We investigate the bidirectional family of commutative binary operations $\mathrm{Op}_m^{(a)}[x,y] = f_a^{(-m)}(f_a^{(m)}(x) + f_a^{(m)}(y))$ ($m \in \mathbb{Z}$) generated by iterating the scaled logarithmic Cauchy isomorphism $f_a(z) = \frac{1}{a}\ln(z)$ ($a > 0$). Our analysis focuses on three structural properties of this hierarchy. First, we show that for all $m \ge -1$ the associated quasi-arithmetic Kolmogorov-Nagumo means $S_{\mathrm{Op}_m}(\mathbf{x})$ admit a closed two-stage operative representation $S_{\mathrm{Op}_m}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{Op}_{m+1}^{(a)}[\mathrm{Op}_m^{(a)}[\mathbf{x}], N_{\mathrm{Op}_{m+1}}(n)]$ with normalization factor $N_{\mathrm{Op}_{m+1}}(n) = f_a^{(-m)}(1/n)$, and prove that this internal operative normalizability via a distributive adjacent level characterizes logarithmic generators among continuously conjugated group operations. Second, we show that for $m \le -2$ and $n \ge 2$ the normalization factor leaves the positive real domain $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, motivating the analytic continuation onto the Riemann surface of the logarithm; there, a fundamental dichotomy emerges between the internal branch-index invariance of $\mathrm{Op}_{-1}^{(a)}$ and the associativity defect $\omega(x,z)$ generated by $\mathrm{Op}_2^{(a)}$. Third, for arbitrary levels $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and sample sizes $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we derive the general covariance pushforward theorem $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{Op}_{m+1}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = f_a^{(-m)}(\mathrm{Cov}(f_a^{(m)}(\mathbf{x}), f_a^{(m)}(\mathbf{y})))$ governing the commutator defect between mean formation and the adjacent operation.

papers.title: The Manhattan cospectrality of the cocktail party graph
papers.abstract: For a graph $G$ of order $N$ with adjacency eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}(G)\geq \cdots\geq\lambda_{N}(G),$ the cospectrality of $G$ is the smallest value of $\sum_{i}\left\vert \lambda_{i}(G)-\lambda_{i}(H)\right\vert $ over all graphs $H$ of order $N$ not isomorphic to $G.$ Abdollahi and Zakeri (Ars Math. Contemp. 22(1) (2022) P1.06) conjectured that the cospectrality of the cocktail party graph $CP_{n}$ is attained exactly at the graph $H_{n}.$ This graph is obtained from $K_{1,2,\ldots,2}$ by attaching a pendant vertex to the vertex of the part of size one. We prove this conjecture for every $n\geq2$ by showing that only three explicit graphs (two for $n=2$) are at distance less than $2$ from $CP_{n}.$ We work with the complement of a competing graph. First we remove its components $K_{2}.$ Then we treat the case in which its main component has a dominating vertex. The remaining cases are reduced to finitely many small graphs. The proof is computer-assisted, and all computations concern explicit finite lists of graphs.

papers.title: Information-Criterion-Driven, Non-linear Deprojection of Angular Imaging Systematics for the SPHEREx Galaxy Clustering Sample
papers.abstract: Imaging systematics that inject false, or suppress true, galaxy clustering signals are of primary concern for current- and next-generation galaxy surveys, such as the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) in its search for local primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}$. As statistical errors shrink with growing galaxy samples, systematic rather than statistical uncertainties come to dominate the cosmological error budget. For effects whose spatial patterns are known or well-modelled \emph{a priori}, a common mitigation approach regresses (deprojects) the density variation associated with a known angular template. In this work we present and demonstrate novel aspects of this procedure as will be applied to the SPHEREx galaxy clustering sample. These include flexible -- but, crucially, constrained and interpretable -- non-linear basis regression with polynomial/spline bases, and aggressive information criterion-driven automated template selection with an associated unbiased two-stage regression, using agreement between two independent selectors as a consistency diagnostic. The method automatically selects a template set of minimal-but-sufficient complexity while limiting the number of templates actually regressed, minimising cosmological information loss and making modern additive-plus-multiplicative approaches tractable. We demonstrate these features on SPHEREx-like lognormal mock catalogues with injected contamination of various spatial profiles, amplitudes, and levels of complexity. Principled, signal-preserving deprojection of the kind demonstrated here is a crucial step towards achieving SPHEREx's goal of $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) < 0.5$.

Current- and next-generation large-scale structure (LSS) surveys, such as DESI (Adame et al., 2025), Euclid (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025), Rubin/LSST (Ivezić et al., 2019), Roman (Eifler et al., 2021), and SPHEREx (Doré et al., 2014; Bock et al., 2026) are or soon will be revolutionising our understanding of the assembly of matter in the Universe with unprecedented statistical samples. With each increase in statistical fidelity, the onus of controlling sources of systematic uncertainty is elevated proportionally, and these unprecedented surveys therefore demand unprecedented levels of care in this regard. Large angular scales (small wavenumber kk) are where a large amount of cosmological information resides, particularly the scale-dependent bias signature of local primordial non-Gaussianity, ∝fNL/k2\propto f_{\rm NL}/k^{2} (Dalal et al., 2008; Doré et al., 2014), which is of particular interest to SPHEREx; however, these same large angular scales are those most severely afflicted by the typical imaging systematics of large-scale structure surveys.

A forced-photometry experiment, as is represented by SPHEREx’s nominal “Level 4” cosmology mission (Bock et al., 2026), may inherit effects on its galaxy selection from the reference catalogue parent surveys that define its target list (which may have sharp or discontinuous features at survey boundaries), as well as from typical astrophysical effects such as dust extinction, stellar contamination, and zodiacal emission, which generally vary smoothly on the sky, and SPHEREx’s own spectrophotometric instrumental effects and selection properties. The addition of misidentified stellar contaminants in a galaxy catalogue, for instance, or even the nigh-unavoidable effect of galaxy sample density loss in crowded stellar regions due to blends and contamination from bright stellar neighbors, will produce a strong variation of power on the large angular scales where the cosmological signal of interest is also strongest.

Various approaches to clustering systematic mitigation have been explored and employed in the past. A common technique is to simply cut the angular scales that are suspected of being contaminated (e.g., setting a strict kmink_{\rm min}) (Agarwal et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2015), which is blind to the nature of the systematic though comes at the significant cost of signal loss. More sophisticated approaches along this line seek to use information about the geometry of the survey/systematics to make more “surgical” sets of cuts (Hand et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2021; Wen et al., 2025; Bruton et al., 2026). Another approach is to forward model the signal transfer function/selection function empirically using synthetic injected sources (Everett et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2025), a technique which provides extremely high-fidelity measurements of certain effects, though is insensitive to others (astrophysical or reference catalogue-induced effects, for instance) and comes with significant computational cost.

This paper focuses on a third common approach, which relies upon contaminating effects with well-known/well-measured spatial patterns. For a contaminant whose pattern on the sky and spectral properties are known a priori, such as dust extinction or, even more cleanly, a parent survey depth pattern, one may construct a spatial template of the contaminating effect, and attempt to account for the modulation of the measured density field due to this effect directly, based on some model for how the contaminant couples to the measured field. These “template deprojection” approaches typically vary in terms of the array and type of templates used, the differing assumptions in how the model couples/is fit, and the approaches taken to mitigate or characterize cosmological signal loss.

The earliest widely used approaches along this line iterated over individual systematic template maps, assigning each galaxy a weight based on the relative contribution in that template relative to the mean density, assuming a linear coupling between the systematic and the density field (Ross et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2012). However, this assumes perfect separability and low correlation between templates (an assumption that is strongly violated by multiple effects which are themselves all correlated with the structure of the Galactic plane). Mode projection seeks to marginalize analytically over the amplitude of the template at a 2-point level (Rybicki and Press, 1992; Slosar et al., 2004; Leistedt et al., 2013; Leistedt and Peiris, 2014; Elsner et al., 2016), which is equivalent to a covariance-aware deprojection, and is still linear in the template. In their default configurations, these approaches treat every template equally as worthy of inclusion/regression, which tends to have the unintended effect of increasing signal loss directly in proportion with the number of additional templates (Elsner et al., 2016; Elsner et al., 2017). For the increasing number of effects and potential templates considered by modern surveys, this represents an increasingly tangible practical barrier.

papers.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
papers.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is typically carried out one domain at a time, since each domain comes with its own data, verifier, and environment. A common recipe is therefore to train domain experts separately from a shared base model and then consolidate them into a single model (Wang et al., 2026b, Ma et al., 2026a). Because new domains and stronger experts keep arriving, this consolidation is not a one-time step but a continual process. Ideally, each new expert would be absorbed like an installed module, such that (i) the model gains what the expert learned in its domain, (ii) everything the model could already do, in the other experts’ domains and in general, is left intact, and (iii) the cost of the update depends only on the new expert, not on how many experts came before.
