Existing approaches fall into two groups. The first consolidates all experts into a single set of weights. Joint multi-task RL must rerun RL on every domain whenever one is added. Sequential RL (Wang et al., 2026a) trains only on the new domain, but earlier gains are susceptible to irreversible damage from later stages. Weight merging (Ilharco and others, 2023, Yadav et al., 2023) combines experts by parameter arithmetic, where their updates can interfere. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) (Wang et al., 2026b, Ma et al., 2026a) must retrain the student against all teachers. All four also apply one fixed mixture to every request and overwrite the base weights, which can degrade performance outside the target domains (Wang et al., 2026c). The second group keeps experts separate and selects them per request. Expert routing depends on a router that is hard to train and must be updated whenever an expert is added, cannot combine experts within a request, and must host a full model per expert. Merging LoRA experts per request (Huang et al., 2023, Prabhakar et al., 2024) avoids these issues but adds adapter computation to every layer at every decoding step.

Both groups keep experts in model parameters. We instead make each expert part of the model’s input, and propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD) (Figure 2). During training, CSPD keeps the pre-RL model frozen and distills each post-RL expert into its own soft prompt (Lester et al., 2021) of 256 vectors, using only that expert’s verifier-filtered responses (Kim and Rush, 2016). Each soft prompt is trained independently. To prepare the prompts for later combination, half of the training examples place a random context prefix before the prompt, so that it works regardless of what precedes it. At inference, the prompts are composed directly by concatenating them in the system message, without any joint training. Adding an expert therefore requires training only its prompt, removing an expert requires only dropping its prompt, and the backbone is never modified. Unlike merged or routed LoRA experts, the prompts are plug-in modules, with no merging coefficient or router to refit when the set of experts changes.

papers.title: Deep conditional distribution estimation via nonparametric exponential tilt models
papers.abstract: Estimating the conditional distribution of a response $Y$ given covariates $X$ is a fundamental problem in statistics, underlying prediction, feature estimation, and dependence assessment. We propose a unified nonparametric representation of the conditional density, a nonparametric exponential tilt model, in which the dependence between $Y$ and $X$ is captured by an interaction function $\phi(x,y)$ while both baseline densities are left unspecified. We establish identifiability and develop a nonparametric likelihood method that profiles out the baselines by empirical likelihood, with non-asymptotic error bounds under general sieve conditions. Because the profile likelihood admits no closed-form or readily tractable population counterpart, standard empirical process arguments do not apply; we therefore establish a new exponential tail bound for the supremum of a canonical U-process under a uniform entropy condition, a result we show to be new to the U-process literature and of independent interest, with a largely self-contained proof. The framework unifies several inferential tasks: mutual density ratio and mutual information estimation; a general theory for conditional features, including means, quantiles and distribution functions, without separate smoothness assumptions on the individual conditional feature functions; and a finite-sample valid permutation test of independence. Under deep neural network sieves, the convergence rates depend on the intrinsic complexity of $\phi$ rather than the ambient dimension. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method attains uniformly smaller estimation errors than existing conditional density and mutual density-ratio estimators, and delivers markedly higher power in independence testing when dependence is oscillatory or high-dimensional, while remaining comparable to established tests in standard settings.

Estimating the conditional distribution of a response 𝐘{\bf Y} given a covariate vector 𝐗{\bf X} lies at the heart of statistical inference: it underpins prediction, classification, and the principled quantification of dependence between random variables. The classical approach is parametric, and the most widely used parametric framework is the generalized linear model (GLM) of [39]; see [37] for a comprehensive treatment. For a scalar response YY, a GLM assumes that the conditional density of YY given 𝐗=𝐱{\bf X}={\bf x} belongs to a one-parameter exponential family, f⁡(y∣𝐱)=f∗​(y)​exp⁡{y​θ​(𝐱)−ψ⁡(θ⁡(𝐱))},f(y\mid{\bf x})=f_{*}(y)\exp\{y\,\theta({\bf x})-\psi(\theta({\bf x}))\}, (1) where f∗f_{*} is a specified baseline (carrier) density, θ⁡(𝐱)\theta({\bf x}) is the natural parameter, and ψ(θ)=log∫ey​θf∗(y)dy\psi(\theta)=\log\int e^{y\theta}f_{*}(y)\,dy is the cumulant function that normalizes the density. The natural parameter is tied to the covariates through a linear predictor, θ⁡(𝐱)=η⁡(𝐱⊤​β)\theta({\bf x})=\eta({\bf x}^{\top}\beta), for a known function η\eta. When η\eta is the identity, so that θ⁡(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​β\theta({\bf x})={\bf x}^{\top}\beta, the model uses the canonical link: the conditional mean μ⁡(𝐱)=ψ′​(θ⁡(𝐱))\mu({\bf x})=\psi^{\prime}(\theta({\bf x})) then satisfies g⁡(μ)=𝐱⊤​βg(\mu)={\bf x}^{\top}\beta with g=(ψ′)−1g=(\psi^{\prime})^{-1}. Familiar special cases include the linear model with normal f∗f_{*} and identity link, logistic regression with Bernoulli f∗f_{*} and logit link, Poisson regression with log link, and Gamma regression with reciprocal link. Model (1) therefore imposes two parametric restrictions: a known baseline f∗f_{*} and a linear (or index) form for the natural parameter.

First, they are developed primarily for a scalar response YY and may not directly apply to a multivariate response 𝐘{\bf Y}. When the response is multivariate, the exponential-family specification in (1) becomes difficult to formulate or justify, and the density ratio and proportional likelihood ratio models require a multivariate baseline whose specification and profiling pose substantial challenges; moreover, the index structure 𝐱⊤​β{\bf x}^{\top}\beta is generally too restrictive to capture the dependence between a covariate vector and a multivariate response. Second, these approaches still impose structural assumptions on the conditional density or distribution of the response: the first direction retains a parametric baseline f∗f_{*}, while the second retains a linear index structure. Whenever the true conditional distribution deviates from these assumptions, the resulting estimators can be biased and the associated inference unreliable. A misspecified model may yield distorted estimates of conditional densities, invalid standard errors and confidence intervals, and misleading conclusions about the relationship between 𝐗{\bf X} and 𝐘{\bf Y}, errors that can propagate into downstream scientific decisions. These considerations motivate a fully data-driven formulation that avoids such restrictions whenever possible and lets the data determine the form of the conditional distribution.

papers.title: SOP Sensing in Hollow-Core Fiber: Forward Sensing using COTS Transponder and Localization with Coherent OTDR
papers.abstract: We experimentally investigate and compare distributed state-of-polarization sensing in support-tube hollow-core and standard single-mode fiber. Despite significantly weaker Rayleigh backscattering and reduced polarization sensitivity in hollow-core fiber, polarization perturbations remain observable and spatially localizable, demonstrating the feasibility of SOP-based distributed sensing in hollow-core fiber

papers.title: Karcher means of structured matrices are asymptotically structured: a study via Schatten estimates for the additive Richardson iteration
papers.abstract: In the present work, we first study the additive Richardson iteration for the Karcher mean of complex Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrix sequences, by obtaining normalized Schatten estimates independent of the matrix dimension. These estimates are used to prove that Karcher means of structured matrices are asymptotically structured and this is proven for input HPD Toeplitz and generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix sequences. More precisely, we provide the a.c.s. approximation, which is the key for demonstrating the GLT closure under Schatten spectral bounds, and the GLT conclusion can be extended to matrix sequences with symbols that are positive definite almost everywhere. Ad hoc numerical experiments illustrate the spectral distribution consequences of these results and few related computational advantages. Concluding remarks and open problems are provided in the final section.

At a fixed matrix size, the Karcher mean can be obtained as the limit of an iteration. While straightforward GLT calculus [12, 13, 6, 7] can identify the symbol of any iterate (see the introduction of [2] and [15, 16]), we need precise information on the Schatten norm asymptotics to conclude the closure of the limit. The normalized Schatten estimates in this paper provide this control. More precisely, under uniform spectral bounds on the input sequences and the initial matrix, the iterates remain in the prescribed interval and satisfy normalized Schatten estimates independent of the matrix dimension. The proposed proof controls the second derivative along the affine segment of the additive step. Ando, Li and Mathias [3] formulated an axiomatic list of properties for multivariate matrix geometric means and it is the basis of our analysis. The Riemannian approach developed by Moakher [21] and Bhatia and Holbrook [8] defines the mean as the minimizer of a sum of squared distances on the positive definite cone. Lawson and Lim [17] proved monotonicity of this least-squares mean and later treated positive definite operators through the Karcher equation [18]. Lim and Pálfia [19] obtained the Karcher mean as a limit of matrix power means; their subsequent work gives existence and uniqueness for probability measures with a finite first moment [20].

papers.title: Large 4-tangles in matroids are characterized by large internally 4-connected minors
papers.abstract: Tangles were first introduced by Robertson and Seymour as an abstract way of treating highly connected substructures in graphs and matroids. For any truly highly connected substructure in a graph or matroid, all of the low-order separations in the object can be oriented towards it. This gives rise to a tangle. A standard question is whether every tangle of a given order in fact arises from some concrete highly connected substructure, such as a minor. It is well known that tangles of order two and three (in both graphs and matroids) are characterized by maximal $2$-connected and $3$-connected minors, respectively. For tangles of order four, it is necessary to consider a weaker notion of connectivity. Carmesin and Kurkofka showed that, for graphs, internal $4$-connectedness suffices. For matroids, Brettell, Jowett, Oxley, Semple and Whittle showed that $4$-tangles arise from weakly $4$-connected minors, that is, minors in which every $3$-separation has a side with at most four elements. In the latter case, the breadth of the tangle (a measure of its complexity) can be preserved exactly, but the authors also asked whether a stronger notion of $4$-connectivity could be used while preserving some fraction of the breadth. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative by showing that, in a matroid, any $4$-tangle of sufficiently large breadth is determined by an internally $4$-connected minor whose unique $4$-tangle also has large breadth.

papers.title: Finite propagation speed for evolutionary equations
papers.abstract: We study finite speed of propagation in the framework of evolutionary equations introduced by Rainer Picard in 2009. We establish sufficient conditions on the material law, which is represented by an analytic and bounded operator-valued function, and the unbounded spatial operator that ensure finite speed of propagation of information for solutions. Assuming a linear-in-frequency coercivity bound for spatially local material laws, we prove propagation on backward light cones for weighted $L_2$ solutions without a finite initial time, thus identifying hyperbolic-type evolutionary equations. The characteristic-speed threshold depends on the coercive coefficient and the principal spatial matrices, but not on bounded memory or delay terms or potential positive fractional temporal contributions. We illustrate the result with the scalar wave equation, Maxwell's equations, a fractional model in elasticity, and dual-phase-lag thermoelasticity.

papers.intro:
Finite propagation speed is a fundamental feature of hyperbolic evolution equations: a disturbance can affect another spatial point only after a positive amount of time. In the classical wave equation, Maxwell’s equations and elastodynamics, this property is expressed by a domain of dependence, or equivalently by a forward or backward region of influence. It provides information beyond temporal causality. Whereas causality excludes a dependence on the future, finite propagation additionally restricts the spatial locations from which a solution can be influenced within a given time interval. For a forced equation, the appropriate statement concerns spacetime: if the forcing vanishes on a backward light cone, then so does the solution.

In the classical wave equation, Maxwell’s equations and elastodynamics, this property is expressed by a domain of dependence, or equivalently by a forward or backward region of influence. It provides information beyond temporal causality. Whereas causality excludes a dependence on the future, finite propagation additionally restricts the spatial locations from which a solution can be influenced within a given time interval. For a forced equation, the appropriate statement concerns spacetime: if the forcing vanishes on a backward light cone, then so does the solution.

The distinction between finite and infinite propagation also arises in models of transport and heat conduction. Fourier’s heat equation has an instantaneous spatial influence, while the telegraph-type processes studied by Goldstein [12] and the relaxation of Fourier’s law proposed by Cattaneo [6] lead to finite-speed models. Gurtin and Pipkin [14] developed a theory of heat conduction with memory and finite wave speeds; see also the subsequent treatment of material response functions by Finn and Wheeler [9]. Further developments include frame-indifferent formulations of Maxwell–Cattaneo heat conduction [8], random-walk descriptions [16], and thermoelastic models with finite wave speeds [15]. For nonlocal models the situation is more varied: finite as well as infinite propagation can occur, depending on the constitutive and spatial operators; see, for instance, [3, 32, 23, 7, 31].

papers.title: Feasibility of Multifrequency Neural Network-Based Wave Inversion in Ultrasound Time-Harmonic Elastography
papers.abstract:
Ultrasound time-harmonic elastography (THE) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft-tissue stiffness. Relying on the same principle of time-harmonic shear wave excitation as established magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), THE offers full field-of-view stiffness mapping at short acquisition times and sub-second temporal resolution across organs. However, reconstruction of shear wave speed maps from acquired tissue wavefields remains challenging due to speckle noise and sparse spatial coverage of the lateral component.
  Deep learning methods have shown promising results for image reconstruction in transient-based ultrasound elastography modalities but remain unexplored in THE. In MRE, MF-ElastoNet, a 2D multifrequency neural network-based wave reconstruction method trained on synthetic physics-based wave data, has shown high generalizability across dynamic ranges and resolutions.
  We investigated the potential of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion for THE, by performing a first feasibility analysis. To this end, we adapted the processing pipeline of MF-ElastoNet from MRE to THE. We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

papers.intro:
Ultrasound elastography is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft tissue stiffness [16]. Already standard of care in the staging of liver fibrosis [21], ultrasound elastography is widely evaluated and validated in tumor characterization [18], including focal liver lesions [19] and thyroid nodules [18], as well as in chronic diseases, including chronic kidney disease [18] and heart failure [14].

Ultrasound elastography is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft tissue stiffness [16]. Already standard of care in the staging of liver fibrosis [21], ultrasound elastography is widely evaluated and validated in tumor characterization [18], including focal liver lesions [19] and thyroid nodules [18], as well as in chronic diseases, including chronic kidney disease [18] and heart failure [14].

Different types of ultrasound elastography techniques include strain imaging and shear wave imaging based on acoustic radiation force impulses (ARFI) or on continuous vibrations as in time-harmonic elastography (THE). Relatively novel THE is of particular interest as it allows a wide field-of-view (FOV), high penetration depth (up to 15 cm), millisecond temporal resolution and inherent comparability to MRE. It captures external vibrations at multiple frequencies through conventional B-Mode ultrasound at framerates of 80 to 100 Hz [10]. From the displacement wavefields obtained, a wave inversion reconstruction is performed, obtaining a shear wave speed (SWS) mapping over the full FOV as a proxy for tissue stiffness. Noise and unknown boundary conditions render this reconstruction ill-posed and highly challenging. Furthermore, state-of-the-art reconstruction methods, including the wavenumber-based multifrequency elasto-visco inversion (k-MDEV) [21] must be tuned to the acquisition settings used for different ultrasound transducers and in different organs.

Deep learning methods in ultrasound elastography have shown promising results in solving the inverse problem in strain imaging [22, 5, 4, 8, 23] and in ARFI-based elastography [9, 24]. Furthermore, in MRE, where external time-harmonic excitation is widely used, several promising approaches for deep learning-based wave inversion have been developed [15, 17, 11, 3, 1, 2]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there have as of yet been no neural network-based investigations for wave inversion in ultrasound THE.

In this work, we performed the first feasibility analysis of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion method for ultrasound THE. To this end, we adapted MF-ElastoNet [1, 2], an uncertainty-aware, multifrequency neural network-based method developed for MRE, to ultrasound THE. We tested the model on phantom datasets from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus (aMEM) Challenge [6], analyzing the ability of the model to resolve homogeneous regions of interest (ROIs) as well as inclusions of different stiffnesses. We additionally tested our approach on in vivo liver THE in both healthy volunteers and patients with focal liver lesions, including benign (focal nodular hyperplasia) and malignant (hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma) cases. In these datasets, we compared our method with k-MDEV [21], the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE.

papers.title: Elementary Factorization For Continuous Orthogonal Matrices
papers.abstract: We prove that every nullhomotopic continuous map, from a finite-dimensional normal topological space X to the complex special orthogonal group, is a product of elementary orthogonal matrices with entries in the ring of continuous functions. The number of factors is bounded by a constant depending only on the size of the matrices and the covering dimension of X. The same factorization result holds for nullhomotopic special orthogonal matrices with entries in a unital commutative Banach algebra.

papers.title: Boundary concentration and Pohozaev identity for the fractional p-Laplacian
papers.abstract: We prove a Pohozaev-like identity for bounded weak solutions of the fractional p-Laplace equation with a locally Lipschitz nonlinearity on bounded C^2 domains, provided that s>max{1/2-1/p,0}. We compare the weak equations for the solution and its spatial deformation to show that the first-order contribution of the energy remainder is concentrated at the boundary. The boundary term involves the weighted trace, with a coefficient expressed by an integral of the one-dimensional boundary profile.

papers.title: InterBand-EMG: A Cross-Band Foundation Model for Generalizable Hand-Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables continuous hand-pose estimation, but learning representations that generalize across users and movements remains challenging. We introduce InterBand-EMG, which combines band-specific quantization with cross-band reconstruction and structured masked code prediction to learn transferable EMG representations for hand-pose tracking. We also introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose dataset comprising 1,227.74 hand-hours from 499 users across 68 movement categories. Experiments on emg2pose and SynapMyo show that InterBand-EMG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in joint-angle accuracy across all three generalization settings on both datasets. The source code and the SynapMyo dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

papers.intro:
Continuous hand-pose estimation recovers the joint-angle trajectories that describe finger articulation during hand movements. It supports applications such as demonstration capture, teleoperation, and human–robot interaction. Vision-based approaches provide accurate hand pose estimates (Banerjee et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022), but their availability can be limited by objects occlusion and movements outside the camera’s field of view (Salter et al., 2024). Surface electromyography (sEMG) offers a complementary sensing modality: skin-mounted electrodes record electrical activity associated with muscle activation, providing information for movement decoding without requiring the hand to remain visible.

Surface electromyography (sEMG) offers a complementary sensing modality: skin-mounted electrodes record electrical activity associated with muscle activation, providing information for movement decoding without requiring the hand to remain visible.

Learning a transferable mapping from sEMG to hand pose is challenging because anatomy, electrode placement, and sensor contact vary across participants and recordings. The emg2pose benchmark provides approximately 370 hours of paired 16-channel sEMG and hand-pose data from 193 participants, with separate evaluations on held-out users, movement stages, and both (Salter et al., 2024). This benchmark establishes a basis for studying generalization in continuous pose decoding. Alongside task-supervised learning, an important question is how pretraining on EMG without pose labels can produce representations that improve subsequent pose estimation under these generalization conditions.

Self-supervised biosignal learning addresses this question through a range of prediction targets and training objectives. Some approaches first discretize continuous signals using vector-quantized (VQ) autoencoders, then learn representations by predicting masked or future codes (Jiang et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2026a; Barmpas et al., 2025). Others learn continuous representations through signal reconstruction, latent prediction, or contrastive objectives, without a separately pretrained discrete tokenizer (Yang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025). For continuous EMG-to-pose estimation, EMG-GPT predicts future codes from a frozen tokenizer and transfers the resulting representations to pose decoding (Magni et al., 2026). Its locally matched tracking evaluation reports higher mean angular errors than the supervised vEMG2Pose baseline across all three generalization splits, although the models retain different input-processing pipelines. These findings motivate further investigation of how EMG pretraining targets influence downstream pose estimation.

Frequency-aware tokenization offers one way to structure these targets. Surface EMG reflects the superposition of action potentials from multiple motor units, with spectral characteristics influenced by muscle properties, tissue filtering, and electrode configuration (Muceli and Merletti, 2024). Allocating separate codebooks to different frequency bands may help retain signal features that a single broadband vocabulary underrepresents. BandVQ follows this principle for EEG by training an independent VQ-VAE tokenizer for each frequency band and using the resulting codes for shared-encoder pretraining (Sukhbaatar et al., 2026). However, its band tokenizers are learned independently: each reconstructs its own band without access to features from the others. This leaves open whether interaction during tokenizer training can produce more useful discrete targets while retaining separate vocabularies for individual bands.

We investigate this question through InterBand-EMG, a self-supervised pretraining framework that combines band-specific quantization with cross-band reconstruction. Our central hypothesis is that coupling reconstruction across bands improves the usefulness of the resulting codes as targets for representation learning. Three encoders with separate codebooks tokenize the low-, mid-, and high-frequency components of EMG. We compare independent reconstruction with three interaction strategies: feature concatenation, band-query attention, and concatenation followed by attention (Figure 1). Our main model uses each band’s quantized features as queries to retrieve context from all bands before reconstruction. Reconstruction losses therefore couple the learning of the band-specific codes while each band retains its own discrete vocabulary. After tokenizer training, we freeze its parameters and use its band-specific code indices as prediction targets. A shared encoder receives masked broadband EMG and learns to predict the codes of all three bands at masked positions. The encoder’s continuous representations are subsequently fine-tuned for hand-pose estimation. This two-stage design allows us to examine whether cross-band interaction during target construction improves downstream representation quality.

To support larger-scale pretraining and evaluation, we also introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose dataset intended for public release. SynapMyo contains 81,564 single-hand recordings, totaling approximately 1,228 hand-hours across 499 participants and 68 annotated gesture and movement categories. The collection includes glove-based recordings acquired using Waveletech EMG wristbands and Manus motion-capture gloves, alongside recordings annotated through vision-based hand reconstruction. Both annotation sources are mapped to a common 20-dimensional UmeTrack joint-angle representation and temporally aligned with EMG. Hand-hours count each hand separately. We establish fixed evaluation splits for held-out participants, held-out movement tasks, and both. Recordings from the same acquisition episode, together with temporally overlapping episodes from the same participant, remain within a single split.

papers.title: Polynomial sequences of Simplex pivots on 0/1-polytopes
papers.abstract:
We study the number of Simplex pivots needed to solve linear programs over $0/1$-polytopes, starting from an arbitrary feasible basis and counting degenerate pivots. It has been known since the 1990s that from any extreme point of a 0/1-polytope there exists a monotone path of linear length to an optimal one. However, translating this into a polynomial sequence of Simplex pivots, i.e., improving basis exchanges, has remained an open question.
  We here provide an affirmative answer, showing that for every 0/1-polytope $\mathcal P \subseteq \mathbb R^d$, an optimal basis can be reached with $O(d^3)$ Simplex pivots, independently of the number of inequalities and of the size of the coefficients.

papers.intro:
The Simplex method, introduced by Dantzig [4], is among the most widely used algorithms for solving linear programs (LPs). Its influence on science and engineering led to its inclusion among the ten most influential algorithms of the twentieth century [6]. Besides its practical importance, the Simplex method remains a candidate for resolving one of the central open questions in discrete mathematics: whether linear programming admits a strongly polynomial time algorithm [14]. However, despite decades of research, its theoretical performance is still poorly understood, even for classes of LPs with considerable combinatorial structure.

The Simplex method, introduced by Dantzig [4], is among the most widely used algorithms for solving linear programs (LPs). Its influence on science and engineering led to its inclusion among the ten most influential algorithms of the twentieth century [6]. Besides its practical importance, the Simplex method remains a candidate for resolving one of the central open questions in discrete mathematics: whether linear programming admits a strongly polynomial time algorithm [14]. However, despite decades of research, its theoretical performance is still poorly understood, even for classes of LPs with considerable combinatorial structure.

The Simplex method starts at a feasible basis of an LP, which corresponds to a minimal set of tight inequalities representing an extreme point solution. At each iteration, it exchanges bases by swapping one inequality with a different one: this operation geometrically corresponds to selecting a direction yy that is improving according to the objective function. Such an exchange is called a Simplex pivot. If a positive step can be taken in the selected direction, the algorithm moves along an edge of the feasible region to a better extreme point. Otherwise, the basis changes while the extreme point remains the same, and the pivot is called degenerate. Thus, the sequence of distinct extreme points visited by the algorithm traces a monotone path on the 11-skeleton11 1 The 11-skeleton of a polyhedron is the graph whose nodes are its extreme points and whose edges are its one-dimensional faces. A path in this graph is monotone if the objective value strictly increases along each extreme point of the path. of the feasible polyhedron, but because of degeneracy, the number of pivots may be much larger than the length of this path.

This distinction is central to the complexity of the Simplex method. Its performance is closely related to the so-called polynomial Hirsch conjecture, which asks whether the shortest path between any two extreme points on the 11-skeleton of a polyhedron can be bounded by a polynomial in its dimension and number of facets [13]. This is a major open question for general polyhedra, but for several important classes polynomial diameter bounds are known, and one can even construct monotone paths of polynomial length from any initial vertex to an optimum. Degeneracy is often avoided by perturbing the LP, but a perturbation may destroy precisely the structure responsible for such bounds. Thus, whether this geometric information can be translated into a polynomial number of Simplex pivots, that is, of improving basis exchanges on the original formulation, is in general not clear.

A further subtlety matters for our paper. At a degenerate vertex one could allow arbitrary degenerate basis exchanges, using them only to reach a basis from which the desired edge can be followed: with such exchanges, translating a short monotone path into a short sequence of basis changes is trivial. We insist instead that every exchange be a Simplex pivot: the entering variable must have positive reduced cost, even when the pivot is degenerate and does not move the current solution. This is essential if the goal is to understand the Simplex method itself, and it is the analogue, at the level of bases, of requiring paths on the 11-skeleton to be monotone: every step must be justified by the objective function. The question we ask is therefore deliberately stronger: given a short monotone path, can its progress be reproduced by a polynomial sequence of Simplex pivots, degenerate ones included?

A prominent example is the class of 0/10/1-LPs, namely LPs defined on 0/10/1-polytopes, whose vertices have all their coordinates in {0,1}\{0,1\}. Such polytopes arise throughout combinatorial optimization, and their geometry is particularly favorable. The Hirsch bound holds for them, even with respect to monotone paths [12, 11], and several geometric rules yield short monotone paths, including greatest-improvement [3], steepest-edge and shadow rules [5, 1, 2]. In other words, for 0/10/1-LPs, the existence of a monotone path of strongly polynomial length from any arbitrary initial feasible extreme point to an optimal one has been known since the 90s. However, the existence of a sequence of Simplex pivots of strongly polynomial length from an arbitrary initial feasible basis to an optimal one has remained open for all these years. This shows a clear gap in our understanding of the Simplex method even for a very classical setting, and in fact the gap between short edge paths and short pivot sequences for 0/10/1-LPs has been explicitly mentioned as an open question in the literature.

papers.title: The Tamura-Shafer Problem for Monoids
papers.abstract: Let \(\Pow(S)\) denote the semigroup of all nonempty subsets of a semigroup \(S\), with multiplication induced from \(S\). We prove that every monoid \(M\) is reconstructible from \(\Pow(M)\), even among arbitrary semigroups: if \(\Pow(M)\cong\Pow(T)\), then \(T\) is a monoid and \(M\cong T\). The resulting isomorphism is uniquely determined by the singleton subsets of units and the two-point subsets \(\{1,a\}\) of nonunits. The main difficulty is to recover multiplication without assuming that an isomorphism of power semigroups preserves singletons. We resolve it by reconstructing finite multiplication cycles and the translation geometry of infinite mixed-power orbits. We also describe the induced split epimorphism between automorphism groups and exhibit examples where nonregular singletons are not preserved.

Positive results have been obtained for several substantial families, including groups [10, 6], semilattices [5], completely 00-simple semigroups [11], Clifford semigroups [2], completely regular semigroups, under the generalized continuum hypothesis [16], and commutative cancellative semigroups [13]. papers.title: How coalition size shapes bill cosponsorship in the U.S. Congress
papers.abstract: Legislation is built by coalitions, yet studied through pairwise ties. Using five decades of U.S. House and Senate cosponsorship (1973-2025), we represent each bill as a group. Prior ties to current members predict who joins better than ties to the sponsor, and group history (earlier co-appearance with pairs of those members) produces a larger likelihood gain than sponsor ties alone. Coalition formation therefore retains a social memory of earlier groups: cooperation is organized around relational histories embedded in the coalition already assembled, which sponsor-cosponsor ties alone cannot recover. Completed coalitions also recur and share subgroups more often than degree- and size-preserving nulls predict. Party sorting peaks in coalitions of a few dozen members; as Congress polarized, small coalitions retained their cross-party share while mid-size coalitions became more partisan. Women are over-represented chiefly in coalitions led by Democratic women, although same-gender sponsor matching is close to zero after adjustment.

papers.intro:
Over the past five decades, roll-call voting in the U.S. Congress has polarized sharply, yet legislators have kept signing on to each other’s bills across party lines [1]. Among the observable traces of political cooperation, bill sponsorship and cosponsorship have proven to be particularly informative proxies for legislative relationships [2, 3], signaling positions to constituents and agenda setters [4, 5]. Early work in political science established that the decision to cosponsor a bill is far from random: it reflects strategic calculations about constituency interests, ideological proximity, and reputational signaling [6, 7]. Building on this foundation, Fowler [8, 9] brought bill cosponsorships into the domain of network science, demonstrating that robust measures of legislative influence (and political cooperation) can be extracted from cosponsorship data. More broadly, whether legislators form broad, cross-partisan coalitions or narrow, ideologically homogeneous ones matters well beyond legislative studies: it speaks to questions ranging from political polarization [10, 11] and normative concerns in democratic theory about how majorities form and minorities are included [12] to the science of collective action [13], where group size and composition shape both the stability and outcomes of cooperative arrangements [14]. A cosponsorship, however, is less a tie between two legislators than a decision to join a group. That group can range from three members to more than four hundred, has its own partisan and gender mix, and often brings together legislators who have worked together before.

The size of a coalition affects what joining it means. Simmel observed that adding a third member transforms a dyad [15], and small-group research finds the sharpest change between dyads and triads [16]. For instance, two legislators co-signing a bill with three total sponsors may imply tighter, deliberate coordination, whereas the same two legislators appearing together on a bill with thirty sponsors may often reflect a broad, symbolic endorsement. Weighted projections (Figure 1a top right) of cosponsorship [9, 17, 11] collapse this difference, and networks aggregated over a session can obscure variation at finer levels of measurement [18]. Well-established regularities have therefore been documented without asking whether they hold for small and large coalitions alike, or how a coalition comes to have the members it has. These include party agenda control [19], persistent bipartisanship [1], women’s coalition building [20, 21, 22] and the electoral calendar [5].

papers.title: Disrupted stars and captured compact objects: Combining observations from multiple messengers to infer the population of massive black holes
papers.abstract: Massive black holes (MBHs) are found in galactic centres, but their formation and evolution remain elusive. Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) both arise from stellar dynamics in the nuclear star clusters around MBHs, and are observed with electromagnetic surveys and gravitational waves, respectively. To overcome the scarcity of coincident detections, we formulate how to combine gravitational-wave detections from LISA-EMRIs with observations from ZTF-TDEs to measure properties of the MBH population. Building on two-dimensional Fokker-Planck simulations of EMRIs and TDEs, we model how their populations are affected by the MBH-host scaling relation, the nucleation fraction and the MBH occupation fraction, and analyse the resulting catalogues using joint hierarchical inference accounting for their individual selection biases. With current ZTF-TDE detections, we can already identify combinations of MBH formation favoured by and consistent with the observed TDE population, and derive corresponding predictions for the EMRI population detectable by LISA. Across a range of astrophysical assumptions, the ratio of detectable TDEs to EMRIs is high: ZTF detecting 2.7-84.3 times as many TDEs as LISA detects EMRIs. TDEs, through their numbers, set the shared mass and redshift distributions: LSST constrains the characteristic MBH mass to a 90% credible width of 0.31 dex and the power-law index of the redshift evolution to a precision of 0.11. EMRIs make up ~3.4% of the joint catalogue, yet carry more information than the whole ZTF sample and are the only probe of MBH spin and orbital eccentricity. TDEs will constrain the abundance of low-mass MBHs before LISA flies, while EMRIs will measure properties that electromagnetic surveys cannot. EMRI and TDE observations offer complementary insights into MBH growth and evolution that neither can provide alone.

\Acp MBH residing in the centre of galaxies are abundant in our Universe. Some of the MBH hosted in low-to-intermediate galaxies (∼108\sim 10^{8}–1011​M⊙10^{11}~M_{\odot}) are surrounded by NSC with densities reaching 10610^{6}–107​M⊙​pc−310^{7}~M_{\odot}~\mathrm{pc^{-3}} (Carollo et al., 1997; Neumayer et al., 2020; Pechetti et al., 2020). These NSC provide a reservoir of CO such as sBH, white dwarfs, neutron and regular stars (Graham and Spitler, 2009; Merritt, 2010; Georgiev et al., 2016; Neumayer et al., 2020). The dynamical evolution of stars and CO in the NSC is driven by the gravitational potential of the MBH and its environment (Merritt, 2013). Interactions between a MBH and the components of its NSC give rise to the possibility of observing EMRI (Amaro-Seoane, 2018; Berry et al., 2019, EMRI; ) and TDE (Gezari, 2021, TDE; ).

Within the NSC, regular stars and white dwarfs undergoing close encounters with the central MBH can be completely or partially disrupted by tidal forces. The nature of the encounter depends on the mass of the MBH and the proximity of the interaction, and a star is tidally disrupted only if the tidal radius lies outside the event horizon. This restricts white dwarf disruptions to MBH masses of ≲105​M⊙\lesssim 10^{5}~M_{\odot} (Sesana et al., 2008) and for regular stars to ≲107​M⊙\lesssim 10^{7}~M_{\odot} (Lodato and Rossi, 2011); above these masses, stars plunge directly into the MBH. Within this regime, the disruption can be partial or full depending on the penetration factor. These disruptions lead to luminous transients with typical light curves (Lodato et al., 2009) that can exceed the MBH Eddington luminosity by orders of magnitude (Lodato and Rossi, 2011). Multiple TDE have been observed (van Velzen and others, 2021; Saxton et al., 2021; Yao and others, 2023; Hammerstein and others, 2023) so far in optical (Bellm and others, 2018), ultraviolet and X-ray (Saxton et al., 2021), and these detections are expected to grow with upcoming observatories like LSST (LSST)/Vera Rubin (Karmen et al., 2026).

Other CO in the NSC (especially sBH) will not be tidally disrupted, leading to two possible outcomes. Most of the sBH in close proximity to the MBH will undergo direct plunges into the MBH. A small fraction of CO can instead become gravitationally bound to the MBH, forming a highly asymmetric-mass binary effectively decoupled from the rest of the NSC (Amaro-Seoane, 2018; Amaro-Seoane and others, 2023). Such a binary system is known as an EMRI (EMRI). As the CO gradually loses energy and angular momentum through GW emission (Peters, 1964; Amaro-Seoane et al., 2007), the orbit shrinks slowly. Due to this mass ratio of the binary, an EMRI can spend ∼105\sim 10^{5}–10610^{6} orbital cycles in the millihertz GW band (∼10−4\sim 10^{-4}–10−1​Hz10^{-1}~\mathrm{Hz}); this makes them a target for the LISA (LISA) mission (Colpi and others, 2024).

The observed TDE light curve is not a direct probe of the disruption itself, but of how the bound debris circularises, accretes, and reprocesses the released energy. The peak luminosity, rise time and decay rate depend on the MBH mass, stellar mass, depth of the encounter, and on the efficiency with which accreted rest-mass energy is radiated (Gezari, 2021; Mockler et al., 2019). papers.title: Elliptic regularization for anisotropic mean curvature flow
papers.abstract: We develop an elliptic regularization scheme for anisotropic mean curvature flow in arbitrary dimension, with general norms serving as surface tension and mobility. Starting from a non-fattening set of finite perimeter, we prove that the vertically rescaled minimizers and translating solitons converge in the Kuratowski sense to the unique generalized level-set motion, and locally in BV to the flat flow. Furthermore, by implementing a restarting and matching procedure prior to curvature identification, we establish for the limit flat flow a coupled phase-transport and surface-energy dissipation balance valid for arbitrary, possibly crystalline, anisotropies. When the surface tension is continuously differentiable (away from the origin) and strictly convex, we further prove that the flat flow is a BV flow and that its reduced boundary defines a unit-density anisotropic Brakke flow. To our knowledge, this is the first construction of unit-density anisotropic Brakke flows valid for every strictly convex differentiable surface tension, in arbitrary dimension and for prescribed non-fattening initial data, without assuming perimeter convergence.

Curvature-driven interface motion is a fundamental model for the capillarity-driven relaxation of microstructures. The role of orientation-dependent surface tension goes back to Herring’s work on crystalline interfaces, while Mullins’ idealized grain-boundary model made the relation between curvature and interface migration explicit [40, 53]. In the vector thermodynamics of Hoffman and Cahn [41, 12], the Euclidean unit normal is naturally replaced in anisotropic capillarity by the Cahn–Hoffman vector ∇ϕ​(ν)\nabla\phi(\nu). In a local two-phase setting, the evolution law (1.1) balances this capillary driving force against the kinetic resistance to interfacial migration; the same law also arises as the sharp-interface limit of phase-field models for the relaxation of a nonconserved order parameter, as in the Allen–Cahn theory of antiphase boundary motion [4].

papers.title: Re-JEPA: Coupling Representation Prediction and Signal Reconstruction for State-Conditioned EMG Tracking
papers.abstract: Improving continuous hand tracking from surface electromyography (sEMG) requires generalization across users and motion types while maintaining sensitivity to subtle movements. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn latent representation spaces through contextual prediction, but their effectiveness for tracking depends on which motion-relevant details these representations preserve and how those details are interpreted as the hand state evolves. We introduce Re-JEPA, a tracking framework that couples representation prediction with signal reconstruction and incorporates state-conditioned motion decoding. During pretraining without kinematic labels, Re-JEPA predicts continuous latent targets at multiple levels from visible EMG patches and reconstructs masked amplitude and phase attributes from the fused predictions. Signal reconstruction imposes an additional constraint on the contextual predictor, encouraging its outputs to retain information needed for signal recovery. For downstream tracking, the Gated Persistent Motion (GPM) decoder conditions EMG-token readout on recurrent state tokens and motion history, then generates continuous trajectories through gated state updates and incremental pose prediction. Under the emg2pose tracking protocol, Re-JEPA reduces angular MAE after full fine-tuning by approximately 10.3%, 19.3%, and 14.9% relative to vemg2pose on the cross-user, cross-stage, and joint cross-user-stage splits, respectively.

papers.intro:
Continuous hand trajectories provide human demonstrations for learning dexterous manipulation in embodied systems (Hoque et al., 2026). Egocentric visual capture, however, is limited by hand–object occlusion and field of view. Surface electromyography (sEMG) records electrical activity associated with muscle activation, offering an alternative source for continuous hand tracking without requiring visual visibility. EMG is not a direct measurement of hand pose: interpreting its movement-related content requires temporal context, while differences in users, sensor placement, and motion patterns complicate cross-user and cross-stage generalization (Salter et al., 2024). Tracking representations must therefore use context to interpret muscle activity while preserving signal differences associated with subtle motion updates. Self-supervised pretraining on EMG without kinematic annotations offers a way to learn such representations.

Physiological foundation models demonstrate the potential of learning transferable representations from large unlabeled datasets. LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain, and SIGMA-PPG use discrete-code prediction or signal reconstruction for physiological signal pretraining (Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026). Reconstruction supervises recoverable detail, but accurate recovery does not ensure that the information is organized for downstream readout; noisy targets may also encourage recovery of predictable, task-irrelevant fluctuations. LeCun and colleagues have explored joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), which estimate target-region representations from visible context. Using learned abstract representations instead of observations as prediction targets allows learning to emphasize structured and semantic relationships without recovering every low-level detail. I-JEPA implements this idea for images without relying on handcrafted view augmentations; V-JEPA extends feature prediction to video, and EEG-JEPA introduces multilevel contextual prediction for physiological signals (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026). These developments motivate EMG pretraining for transferable contextual relationships. Continuous tracking, however, also depends on small observational differences that may encode motion updates. Representation matching alone does not directly require every such difference to be retained. We therefore seek to preserve the benefits of contextual prediction while constraining its intermediate representations to retain fine-grained signal information.

We propose Re-JEPA, an EMG pretraining framework that first predicts in representation space, then decodes the predictions into signal space under a recovery constraint (Figure 1). The model predicts the continuous representations of a momentum target encoder at multiple depths from visible patches. It fuses these predictions, restores their positions in a complete token grid, and uses amplitude and phase decoders to recover the signal attributes of target regions. Reconstruction gradients propagate through the predictor to the online encoder, exposing the same intermediate predictions to representation matching and signal recovery. This path incorporates signal recoverability into contextual representation learning, retaining information that continuous tracking may require. Overlapping patches refine the temporal grid, while masking physical regions in the original signal controls the visibility of target content.

Using these pretrained tokens for continuous tracking further requires interpreting EMG observations in light of motion history. We introduce the Gated Persistent Motion (GPM) decoder, which maintains recurrent state tokens and explicitly conditions on the previous pose estimate and motion increment. GPM reads EMG tokens through attention, updates its latent state through a gate, and predicts the next pose increment for accumulation. It connects context-dependent signal representations to state-conditioned motion decoding. Frozen readouts, full fine-tuning, and pretraining-objective comparisons evaluate continuous tracking and cross-user and cross-stage generalization.

papers.title: $\varepsilon$-SegFormer: Multi-Resolution Vision Transformers for Sparsely Supervised Segmentation in Electron Microscopy
papers.abstract: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. We introduce $\varepsilon$-SegFormer, a multi-resolution Vision Transformer for sparsely supervised semantic segmentation, which builds on the architecture of MuViT and extends the training method of $\varepsilon$-Seg. For each labeled pixel, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer samples views at three physical resolutions centered on it, embeds their patches into a single token sequence, and encodes every token's position in image coordinates, so that attention relates all views in one shared frame. A segmentation head classifies the pixel from the tokens around it; during training, the pixel's own token is hidden, so the label must be predicted from context rather than local appearance. The model is trained in a single stage, without pretraining, with an auxiliary reconstruction loss. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer learns from about 10,000 labeled pixels among the 670 million voxels inside three cells, and, given the cell mask, segments nuclei, mitochondria and insulin granules in a slice of a fourth, unseen cell with an average Dice of 0.89 (0.91 after post-processing). Ablations show that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best, with the wider context entering through attention in the encoder.

papers.intro:
Volume electron microscopy (vEM) images entire cells at nanometer resolution and shows every organelle in its native context [30, 38]. Turning such volumes into biological insight requires segmenting the organelles, and a single cell imaged by focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) easily spans hundreds of millions of voxels. Deep networks segment organelles well when trained on dense annotations [20, 12], but producing these annotations takes experts months [11], and models trained on one dataset often need new annotations for the next [12]. Annotation, more than imaging, has become the bottleneck of quantitative vEM.

Sparse supervision addresses this bottleneck directly: instead of painting masks, annotators label a few scattered pixels. Interactive tools have long trained pixel classifiers from such input [6, 2], point and scribble labels are established for natural images [5, 25], and ε\varepsilon-Seg [32] showed that deep networks can learn to segment organelles in EM from labels on 0.05% of the pixels or fewer. A single labeled pixel, however, contains no information about its spatial context, although the class of a pixel is often determined by context spanning many pixels, particularly in high-resolution EM images. A small cross-section of a mitochondrion can resemble an insulin granule, and the interior of a nucleus can look like cytoplasm until its envelope comes into view. A model that learns from sparse labels should therefore see well beyond each labeled pixel, yet the effective receptive field of convolutional networks grows only slowly with depth [27], and enlarging the input at full resolution is expensive, since memory grows quadratically with the field of view in 2D; μ\muSplit therefore fed the wider surroundings at reduced resolution [3].

For each labeled pixel, we sample three views centered on it, with increasing field of view and decreasing resolution, split all of them into tokens, and encode the joint sequence with one transformer whose rotary position embeddings [35, 21] place all views in the same slice coordinates. With 867 tokens, the model sees 680 pixels (about 11 μ\mum) across while keeping full resolution near the labeled pixel (Figures 1 and 2). papers.title: FR3-Band Capacitive-Piezoelectric Thin-Film LN Resonator for Heterogeneous Integration
papers.abstract: This letter presents a capacitively coupled piezoelectric lateral-field-excited bulk acoustic wave resonator (XBAR) in single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) for frequency range 3 (FR3, 7.125-24.25 GHz). We develop a platform that simultaneously maintains high electromechanical efficiency (\(k_t^2\)) and quality factor (\(Q\)) while alleviating challenges associated with parasitic galvanic interconnections and is fit for heterogeneous integration above integrated circuits. A 100 nm air gap excites the second-order symmetric Lamb wave (S2) mode in a 500 nm thick periodically poled piezoelectric film (P3F) LN from a fused silica substrate via flip-chip bonding, yielding a resonance frequency (\(f_s\)) of 7.16 GHz with an extracted \(k_t^2\) of 12.25\% and \(Q\) of 100, facilitating a high \(Q\cdot k_t^2\cdot f_s\) product of 87.71. The results demonstrate strong piezoelectric transduction through a nanoscale air gap, supporting further development of the platform for heterogeneous integration of compact, low-loss microwave components.

Piezoelectric acoustic resonators are ubiquitously utilized as compact and low-loss frequency references for timing applications, enabling modern 5G communication technologies [1, 2, 3]. High-frequency bulk acoustic wave (BAW) devices in aluminum nitride (AlN) and scandium aluminum nitride (ScAlN) have been integral in realizing miniature oscillators fit for co-packaging or monolithic CMOS integration, presenting size advantages over well-established quartz crystals [4, 5, 6, 7]. However, these platforms have faced significant challenges in frequency scaling, inhibiting their adoption past 7 GHz for emerging 6G bands such as frequency range 3 (FR3, 7.125-24.25 GHz) [8, 9, 10].

papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

A probabilistic reconstruction can represent these alternatives and provide a basis for estimating instantaneous and statistical features that the instrument cannot resolve directly.

Limitations take different forms across cardiovascular imaging modalities. Transthoracic echocardiography is portable and relatively inexpensive [20] and provides real-time images [28]. By comparison, time-resolved three-dimensional phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (4D-flow MRI) acquires volumetric velocity data over several minutes, with a trade-off between acquisition time and spatial and temporal resolution [2]. Respiratory motion during acquisition can introduce additional artifacts in the measured velocity fields [2]. Color-Doppler echocardiography illustrates the incompleteness of flow measurements: it captures only the velocity component along the ultrasound beam [21]. Aliasing and noise can corrupt the measured velocities [22], acoustic shadowing can obscure the color-Doppler signal [26], and tissue clutter and the filtering used to suppress it can affect the available flow data [35]. More generally, missing or unreliable measurements can occur in regions where a complete velocity field is needed to characterize jets, vortices, and blood transport.

Several reconstruction strategies have been developed to extract more complete hemodynamic information from these measurements. Signal-processing approaches can jointly denoise and dealias color-Doppler data [22], while intraventricular vector-flow methods (iVFM) infer unmeasured velocity components by imposing kinematic constraints [35]. The Doppler Velocity Reconstruction method uses a streamfunction–vorticity formulation to recover two-component ventricular flow fields. In tests using synthetic Doppler data derived from CFD, it was more robust to added noise and changes in probe placement than the two iVFM formulations compared in that study [21]. More recently, AI-VFM has combined Doppler observations with planar mass and momentum conservation in a physics-informed neural network to reconstruct two-component velocity and spatial pressure fluctuations, including regions or time frames without color-Doppler input [19]. These developments demonstrate that neural networks and physical constraints can restore information absent from the measurement. These advances have been validated against simulated flow fields and illustrated with in vivo data [21, 35, 19], but recovering fine-scale fluctuations remains challenging. Vixège et al. [35] explicitly note that the spatial and temporal averaging inherent in color Doppler prevents their iVFM approach from resolving turbulent fluctuations. For AI-VFM, Maidu et al. [19] report that spectral bias in the neural network smooths the reconstructed fields and leads to underestimation of peak pressure fluctuations. In the formulations presented in these studies, reconstruction yields a velocity-field estimate rather than a sampled conditional distribution of compatible fields [21, 35, 19]. Here, we take a step forward by investigating the problem with a probabilistic approach. Furthermore, we provide for the first time a systematic assessment of the entire range of turbulent velocity fluctuations, by examining the resulting ensembles through velocity, gradient, and multiscale increment statistics. Reconstructing a large missing region is intrinsically non-unique: several flow configurations may be compatible with the same limited observation. This ambiguity is key in the presence of turbulent flows, whose high-dimensional and chaotic dynamics allow multiple realizations within the missing region to be consistent with the available data [14]. Patient-specific cardiac simulations reveal strongly intermittent velocity fluctuations over a broad range of time scales [11], while conventional color-Doppler measurements average over spatial and temporal scales that can obscure fine-scale fluctuations [35]. A distribution of plausible fields could help estimate the likelihood of such unresolved events, which an average reconstruction alone cannot provide.

papers.title: From Giant Vortex States to Bright Solitons in Rapidly Rotating Bose--Einstein Condensates with Attractive Interactions
papers.abstract: We study the ground state of a Bose--Einstein condensate (BEC) with attractive interaction of strength $ a_\Omega $, confined by a two-dimensional anharmonic trap rotating at angular velocity $ \Omega $. We prove the occurrence of a phase transition, as $ \Omega \to\infty $, from an annular giant vortex state to an angularly localized bright soliton. More precisely, we distinguish three regimes according to the relative sizes of the radial and angular concentration scales. In the weak coupling regime $ a_\Omega = \mathcal{O}({\Omega}^{-1/2}) $, the limiting angular profile is governed by a variational problem on the unit circle showing rotational symmetry breaking: below a given sharp threshold, the condensate remains uniformly distributed in the annulus and has a giant vortex profile with a vortex-free bulk and macroscopic circulation; above it, rotational symmetry is broken. In the intermediate coupling regime $ \Omega^{-1/2} \ll a_\Omega \ll 1 $, the condensate localizes at a point on the unit circle with radial and angular widths of order $ \Omega^{-1/2} $ and $ a_\Omega \sqrt{\Omega})^{-1} $, respectively. After rescaling, the limiting profile factorizes into the ground state of the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator in the radial variable and a one-dimensional bright soliton in the angular variable. In the regime $ a_\Omega = a \in (0,a^*) $, corresponding to stable attraction below the collapse threshold $ a^* $ both the radial and angular widths are of order $ \Omega^{-1/2} $; consequently, the limiting profile is no longer a product but rather a genuinely two-dimensional localized state.

papers.intro:
The physical phenomenon of superfluidity is responsible for some of the most striking manifestations of quantum mechanics at the mesoscopic or macroscopic level [Leg06]. Such a quantum phenomenon often occurs together with Bose-Einstein condensation in cold interacting Bose gases [BDW08, PS08, PS16], although it is known that the two phase transitions are not directly linked to one another. The experimental realization of Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) in dilute atomic gases [AEM+95, DMA+95] has provided a highly controllable setting for testing superfluidity and its macroscopic features, typically by setting BECs under rotation: any superfluid can indeed store angular momentum only through the nucleation of quantized vortices, i.e., isolated singularities of the phase of the condensate wave function, where the condensate density is depleted [Fet09]. The occurrence of such topological defects has also been observed in the experiments [MCWD00], as well as their spectacular arrangement in periodic regular structures (vortex lattices) [ARVK01], and the emergence of a quantum Hall regime for angular velocities close to the harmonic trap frequency [SCEM+04].

For all the above experimental observations, the sign of the interaction potential plays a crucial role, since stability of the condensate can be achieved for all values of the parameters only for repulsive systems. On the opposite, attractive BECs collapse above a finite critical particle number [BSH97, SGWH99]. When the attraction combines with the imposed rotation or a global quantization of the circulation, new phenomena may occur [Adi01, Adi02, CC06, KJB04], depending on the interaction strength and confinement, such as vortex splitting or vortex state instability [SU02, SU04] and center-of-mass rotation [LCS04]. Even more intriguing is the transition from vortex states to bright (Townes) solitons predicted for condensates confined to annular traps [KSU03] and observed experimentally when the interaction undergoes a fast change from repulsion to attraction [BZTT+25], which is the phase transition we are analytically deriving in this work. In this last paper, indeed, in an experiment with Cesium atoms, it is observed that a sudden change of the interatomic interaction from repulsive to attractive is responsible for the formation of an annular vortex state. Such a state, however, shows angular instabilities leading for stronger attraction to the fragmentation of the wave function into different components with the typical Townes soliton behavior. These features are also confirmed by numerical experiments in the framework of the Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory.

In the theoretical physics and mathematical physics literature, many works have been devoted to the analysis of rotating BECs within the Gross-Pitaevskii theory. Most of the works however deal with the repulsive case, where a clear picture of different regimes and phase transitions as the angular velocity increases has been derived (see, e.g., [Kav26, PK26] for a heuristic description of such phases). To summarize, for slow rotation, no effect is observed at the level of the (GP) minimizer, since a BEC can store angular momentum only in multiples of a fundamental quantum. As a first threshold is crossed, corresponding to the first critical velocity, quantized vortices are nucleated in the sample and their number and distribution are determined by the minimization of suitable renormalized interaction energies [IM06a, IM06b]. For angular velocities of the same order of the first critical velocity, the vortices cover a significant portion of the sample and their distribution is to leading order uniform but there are corrections due to the trap inhomogeneity [CR13]. In anharmonic traps, as the rotational speed gets higher, the vortices occupy the whole sample and arrange in the famous Abrikosov lattice until a two subsequent thresholds are reached corresponding to the formation of a macroscopic hole and of a giant vortex state, where the bulk becomes annular and vortex free [CRY11, CPRY12, Rou11]. Harmonically trapped BECs are in this respect special, because the angular velocity can not reach arbitrarily large values without destroying the trap, and when it approaches the harmonic trap frequency, a lowest Landau level regime sets in [ABN06, NR22].

papers.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
papers.abstract: There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.

papers.intro:
State machine replication (SMR) is the foundation of fault-tolerant distributed systems and blockchains [1, 2]. Over the last decade, consensus protocols built over a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of blocks have become an established architecture for high-throughput replication (Section VIII). Among them, uncertified DAG protocols [3, 4, 5, 6] have been deployed in Hedera, Sui, and IOTA because of their low latency. In DAG protocols every validator proposes a block of transactions in every round and references a subset of blocks from the preceding round. This structure separates data dissemination from transaction ordering [7] leading to a sepration of concerns. For the bulk data-dissemination validators batch and broadcast transactions concurrently, while for the delicate agreement protocol causal references of the DAG encode the votes. Once the DAG is constructed, validators totally order all blocks by deterministically interpreting their local view of the graph without sending additional consensus messages [8, 9].

papers.title: Latent Space Planning with Sequential Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.

papers.intro:
World models learn compact representations of environments from observations and predict how they evolve under actions, enabling inexpensive simulation for planning (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Terver et al., 2025). Planning with these models requires finding goal-reaching action sequences, typically by minimizing a cost that compares the predicted representations with the representation of a goal observation. Sampling-based planners, such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026), draw action sequences from a Gaussian and refit it to the lowest-cost samples. While they require only cost evaluations, their performance degrades with longer planning horizons and higher action dimensionality (Psenka et al., 2026). Gradient-based planners, on the other hand, differentiate the cost through the world model and perform well on tasks where the goal is greedily reachable (Terver et al., 2025). However, they can become trapped in local minima (Terver et al., 2025). Additional strategies have been proposed to overcome this, including optimizing the intermediate states alongside the actions with Langevin-style perturbations of these states, as in GRASP (Psenka et al., 2026).

MPPI (Williams et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2017) takes a complementary approach, alternating between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from these samples and updating the plan from this estimate. MPPI may thus be viewed as a form of expectation-maximization (EM), whose expectation step estimates the mean of the target from samples and whose maximization step moves the plan to this mean Cuin et al. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian centered on the plan (Williams et al., 2016, Alg. 1) and reach the target only through importance weights. The target distribution that favors goal-reaching action sequences is generally intractable to construct directly. Instead, it can be approached through a sequence of intermediate distributions, beginning with a Gaussian centered at the initial plan and gradually shifting toward lower-cost sequences as the plan is updated. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a principled means of approximating such a sequence of distributions (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral, 2004). SMC samplers (Del Moral et al., 2006), extending annealed importance sampling (Neal, 1998), maintain a population of particles that is propagated between successive distributions using Markov kernels, with importance reweighting and resampling to maintain an approximation to each distribution (Arbel et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2025).

Our key insight is that latent-space planning can be formulated as optimization guided by SMC. The two methods complement each other, each carrying out one step of the EM view of MPPI. As the plan changes by one optimizer step per iteration, the targets of consecutive iterations form a sequence of evolving distributions. SMC carries a population of action sequences from one target to the next through sequential reweighting and resampling. The optimizer then updates the plan using this weighted population, thereby re-centering the target for the next iteration. This combines the population-based updates of MPPI with the gradient-based updates of conventional planners.

The tilting of action sequences toward the goal is determined by a cost function that assigns lower costs to more desirable sequences. A natural choice is the Euclidean distance between the final predicted latent and the goal latent, which is commonly used as an optimization objective in latent world-model planners (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026). papers.title: Kidney Exchange in Deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ Time
papers.abstract: Kidney exchange admits a randomized $O^*(4^t)$ algorithm parameterized by the target number $t$ of transplants, but the best previous deterministic algorithm requires $O^*(6.855^t)$ time. We nearly close this gap by developing a deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ algorithm. Our approach uses Dynamic Representative Sets to execute the semi-feasible packing recurrence under a global cardinality budget of $2t$, exploiting a residual extension-budget invariant to avoid repeated static representative-family compression. To handle admissible cycles containing at least $t$ vertices, we establish a deterministic $O^*(4^{k+o(k)})$ algorithm for finding a shortest simple directed cycle of length at least $k$. Beyond feasibility, our framework supports additive optimization, yielding the same running-time bound for maximizing arc utility among packings with exactly $t$ transplants. Consequently, a packing that lexicographically maximizes the number of transplants and then additive utility can be computed deterministically in $O^*(4^{\tau+o(\tau)})$ time, where $\tau$ is the maximum achievable number of transplants.
