papers.title: Parity-violating optical rotation in the Th-229 nuclear clock transition
papers.abstract: The exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition in $^{229}$Th provides a new opportunity to study hadronic parity violation (PV) by optical methods. The PV nucleon--nucleus interaction admixes opposite-parity nuclear states into the $5/2^+$ ground state and the $3/2^+$ isomer, thereby inducing an electric-dipole amplitude $E1_{\rm PV}$ that interferes with the magnetic-dipole clock transition amplitude $M1$. In a single-valence-neutron Nilsson model, we find $|E1_{\rm PV}/M1| \sim 2\times10^{-5}$. This interference can be detected as a parity-violating nuclear optical rotation (PVNOR) of resonant laser light transmitted through a $^{229}$Th-doped crystal. For a highly-doped CaF$_2$ crystal fiber, the estimated rotation is of order $10^{-6}\,{\rm rad}$. A crossed-polarizer measurement can reach this sensitivity with existing ultraviolet laser technology. We also analyze systematic effects in the form of optical birefringence, stray magnetic-field-induced Faraday rotation, and local crystal defects. Such a measurement would provide the first direct probe of the PV neutron-nucleus interaction constant, $g_n$.

papers.intro:
Studying the effect of the weak interaction in low-energy bound systems such as atoms and nuclei is a longstanding effort, complementary to experiments at high energy colliders [18, 31]. In particular, the parity-violating (PV) component of the nucleon–nucleon interaction is a low-energy manifestation of the electroweak interaction between quarks. Its experimental study is difficult because weak nuclear amplitudes are masked by the much larger strong and electromagnetic interactions. Nevertheless, PV observables have been measured in nucleon scattering, compound nuclear resonances, nuclear electromagnetic transitions, and atomic systems through nuclear anapole moments; see, for example, Refs. [20, 10, 12, 11, 9]. These measurements are complementary because they probe different combinations of the underlying PV meson–nucleon couplings and have very different nuclear-structure uncertainties.

[20, 10, 12, 11, 9]. These measurements are complementary because they probe different combinations of the underlying PV meson–nucleon couplings and have very different nuclear-structure uncertainties.

For single-particle estimates, the PV nucleon–nucleus interaction is conventionally parameterized by effective proton and neutron constants gpg_{p} and gng_{n} [10]. The nuclear anapole moment measured in 133Cs, an odd-proton nucleus, primarily constrains the proton constant gpg_{p}. By contrast, the low-lying states of the odd-neutron nucleus 229Th are dominated by a valence neutron and therefore provide direct sensitivity to gng_{n}. In the meson-exchange description, gpg_{p} is dominated by the sum of the ρ\rho-meson and pion contributions, whereas these contributions enter gng_{n} with opposite signs. This information is also complementary to compound-nucleus experiments, whose large statistical and kinematical enhancements [36, 14] come at the cost of an interpretation based on ensembles of resonances and statistical nuclear theory. Note that the compound-nucleus results are mainly sensitive to gpg_{p}, which is expected to be larger than gng_{n} [13].

papers.title: Puzzles, People, and Publications: Measuring Shared Significance in Crosswords from 1942 to 2024
papers.abstract: Crossword puzzles are cultural objects that encode shared significance. We use interpretable, large-scale computational methods to analyze how crossword constructors, editors, and publications have adopted and adapted language to convey significance. Focusing on approximately 2.4 million crossword clue/answer pairs published in The New York Times between 1942 and 2024, we find shifting significance and differing editorial practices to be quantitatively measurable. By computationally measuring shared significance over time in crossword puzzle production, we are able to better understand cultural changes in the United States through the 20th and early 21st centuries.

papers.title: Water-ice formation in Ophiuchus follows the local irradiation
papers.abstract: Water ice only appears on interstellar dust grains beyond a certain depth into a molecular cloud. This depth has so far been quoted as one extinction threshold per cloud. We measured the threshold along 43009 sightlines through the Ophiuchus cloud with the ice color-excess method, which converts archival WISE and Spitzer photometry of background stars into the peak optical depth of the 3 $\mu$m water-ice band. We sorted the sightlines by the 12 $\mu$m surface brightness of the cloud at fixed extinction, a proxy for the ultraviolet field that excites the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons at the cloud surface. The onset of ice formation lies at higher extinction toward sightlines with brighter 12 $\mu$m emission, ranging from $A_{K_S}^{\rm th} = 0.67$ to $1.15$ mag. It increases by 0.58 to 0.90 mag in $A_{K_S}$ per factor of ten in 12 $\mu$m brightness, depending on the adopted reddening coefficient. Because the 12 $\mu$m-bright and -faint sightlines lie in different parts of the cloud, we repeated the comparison within each of the five subregions, and four of the subregions show the same trend. The trend also persists among sightlines with a similar amount of diffuse material around them. A later onset in more strongly irradiated gas is expected from photodesorption by external ultraviolet light, although a comparison of its size with models requires a calibration of the 12 $\mu$m brightness against the strength of the field. The extinction at which water ice appears thus varies with the local environment, which complicates comparisons between clouds. Photometric ice maps resolve this variation across entire clouds, and the SPHEREx and JWST ice surveys can test it spectroscopically.

papers.intro:
Water ice is the dominant solid molecular reservoir in molecular clouds and the starting point of the chemistry that ends in comets and planets (Boogert et al., 2015). Its presence is measured through the broad O–H stretching band at 3 μ​m3\text{\,}\mathrm{\muup m} in the spectra of stars behind the cloud. The first systematic surveys already showed that the band only appears above a certain amount of dust extinction, the so-called ice formation threshold. In Taurus, ice absorption starts at AV≈3.2 magA_{V}\approx$3.2\text{\,}\mathrm{mag}$ and then grows linearly with extinction (Whittet et al., 1988; Whittet et al., 2001). The threshold is understood as the depth at which the far-ultraviolet (FUV) photons that desorb water molecules from the grain surfaces are attenuated enough for freeze-out to prevail (Hollenbach et al., 2009; Öberg et al., 2009; Cuppen & Herbst, 2007). It marks where the ice mantle becomes thick enough to detect, and grains below it can already carry some ice. Stars and planets form much deeper in the cloud, but ice formation in the irradiated outer layers matters in its own right. Ice-coated grains coagulate more readily than bare ones (Ormel et al., 2009), so grain growth can speed up once ice forms and change the infrared extinction law (McClure, 2009). FUV irradiation also processes the ice and creates radicals (Öberg, 2016).

papers.title: Tensor Hypercontraction of the Coupled Cluster Doubles Amplitudes using a Space-Time Interpolation Grid
papers.abstract: We present a tensor hypercontraction (THC) approach for compressing coupled-cluster doubles amplitudes using a joint grid in real space and imaginary time. The proposed method extends interpolative separable density fitting (ISDF) to imaginary-time-propagated orbital-pair densities, enabling the direct construction of a compact, separable representation of the doubles amplitudes without explicitly forming or decomposing the full four-index amplitude tensor. Interpolation points are selected through a pivoted Cholesky decomposition of the space-time pair-density Gram matrix, yielding a basis that is particularly well suited to representing the doubles amplitudes in second-order M{\o}ller-Plesset (MP2). We investigate the accuracy and transferability of this basis within a rank-reduced coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) framework. Using a THC rank equal to eight times the number of molecular orbitals, CCSD correlation-energy errors remain below $0.1\%$ for all systems considered. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed approximation accurately reproduces relative CCSD energies for both intramolecular rotations and intermolecular dissociation curves, with deviations below 0.1 kcal mol$^{-1}$ at sufficiently large THC ranks. Although the present implementation is designed to assess accuracy rather than computational efficiency, the proposed representation provides a route toward CCSD calculations with quartic computational scaling and offers a promising foundation for extensions to periodic and finite-temperature systems.

papers.title: Minimal chiral $p$-wave superconductor
papers.abstract: Chiral $p$-wave superconductors are among the most intriguing topological phases: their vortices bind Majorana zero modes and their edges carry chiral Majorana modes, yet no material has been unambiguously identified as one. Here, we carry the bottom-up approach of Kitaev chains to two dimensions, proposing a minimal chiral $p$-wave superconductor from a square array of quantum dots coupled via Andreev dots. Rashba spin-orbit coupling in the tunnel barriers provides the $p$-wave winding, and a Zeeman field renders the dots spinless. At a sweet spot, the edge states are confined to the outermost row, so that a chiral thermal conductance and a vortex-bound Majorana zero mode with sub-percent splitting emerge already in $3\times3$ and $5\times5$ arrays. Our setup is realizable with existing InAs and Ge quantum-dot arrays.

papers.title: Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
papers.abstract: Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.
papers.intro:
Predictive coding (PC) (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005) is a brain-inspired learning algorithm that performs credit assignment by relaxing an energy functional defined over neurons. Its computations are local in space and time, so it can in principle train architectures of any topology, including looped ones (Salvatori et al., 2022a). Yet, these properties have rarely been exploited in practice, as recent work has largely used this relaxation to reach the equilibrium needed for credit assignment of feedforward architectures with a fixed number of layers (Pinchetti et al., 2025). Predictive coding (PC) (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005) is a brain-inspired learning algorithm that performs credit assignment by relaxing an energy functional defined over neurons. Its computations are local in space and time, so it can in principle train architectures of any topology, including looped ones (Salvatori et al., 2022a). Yet, these properties have rarely been exploited in practice, as recent work has largely used this relaxation to reach the equilibrium needed for credit assignment of feedforward architectures with a fixed number of layers (Pinchetti et al., 2025). This choice was pragmatic: Since predictive coding approximates backprop on feedforward networks, the architectures, initializations and optimization techniques developed in deep learning could be reused almost unchanged, which allowed a small community to scale PC from MNIST to ImageNet in a few years (Whittington and Bogacz, 2017; Kerjan et al., 2026). The downside, however, is that research directions such as the study of novel architectures and different ways to exploit the energy minimization process have been overlooked, which in the long term could help solve some of the underlying problems of this algorithm.

The main problem of predictive coding models is depth: their performance degrades once they grow beyond roughly seven layers, because the energy of the model concentrates near the output and early layers receive almost no learning signal (Pinchetti et al., 2025; Innocenti et al., 2026). Question. Can energy-based relaxation be turned into a form of effective depth, and what architectural structure is required for such behavior to emerge?

Question. Can energy-based relaxation be turned into a form of effective depth, and what architectural structure is required for such behavior to emerge?

Our answer is to close a shallow feedforward PC network into a loop, by identifying its first and last hidden layers. In the resulting circular predictive coding network (CPCN), effective depth is set by how long the energy relaxes, not by how many layers are stacked, while the error signal only travels around a loop of at most four hidden layers. Closing the loop, however, breaks the two correspondences that allowed PC to reuse the machinery of backprop. Luckily, there is another literature from which we can take inspiration: that of deep equilibrium models (DEQs) (Bai et al., 2019), whose output is the fixed point of a single transformation, and whose parameters are trained via the implicit function theorem (IFT). We will show how both correspondences can be re-derived in this case, using recent work that connects predictive coding to equilibrium propagation (Kerjan et al., 2026), and equilibrium propagation to the IFT (Zucchet and Sacramento, 2022). Our contributions are briefly as follows: • We formally prove that in CPCNs trained via predictive coding (i) the free phase has a unique zero-energy equilibrium, which coincides with the fixed point of an equivalent DEQ; and (ii) building on (Zucchet and Sacramento, 2022), training a CPCN with EP approximates the implicit gradient of this DEQ. As such results are either approximations, or may not hold under machine precision, we verify them empirically in GPU simulations; • We test CPCNs on image classification tasks, showing that it reaches performance comparable to much larger PC-based ResNet18 models on CIFAR10/100, using substantially fewer parameters, and scales to ImageNet32 . We further provide evidence that the trained model uses the effective depth of the loop, as multiple test images converge to the correct prediction only after tens of different forward passes. • We test CPCNs on Sudoku-hard, the first application of PC to constraint satisfaction tasks. Here, we observe adaptive computation properties, as harder puzzles are solved by allocating more relaxation steps than the ones the model was trained on. papers.title: Cluster Editing in Subexponential Fixed-Parameter Time
papers.abstract:
Cluster Editing asks whether at most $k$ edge additions and deletions turn a given $n$-vertex graph into a disjoint union of cliques. For more than a decade, the fastest algorithm for it was the golden-ratio algorithm of B\"ocker with running time $O(1.62^k+n^{O(1)})$. Cao and Chen had conjectured that the subexponential running time $2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$ is possible, but this contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself.
  Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.

papers.title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
papers.abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.

papers.intro:
Co-speech gestures are an essential means of communication: performed alongside speech, hand and arm movements emphasise what is said or convey meaning that complements it [22, 35, 11]. How people produce and interpret gestures with speech is still largely an open question, and answering it at scale requires large annotated corpora. Annotating gestures in video, however, is labour-intensive, typically taking a human annotator several hours per hour of video.

Since these methods were evaluated on different data, often in-house, with different objectives and metrics, their results are not directly comparable, leaving the state of the art unclear and the practical reliability of existing detectors uncertain.

In this paper, we address this gap with the following contributions. (1) We build a framework that evaluates existing gesture detection methods on the same data and with the same objectives: rule-based, pre-trained and trained methods are run on the same cross-validation folds of three datasets, MULTISIMO, GESRes and CABB-S, and scored per frame, per gesture span and per window. (2) We show that the early reported success could not be replicated, because performance varies strongly across datasets, above all with how frequent gestures are. (3) We show that models trained on the target data remain the most reliable, while cross-domain training and co-training with silver labels help only as far as the training data matches the test data. (4) We propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL [10], on CABB-S.

papers.title: AnimalFarm: Auditing the Generation and Detection of Hateful Images Featuring Anthropomorphic Characters
papers.abstract:
Anthropomorphic non-human characters have long been used to convey hateful messages targeting human groups, from Nazi-era propaganda to recent AI-generated imagery on social media. However, the safety risks posed by such imagery remain largely unexplored. We thus conduct the first systematic study of hateful image generation and detection involving anthropomorphic non-human characters. We construct a benchmark from conservatively screened source scenes, covering five character types and three image generation tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, and conversational image generation. Across 14,250 scheduled queries, image generation systems produce images for 92.1\% of queries, of which 95.9\% contain hateful content. We further collect 4,370 hateful images and evaluate five popular hateful-content detectors. Even the strongest detector, GPT-5.5, identifies only 73.9\% of hateful images, while most detect fewer than 58\%. Our analysis reveals that existing detectors often misclassify hateful images as benign when their main subjects are non-human characters. We explore two effective mitigation approaches: a training-free pipeline that maps non-human characters back to human representations before classification and a detector fine-tuned for this type of hateful content. These approaches achieve F1 scores of 0.962 and 0.979, respectively. Our findings expose significant safety gaps in both image generation and hateful-content detection.

papers.title: Seabird-Aware Multi-Objective Offshore Wind Capacity Allocation: A Gippsland Case Study
papers.abstract: Offshore wind planning requires balancing capital cost, wind-resource potential, and seabird exposure. We formulate a spatial tri-objective mixed-integer linear program for offshore wind capacity allocation, minimizing capital cost and modeled seabird exposure while maximizing wind-weighted capacity. Applied to Australia's Gippsland offshore wind area, the model identifies exposure reductions of 23-44% at capital-cost premiums of 0.8-6.1% across 15 wind-weighted capacity requirements. We benchmark exposure-aware optimization against 19 percentile-based exclusion thresholds. At a fixed wind-weighted capacity requirement, the 5th-percentile threshold reduces exposure by 30.1% at a 37.6% cost premium, versus at least 30.1% at a 1.4% premium with optimization. Under a fixed capital budget, exclusion screening reduces exposure by 48.2% with a 26.9% capacity loss, compared with 48.5% and 7.6%, respectively, under optimization. These results highlight the value of explicitly optimizing graded seabird exposure.

One important environmental concern is the potential impact of offshore wind development on seabirds, including collision, displacement, and barrier effects [2]. Because seabird distributions vary spatially, the location of offshore wind development can influence seabird exposure.

A common approach to addressing environmental concerns in offshore wind planning is spatial exclusion, whereby protected or ecologically sensitive areas are removed from development consideration [3]. Seabird sensitivity maps can inform such screening [4], but applying a threshold converts graded sensitivity information into a binary distinction between eligible and excluded sites. Although exclusions are necessary where development is prohibited, threshold-based screening alone does not account for differences in exposure among eligible sites when allocating capacity. It may therefore overlook alternative capacity allocations with lower modeled seabird exposure.

papers.title: Very weak solutions of nonlinear elliptic systems with Orlicz growth
papers.abstract:
In this work we consider non-linear elliptic equations with respect to Orlicz growth, for instance equations of the form
  $$
  \mathrm{div}(\varphi(\vert 
abla u \vert) 
abla u)= 0.
  $$ We study very weak solutions to this system, that is, solutions that are not a priori in the correct energy space to this equation ($\varphi(\vert 
abla u \vert) \vert 
abla u \vert^2 \in L^1$). On the one hand, using rather mild assumptions on the corresponding Orlicz space (we need either the $\Delta_2$ or $
abla_2$ condition, but not both at the same time), we can show that the integrability of very weak solutions improves to the energy space, provided that the initial integrability is close enough to the energy space. On the other hand, mirroring the construction of Colombo and Tione (Non-classical solutions of the $p$-Laplace equation, J. Eur. Math. Soc., 2024), for the $p$-Laplacian, we give a construction of 'wild' solutions for a $L \log L$-type Laplacian.

papers.title: The Fiscal and Economic Implications of Green Mandates: a Boltzmann Approach to Public Governance
papers.abstract: Public authorities increasingly need to translate multifaceted policy objectives into concrete fiscal and investment choices while accounting for their socioeconomic consequences. A credible ex-ante impact assessment should report downstream implications attributable to the historical baseline and specified policy targets, without introducing discretionary assumptions about unknown administrative, socioeconomic or other physical processes. Bringing the large-scale perspective of statistical physics to public governance, we construct such an ex-ante impact assessment. Its scope encompasses policy objectives that condition a finite number of generalized moments of observables in the historical baseline, which comprises a sufficiently large collection of projects or public programmes. As a proof-of-principle application, we consider the green transition in the energy-generation sector using the historical baseline of many infrastructure projects from the World Bank. Our earlier results deriving closed-form expressions for coarse-grained combinatorial probabilities enable a tractable statistical and downstream assessment. We assess the statistical compatibility of the historical baseline with different levels of green-power surplus and demonstrate how the same statistical-physics construction can estimate any downstream metric expressible through arbitrary functions of generalized moments of the baseline observables. In the absence of more detailed knowledge about the processes forming the historical baseline, large-scale universality, whenever many unknown influences on collective phenomena become negligible, unambiguously offers a principled route to a self-contained ex-ante impact assessment.
papers.intro:
A climate mandate often requires a reallocation of various resources towards a specified policy objective. Policymakers seeking to accelerate a transition towards greener infrastructure need to assess not only whether the objective can be realized, but also what its implementation would imply for investment allocation and project costs, the technological mix, as well as further geographical and economic aspects. Within EU economic and fiscal governance, green budgeting provides a framework for integrating environmental objectives into budgetary decisions and assessing their broader fiscal and socioeconomic implications. In particular, the fiscal implications of climate objectives can vary substantially with the policy instruments employed, with respect to the balance between public expenditure, private investment, subsidies, and revenue-side measures [3].

In fact, most policy objectives are inherently multidimensional. In settings where policymakers have access to the historical baseline of an existing repository comprising public programmes with their expenditure or projects with their investments, a series of ex-ante questions arise. Can a policy target be even realized with current technological capabilities and budget constraints? What would its implementation imply for capital reallocation across technologies and regions? What would happen to private investment and other dimensions that are not themselves under the policymaker’s direct control? And, before proceeding with any restructuring, is the existing institutional and market environment, as reflected in the historical baseline, already plausibly compatible with the policy objective? Notice that such questions concern the implications of meeting a mandated target, rather than the estimation of an assumed underlying population model.

To answer such questions, the policymaker investigates the downstream consequences implied by a mandated target in an ex-ante impact assessment, which precedes and informs the strategic planning of an actual intervention pursuing this target. Such implications may include changes in fiscal expenditure, economic indicators, technological composition, regional distributions, or other relevant quantities. The policymaker can compare these implications with the applicable fiscal, economic, and policy constraints in order to assess whether the planned intervention is compatible with the governing framework. To this end, principles of public governance, including proportionality and sound financial management, form part of the normative basis against which the magnitude and nature of downstream consequences are to be evaluated.

For reported consequences to be meaningful and interpretable, their provenance must be clear from the assessment itself. Established frameworks for evidence-based ex-ante impact assessment in EU and OECD regulatory governance emphasize that policy assessments should be grounded in clearly specified policy objectives, available evidence and an appropriate baseline, and should examine the consequences of alternative courses of action in relation to those objectives [14, 28]. Following these guidelines still does not determine a unique quantitative assessment, since the same historical evidence and policy objective can support different analyses, depending on the choices made in their design. Such discretion creates scope for analysts, experts, and other stakeholders to substantially influence assessment outcomes and, consequently, the conclusions drawn from them [19]. More fundamentally, diverse assessments of the same policy objective raise the practical issue of selecting one estimate among several for the same metric; see e.g. a related concern in [18].

To facilitate pluralism in democratic deliberation, we need one quantitative answer to a clearly specified question – not to settle the debate, but to give it common ground from which meaningful disagreement and informed decisions can emerge. After designating a historical project repository from the available baseline, the ex-ante analysis of any policy objective should specify the mandated targets, relevant structural conditions, and, at most, a set of independently adopted principles relevant to public governance. An ex-ante impact assessment should be able to clearly isolate the contribution of these core inputs to the reported consequences, disentangling it from choices made by analysts, experts, or other third parties. We refer to this methodological requirement as attributability.

Although we apply the proposed framework to the climate mandate of green transition, the underlying logic is not specific to climate policy. Our framework is readily generalizable to the ex-ante statistical assessment and downstream analysis of policy mandates in other areas of public governance.

Conventional quantitative approaches draw on statistical inference, predictive modelling, engineering models, or combinations thereof. Although these approaches can serve important scientific and predictive purposes, their design is not necessarily aligned with the ex-ante policy question considered here. The latter is concerned with the implications of meeting specified policy targets on the basis of an agreed historical repository. The assessment thus centres on attributability, rather than on inferring an underlying data-generating process or predicting future outcomes. Moreover, modeling the multitude of real-world influences relevant to such questions becomes not only computationally intractable, but also renders an exhaustive description of the problem epistemically impossible.

papers.title: An affine surface with 3-step nilpotent fundamental group
papers.abstract: We construct a smooth complex affine surface $Y$ such that $\pi_1(Y)$ is virtually $3$-step nilpotent, but not virtually $2$-step nilpotent. This gives a negative answer to the quasi-projective version of Campana's nilpotency problem.

This is, of course, a special case of Serre’s problem on which finitely presented groups are fundamental groups of compact Kähler manifolds (Kähler groups). Whether there exists nilpotent Kähler groups of nilpotency higher than 22 remains open.

papers.title: Rigidity in the Lichnerowicz inequality for word-length semigroups
papers.abstract: We give an operator-algebraic characterization of Cayley graphs that are partial cubes, that is, embed isometrically into a hypercube. More precisely, noncommutative versions of the Lichnerowicz inequality control the spectral gap of the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup by the constant in the complete $\Gamma_2$-criterion of Junge and Zeng or the constant in the geometric Ricci criterion of Junge, LaRacuente and Li. We show that for word-length semigroups on group von Neumann algebras, equality in either of these inequalities occurs exactly when the Cayley graph is a partial cube.

papers.intro:
In Riemannian geometry, the Lichnerowicz inequality [12] gives a lower bound for the spectral gap of the Laplace–Beltrami operator in terms of a lower bound on the Ricci curvature. In recent years, a number of approaches have been developed to extend the notion of lower Ricci curvature bounds beyond Riemannian manifolds, including the setting of metric measure spaces, discrete graphs and general (quantum) Markov semigroups. While not all of these cases support a notion of dimension, in each case a dimension-free version of the Lichnerowicz inequality is known [1, 13, 9, 11].

While not all of these cases support a notion of dimension, in each case a dimension-free version of the Lichnerowicz inequality is known [1, 13, 9, 11].

A natural question is to ask when the Lichnerowicz inequality is saturated. For the dimension-dependent inequality for Riemannian manifolds, Obata’s theorem [14] states that the equality cases are exactly the round spheres. More generally, for RCD spaces, the equality cases are exactly the spherical suspensions by a result of Ketterer [10]. Recently, versions of Obata’s rigidity have also been obtained for discrete graphs and quantum Markov semigroups induced by free difference quotients [4, 5, 6].

papers.title: Atomistic theory of the $d$-wave phonon angular momentum splitter effect
papers.abstract: Phonons offer a bosonic route to angular-momentum transport in solids, but how their momentum-space textures manifest in transport remains unclear. Here we develop an atomistic theory of the phonon angular momentum splitter effect in an antiferromagnetic square lattice with checkerboard-modulated elastic couplings, analogous to the spin-splitter effect in $d$-wave altermagnets. We calculate the transport and accumulation of phonon angular momentum driven by a temperature gradient and find that the transverse response separates into Hall and $d_{xy}$-wave splitter contributions. The splitter contribution requires both the antiferromagnetic order and the checkerboard elastic modulation and exhibits a characteristic $d_{xy}$ angular dependence, whereas the Hall contribution is nearly isotropic. Their combination enables directional control of the edge phonon angular momentum accumulation.

Altermagnets are compensated magnets whose sublattices with opposite spins are connected by crystal-rotation symmetries, producing momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting despite vanishing net magnetization [1, 2, 3, 4]. In dd-wave altermagnets, the spin splitting forms a quadrupolar pattern in momentum space, enabling the spin-splitter effect: a longitudinal electric field drives spin-up and spin-down currents along different directions and generates a transverse spin current without relying on the conventional relativistic spin Hall mechanism [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Spin-splitter torques and tilted spin currents have been reported in RuO2-based heterostructures [10, 11].

Phonons provide an alternative bosonic route to angular-momentum transport, as circular or elliptical ionic motion carries phonon angular momentum (PAM) [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. Under a temperature gradient, PAM can be driven out of equilibrium, generating a PAM density through a phonon analogue of the Edelstein effect [18], and, through the PAM Hall effect, a transverse PAM current with opposite accumulations at the sample edges, analogous to the spin Hall effect [19, 20, 21]. PAM can further be induced by an electric field or a charge current [22, 23]. Experimental evidence includes the mechanical detection of thermally generated PAM in chiral tellurium, chirality-selective transport in quartz, and chiral-phonon-activated spin and orbital Seebeck effects [24, 25, 26, 27].

Of particular relevance here, a phonon analogue of the spin-splitter effect has been proposed in dd-wave altermagnets through magnon–phonon hybridization and orbital mechanisms [34, 35]. These studies show that altermagnetic order can imprint its momentum-space symmetry on PAM, but how this texture manifests as a PAM current in real space and as a measurable edge accumulation in a finite sample remains unresolved.

Here, we develop an atomistic theory of the PAM splitter effect, illustrated in Fig. 1. We consider an antiferromagnetic square lattice in which the diagonal force constants alternate in a checkerboard pattern and the magnetic order couples directly to PAM. This minimal model supports a dx​yd_{xy}-wave PAM response alongside a PAM Hall contribution. Using the nonequilibrium steady-state covariance framework we developed for PAM transport in Ref. [21], we calculate the covariances of the atomic displacements and velocities, from which we obtain the local PAM, bond-resolved PAM current, and edge accumulation induced by a temperature gradient. We find that the transverse response separates into PAM Hall and dd-wave components, with the latter changing sign upon rotating the temperature gradient by 90∘90^{\circ}. Their combination enables directional control of the transverse PAM current and edge accumulation, providing a signature of the dd-wave PAM texture in real space.

papers.title: Frustration-Stabilized Hexamerons and Their Topological Magnons in Janus MXene
papers.abstract: Frustrated magnets on triangular lattices favour noncollinear order, and when inversion symmetry is broken they can host localized topological textures on top of that order. Here we show that the Janus MXene MnHf2C2FI is such a system. Combining first-principles calculations with atomistic spin simulations, we find that magnetism is confined to the Mn layer, where a strong antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor exchange together with a sizable Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction stabilizes a frustrated 120 Neel ground state. On top of this ground state we identify a metastable hexameron: a composite of six merons and antimerons, one vortex-antivortex pair on each of the three sublattices, whose sublattice-resolved topological charges compensate. Linear spin-wave theory confirms that the hexameron is a local energy minimum, and its noncoplanar cores act as potential wells that bind discrete in-gap magnon modes below the bulk continuum. In a periodic hexameron array the magnon bands carry nonzero Chern numbers, and the resulting Berry curvature produces a magnon thermal Hall response whose sign depends on which of the two time-reversal partners of the hexameron is realized. Our results establish Janus MXenes as a two-dimensional platform in which frustration, broken inversion symmetry, and spin-orbit coupling combine to produce metastable antiferromagnetic solitons with distinct spectroscopic and transport fingerprints.

papers.intro:
Magnetic frustration plays a crucial role in the emergence of exotic magnetic phenomena, including noncoplanar magnetic order[2, 3, 23, 99], quantum spin liquids [106, 13, 22, 31, 70, 24, 57, 75], topological spin freezing and spin-glass behavior [56], antiferromagnetic (AFM) topological textures[94, 96, 132, 132, 10, 17, 135, 117, 76] and incommensurate magnetic order [28, 51, 135, 27, 81]. Frustration arises when competing interactions or the geometry of the lattice prevent all magnetic interactions from being simultaneously satisfied. These situations are commonly referred to as interaction-induced frustration and geometric frustration, respectively. One of the consequences of magnetic frustration is the prevention of the Néel state or magnetic states characterized by long-range order. Consequently, one expects the magnetic susceptibility to exhibit paramagnetic behavior, persisting even down to the lowest temperatures. This implies that the system fails to develop long-range magnetic correlations. Frustrated systems (such as spin liquids) differ from standard paramagnetic states in which magnetic moments fluctuate independently, by the presence of short-range correlations. This led Villain [126] to introduce the concept of ”cooperative paramagnetism.”. A prototypical example is the nearest-neighbor Ising antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, where the three spins on each elementary triangle cannot satisfy all three antiferromagnetic interactions simultaneously. As a result, the system has an extensively degenerate manifold of ground states and a finite residual entropy in the thermodynamic limit. Wannier’s exact solution, later corrected by an erratum, gives a residual entropy of S0/N≃0.3231​kBS_{0}/N\simeq 0.3231\,k_{\mathrm{B}} per spin [129, 130], about 46.6%46.6\% of the infinite-temperature entropy kB​ln⁡2k_{\mathrm{B}}\ln 2 per spin. For this reason, the two-dimensional triangular lattice is the prototypical frustrated geometry, especially when it hosts antiferromagnetically interacting spin moments 1/21/2 [84]. The interplay of frustration, competing exchange interactions, and spin–orbit coupling (SOC) can lead to a wider variety of magnetic states, including noncollinear and noncoplanar order as well as topologically nontrivial spin textures[9, 135]. In triangular and kagome magnets, competing exchange interactions can still favor noncollinear configurations even in the absence of SOC[120, 136, 128, 14]. When SOC is present, the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), which originates from the antisymmetric part of the exchange interaction and is allowed when the relevant bond lacks inversion symmetry, can favor a particular sense of spin rotation. In competition with symmetric exchange, magnetic anisotropy, and external magnetic fields, DMI can stabilize chiral spin textures, including magnetic skyrmions[48, 113, 94, 19, 63]. In other words, inversion symmetry breaking and spin-orbit coupling work together to create a spin texture in momentum space. These considerations motivate studying antiferromagnetic (AFM) frustrated magnetic systems with broken inversion symmetry as potential hosts of unconventional magnetic order and topological spin textures.

Recent progress in the experimental study on topological magnetism [60, 45, 97, 44, 8], driven by its potential for information technology, has renewed interest in antiferromagnets (AFMs)[98, 43, 134, 60, 30]. Their spin dynamics can be several orders of magnitude faster than those of ferromagnets (FMs) [64, 12, 16]. In particular, AFM spin textures with swirling, topologically nontrivial configurations are attractive because they can behave as particle-like objects and may serve as robust information carriers. Manipulating them is expected to require low energy [110, 15, 134, 58, 44, 37, 72, 114, 59, 116]. Moreover, AFM textures can be driven by electric currents [15, 7, 134] without the transverse deflection associated with the skyrmion Hall effect, which affects their FM counterparts [79, 80]. Therefore, AFM skyrmions can travel long distances without reaching the sample edge. Consistent with these developments, researchers have experimentally realized synthetic AFM skyrmions in coupled magnetic bilayers, where two FM skyrmions in separate layers are antiferromagnetically coupled across a nonmagnetic spacer layer [32, 26]. To date, intrinsic AFM skyrmions, i.e., skyrmions forming within a single AFM layer, have not been experimentally observed [18, 100, 74].

Since the discovery in 2011, two-dimensional transition-metal carbides and nitrides, known as MXenes [95], have been studied extensively. Their general formula is Mn+1XnTx, where M is an early transition metal, X is C or N, and Tx denotes surface terminations such as –O, –OH, or –F. Their metallic conductivity, chemical stability, and tunable surface chemistry have made them attractive for energy-related applications [69, 122, 123, 5]. Surface terminations strongly influence the band gap, Fermi level, and charge-transfer characteristics [93, 85, 21, 52], and heterostructure formation and defect engineering have improved light absorption and charge separation [123, 103, 82]. However, the magnetic properties of MXenes have received considerably less attention, even though MXenes containing magnetic transition metals such as Mn and Cr offer a natural platform for two-dimensional magnetism[11, 42, 78, 65]. Moreover, Janus MXenes can be synthesized[6, 25, 105, 49, 104, 71, 125, 36], in which asymmetric surface terminations break inversion symmetry, can enable spin–orbit-driven interactions such as the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI) and may host frustrated and noncollinear magnetic states [61, 86]. They therefore provide a platform for studying the interplay of frustrated exchange interactions, broken inversion symmetry, and spin–orbit coupling (SOC), which together promote unconventional magnetic order and topological spin textures[9, 135].

papers.title: PAWS: A Parametric Model of Canine Pose and Shape
papers.abstract:
We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape.
  We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

Beyond companionship, they serve in working and service roles, from hunting and herding to search and rescue, protection, and olfactory detection. Recognizing the range of human-dog interactions motivates a better understanding of their anatomy, locomotion, behaviour and communicative cues.

Despite this importance, building a realistic, anatomically plausible 3D model of dogs remains a challenge. Existing models often fail to capture relevant regions, such as the ears, with desired realism, and limit realistic deformations, while other joints (wrist and elbow joints) are often modelled with excessive degrees of freedom, allowing for unnatural poses. Addressing these shortcomings requires balancing anatomical accuracy with controlled flexibility, constraining the model to abide by anatomical constraints while retaining sufficient expressiveness to capture relevant properties.

Existing models often fail to capture relevant regions, such as the ears, with desired realism, and limit realistic deformations, while other joints (wrist and elbow joints) are often modelled with excessive degrees of freedom, allowing for unnatural poses. Addressing these shortcomings requires balancing anatomical accuracy with controlled flexibility, constraining the model to abide by anatomical constraints while retaining sufficient expressiveness to capture relevant properties.

In this work, we present an approach for modelling the articulated 3D surface of dogs using surface scans of real dogs. Using a multi-camera scanner, we captured 31 dogs spanning different breeds and body shapes, each performing a variety of natural movements. We focused on dogs with short to medium fur length to capture body shape directly, avoiding interference from long coats. Finally, we show that our model captures the relevant degrees of freedom, enabling a regression pipeline that estimates model parameters directly from images.

papers.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
papers.abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.
papers.intro:
Emotion recognition from short texts is a well-established task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from public opinion analysis and customer service support to the detection of mental-health signals in online communities. Research in this area has further been supported by the availability of publicly accessible datasets across multiple languages. A common approach consists of fine-tuning pre-trained multilingual encoder models, such as XLM-R [1], on labelled data from the target domain. An example is XLM-EMO [2], developed to recognise four basic emotions across 19 languages. While this approach can achieve strong performance when labelled data are available, collecting and annotating data for each new domain, platform or language is costly. Moreover, models trained on a specific dataset often exhibit limited generalisation to other datasets [3].

While this approach can achieve strong performance when labelled data are available, collecting and annotating data for each new domain, platform or language is costly. Moreover, models trained on a specific dataset often exhibit limited generalisation to other datasets [3].

When labelled data for a target domain are unavailable, several alternative approaches can be considered: reusing a model fine-tuned on a different dataset, directly applying a publicly available emotion model, or adopting a zero-shot approach, which requires no task-specific training. Two categories of zero-shot approaches are available. The first comprises general-purpose large language models (LLMs), which can be prompted to assign a label to each input text. Although LLMs achieve performance comparable to that of fine-tuned models on simple sentiment analysis tasks, they tend to underperform on finer-grained affective tasks [4]. Furthermore, their predictions may be sensitive to the wording of the prompt and to the order of the candidate labels [5, 6, 7]. The second category, several implementations of which were released between September and October 2026, is represented by decision models: systems designed to process a question together with a predefined set of candidate options and return a probability distribution over these options rather than generating free-form text [8, 9, 10].

The second category, several implementations of which were released between September and October 2026, is represented by decision models: systems designed to process a question together with a predefined set of candidate options and return a probability distribution over these options rather than generating free-form text [8, 9, 10].

By design, decision models are constrained to a predefined set of options, and their output scores can be directly interpreted as confidence values. Their providers also claim low inference latency and robustness to variations in prompt formulation. This class of models is defined by its interface rather than by a specific mechanism. For closed-source systems, the internal inference procedure is not publicly documented and may, for instance, merely involve extracting the probabilities assigned by an LLM to the candidate labels through a dedicated interface. We therefore evaluate these systems as black boxes, exactly as offered. To date, the only independent study, Emo-Jev [11], evaluates a single decision model in single-run experiments, without reporting confidence intervals or conducting statistical significance tests (Section 2). To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has systematically compared multiple decision models with fine-tuned encoders across languages while accounting for statistical uncertainty.

This paper fills that gap with a controlled comparison on a common task. We compare five zero-shot systems, three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions and Strands Decider 2B) and two general LLMs (GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.5-2B), with two multilingual emotion encoders, XLM-EMO and tabularisai, fine-tuned on each dataset. The task is to assign one of four emotions (joy, sadness, anger or fear) to texts from 10 social-media datasets in five languages. Quality is measured with macro-F1, the mean of the F1 scores of the four classes, and differences are given in points, where one point is 0.01 macro-F1. All zero-shot systems receive the same instructions, written once in Italian (Section 3.3); complementary runs test instructions in English and in the language of each text.

The study addresses two main questions and one cross-cutting question. The first is whether zero-shot systems, decision models and general LLMs alike, can replace fine-tuning on labelled data (H1 and H2). The second is whether a decision model is preferable to a general LLM for the same task, in quality and latency (H3). The cross-cutting question is how robust all zero-shot systems are to the wording of the prompt and to the order of the options (H4). We do not vary the amount of labelled data: the first question is answered by comparing the zero-shot systems with encoders fine-tuned on the full training split of the target dataset and on other datasets, and, in an exploratory comparison, with public emotion models used as they are. H1, H3 and H4 use a margin of two points: a smaller difference is treated as negligible in practice, and two systems are called equivalent when the data exclude any difference larger than the margin. H1 The best zero-shot systems reach the quality of an encoder fine-tuned in-domain, that is, on the training split of the dataset on which it is tested: they are equivalent to it within two points. This is the most demanding comparison for a zero-shot system, because the encoder has seen texts from the same source, annotated with the same guidelines. With test sets of the size available here this equivalence cannot be demonstrated (Section 3.5), so we also report how large a gap the data can exclude. H2 (a) A fine-tuned encoder loses quality when applied to a dataset other than its training dataset, and (b) zero-shot systems outperform it in that setting. This is the realistic situation of a practitioner who reuses a model trained elsewhere. H3 For the same task, a decision model is preferable to a general LLM: at least as good in quality and faster. Two pairs make this test partly controlled: OpenAI Decisions runs on the same model as GPT-6 Luna, and Strands Decider 2B is built on the same base model as Qwen3.5-2B. H4 The quality of zero-shot systems is insensitive to the wording of the question and to the order of the options, in the sense that it varies by less than the margin of two points; a variation that is detectable but smaller than the margin is consistent with H4.

H1, H3 and H4 use a margin of two points: a smaller difference is treated as negligible in practice, and two systems are called equivalent when the data exclude any difference larger than the margin.

The best zero-shot systems reach the quality of an encoder fine-tuned in-domain, that is, on the training split of the dataset on which it is tested: they are equivalent to it within two points. This is the most demanding comparison for a zero-shot system, because the encoder has seen texts from the same source, annotated with the same guidelines. With test sets of the size available here this equivalence cannot be demonstrated (Section 3.5), so we also report how large a gap the data can exclude.

papers.title: No Audio, No Transcripts, No Problem: LLM-based ASR Adaptation Using Only Domain Documents
papers.abstract: Can a speech recognizer be adapted to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, using only written documentation? This is the realistic onboarding setting: a new customer hands over raw documentation, not the transcripts that text-only adaptation normally assumes. We turn a domain's documents into adaptation text in two ways, directly as written sentences or rendered by a large language model (LLM) into synthetic spoken dialogs, and feed them to a recently proposed denoising-based text-only adaptation method. We show that, across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, document-only adaptation can match or closely approach real transcriptions; whether written or conversational rendering is best depends on speaking style and the amount of text generated. To our knowledge, this is the first study of document-only adaptation of LLM-based ASR. As no existing corpus pairs audio, transcripts, and documents, we also built and released a document-grounded benchmark.

A recurring and largely unexamined assumption underlies this line of work: the available target-domain text consists of ground-truth transcriptions of spoken conversations. Prior text-only adaptation methods for conventional end-to-end ASR [8, 9, 10] and for LLM-based ASR [11, 12, 13, 14, 15] all adapt on transcripts. Yet in the most realistic onboarding scenario (a new client hands over their materials so an ASR can be delivered for their domain), transcripts of in-domain calls are exactly what is not available. What is available is raw documentation: company websites, product and service descriptions, manuals, policies, etc. Obtaining transcripts instead presupposes the very audio collection and annotation that text-only adaptation is meant to avoid. Beyond practicality, document-based adaptation suits privacy-aware deployment: adapting from a company’s existing documentation avoids recording and transcribing sensitive customer conversations.

All this motivates the central question of this paper: can an ASR system be adapted to a new domain using only raw documents, with no target-domain audio and no target-domain transcripts? We answer this question in the affirmative. Our key insight is that documents and transcripts differ not only in content but in form: a document states facts in written prose, whereas a transcript realizes those facts as spontaneous, often disfluent, turn-based speech. We therefore turn the domain’s documentation into adaptation text in two ways: used directly as written sentences or rendered by an LLM into synthetic spoken dialogs (a conversational grounded in the document), and feed them to the multi-view denoising adaptation method of [13]. We find that document-only adaptation is competitive with ground-truth transcriptions across domains and regimes, and that whether written or conversational rendering is preferable depends on the target’s speaking style (form) and the amount of generated text (quantity). To expose the form dependence, we evaluate on two deliberately contrasting corpus types, spontaneous customer–agent conversations and presentation-style talks and lectures: their registers sit at opposite ends of the speaking-style spectrum, with the conversational corpus matching the synthetic dialogs and the presentation corpus being closer in style to the original documents. papers.title: Probing for relativistic outflows in the Ultraluminous X-ray pulsar RX J0209.6-7427
papers.abstract: Context. Relativistic winds have been observed in Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), but their detection at large distances remains limited. Galactic neutron stars accreting matter from Be-star companions provide a valuable opportunity to improve our understanding of these outflows. Aims. RX J0209.6-7427 is a Be-XRB, powered by a neutron star with a spin period of 9.3 seconds, that underwent an outburst in 2019, exceeding a bolometric luminosity of $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at its peak. Owing to its relatively low distance and a high-resolution XMM-Newton observation, this source is a strong candidate for investigating outflows associated with super-Eddington accretion. Methods. The RGS spectrum yields 105,000 counts, a factor of two higher than any other deep ULX RGS spectrum. RGS and EPIC-pn data sets were modelled with a phenomenological continuum accounting for emission from the accretion disc and accretion column. The emission and absorption features were fitted with the optically-thin plasma models available in SPEX, exploring the temperature-velocity parameter space. Results. The modelling of emission features suggests the presence of a multiphase photoionised plasma approximately at rest with respect to the source. The absorption features can be reproduced either by blueshifted photoionised absorbers moving at approximately $0.1c$ and $0.2c$, the latter being more tentative, or by an alternative collisionally ionised absorption model, which provides a comparably acceptable fit. The presence of ultrafast outflows therefore remains a plausible, but non-unique, interpretation of the data. If associated with outflows, the inferred column densities appear lower than those reported for some persistent ULXs, potentially reflecting differences in the accretion-flow properties or the shorter super-Eddington phase of RX J0209.6-7427.

papers.intro:
Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are mainly extragalactic, off-nuclear sources characterised by an X-ray luminosity ≥1039​erg/s\geq 10^{39}\ \rm erg/s and higher than the Eddington limit for an accreting 10 M⊙\odot black hole (BH), reaching luminosities of 1041​erg/s10^{41}\ \rm erg/s in the canonical X-ray band alone (0.3 - 10 keV; Kaaret et al. 2017; Pinto and Walton 2023 for a recent review). The high luminosities exhibited by these sources were originally thought to arise from accretion onto black holes with masses of up to 104−5​M⊙10^{4-5}\rm\ M_{\odot}. This scenario was challenged by the discovery of pulsations in a few ULXs (pulsating ULXs, pULXs), revealing that at least ∼20%\sim 20\% of ULXs are thought to be powered by accreting neutron stars (NSs; Bachetti et al. 2014; Israel et al. 2016; Rodríguez Castillo et al. 2020). In order to explain super-Eddington luminosities in NSs, a correlation between a very high strength of the NS magnetic field (at least ∼1013​G\sim 10^{13}\rm\ G), the luminosities and the mass accretion rate has been invoked (Mushtukov et al. 2015). The strong magnetic field would diminish the electron scattering cross-section favouring super-Eddington luminosities. M82 X-2 and M51 ULX-7 are two sources for which such high magnetic fields values (∼1013−14​G\sim 10^{13-14}\ \rm G) have been suggested (Bachetti et al. 2020; Vasilopoulos et al. 2020). However, several properties characterising the pULXs can be explained by a lower magnetic field strength, ranging between 1011−13​G10^{11-13}\rm\ G (King and Lasota 2019). The main example is NGC 300 ULX-1, where Walton et al. (2018) tentatively detected a cyclotron line in this source, which suggests a magnetic field of 1012​G10^{12}\ \rm G (see also Vasilopoulos et al. 2019). The presence of a relatively low magnetic field is also supported by the detection of a 0.2c ultrafast outflow (UFO; Kosec et al. 2018b). Moreover, the radiative mechanism of the NS accretion column at super-Eddington accretion rates and its geometry are still unknown (West et al. 2017). The distance of the very few persistent pULXs and the limited capabilities of the current X-ray observatories prevent a detailed study of these sources.

Among Galactic high-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs), we may identify two distinct types of system: persistent and transient, such as an X-ray transient accreting from an Oe/Be-type main sequence donor in an eccentric binary. One source of this last XRB class is RX J0209.6-7427, which offers the chance to improve our knowledge of pULXs for two main reasons: a) it is a nearby source that recently, in 2019, underwent an outburst, and, by following its evolution, we can gain insight into the radiative processes in the accretion column and the formation of the shock above the NS surface, which is believed to define the transition between subcritical and supercritical accretion regimes; b) this is a highly variable source located in the outer wing of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) at a distance of 55 kpc. This system, in fact, is a Be X-ray binary system, where an accreting pulsar, with a pulse period of 9.3s (Iwakiri et al. 2019), accretes matter from a donor Be star that loses material through a slow moving equatorial wind (or decretion disc, see Reig 2011). If the binary plane is misaligned with this equatorial wind or the NS orbit is highly eccentric, the mass transfer may be highly variable, resulting in these powerful outbursts during which the luminosity of the source surpasses the Eddington limit. During these episodes, RX J0209.6-7427 may enter an accretion regime analogous to that observed in ULXs. Powerful winds are expected in super-Eddington accretion flows, and mildly relativistic outflows have been spectroscopically detected in several ULXs (Pinto et al. 2016; Pinto et al. 2017; Kosec et al. 2018a; Pinto et al. 2020b). However, among confirmed pULXs, direct evidence for a relativistic outflow has so far been reported for NGC 300 ULX-1 (Kosec et al. 2018b) and in the transient Be/X-ray binary A0538-66 (Ducci et al., 2026).

The paper is structured as follows: in Sect. 2 we report on the observation of the source and the spectral modelling in Sect. 3. In Sect. 4 we discuss the results of the analysis and the conclusion in Sect. 5.

papers.title: Parameterized Subset Sum for Integers and Solvable Permutation Groups
papers.abstract: We show that parameterized subset sum for binary-encoded integers belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2]$, where the parameter is the number of selected integers. This improves a result of Buss and Islam, who proved membership in $\mathsf{W}[3]$. The proof uses an fpt-reduction to weighted CNF satisfiability without changing the parameter. For every fixed integer $d\geq1$, we also show that parameterized subset sum for permutation groups of derived length $d$ belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2d]$. The proof combines positive CNFs for addition in small abelian groups with an affine decomposition of a solvable permutation action. This gives circuits of weft at most $2d$ and depth depending only on $d$ for product evaluation. For every fixed nilpotency class, we obtain the stronger bound $\mathsf{W}[2]$ by an fpt-reduction to subset sum in abelian permutation groups. The reduction uses Hall's polynomial coordinates in a free nilpotent group and the Magnus embedding. For nilpotent permutation groups without a fixed class bound, we prove $\mathsf{W}[2]$-hardness, already for permutation $2$-groups.
papers.intro:
The classical subset sum problem asks whether some of the integers in a given list sum to a given target integer. With binary-encoded integers, it is one of the fundamental 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete problems [27]. Its algorithmic complexity continues to attract considerable attention. For positive integers, Bringmann [5] gave a randomized pseudopolynomial algorithm whose running time is near-linear in the number of input integers plus the target integer, up to logarithmic factors. Chan [9] recently obtained a deterministic algorithm with the same bound, up to logarithmic factors. Independent recent preprints by Chen, Mao, and Zhang [11] and Jin and Mao [25] give deterministic pseudopolynomial algorithms with almost-linear dependence on the largest absolute value of the input integers.

In this paper, we study the parameterized complexity of subset sum, where the parameter k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} is the number of selected integers from the input list. Parameterized algorithms aim to confine the expensive part of a computation to a parameter that is determined by the input but may be small compared to the total input length. A problem belongs to the class 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT} (for fixed-parameter tractable) if it can be solved with an algorithm that for input length n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} has a running time of f⁡(k)⋅ncf(k)\cdot n^{c}, where f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} is computable and c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N} is a constant independent of kk. Attempts to define an analogue of 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP} in the parameterized world led to the 𝖶\mathsf{W}-hierarchy, 𝖶⁡[1]⊆𝖶⁡[2]⊆⋯\mathsf{W}[1]\subseteq\mathsf{W}[2]\subseteq\cdots. Hardness for one of these classes gives evidence against fixed-parameter tractability, whereas membership results relate a problem to standard problems in the 𝖶\mathsf{W}-hierarchy such as parameterized clique or weighted satisfiability. We refer to the books of Downey and Fellows [16] and Flum and Grohe [20] for the foundations of this theory.

Repetitions are allowed, and the order of the chosen permutations is unrestricted. Even and Goldreich [18] proved that the problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete when kk is encoded in unary. For binary-encoded kk, Jerrum [24] proved 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness, even for two input generators. In a recent preprint, Thumm and the author [30, Theorem 1.2] established a sharp distinction for nilpotent groups: the binary length problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete for 22-step nilpotent permutation groups and 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete already for permutation groups that are simultaneously 33-step nilpotent and metabelian.

We next turn to permutation groups, where addition is replaced by composition of permutations. Given a list of permutations, a target permutation, and a length bound k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the length problem asks whether the target is a product of at most kk permutations from the list. Repetitions are allowed, and the order of the chosen permutations is unrestricted. Even and Goldreich [18] proved that the problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete when kk is encoded in unary. For binary-encoded kk, Jerrum [24] proved 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness, even for two input generators. In a recent preprint, Thumm and the author [30, Theorem 1.2] established a sharp distinction for nilpotent groups: the binary length problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete for 22-step nilpotent permutation groups and 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete already for permutation groups that are simultaneously 33-step nilpotent and metabelian.

When the length bound kk is the parameter, the exact-length version (where a product of exactly kk permutations from the input list must yield the target) is called Permutation Group Factorization by Cai, Chen, Downey, and Fellows [7]. They proved that it is 𝖶⁡[1]\mathsf{W}[1]-hard [7, Theorem 6]. In the same paper, they proved 𝖶⁡[2]\mathsf{W}[2]-hardness for the corresponding factorization problem in transformation monoids, whose elements are arbitrary self-maps of a finite set [7, Theorem 7]. Lohrey and Rosowski [29] denote Permutation Group Factorization by 𝗉𝖥⁡[S∗]\mathsf{pF}[S_{*}], where 𝗉𝖥\mathsf{pF} stands for parameterized factorization and S∗S_{*} is the class of all symmetric groups. In the present paper, we write Sym⁡(∗)\Sym(*) for this class and hence 𝗉𝖥⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pF}[\Sym(*)] for the problem. The related parameterized subset sum problem 𝗉𝖲𝖲𝖲⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pSSS}[\Sym(*)] asks whether a target permutation is an ordered product of kk entries selected from a given list of permutations, with each list element used at most once and the list order preserved. There is a simple fpt-reduction from 𝗉𝖥⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pF}[\Sym(*)] to 𝗉𝖲𝖲𝖲⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pSSS}[\Sym(*)] that works for arbitrary groups and does not change the ambient group generated by the input group elements; see Lemma 5. In the rest of the introduction we only consider the exact-length variants 𝗉𝖥⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pF}[\Sym(*)] and 𝗉𝖲𝖲𝖲⁡[Sym⁡(∗)]\mathsf{pSSS}[\Sym(*)], but all our results also hold for the variants where the target has to be produced by at most kk elements from the input list.

papers.title: Optimizing MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with burst-mode free-electron laser operation
papers.abstract: Burst-mode X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide a powerful platform for X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments with sub-microsecond temporal resolution, but the achievable performance is constrained in practice by both photon statistics and the sample's dose tolerance. Here, we develop an analytical framework for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of pulsed XPCS measurements, including pulse-to-pulse fluctuations of the incident intensity. We combine this description with dose constraints and show that, for a fixed maximum dose, acquiring fewer frames at higher per-pulse intensity yields a higher SNR than distributing the dose over a larger number of low-intensity frames. The framework is validated against measurements at the European XFEL, where the intensity fluctuations of the investigated operation mode are found to cause only a negligible reduction in SNR. We further introduce and experimentally demonstrate a rolling bunch pattern with three pulses per train and variable pulse spacings. This scheme enables more than an order-of-magnitude increase in the accessible per-pulse intensity while maintaining equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide practical guidelines for optimizing dose-efficient MHz-XPCS experiments and for evaluating future XFEL operation modes.

papers.intro:
X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) is a coherent-scattering technique for measuring structural dynamics over nanometer to atomic length scales [23, 19]. By correlating scattered speckle intensities at different times, XPCS provides access to the intermediate scattering function and hence to relaxation processes such as diffusion, caging, aggregation, and structural rearrangement. The short X-ray wavelength further enables measurements at scattering vectors that are inaccessible to conventional dynamic light scattering, making XPCS particularly useful for concentrated or opaque soft-matter and biological systems.

The availability of high-repetition-rate X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) has extended XPCS applications toward time scales that are difficult to impossible to access at storage-ring sources. Early XFEL-XPCS experiments demonstrated the feasibility of correlating speckle patterns from individual pulses at low repetition rates [4, 18, 20]. The development of superconducting-linac-based facilities, in particular the European XFEL, subsequently enabled sequential XPCS at megahertz (MHz) intra-train repetition rates [17, 24]. In this regime, successive femtosecond X-ray pulses provide a sequence of structural snapshots with sub-microsecond temporal separation, while the pulse trains are repeated at a much lower rate that allows for sample translation [8, 21].

Experiments have revealed beam-heating-modulated diffusion and non-equilibrium dynamics in nanoparticle suspensions [17, 6], while related pump-probe strategies have used the X-ray beam itself to trigger and follow rapid structural transformations [7]. Measurements on antibody and protein solutions have further shown that equilibrium dynamics can be accessed before radiation-induced aggregation becomes dominant, motivating the concept of “correlation before aggregation” [28]. Despite these advances, XPCS at a pulsed XFEL is not simply a faster version of XPCS at a quasi-continuous source. At a synchrotron radiation source, the measurement statistics are commonly described in terms of a continuous photon flux and an integration time, whereas at an XFEL the data are acquired as a sequence of individual pulses. The number of pulses per train as well as the number of trains, the photons detected per pulse and the pulse-to-pulse intensity fluctuations all influence the achievable signal-to-noise ratio. At the same time, the high peak intensity of XFEL pulses can make radiation damage the primary experimental constraint, particularly for soft and biological materials. The discrete source structure therefore provides not only access to shorter delays, but also opportunities for flexible allocation of dose across space and time.
