In this work, we derive an analytical expression for the signal-to-noise ratio of XPCS at pulsed XFEL sources, explicitly accounting for the discrete pulse structure and pulse-to-pulse intensity fluctuations. We combine this description with an absorbed-dose constraint to establish scaling relations for the optimization of pulse intensity and the number of exposures. The resulting predictions are compared with experimental data and used to evaluate dose-limited acquisition strategies at the European XFEL. In particular, we investigate how the flexible pulse structure of burst-mode operation can be used to redistribute the dose across time points and compare conventional sequential acquisition with a variable, rolling pulse pattern. Our results demonstrate the potential of pulse-pattern optimization to improve the per-pair signal-to-noise ratio and reduce data volumes, while parameterizing these improvements with respect to scattering strength, sample tolerance, temporal coverage, and repetition rate.

papers.title: Strong Functional Observability and Strong Functional Detectability: Applications to Functional Observer Design for Systems with Unknown Inputs
papers.abstract: This paper investigates strong functional observability, strong functional detectability, and strong$^*$ functional detectability for continuous-time linear systems with unknown inputs in both the state and measurement equations. Extending Kratz's finite algebraic approach \cite{26}, zero-output trajectories are characterized through the projected kernel of a finite matrix, without differentiating the unknown inputs. This characterization yields a necessary and sufficient rank condition for strong functional observability. For strong functional detectability, a frequency-dependent rank criterion involving only the original system matrices is derived, along with an equivalent finite test based on reduced zero-output dynamics. Strong$^*$ functional detectability is then characterized by an additional algebraic rank condition, and its relationship with the existence of stable functional observers is examined. A constructive observer design procedure based on constrained Sylvester equations is also developed. Particular cases and a numerical process example illustrate the theoretical results.

papers.intro:
Observability is a fundamental structural property of dynamical systems and plays a central role in estimation, control, monitoring, and fault diagnosis. Since the pioneering contributions of Kalman [1] and Luenberger [2, 3], observability theory has become a cornerstone of modern systems and control theory. Classical observability concerns the reconstruction of the complete state vector from available output measurements and provides the theoretical foundation for state observer design. In many practical applications, however, only a prescribed linear function z⁡(t)=L​x​(t)z(t)=Lx(t) needs to be estimated. Such a function may represent a performance variable, a physical quantity of interest, a fault indicator, or a combination of state variables used for monitoring and control. Direct estimation of these quantities can reduce the observer order and computational complexity, particularly in large-scale and interconnected systems, without requiring complete state observability [4]-[21], [29], [33]-[34] .

Direct estimation of these quantities can reduce the observer order and computational complexity, particularly in large-scale and interconnected systems, without requiring complete state observability [4]-[21], [29], [33]-[34] .

These considerations have motivated the development of functional observability and functional observer design, notably through the contributions of Fernando and coauthors [7]–[10]; see also [15]-[17]. Functional observability concerns the reconstruction of a prescribed function of the state rather than the entire state vector. Various algebraic and geometric characterizations, together with constructive observer design methods, have been developed in [16]–[19]. A closely related concept is functional detectability, which ensures the asymptotic reconstruction of the prescribed linear function of the state [16], [28].

In practice, many engineering systems are affected by unknown disturbances, faults, or unmeasured inputs, which further complicate state estimation. In particular, unknown inputs may generate nonzero state trajectories while leaving the measured outputs identically zero. This difficulty has motivated the study of strong observability and strong detectability [30]-[32]. Hautus [28] investigated strong detectability and its relationship with observer design, while Kratz [26], [27] developed a finite algebraic construction for strong observability without requiring differentiability of the unknown inputs. These developments provide an important theoretical foundation for unknown-input observer (UIO) design [35], [38]-[41], whose objective is to estimate the system state despite the presence of unknown disturbances. papers.title: Additive cubes are avoidable by a non-uniform morphism of length $6$ over $\{0,a,b\}$ (with $b \ge 4$ and $\gcd(a,b) = 1$)
papers.abstract: We prove that additive cubes are avoidable over every ternary alphabet $\{0, a, b\}$ with $1 \le a < b$, $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, and $b \ge 4$, thereby solving and extending Rao's~(2015) conjecture from $b \ge 6$ down to $b \ge 4$. Our construction applies a single dual pair of parameterized non-uniform morphisms of image length at most~$6$ to the additive-cube-free word $\mathbf{w}$ of Cassaigne et al.~(2014). For $b \ge 10$, we prove that every additive square in the image is an abelian square, reducing additive cubes to abelian cubes; the absence of abelian cubes and the $24$ finite cases with $4 \le b \le 9$ are then certified via the finite-graph method of Jamet and Rosenfeld~(2026).

papers.title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning Architectures for Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Chemical Processes
papers.abstract: Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) is crucial for both maintenance and control in chemical industries, where early fault detection can prevent costly failures and optimize operations. This is particularly critical in pilot units like those at IFP Energies Nouvelles (IFPEN), which operate under short-term experimental conditions with frequently varying operational parameters. This study conducts an extensive benchmarking analysis using the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP), a widely used simulated chemical process dataset, to evaluate multiple approaches for fault detection and diagnosis, featuring numerous continuous operations with different sensors and faults. Several methods were implemented and compared including Multi Scale PCA (MS-PCA), AutoEncoder, Ensemble Learning, and LSTM models for fault detection, alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and BLSTM (Bidirectional LSTM) for fault diagnosis. Our results demonstrate that Ensemble Learning achieves detection rates ranging from 80% to 100% across various fault scenarios. For the fault diagnosis task, BLSTM achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 98.76%. The study reveals that ensemble-based approaches consistently outperform individual models in handling the complex, multivariate nature of chemical process data, due to its robustness in combining multiple perspectives, comprehensive data capture, and localized detection capabilities. Furthermore, the superior performance of the BLSTM is due to its ability to capture both past and future temporal dependencies in the sequential data, particularly important in chemical processes where fault patterns may manifest with complex temporal relationships. This research contributes to the field of Fault Detection and Diagnosis by providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of ensemble methods and Bidirectional LSTMs in order to address industrial FDD applications on chemical processes.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
papers.abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

papers.title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
papers.abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9\% and coverage of failure rate for all three blocks and of throughput for two of three. A fidelity paradox was observed: accurate process-level parameters did not ensure system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors driven by misinterpreted observation-window truncation and absent system-level calibration. These results demonstrate that local open-weight models can perform DES generation at accuracy comparable to cloud-based alternatives, while identifying parameter extraction as necessary but insufficient for behavioral validity. Source code and results are available at https://github.com/RaikoPipe/genai4simpy

Discrete-event simulation (DES) and Digital Twins are essential technologies for evaluating scenarios, identifying bottlenecks, and optimizing production processes [8, 26]. However, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) frequently lack the domain expertise, digital infrastructure, and specialized technical skills required to develop and maintain such models [26, 6, 19]. This accessibility gap risks a “selective industrial revolution,” where only large corporations benefit from Industry 4.0 and 5.0 technologies [5, 7].

While Automated Simulation Model Generation (ASMG) approaches reduce manual modeling efforts, they often remain rigid and technically complex for SMEs [19]. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) could abstract this complexity, but current applications rely heavily on proprietary, cloud-based models, which introduces severe data privacy concerns in industrial contexts [14]. To bridge this gap, this paper investigates how agentic AI workflows powered by local, open-weight language models can automate the generation of DES from raw event logs. papers.title: Dynamical friction on an extended satellite revisited
papers.abstract: The original formulation of Chandrasekhar dynamical friction (DF) was developed for a point-like particle moving in a infinite and homogeneous medium. However, despite very useful order of magnitude estimates of the slowing-down time scales of a test mass in more realistic finite-sized models, high resolution $N-$body simulations often hint at a breakdown of Chandrasekhar's formalism (typically overestimating the effect of DF) for massive satellites sinking in the host galaxy. More advanced semi-analytical treatment of the DF expression managed to partially reduce said discrepancy, even though an accurate comparison with numerical simulations still remains difficult, specifically due to the interplay between the DF force and the tidal stress effects on an extended stellar systems sinking in the gravitational potential of the parent galaxy or halo. In this study we perform ad hoc $N-$body simulations of a satellite orbiting in a simple spherical galaxy model, for different values of the initial orbital eccentricity, satellite mass, scale radius and velocity anisotropy profile of the host model. We adopt an $N-$body code where the self-consistent interaction among the particles representing the galaxy can be substituted by the effect of the static smooth potential of the system's continuum limit. Moreover, the satellite itself is either modeled with $N_{\rm sat}$ particles or represented by a single particle with an effective size parametrized in the form of the force exchanged with the other simulation particles representing the galaxy. We find that, at fixed galaxy model and satellite mass, the more extended the satellite, the weaker is the effect of DF. This trend, which is found for both isotropic and radially anisotropic host systems, is particularly evident for orbits with initial orbital eccentricity exceeding $\approx0.3$.

papers.title: Stochastic Differential Equations on the Simplex
papers.abstract: We propose a framework for simplex-valued diffusion processes, formulated as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion. Our edge-wise representation includes the multivariate Jacobi processes and the general class of continuous simplex-valued polynomial diffusions. Also, it allows bounded, locally Lipschitz state-dependent drift rates and edge weights. We establish weak solutions, as well as global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness for strictly positive initial states under a sufficient boundary non-attainment condition.

papers.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.

papers.intro:
Type disciplines make programs safe by construction. A type states what a component may do, a checker verifies each component against the types of the others, and in a sound discipline the components that pass the check compose into a program that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Typestates [1] add protocols, so that the operations a component may perform depend on its state, and typestate checkers verify such protocols statically [2]. Reinforcement learning (RL) agents that act in a shared space need this kind of guarantee: every action that a learner tries, in training as in execution, must be safe. A type discipline offers it in a form suited to learning. A type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy that the learner produces. Agents rely on each other’s types, which act as interfaces [3], rather than on each other’s policies, which keep changing during training. Each agent is checked separately, before learning starts, so the checks remain per agent as teams grow. With several agents, whether an action is safe also depends on what the other agents do and on parts of the world that the acting agent cannot sense: an agent’s safety depends on another that it cannot see. Shields [4] are an established way to keep learners safe. With several agents, they handle such dependencies through a model of the whole team: they are synthesised over joint states or their projections [5, 6], decomposed from a centralised shield [7], projected from a global machine [8], or certified together over a global model [9]. These constructions require a finite joint model or abstraction, and whether an agent can then run its shield from its own information, without communication, is a property of the derived shield.

Each agent runs its type on its own observations, so execution needs no communication. We implement epistemic typestates in an engine that builds, analyses and runs types. Its input is the model of each agent, e.g., its worlds, their dynamics, its observations, together with the public types of the other agents. The engine synthesises a type when the agent’s reachable beliefs are finite, or builds a type from a guard, i.e., a rule that gives the permitted actions from the agent’s observation. papers.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

papers.intro:
Language models (LMs) have finite capacity to store factual knowledge in their parameters (Morris et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a), which can limit their performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. This poses a particular challenge for smaller models, as facts that cannot be inferred from general patterns must be memorized during pretraining (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024). Even when successfully encoded, knowledge in weights can become outdated as real-world facts change (Vu et al., 2023). Teaching an LM to search address these limitations by allowing factual knowledge to remain externally retrievable, with sources that can be updated without retraining the model. Prior work has explored several ways to incorporate retrieved knowledge at inference time (Lazaridou et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022; Shuster et al., 2022; Asai et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025). These capabilities are typically introduced during post-training (OpenAI et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026), after the model has been pretrained to predict the next token without access to search.

To teach the search ability during pretraining, we augment the training corpus with inline web-search tool calls and corresponding web-retrieved evidence that help predict the original document continuation. These augmentations demonstrate when to seek information beyond the available text, what to search for, and how to use the returned evidence to predict the continuation. We construct search-augmented pretraining corpora from the knowledge-rich Wikipedia corpus and DCLM-Edu, which represents a realistic pretraining setting. The augmented DCLM-Edu corpus contains over 100B tokens of document text, search queries, and retrieved responses. Using these corpora, we train QueryLM models from scratch at scales from 360M to 3.3B parameters. When search is available, QueryLM improves on knowledge-intensive tasks compared with FLOP-matched baselines (Section 5.1). Our 400M model with search also exceeds the average QA performance of SmolLM3-3B evaluated without search, despite using approximately 6,700 times less pretraining compute (Figure 1). The advantage over FLOP-matched baselines persists after both models undergo search-augmented fine-tuning, showing that the tested post-training recipe does not fully recover the benefit of learning search during pretraining (Section 5.1). Beyond answering more questions correctly, QueryLM more readily adjusts its predictions to supplied evidence, including evidence that contradicts facts seen during training (Section 5.2). General capabilities remain broadly comparable after search fine-tuning (Section 5.3), while our ablations examine how retrieval quality, response length, and insertion frequency affect performance and training cost (Section 6). These results support Search-Native Pretraining as a scalable approach to teaching models to search for and use external information from the start of training.

papers.title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

Remote sensing agents autonomously plan and invoke perception models and geospatial analysis tools to perform Earth observation tasks [29, 9, 23, 21, 22] according to users’ queries. However, user requests sometimes exceed a system’s current capabilities in practical deployment. As illustrated in Fig. 1, an agent may understand a request [33, 10, 28, 15] and formulate a reasonable plan [2, 31, 25, 17], yet still fail to complete the task because a required specialized tool is unavailable. To support users’ analytical queries over time, remote sensing agents must develop self-evolving capabilities, autonomously identifying and addressing capability gaps during execution, and retaining verified improvements for reuse in subsequent tasks.

To achieve self-evolution, recent remote sensing agentic systems have explored various strategies, ranging from workflow repair and experience accumulation [24, 2, 25, 4] to on-demand script generation by proactively consulting documentation [35]. Despite this progress, these approaches primarily focus on optimizing their internal logic or generating simple rule-based scripts. Such script-level adaptations remain fundamentally constrained when task requirements exceed the perception capabilities supported by the agent’s existing toolset. Workflow adjustment and code generation alone cannot provide specialized capabilities that require pretrained models. To bridge these gaps, agents need to autonomously discover, acquire, and integrate pretrained models from external resources.

Consequently, modifying harness allows the system to seamlessly archive and reuse acquired capabilities across tasks. This external integration inherently bypasses the continuous training overhead required by approaches that attempt to internalize new capabilities through model parameter optimization [32, 26].

Motivated by these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, a self-evolving harness for remote sensing agents that connects capability acquisition with the accumulation of reusable experience. With the base model parameters frozen, it supports continued capability growth through two complementary mechanisms: dynamic toolset expansion and skill library consolidation. Dynamic toolset expansion enables agents to autonomously acquire and integrate pretrained models from open-source repositories as task requirements evolve. Skill library consolidation distills verified successful executions into reusable procedures that guide subsequent tasks. Crucially, successful workflows involving newly acquired tools can also be consolidated into reusable skills, allowing new capabilities to be retained together with the procedural knowledge needed to apply them. It enables remote sensing agents to build on both advances in the external model ecosystem and their own accumulated execution experience across tasks.

papers.title: Network Traffic Dynamics in Urban Low-Altitude Air Transport with Projected-Space Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams
papers.abstract: The growth of Low-Altitude Air Transport (LAAT) systems calls for effective macroscopic modeling tools to manage dense drone traffic. The Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) offers a promising framework for this purpose, but its conventional formulations do not directly account for the three-dimensional interactions and path deviations that characterize drone operations. To address this challenge, we introduce a projected-space framework that represents drone motion using projected speed and shortest origin-destination (OD) distances, eliminating the dependence on realized trip lengths that are unknown at trip generation. Under suitable assumptions, we prove the steady-state exactness of the projected-space accumulation-based model and establish deterministic finite-window error bounds for the trip-based estimator. The projected-space accumulation-based formulation is further extended to heterogeneous multi-class systems to accommodate different drone characteristics and operational priorities. Microscopic simulations validate the projected-space formulations under stationary and transient traffic conditions, including hysteresis. Moreover, simulations involving heterogeneous priority classes demonstrate that mixed-priority operations can improve network outflow under the investigated scenarios. These findings establish a theoretical foundation for projected-space macroscopic modeling of LAAT systems and support its application to real-time traffic estimation and future airspace management and control.

papers.intro:
Urban Air Mobility (UAM) has attracted increasing interest as an emerging component of urban transportation systems, supported by advances in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, and autonomous flight technologies (Straubinger et al., 2020; Sengupta et al., 2025). Beyond monitoring, where UAVs equipped with high-resolution cameras have provided new opportunities for urban traffic monitoring and data collection (Barmpounakis and Geroliminis, 2020; Paipuri et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2025), the development of low-altitude air transport (LAAT) systems may enable new passenger and cargo services, particularly for time-sensitive applications such as medical supply delivery and urban logistics (Li et al., 2020; Archetti et al., 2022). The prospect of large-scale LAAT operations, however, raises important challenges concerning airspace congestion, traffic efficiency, and the coordination of interacting aerial vehicles. Recent studies have further highlighted system-level challenges from complementary perspectives, including capacity limitations induced by dense multi-agent interactions and safety-oriented network planning for vertiports and contingency landing infrastructure (Zhao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2027). While trajectory-based approaches can describe individual aircraft movements and interactions (Safadi et al., 2023; Weng et al., 2026), they do not directly provide a compact representation of network-wide congestion dynamics, motivating the development of macroscopic traffic models for large-scale LAAT management.

The Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD), which relates network accumulation to aggregate traffic production or outflow, provides a compact and computationally efficient framework for modeling and managing large-scale transportation systems (Daganzo, 2007; Geroliminis and Daganzo, 2008). Originally developed for urban road networks, MFD-based models have been widely applied to traffic state estimation and perimeter control (Haddad, 2015; Sirmatel and Geroliminis, 2019; Li et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2026), route guidance (Sirmatel and Geroliminis, 2018; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026), pricing (Yang et al., 2019; Loder et al., 2022), and public transport operations (Ramezani and Nourinejad, 2018; Beojone and Geroliminis, 2023; Li et al., 2026). Recent studies have also investigated MFD estimation under sparse sensor coverage (Maiti et al., 2025). In conventional MFD-based traffic dynamics, the accumulation-based (AB) model represents network outflow using traffic production and a representative trip length. However, its accuracy may deteriorate under transient traffic conditions, where trip completions depend on the recent evolution of the traffic state (Mariotte et al., 2017; Leclercq and Paipuri, 2019). Trip-based (TB) and bathtub models address this limitation by explicitly representing trip progression and heterogeneous travel distances (Arnott, 2013; Daganzo and Lehe, 2015; Lamotte and Geroliminis, 2018). Subsequent developments have incorporated remaining travel distance as an additional state (Sirmatel et al., 2021), introduced time delays into AB models (Haddad and Zheng, 2020), formulated agent-based bathtub dynamics in a relative space defined by the remaining distance to destinations (Martínez and Jin, 2024), and developed MFD calibration and uncertainty quantification across congestion loading and recovery phases (Ma et al., 2026).

More recently, MFD-based modeling has been extended to low-altitude aerial transportation. Haddad et al. (2021) introduced an MFD-based modeling and feedback-control framework for LAAT, while Safadi et al. (2023) developed a microscopic–macroscopic simulation framework demonstrating the existence of LAAT MFDs under different operational configurations. Cummings and Mahmassani (2024) investigated macroscopic flow relationships in unstructured urban airspace, and Knoop et al. (2025) examined empirical aviation MFDs using effective travel distances to characterize route inefficiency. Further developments have addressed LAAT network equilibrium and traffic management (Weng et al., 2025), route guidance with decentralized collision avoidance (Weng et al., 2026), and structured airspace for heterogeneous aerial traffic (Fu et al., 2026). Nevertheless, LAAT differs fundamentally from conventional road traffic: multidirectional movement in three-dimensional airspace requires frequent collision-avoidance maneuvers, introducing substantial trajectory deviations and traffic-dependent travel distances. For illustration, Figure 1 presents an LAAT MFD obtained from a detailed microscopic simulator (Safadi et al., 2023), together with representative drone trajectories below and above the critical accumulation, respectively. Drone trajectories exhibit deviations from their shortest OD paths in both regimes, with substantially more pronounced detours under high accumulation due to increasingly frequent collision-avoidance interactions, highlighting the challenge of relating microscopic drone motion to macroscopic traffic performance.

Emergency missions, such as medical deliveries, search-and-rescue, and firefighting support, often require faster responses than routine commercial operations. For example, Chen et al. (2026) investigated medical drone pre-positioning for cardiac-arrest response, while priority airspace access for public-safety drones has also been demonstrated (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2026). However, these aerial studies primarily address operational-level priority mechanisms, while the resulting macroscopic dynamics of interacting priority classes remain relatively unexplored.

papers.title: The Garnett--Jones distance theorem for rectangles
papers.abstract: For the family of all axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb R^d$, $d>1$, we characterize the distance of a real- or complex-valued function of rectangular bounded mean oscillation (little bmo) to $L^\infty$ by the reciprocal of its critical exponential integrability exponent. For each $\alpha>0$ at which the rectangular exponential moment of $f$ is finite, we construct a bounded correction so that the residual has mean absolute oscillation bounded by a dimension-dependent constant times $1/\alpha$ on every rectangle. The proof bounds products of coordinate maximal operators between two sets in terms of the supremum of their density product over common test rectangles. Selecting a longest interval along each path lets us remove repeated visits to a coordinate, so the density exponent is independent of the number of factors. The maximal-operator estimate holds with every positive density exponent below $1/6$ in two dimensions and below $1/24$ in three dimensions.

papers.title: Adesktop learning factory for smart and resilient manufacturing based on digital twin and AI
papers.abstract: Learning factories have been increasingly applied in engineering research and education. In this paper, we develop a small-scale, low-cost, fully open-sourced learning factory that leverages AI and digital twins to demonstrate smart and resilient manufacturing. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.

papers.intro:
Learning Factory is an educational platform that closely integrates teaching with the simulation of real production environments [1]. For example, Free University of Bolzano developed a mini-factory to demonstrate modular reconfigurability through integrated robotics solutions [1] . EAFIT University’s learning factory [2] adopts comprehensive ICT(Information and Communication Technology) infrastructure to achieve Industry 4.0 compliance, enabling real-time data acquisition and analysis throughout production elements.

Learning Factory is an educational platform that closely integrates teaching with the simulation of real production environments [1]. For example, Free University of Bolzano developed a mini-factory to demonstrate modular reconfigurability through integrated robotics solutions [1] . EAFIT University’s learning factory [2] adopts comprehensive ICT(Information and Communication Technology) infrastructure to achieve Industry 4.0 compliance, enabling real-time data acquisition and analysis throughout production elements.

Existing learning factories, as reviewed before, share a few common challenges. First, most existing learning factories use industrial robots and controllers. These industrial equipment is usually expensive, which limits the applicability of the learning factory. Industrial equipment also takes up considerable space, making reconfiguration time-consuming and labor-intensive. Another significant drawback of the learning factories designed with industrial equipment is that, the industrial equipment is usually closed and it is difficult to design and implement new functions freely. Second, most of the existing learning factories still focus on traditional production processes. Emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital twin are not well-integrated in the existing learning factories. Also, predictive maintenance and how to maintain a resilient production system, although important in practice, do not receive sufficient attention in the design of learning factories.

To address these issues, we propose a low-cost, fully open, "desktop-level" learning factory to demonstrate resilient production line operation based on AI and digital twins. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, and two conveyors. The AGV and robotic arms are fully open and built on Robot Operating System (ROS), supported by a user-friendly graphical programming interface. This significantly lowers the entry barrier for beginners while leveraging open-source resources for rapid iteration. Additionally, this solution incorporates deep learning (e.g., image recognition and imitation learning) and digital twin technology, aligning closely with industry 4.0 trends.

papers.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.
papers.intro:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely considered to be the best available models of visual cognition (Kubilius et al., 2019; Lindsay, 2020; Yamins & DiCarlo, 2016). This is due to the alignment between the neural activity within DNNs and that recorded in visual cortex (Conwell et al., 2024; Schrimpf et al., 2020; Khaligh-Razavi & Kriegeskorte, 2014), and the human-level performance in tasks such as object recognition and image segmentation. However, more rigorous and comprehensive evaluations of the behaviour of DNN image classifiers reveal that they exhibit many robustness and generalisation issues not seen in humans (Har-Shalom & Weiss, 2025; Geirhos et al., 2018; Bowers et al., 2023; Ilievski et al., 2025; Wichmann & Geirhos, 2023; Malhotra et al., 2020; Sa-Couto & Wichert, 2021; Geirhos et al., 2020; Recht et al., 2018; Yadav & Bottou, 2019; Recht et al., 2019). A particularly prominent issue is that DNNs make highly confident predictions even when they are wrong. This issue is not limited to discriminative DNNs applied to image classification, but seems pervasive in modern AI systems. For example, an analogous issue occurs with generative DNNs, such as large language models, which present false information as fact with high confidence (so called “hallucinations”) (Zhou et al., 2024; Marcoccia et al., 2026).

DNN models of visual perception are prone to making confidently wrong predictions for samples from both unknown and known classes. Examples of the former include test images from classes that the DNN was not trained on (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2017; Vaze et al., 2022), metamers (Feather et al., 2023), and “fooling images” that look like pure noise to humans (Nguyen et al., 2015; Kumano et al., 2022). The primary example of the latter are adversarial perturbations which cause the DNN to confidently predict that a sample from one of the training classes comes from a different class (Szegedy et al., 2014; Akhtar & Mian, 2018; Biggio & Roli, 2018; Goodfellow et al., 2015; Kurakin et al., 2017; Eykholt et al., 2018). The former behaviour shows that DNNs lack sensitivity to large image differences that for humans are clearly perceivable and which mean that the image contains no recognisable object. While the latter shows that DNNs are simultaneously over-sensitive to small changes which are typically imperceptible or irrelevant to humans.

We hypothesised that these pervasive issues might be a consequence of the design of DNNs which led us to rethink the implementation of some of the fundamental building blocks used by neural networks (NNs). Confidently wrong predictions suggest that the neurons in DNNs are insufficiently selective. Hence, we propose a novel, more selective, integration function (ZINC, Section 3.1). In addition, we introduce a novel pooling layer (SCAM, Section 3.2) that aims to enhance tolerance to class-preserving appearance changes so as to facilitate successful generalisation despite the increased selectivity of the integration layers. We train such networks using a recently introduced loss (HEM, Section 3.3). From these re-designed components we build DNNs consisting of alternating integration and pooling layers that we call STEAL (Selectivity and Tolerance Enhanced Alternating Layer) networks.

In addition, we introduce a novel pooling layer (SCAM, Section 3.2) that aims to enhance tolerance to class-preserving appearance changes so as to facilitate successful generalisation despite the increased selectivity of the integration layers. We train such networks using a recently introduced loss (HEM, Section 3.3). From these re-designed components we build DNNs consisting of alternating integration and pooling layers that we call STEAL (Selectivity and Tolerance Enhanced Alternating Layer) networks.

STEAL Nets have the same structure as early DNNs models of object recognition (Fukushima, 1980; Fukushima, 1988; Riesenhuber & Poggio, 1999; Serre et al., 2007; Serre et al., 2002) which were the fore-runners of convolutional neural networks (CNNs; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; LeCun et al., 1998), however, the standard mechanisms for performing integration and pooling (cross-correlation and max-pooling) are replace by our proposed mechanisms. In both early CNNs and STEAL Nets, the integration and pooling layers can be interpreted as simplistic models of the simple and complex cells observed in primary visual cortex (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962). Furthermore, as with simple CNNs, STEAL Nets contain two different types of layer as different mathematical processes are required to generate more selective and more tolerant neural responses (Riesenhuber & Poggio, 1999; Spratling, 2005). A more selective representation is produced by a neuron responding to a conjunction of co-active synaptic inputs, whereas a more tolerant representation results from a neuron responding to any one of multiple inputs. In contrast to existing CNNs, our models are designed to more rapidly build-up selectivity to complex stimuli, while simultaneously more rapidly building-up tolerance to changes in appearance. This allows us to create relatively shallow NNs that have competitive performance to modern very deep DNN architectures. The depth of our networks is more consistent with the depth of the ventral stream, which increases the prospect of having a more direct correspondence between DNN stages and cortical regions. The relative shallowness of our architectures also has relevance to machine learning as hierarchical NNs require the output of one layer to provide the input to the next. Hence, even on parallel hardware, the number of layers defines the minimum number of sequential operations that must be performed. As our networks have relatively few layers they have the potential to improve inference speed and address one concern of frugal AI (Girdhar et al., 2025).

papers.title: FlowScope: 3D Scene Flow Pretraining Improves Surgical Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels. We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost. On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head. Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains. Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.

papers.intro:
Robot-assisted surgery is a promising but underexplored frontier for robot learning. Automating even routine suturing subtasks, such as needle pickup or needle handover, could reduce surgeon fatigue and ultimately improve patient outcomes. Imitation learning has recently made dexterous behaviors like these tractable in general-purpose manipulation [48, 11, 3], following a simple recipe: collect more demonstrations, train better policies. In surgical robotics, the first half of this recipe is the bottleneck.

Surgical demonstrations are scarce and expensive. Each one requires an expert operator, often an experienced robotic surgeon, a carefully prepared physical setup, and time on a costly system. Simulation offers a potential alternative, but accurately modeling deformable tissues and realistic endoscopic scenes remains challenging, limiting reliable transfer of learned policies to physical surgical robots [19, 28, 39].

Pretraining offers another way to reduce the demonstration burden. It has transformed language [36, 37, 14] and vision [20, 31, 41]. Robotics has followed, from the RT series [5, 4, 32] to vision-language-action models built on web-scale data [3, 35]. The natural next step is to fine-tune these generalist models on surgical tasks. Yet vision models pretrained on general-domain images transfer poorly to surgical scenes [18, 34, 13], and the robot data behind generalist policies looks nothing like the inside of a patient. Indeed, in our experiments, a fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} trails FlowScope on both surgical tasks (Sec. 4). Surgical policies need surgical pretraining data.

What, then, should a surgical policy learn from unlabeled stereo video? Our answer is motion. What a surgeon does is visible in how the scene moves: the instruments sweep toward the needle, the needle lifts from the tissue, and the tissue deforms under traction. Because the endoscope is stereo, this motion can be estimated in metric 3D with off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. On both tasks, FlowScope substantially improves real-robot success over training from scratch: from 54% to 90% on pickup, and from 4% to 52% on the first handover of regrasp. It also outperforms Diffusion Policy [11] and the finetuned vision-language-action model π0.5\pi_{0.5} [35]. The gains are not tied to ACT’s regression head; they persist when we replace it with a generative flow-matching head. papers.title: Square-root cancellation in three hyperbolic counting problems via maximal estimates
papers.abstract: We study three counting problems for lattice orbits in hyperbolic space: counting orbit points within a prescribed distance of a fixed closed geodesic or a totally geodesic hyperplane, and counting orbit points above a prescribed height at a cusp. For almost every base point, we obtain error bounds of square-root size up to logarithmic factors. For the geodesic and hyperplane counts, these bounds match the conjectured exponents and improve earlier results due to Good and Laaksonen. For these two problems, we adapt the method of maximal estimates developed by Chatzakos and Dimakis for hyperbolic lattice counting, formulating it in both a discrete and a continuous framework. For the hyperplane problem, we also obtain an asymptotic formula for the spatial second moment of the error term, involving an almost periodic function. For the cusp problem, the square-root bound can be deduced from work of Yu, which incorporates Schmidt's dyadic maximal argument. We present a proof, together with an $\Omega$-result supporting the optimality of the exponent $1/2$ for at least one cusp of any group that is not essentially cuspidal. In contrast, for the modular group, we obtain a power saving over the exponent $1/2$ for every base point.

papers.title: The weighted fundamental lemma for non-split groups
papers.abstract: In this work, we prove the Weighted Fundamental Lemma for Lie algebras for general (quasi-split) unramified $G$. The strategy is to adapt the proof of Chaudouard--Laumon from the split case. In particular, we define the notion of a $\xi$-stable Higgs bundle for a quasi-split reductive group scheme $G$ on a curve, and prove that the stack of such form a proper, finite-type Deligne--Mumford stack over the Hitchin base when $G$ has anisotropic center. We then adapt the global cohomological theorem of Chaudouard--Laumon to the quasi-split setting, and perform the required Frobenius-point count to obtain an identity of adelic orbital integrals. A local-to-global argument deduces the WFL for Lie algebras. In the last chapter, we perform a parallel reduction to deduce Waldspurger's nonstandard WFL from a global version which follows from the same geometric theory. Our work implies the Twisted Weighted Fundamental Lemma in good characteristic, which completes Moeglin--Waldspurger's stabilization of the twisted Arthur--Selberg trace formula. We therefore render unconditional the endoscopic classification for classical groups and an array of downstream consequences in automorphic theory.

papers.title: On the chromatic splitting conjecture in coheight $1$
papers.abstract: This article confirms predictions made by Hopkins' chromatic splitting conjecture in stable homotopy theory. A consequence of our main theorem is that a certain map of $K(h-1)$-local $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-rings $\mathbb{S}_{K(h-1)}^{B\mathbb{Z}}\to L_{K(h-1)}\mathbb{S}_{K(h)}$ admits a retract, so long as $p-1$ does not divide $h-1$. If $h=2$ and $p$ is odd, we show this map is an isomorphism. We use methods from the theory of $p$-divisible groups and $p$-adic geometry. Along the way we prove an entirely new kind of "two-tower isomorphism," in analogy with Faltings' isomorphism between the Lubin--Tate and Drinfeld towers, which parametrizes $p$-divisible groups over characteristic $p$ perfectoid spaces with fixed generic fiber in terms of negative Banach--Colmez spaces. Using the two-tower isomorphism, we gain control over the continuous cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group $\mathbb{G}_h$ with coefficients in $\pi_*L_{K(h-1)}E_h$. To study the continuous action of $\mathbb{G}_h$ on $L_{K(h-1)} E_h$, it was necessary to develop the theory of solid Lubin--Tate spectra. Adapting Lurie's constructions, we attach a solid Lubin--Tate spectrum to $p$-divisible groups over a broad class of solid rings in characteristic $p$.

papers.title: Bayesian Optimal Stopping: Invincible Prophets and Achievable Philosophers
papers.abstract:
We study Bayesian optimal stopping: a hidden world $H$ is drawn from $K$ worlds according to a known prior and determines the joint distribution of $n$ observations. A decision-maker selects one observation irrevocably to maximize its value, learning about the world as observations arrive. We compare algorithms against the Bayes-optimal online policy (the philosopher) and the offline optimum (the prophet).
  Our results show that the philosopher is achievable in that we find a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of the Bayes-optimal policy that runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal{I}|^{\log^* |\mathcal{I}| + 1/\varepsilon} \cdot (1/\varepsilon)^{1/\varepsilon^2})$, where $|\mathcal{I}|$ is the size of the input. By contrast, the prophet is invincible and no algorithm can obtain a competitive ratio that substantially exceeds the worst-case guarantees. When the observations are conditionally independent and identically distributed given $H$, the secretary's rule is $1/e$-competitive. We show that no algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio better than $1/e + 1/\mathrm{poly}(K)$ and this bound is attainable.
  Our approximation scheme builds on a primal improvement subroutine connecting the two benchmarks. Given an $\alpha$-competitive algorithm against the prophet, we construct an algorithm with a strictly better approximation factor against the philosopher. We randomize between the baseline algorithm and a threshold algorithm based on dual martingales that exploit the Bayesian structure. Each improvement yields a tighter dual martingale, enabling repeated primal-dual updates. We approximate these martingales in polynomial time using importance-weighted Monte Carlo sampling. Dual martingales also establish our upper bound on the competitive ratio and may be useful for more general Bayesian online optimization problems.

We propose a Bayesian framework for online algorithm design in which a prior over world models induces a mixture distribution over IID inputs. Through the observations in the online phase, the algorithm learns about the world while making decisions. This model interpolates between adversarial and IID models, and captures the stochastic correlations in the input. Within this Bayesian framework, we develop a theory of optimal stopping—a canonical online selection problem—and use it to design and analyze new algorithms.

In our model, the ground truth world HH is drawn from KK worlds according to a known prior π\pi but is hidden to the decision-maker. The world HH then determines the distribution of nn IID observations X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n}. The decision-maker selects one observation irrevocably without knowing the future observations or HH, and its reward is the value of the selected observation. This model interpolates smoothly between classical settings: the known distribution prophet inequalities model of Samuel-Cahn, (1984) corresponds to our setup when the prior has a single component and the observations are conditionally independent given the world; conversely, by Yao’s minimax principle, the unknown IID model corresponds to arbitrary mixtures with any number of components, i.e., K=∞K=\infty.11 1 A minimax argument shows, informally speaking, that in more general online decision-making problems, the competitive ratio of the optimum online algorithm on the worst-case Bayesian problem is equal to the best possible competitive ratio in the adversarial model (see Kesselheim et al., (2026, Theorem A.1) for a formal statement). Our setup can then capture the spectrum between these two extremes, providing the flexibility to model various levels of uncertainty for decision-making. In fact, our results are for more general models, where (i) the observations are conditionally independent given HH but may have different distributions, or (ii) even conditional on HH, the observations may be correlated.

A key advantage of this Bayesian model is that it provides a framework for designing and analyzing online algorithms that learn while making decisions. The two extreme models discussed above often obscure the value of online learning: when the distribution is known, there is nothing to learn; when it is unknown, an elegant result of Correa et al., (2019) shows that no amount of additional online learning can overcome the worst-case barrier of 1/e1/e, which the classical secretary rule (Dynkin, 1963) already attains. This example shows that a good Bayesian algorithm must adapt its decisions to what it learns from past observations. Such adaptivity has been largely absent from prior work on algorithms with partial information.22 2 For instance, in the context of optimal stopping with distributional advice, Bai et al., (2025) note: “Our framework is limited in that it does not adjust thresholds adaptively based on the observed values. Intuitively, a learning algorithm may adjust thresholds toward [the robust algorithm] if the observed values are unlikely to be from the predicted prior, and conversely, toward the [consistent] algorithm […] if the observed values are consistent with the predicted prior.” The reason is that while adaptivity enables better algorithms, finding good adaptive policies is, in general, computationally challenging.
