papers.abstract: The utilisation of Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices (SQUIDs), a loop of superconducting material hosting two Josephson junctions, has long been at the forefront of quantum sensing. To enhance performance and signal power, modern architectures connect multiple SQUIDs into two-dimensional series-parallel arrays called Superconducting Quantum Interference Filters (SQIFs). A major recent advancement, called a mixed-SQUID array, integrates junction-free ``bare" loops alongside active SQUID loops, offering a promising strategy to engineer high-performance alternatives to traditional SQIF technology. However, a rigorous theoretical optimization and performance scaling analysis for this novel geometry remains lacking. In this work, an analytical framework, validated against full numerical simulations, is developed to establish fundamental design rules for this technology. This work systematically examines how key quantum sensing parameters evolve as a function of loop inductance, parasitic coupling, and overall array dimensions. Crucially, it is demonstrated that these mixed SQUID arrays circumvent the severe inductive screening losses inherent to conventional SQIF designs, achieving a performance boost in flux sensitivity in the range of $2-4\:\times$ under realistic device parameters.

papers.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
papers.abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

papers.title: Omo: Giving Continuing AI-Agent Work a Place to Return To
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now keep working while the people who started them are away. Coming back is the hard part: a session list tells you which agent is where, but not what it was asked to do, what it changed, or what to tell it next. We present Omo, which gives each piece of continuing agent work a persistent place to return to. We built the idea twice. Omo Space is an open-source Minecraft mod in which rooms and screens that people build are live terminals on their own machine. Omo Theia brings the same rooms and desks into a customizable IDE, one step away from the editor and the Git patch. Both keep agent sessions running on the host after the view is closed. We describe the two systems, four lessons from building them, and a study designed to test whether returning to a place helps people pick up agent work correctly.

papers.title: DermKG: A Concept-Centric Knowledge Graph for Interpretable Skin Disease Diagnosis from Dermatological Morphology
papers.abstract: Dermatologists describe lesions with a standardized morphological lexicon, which makes concept-based models attractive for interpretable skin disease diagnosis. How much diagnostic information these concepts actually carry, however, is rarely quantified. We present DermKG, a concept-centric knowledge graph built on the expert-annotated SkinCon subset of Fitzpatrick17k (3,230 images, 48 concepts, 113 diseases). DermKG has 3,452 nodes of 8 types and 19,365 edges of 11 relation types, and encodes disease concept profiles, concept co-occurrence, a three-level diagnostic hierarchy, and 20 clinical morphology rules, all of which are supported by the training data (15 strong, 5 moderate). An information-ceiling analysis shows that the 3,230 lesions collapse onto only 813 distinct concept vectors, bounding concept-only top-1 accuracy at 38.9\% for diseases and 77.6\% for the nine categories. Within this bound, DermKG-Net, a graph neural network that scores lesions against disease prototypes and aggregates them along the hierarchy, raises category-level balanced accuracy from 0.257 to 0.411 over the strongest of 11 baselines (paired bootstrap difference $+0.150$, 95\% CI $[0.073, 0.231]$) and more than doubles minority-category recall. Ablations show that most of this gain comes from the hierarchical prototype objective, with a smaller contribution from graph structure. DermKG further yields rule-based reasoning chains and concept-level explanations for individual predictions.

papers.title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
papers.abstract: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.

authors.name: Zeyu Chen
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Nonlinear stability of periodic waves in the Benjamin-Ono equation
papers.abstract: We construct the Lyapunov functional for the periodic waves of the Benjamin-Ono equation based on the conservation of momentum, energy, and a higher-order energy, which exists due to integrability. Positivity of the second variation of the Lyapunov functional for perturbations in Sobolev space $H^1(\mathbb{R})$ is established by utilizing the basis properties of eigenfunctions of the linearized Benjamin-Ono equation in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Coercivity of the Lyapunov functional for co-periodic and multiple-periodic perturbations yields the nonlinear orbital stability of the periodic waves in the periodic domain.

papers.title: Algebraic dark solitons versus rogue waves in the massive Thirring model
papers.abstract: We address the existence of algebraically decaying solitary waves on the nonzero wave background in the massive Thirring model (MTM) in laboratory coordinates. We find the precise condition of the spectral stability and instability of the nonzero wave background. In the case of instability, we distinguish modulational, side-band, and full-band instabilities and show that the rogue wave exists if and only if the nonzero wave background is modulationally unstable. For the other unstable cases and in the case of stability, we show that there exist exactly two algebraic dark solitons which correspond to the end points in the admissible range of the wave speed for the dark soliton propagation.

papers.title: PP-CFG: Polarity-Preserving Guidance for Controllable Few-Step Image and Video Generation
papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.

papers.title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

authors.name: Lam Nguyen
authors.institution: United States Army Combat Capabilities Development Command

papers.title: Real-analytic actions of lattices in $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$ on compact $n$-manifolds
papers.abstract: We classify real-analytic actions of arbitrary lattices in $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$ on compact connected $n$-manifolds without boundary, $n\geq 3$, with no invariant-volume assumption. After finite-index restriction, the action has finite image, extends to a connected Lie group locally isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)$ with an equivariant finite cover when needed, or is obtained by analytic surgery with at least one torus piece. In the last case the lattice is commensurable with a conjugate of $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb Z)$. As a main input, we prove a general cocycle superrigidity theorem for real analytic germs.

papers.title: Real-analytic actions of higher-rank lattices preserving an ergodic volume
papers.abstract: We classify real-analytic actions of higher-rank lattices that preserve an ergodic smooth volume on a compact manifold. On an invariant open dense set of full volume, the action is analytically conjugate to the restriction of an affine action on finitely many copies of one double quotient. The conjugacy carries Haar probability to the given volume. Analytic germ superrigidity supplies local coordinates with measurable dependence on the center. The conditional measures on coarse Lyapunov manifolds determine the law of a displaced center. A two-point joining pairs charts whose evaluations agree there and gives the change of coordinates. The resulting analytic frame bundle carries a coframe whose vector fields integrate to the homogeneous model. This gives the open homogeneous classification in Zimmer's program.

papers.title: INCISE: Training-Free In-Context Segmentation of Surgical Videos
papers.abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.

papers.title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.

authors.name: Ming Du
authors.institution: Second Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University

papers.title: Diameter Growth of $\mathrm{U}(2^N)$ under Cliff Metrics
papers.abstract: Cliff metrics are right invariant Riemannian metrics on the unitary group $\mathrm{U}(2^N)$ introduced by Nielsen and his collaborators in the geometric approach for gate complexity in quantum computations. In this paper, we compute the exponential growth rate for the diameter of $\mathrm{U}(2^N)$ equipped with cliff metrics as $N \rightarrow \infty$. We prove that if the norm of most generalized Pauli matrices are sufficiently large, this growth rate coincides with the growth rate of maximal gate complexity obtained by Knill.

authors.name: Xiaobo Liu
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Instant-LIVO: Efficient LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry with Compact Geometry and a Bounded Single-Reference-Frame Map
papers.abstract: LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) is a fundamental technology for autonomous systems; however, deployment on resource-constrained platforms remains challenging due to physical limitations. This paper presents Instant-LIVO, a tightly coupled, high-speed, real-time LIVO system. The system introduces a compact geometric map based on spatial-hashed OctVox and accelerates local-neighborhood retrieval and plane fitting through cache-assisted heuristic staged K-nearest-neighbor searches. It also employs a bounded single-reference-frame visual map that adaptively updates the reference frame according to the tracking status, while using Schmidt-type uncertainty-aware photometric fusion to maintain the correlation between the reference pose and the current state. The system performs multisensor fusion through a sequential process consisting of IMU prediction, LiDAR geometric correction, and visual photometric correction. It was evaluated on 32 public benchmarks and custom datasets. While maintaining competitive accuracy on both X86 and ARM platforms, Instant-LIVO achieves average processing-speed improvements of approximately 2.3x and 2.1x, respectively, and reduces peak memory usage to approximately 1/20 and 1/13, respectively. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing LIO and LIVO baselines in both accuracy and computational efficiency.The implementation is available at: https://github.com/Faker-0714/Instant-LIVO.git.

authors.name: Wenxin Li
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

papers.title: Proper Conflict-Free Coloring of Cocomparability, Co-Bipartite, and Distance-Hereditary Graphs
papers.abstract: A proper conflict-free coloring is a proper vertex coloring in which every non-isolated vertex has a neighbor whose color occurs exactly once in its open neighborhood. We prove that deciding whether $\omega(G)$ colors suffice is NP-complete on connected cocomparability graphs of diameter two and independence number three. The reduction supplies a partition into three cliques, a maximum clique, an optimal ordinary coloring, and a dominating edge. Every constructed graph needs either $\omega(G)$ or $\omega(G)+1$ PCF colors. The result also gives NP-completeness on AT-free graphs. For the co-bipartite subclass, we give a complete matching characterization and an $O(n^6)$-time algorithm for an optimal coloring. The cocktail-party graphs are exactly the co-bipartite graphs requiring two more colors than their ordinary chromatic number; every other co-bipartite graph needs at most one additional color. The matching method extends to all graphs with independence number at most two, giving an $O(n^6\log n)$-time optimization algorithm. Finally, for distance-hereditary graphs, we decide whether $k$ colors suffice in $O(n+m+nk^{10})$ time and compute an optimal coloring in $O(n^{11}+m)$ time without fixing the palette size. The algorithm uses a binary decomposition and groups colors according to five possible behaviors at the boundary of a subgraph.

authors.name: Gautam K. Das
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Guwahati

papers.title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Identifying scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms requires both domain knowledge and fluency in quantum algorithm design, expertise that rarely resides in one person. We report results from QuASAR, an experimental, two-agent, LLM-driven pipeline intended to bridge this gap. One agent screens scientific literature for computational kernels with a plausible quantum-algorithmic analogue and proposes candidates, each backed by citations. A second agent independently verifies those citations. For candidates that survive verification, it reconstructs the source's computational structure, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and executes a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. We applied this pipeline to ten candidate computations drawn from the astrophysics literature. Nine candidates were carried through to a small-scale, benchmarked prototype. We report three in detail, chosen as the clearest examples with the least redundancy across the set. They span combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference. The pipeline attempted to supply quantum-design expertise a domain scientist might lack, reconstructing source algorithms where one existed and building original, disclosed mappings where none did. None of the three case studies achieved quantum advantage at the tested scales, and their astrophysical framing has not yet undergone expert validation. What the experiment does show is that the pipeline can turn a published idea into a runnable prototype, which a scientist can then inspect, test against classical methods, and decide whether to pursue. QuASAR is an exploratory framework, offered to the community for evaluation, critique, and further development, with an approach that could broaden the use of quantum computing in scientific research and extend to computational improvements more generally.

papers.title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.

papers.title: Bel: Step-Level Policy Improvement of Visual Agents Without Training
papers.abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.

papers.title: Causal Event Networks: Entangled Tensor Graphs, Connectome Quotient Topology, and Subjective Experience as Geometric Dual
papers.abstract: We introduce a chromatically constrained tensor-product construction that generates sparse recurrent computational graphs whose coloring bounds the number of sequential execution phases: vertices are computational units, edges are causal message-passing channels, and the graph can grow arbitrarily large while its chromatic causal depth stays fixed. Coarsened to the scale of the Budapest Reference Connectome, the community quotient of a simple local construction reproduces the connectome's broad degree profile, passes a nine-criterion topological test and comes close to the connectome on most of a further battery of complexity, spectral, controllability and clique measures, while the fine parent graph shows a scale separation: multiscale organization is intrinsic to the fine graph, and short-path integration appears only under coarsening. Placing short-path integration directly in the fine substrate, with chromatically admissible bridges and targeted sparsification, yields quotients far less modular than the connectome across a wide range of coarsening schemes. Relocating edges into the interiors of quotient nodes instead produces a quotient that matches the connectome's degree profile, edge count and fiber-bundle distribution, passes the full nine-criterion test and comes close on most complexity and spectral measures; its fine substrate fails only the two near-random path criteria. Used as the deep-feature pathway of a U-Net encoder-decoder, the graph-derived recurrent module improves image inpainting over the convolutional baseline. We close with a conjectural, structural account of subjective experience in holographic terms: the graph acts as an evolution operator that fixes the admissible causal order and the geometries the substrate can support, and experience occupies the position of the bulk dual of a particular activity state.

papers.title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
papers.abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

authors.name: Jiangfan Zhang
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Idempotent generically stable measures in NIP groups
papers.abstract: Let $\mu$ be a global generically stable Keisler measure on a type-definable group in an NIP theory. Then $\mu$ is idempotent if and only if it is the unique translation-invariant measure on its type-definable stabilizer subgroup. This resolves the NIP case of the Idempotent Measure problem studied by Chernikov, Gannon, and Krupi\'nski.

papers.title: Monomial Ideals Of VEW Graphs
papers.abstract: Let $D$ be a $k$-edge weighted VEW graph and $I=I(D)$ be its edge ideal. In this paper, we characterize the irredundant irreducible decomposition of edge ideal $I$. Also, we study the Cohen-Macaulay property and Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of different classes of $k$-edge weighted VEW graphs.

papers.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
papers.abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.

authors.name: Anqi Li
authors.institution: Hunan Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Wei Qiu
authors.institution: United States Food and Drug Administration

papers.title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
papers.abstract: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. On 189 breast report questions, frontier models that read a written description of the slide or look at a thumbnail and tiles of it answer at 0.50 to 0.66, below the majority class at 0.67. A description is written before the question is known, and a look covers a handful of tiles. We present Opsis, which lets the model ask instead: a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder. A slide is encoded once, a question names an operator, arguments and candidates given at runtime, and the answer is a probability over the candidates. We build it as a 10 M parameter decoder on frozen Virchow2 tokens (Opsis-S) and inside Qwen3-VL-8B (Opsis-V). Asking Opsis-S, four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79, and on 3,797 pan cancer questions asking is 8.6 points above reading. On 995 composite questions that Opsis-S was never trained on, a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, against 0.69 when it looks at the slide and 0.78 for ABMIL trained on each composite. On a pan cancer question set over 10,712 TCGA slides, one Opsis-S decoder matches linear probes trained per question on TITAN and PRISM2 embeddings (average accuracy 0.69 against 0.70 and 0.68). Opsis-S also separates CAMELYON16 metastases without training on that cohort (AUROC 0.86) and localises necrosis from report labels alone (tile AUROC 0.93).

authors.name: Wei Qiu
authors.institution: United States Food and Drug Administration

papers.title: General Transport Signatures of Odd-Parity Magnets: Charge--Spin Selection Rules and Temporal--Spectral Separation
papers.abstract: While even-parity altermagnets are known for spatially separating charge and spin currents via the crystal spin Hall effect, the defining transport counterpart for odd-parity magnets remains to be established. Here, we establish temporal and spectral charge--spin separation as a general transport signature across all spin-splitting classes of collinear and noncollinear odd-parity magnets with unitary spin-flip inversion $\mathcal U=[C_2^\perp\Vert P]$. This symmetry restricts charge responses to odd orders and $z$-polarized spin responses to even orders, independent of microscopic mechanism and without requiring spin conservation. For ac drives that reverse sign after half a period, charge and spin currents exhibit opposite half-period parities, and their spectra contain only odd charge and even spin harmonics. This allows dc spin rectification without a dc charge counterpart, even in longitudinal transport and beyond weak fields. We show that although antiunitary $\mathcal T\tau$ enforces odd-parity bands, it reverses the charge--spin selection of Berry-curvature and Berry-curvature-dipole responses, providing a direct transport fingerprint distinguishing the two protecting symmetries. We verify the selection rules for all linear and second-order transport mechanisms and demonstrate harmonic separation in a minimal odd-parity model, representative Floquet-engineered collinear MnPS$_3$, and the equilibrium noncollinear VCl$_2$ family.

papers.title: The Effect of Dust Grain Growth and Stellar Metallicity on Gas Giant Planet Formation by Disk Instability
papers.abstract: The formation of gas giant planets by the gas disk gravitational instability (GDGI) mechanism depends sensitively on the thermodynamics of the protoplanetary disk gas: disk gas must be able to cool on orbital timescales for dense clumps to become gravitationally unstable and contract to form protoplanets. Since disk cooling is regulated by the opacity of the dust grains embedded in the gas, the properties of these dust grains are critical for the GDGI mechanism. Grain growth to larger sizes than assumed in traditional opacity models for solar metallicity, as well as protostars with sub-solar metallicity, should have lower opacity disks that are more conducive to planet formation by GDGI. Here we use a three dimensional radiative hydrodynamics and gravitation code to compute the evolution of the GDGI in $0.091 M_\odot$ disks with varied initial minimum values (1.3 to 2.7) of the Toomre criterion orbiting solar-mass protostars. Three sets of eight models are computed: one with the standard opacity, and two more with the opacity reduced by arbitrary factors of 10 or 100. As expected, the reduced opacity models result in enhanced disk fragmentation by the GDGI and the production of more self-gravitating clumps than the standard opacity models. Nevertheless, all three opacities form similar self-gravitating clumps at this early phase of clump evolution, with masses of 0.2 to 0.7 $M_{Jup}$ and semimajor axes between 6 and 13 au. Significant dust grain growth should enhance the ability of the GDGI to form protoplanets around super-solar metallicity protostars.

papers.title: Accretor Luminosity as Probe of Orbital Evolution and Magnetic Braking in AM CVn Binaries
papers.abstract: AM CVn binaries are ultracompact systems with orbital periods $P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 70$ min, where a white dwarf accretes from a He-rich semidegenerate donor. At short orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 20$ min), rapid accretion reheats the accretor. As the system widens and the mass transfer rate decreases, the accretor follows standard white dwarf cooling at longer orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \gtrsim 30$ min). The accretor cooling luminosity then acts as a powerful probe into the orbital evolution of the binary. Recent observations show that the accretor appears brighter (younger) at long orbital periods, compared to models where orbital angular momentum loss is solely set by gravitational wave emission. We show that additional angular momentum loss, which we ascribe to magnetic braking of the donor, can better reproduce observations of accretor luminosity. We test and constrain various proposed magnetic braking formalisms, for the white dwarf, helium star, and evolved cataclysmic variable (CV) channels for AM CVn formation. None of the magnetic braking formalisms in their original form can reproduce the observations, but the widely popular magnetic braking proposed by Rappaport et al. 1983 boosted by a factor $\approx 5$, or the saturated magnetic braking proposed by Matt et al. 2015 boosted by a factor of $\approx 150$, yields satisfactory results. We also find that the CARB formalism, recently applied to the evolved CV channel, is strongly in tension with observations of accretor luminosity. Our models motivate UV spectroscopy observations, and dedicated WD atmosphere models for AM CVn accretors.

papers.title: Multi-scale dynamic latent space models improve inference for a social predator
papers.abstract: Social networks are dynamic in nature. Examining changes in dynamic networks provides insights into the drivers and consequences of social interactions. Dynamic latent space models (DLSMs) quantify social tie strength through a distance measure between latent positions in an unobservable, low-dimensional space. Conditional on the latent positions, ties are assumed independent, and temporal dynamics are introduced through autocorrelated trajectories. These trajectories are typically modeled as random walks; however, random walks lack the mechanism to characterize network clustering, where individuals from the same group tend to form stronger ties than those across groups. Therefore, we extend the framework of DLSM to distinguish within-group dynamics from between-group dynamics. Our approach employs coupled movement models operating at two scales in the latent space to encode community structure using autoregressive processes with attraction. Through simulation studies, we show that when cluster separation is high, our framework improves coverage of linear predictors and enhances overall model fit relative to a naive DLSM. When cluster separation is moderate, performance remains comparable to that of the naive approach. In addition, our method demonstrates empirical computational advantages over the naive DLSM, with potential for further efficiency gains. We apply our framework to a case study of gray wolf (Canis lupus) interactions over three decades in Yellowstone National Park, where it provides improved model performance and novel insights into wolf social dynamics.

papers.title: On generation of the coefficient field of a primitive HMF by a single Fourier coefficient: An application of Nekov\'a\v{r}'s Theorem
papers.abstract:
Let $f$ be a non-CM primitive Hilbert modular form (HMF) over a totally real number field, of parallel even weight $k\geq 2$, with coefficient field $E_f$, and let $F_f \subseteq E_f$ denote the field fixed by the inner twists of $f$.
  In this article, we establish an analogue of Ribet's large image theorem for the residual Galois representations associated with $f$, by applying Nekov\'a\v{r}'s large image theorem (cf.~\cite[Theorem B.5.2]{Nek12}) to the automorphic representation $\pi(f)$ associated with $f$. As a result, we prove that if $f$ has no nontrivial inner twists, then $E_f$ is generated by a single prime Fourier coefficient, for a set of prime ideals of Dirichlet density one. We derive this result as a consequence of a more general theorem established for $F_f$.

papers.title: The Power Of Enumerations
papers.abstract:
We study the computational strength of enumerations of generic and random sets, particularly its interplay with computing these `typical' sets. We show that, while enumerations of $2$-generics can compute $2$-generics, this fails at higher levels---every $3$-generic has an enumeration which computes no weak $3$-generic. The analogous statement holds for randoms---every weak $2$-random has an enumeration which computes no $1$-random.
  We then analyze the total degrees above a quasiminimal enumeration degree, showing certain restrictions as well as certain positive results on the possible Turing degrees in such a cone. This answers a question of Slaman and Sorbi, by showing that there are quasiminimals with no minimal Turing degrees above them. We also show that while every total degree above some quasiminimals compute dimension $1$ sets, the total degrees above any quasiminimal fail to be a subset of the PA degrees.

papers.title: Claw-free difference graphs of finite groups
papers.abstract: Let $\D(G)$ be the difference graph of a finite group $G$: the graph on the non-isolated vertices of $\PE(G)-\Pg(G)$, where $x\sim_{\D} y$ if and only if $\gen{x,y}$ is cyclic and neither of $x,y$ lies in the cyclic group generated by the other. A claw is the graph $K_{1,3}$ and a graph is claw-free if it has no induced claw. We prove that for every finite group $G$, $\D(G)$ is claw-free if and only if it is a disjoint union of copies of the path $P_3$, if and only if the element orders of $G$ are prime powers or $6$, every element of order $3$ has at most one involution in its centralizer, and every involution has at most one subgroup of order $3$ in its centralizer (equivalently: $C_G(a)$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup of order at most $2$ for every $a$ of order $3$, and $C_G(u)$ a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup of order at most $3$ for every involution $u$). Consequences: a nilpotent group that is not a $p$-group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if $G\cong C_6$; $\D(\Sym_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 5$; $\D(\Alt_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 6$; a non-abelian simple group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if it is EPPO or $\PSL_2(11)$ or $\PSL_2(13)$, proved family by family (this uses the classification of finite simple groups). For soluble groups we obtain a complete classification: the non-EPPO soluble groups with claw-free $\D$ are $C_6$, $D_{12}$, $C_3\rtimes C_4$ and the Frobenius groups $N\rtimes K$ with $N$ an abelian $r$-group, $r\ge 5$, and $K\cong C_6$ or $C_3\rtimes C_4$. For every group with claw-free non-empty $\D$ we show $|O_2(G)|\le 2$ and $|O_3(G)|\le 3$, and we give non-soluble examples ($\Sym_5$, $\PGL_2(7)$, $\PSL_2(11)$, $\PSL_2(13)$). We also prove that the full enhanced power graph is claw-free only for cyclic groups and clarify the relations between claw-freeness of $\D(G)$, $\Pg(G)$ and $\PE(G)$.

papers.title: On the prime index elements graph of finite groups
papers.abstract: For a finite group $G$, the prime index elements graph $\G(G)$, introduced by Anitha and Rajkumar, has vertex set $G$, two distinct elements being adjacent if the cyclic subgroup generated by one has prime index in that generated by the other. We show that $\G(G)$ is a bipartite blow-up of a weighted graph $\Hq(G)$ on the cyclic subgroups of $G$, which is a cartesian product of trees when $G$ is nilpotent, and use this to study several graph invariants. We characterize the groups for which $\G(G)$ is a star, a cograph, a chordal graph, or has a perfect code. We compute the sharp bounds for the independence and domination number. We give an exact formula for the strong metric dimension, bound the metric and strong metric dimensions in terms of the quotient graph, show that the upper bounds for the strong metric dimension are attained for cyclic p-groups, and all upper bounds for groups whose prime index elements graph is complete bipartite, and determine the groups attaining the lower bounds: the strong metric dimension attains it only for $\Z_p$ with $p$ odd, and we give a criterion for the metric dimension, which we solve completely for cyclic groups. For nilpotent $G$ we give necessary conditions for $\G(G)$ to be Hamiltonian, in terms of the numbers of covers of cyclic subgroups in the Sylow subgroups, and prove that they are also sufficient when all Sylow subgroups but one are cyclic. We also show that a nilpotent group with a Hamiltonian path is $\Z_3$ or of the form $K\times\Z_2$ with $|K|$ odd, and that in the abelian case above a Hamiltonian path exists exactly when a Hamiltonian cycle does. Finally, we characterize the finite groups $G$ for which $\G(G)$ is planar, toroidal or of genus two.

papers.title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
papers.abstract: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.

papers.title: Don't Discard Your Rollouts: Reusing Teacher RL Traces for Student Distillation
papers.abstract: RL post-training methods such as PPO and GRPO are computationally expensive, with substantial resources devoted to sampling rollouts, which contain multiple completions per prompt along with their respective rewards. Canonical distillation, however, discards these traces and uses more compute to regenerate data from the final teacher. We ask if and how we can reuse the saved teacher RL rollouts to distil student models. Reusing rollouts is non-trivial: naive SFT on the rollouts underperforms canonical distillation, and naive DPO, while performant, is unstable, collapsing on weaker students. We show that treating rollout reuse as a data selection problem using metadata already recorded during GRPO substantially reduces this gap. We use prompt pass rates to order the data, using the easiest prompts for an SFT warm start prior to using mixed-success prompts for DPO. For each prompt, we use saved teacher log-likelihoods as a proxy for selecting student-compatible completions. Across mathematical reasoning and Python coding tasks, with students from multiple model families, our two-stage recipe achieves comparable average performance to canonical distillation, while incurring no additional inference cost for dataset construction.

papers.title: Modeling Attributional Style at Scale: A Dataset and Analysis for Psychological Attribution Assessment and Reframing
papers.abstract: According to the reformulated Learned Helplessness theory, repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can foster a depressogenic attributional style, increasing susceptibility to depression yet remaining a tractable target for cognitive therapy. Computational research on attributional cognition, however, is hampered by the lack of large-scale datasets and robust evaluation protocols. In this work, we introduce the Attributional Style Transfer Dataset (ASTD) along with dedicated evaluation metrics, the first benchmark designed to model, assess, and reframe attributional explanations at scale. Constructed via a Prevent-Filter-Validate pipeline that integrates LLM-based generation with specialist validation, ASTD contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions spanning seven styles. Using this dataset, we address two key challenges: (1) scalable assessment of attributional style via both supervised classifiers and zero/few-shot LLMs; and (2) attributional reframing and evaluation, where we propose automatic evaluation metrics to quantify psychological validity. Furthermore, we leverage our proposed metrics to construct a preference dataset, fine-tuning LLMs with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and achieving substantial gains in reframing quality. Together, our dataset, metrics, and methodology offer a new paradigm for understanding and modeling attributional style, with direct implications for scalable and adaptive mental health interventions. Code and data: https://github.com/qzhou711/ASTD

papers.title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
papers.abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

papers.title: Droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction via pulsed electrohydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations based on the phase-field lattice Boltzmann method are employed to investigate droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction microchannel under pulsed electrohydrodynamics. The applied electric field modulates the interfacial morphology, thereby altering the hydrodynamic stress distribution acting on the liquid-liquid interface. Three configurations are examined: no electric field, top-biased electrode, and bottom-biased electrode. The results show that the top-biased electrode promotes rapid transverse migration of the dispersed phase towards the upper wall, thereby accelerating the transition to the channel-blocking stage. By contrast, under the bottom-biased electrode, the dispersed phase first adheres to the lower wall and subsequently deforms upward under the electric force. As a result, the droplet formation dynamics are strongly affected by the spatial distribution of the electric field. The droplet generation process is further divided into a filling stage and a squeezing stage based on theoretical analysis. During the filling stage, the electric force modifies the filling duration but has little influence on the filling flux. During the squeezing stage, the necking rate and breakup time are governed by the pinning of the dispersed-phase contact line on the channel wall. Compared with constant electric forcing, pulsed electric forcing introduces an additional temporal degree of freedom, enabling stage-dependent modulation of interfacial evolution and breakup dynamics. Finally, droplet sequence diagrams and regime maps are presented for different pulse parameters. The results demonstrate that pulsed electrohydrodynamics in a T-junction enables active and programmable control of consecutive droplet generation.

authors.name: Bin Gong
authors.institution: Shandong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Federated and Balanced $k$-means: Communication Efficiency, Privacy, and Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Collaborating on data across organizations in healthcare and finance demands methods that preserve privacy while enabling effective analysis. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates clustering across data where different parties hold different features of the same entities without sharing raw data. However, existing VFL clustering methods suffer from two key limitations: vulnerability to information leakage and the creation of imbalanced clusters. To address these limitations, we propose Fabric, a balanced and privacy-preserving federated $k$-means algorithm. Our method decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent subproblems for each client, using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently handle the balance constraints. Under the semi-honest model, Fabric provides provable privacy guarantees by injecting calibrated noise into local objective evaluations. Extensive evaluations on ten real-world datasets show that Fabric achieves a superior utility-privacy trade-off compared with state-of-the-art methods and converges faster. Specifically, Fabric reduces SSE by 29.1\% on average and improves balance performance by 1.41$\times$, while being 26$\times$ faster on average.

papers.title: Highly Efficient Vertical Federated Clustering with Triangle-Inequality-based Pruning
papers.abstract: In many real-world scenarios, multiple parties hold complementary feature subsets for the same samples but cannot share raw data. This makes efficient clustering over distributed feature subsets an important and challenging problem. While vertical federated learning (VFL) enables such collaboration, existing VFL clustering methods often require many communication rounds or substantial local computation. To address these limitations, we first propose TriCD, an exact pruning method for CDKM that preserves the same cluster assignments under the same initialization. TriCD constructs triangle-inequality bounds on demand to skip redundant objective evaluations with negligible extra space. Building upon this, we propose FedTriCD, an efficient federated clustering algorithm. By decomposing the global objective into client-local subproblems, FedTriCD enables pruning-based local optimization using only local data. FedTriCD further reduces communication by allowing multiple local updates between server synchronizations. A proximal regularization term is introduced to control the drift caused by infrequent communication. Our theoretical analysis establishes the exactness and finite convergence of TriCD and provides a bounded-error server-side update guarantee for FedTriCD. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficiency and clustering quality of the proposed methods. TriCD achieves up to a 50.07$\times$ speedup over \Lloyd's algorithm. Moreover, FedTriCD achieves competitive clustering quality while requiring fewer local evaluations and fewer communication rounds than state-of-the-art federated clustering methods.

papers.title: Quantum effects on the Peierls stress for screw dislocations in {\alpha}-Fe
papers.abstract: The large discrepancy between the Peierls stress calculated using atomistic methods and that measured in experimental studies is well known. Despite significant research efforts over the past decades, our understanding of this mismatch remains limited. This work presents a multiscale study on the kinetics of screw dislocations in {\alpha}-Fe at 0.7K, employing the phonon description of temperature and using the Concurrent Atomistic-continuum (CAC) method as the simulation tool. Our simulations are shown to preserve the Bose-Einstein distribution of phonon modes and reproduce the nucleation and propagation of kink pairs. Large-scale CAC simulations with dislocation line lengths ranging from 0.1 to 2.1 microns, a typical range of lengths for screw dislocation lines, are performed, providing a quantitative and mechanistic understanding of the phonon-dislocation in {\alpha}-Fe. The experimentally measured Peierls stress in {\alpha}-Fe has been successfully reproduced, and the quantum effects on Peierls stress are quantified. Dependencies of phonon-dislocation interactions on dislocation line length and specimen size are explored and discussed.

papers.title: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.

papers.title: Linear-Size Spectral Sparsification by Sign Descent
papers.abstract:
Given an undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and arbitrary positive weights, we construct a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-spectral sparsifier with $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ edges. For every $0<\varepsilon<1$, the algorithm succeeds with high probability and runs in time \[
  O\!\left(n+\varepsilon^{-3}\bigl[m\log^2 n+n\log^3 n\,(\log\log n)^4\bigr]\right). \] In each phase we seek a reweighting that brings many edge weights to zero or twice their current value while keeping the relative change in every graph energy small. Reversing the weight changes preserves the error and exchanges deletion with doubling, so one choice deletes at least half the edges that reach an endpoint. We balance a smooth penalty for spectral error against a linear reward for alignment with independent random signs. Each step changes the free weights by a fixed fraction of their values at the start of the phase, with directions chosen from the estimated signs of the negative gradient. A weight stays fixed once it reaches an endpoint. We show that while few weights are fixed, the remaining edges admit a direction whose gain in reward exceeds its first-order spectral cost by a constant. The objective is bounded below, so this decrease forces a constant fraction of the weights to an endpoint. We repeat the partial coloring on the surviving edges, choosing the tolerances to keep the total relative error within $\varepsilon$.

papers.title: Hierarchical Agentic Mid-Band Agility for Reliable Low-Latency Space-Air-Ground Integrated V2X Networks
papers.abstract: Upper-mid-band spectrum offers bandwidth opportunities for the integrated networks of ground vehicles, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to support 6G wide-area vehicle-to-everything (V2X) connectivity. However, V2X services' latency and reliability are sensitive to the mid-band selection due to frequency-dependent propagation and rain attenuation. This paper investigates environment-aware spectrum agility over candidate frequency range 3 (FR3) bands within 7.125-24.25 GHz, jointly with end-to-end (E2E) multi-path traffic splitting and transmit power control. Each data packet is partitioned into non-overlapping subflows over direct and UAV-assisted paths, with failed sky-link subflows selectively retransmitted subject to retransmission and freshness constraints. We formulate latency- and reliability-oriented problems, followed by a unified sequential optimization problem incorporating band-switching costs and average quality-of-service (QoS) violation budgets. To coordinate optimization decisions across heterogeneous timescales, we develop an agentic AI-assisted hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (AA-HMARL) framework. A high-level agentic supervisor integrates recurrent memory, analytical evaluation of candidate bands, and event-triggered replanning to coordinate slow environmental adaptation with fast channel and retransmission dynamics, while distributed ground vehicles and UAV agents optimize data splitting and power using constrained MAPPO. Simulation results demonstrate an adjustable reliability-latency trade-off. Particularly, AA-HMARL reduces the mean E2E completion latency and the mean number of retransmission rounds among successfully delivered updates by 17.8-25.5% and 57.6-61.5%, respectively, and reduces the mean age of information (AoI) by 12.7-14.6% relative to fixed-band MAPPO across two traffic types.

papers.title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

papers.title: BitPrefill: W1.58A4 Tensor-Core Acceleration for Compute-Bound LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces large language model (LLM) inference cost, yet implementations optimized for memory-bound decode can leave compute-bound prefill on BF16 tensor cores. This gap matters for input-heavy workloads, including long-context and multimodal applications, where prefill can account for a substantial fraction of inference latency. We propose a W1.58A4 operator that quantizes weights to ternary values and activations to 4-bit, while executing the linear projection on native INT4 general matrix multiply (GEMM) tensor cores, turning prefill from a full-precision matrix multiply into a low-bit one. We deploy the operator for BitNet-b1.58 on a single RTX 4090 and a Jetson Orin Nano edge device, and report GEMM-kernel latency, end-to-end LLMs prefill latency, and task accuracy against bf16 and BitNet/BitBLAS baselines. Our proposed kernel achieves ~1.42x acceleration compared to the original BF16 prefill phase, with negligible reduction on model accuracy.

papers.title: Atomic layer etching of niobium via alternating O$_2$ and H$_2$/SF$_6$ plasma exposures
papers.abstract: Niobium thin films are a key component of superconducting detectors and electronics, and film surface quality, surface roughness, and geometrical dimensional accuracy affect many performance metrics. Atomic layer etching (ALE) is of interest for modifying film surfaces owing to its Angstrom-scale etching precision and surface smoothing characteristics. Here, we report a plasma-enhanced ALE process for Nb based on sequential O$_2$ plasma and H$_2$/SF$_6$ plasma exposures. The process achieves an etch per cycle of 5-7 Angstrom/cycle and exhibits surface smoothing. The superconducting transition temperature of the ALE-treated films is maintained up to the expected decrease associated with reduced film thickness. Our ALE process could find applications in superconducting electronics for which surface quality and precise thickness control are of high importance.

papers.title: Constructing toric diagonal modules with short linear resolutions
papers.abstract: For a complete simplicial toric variety $X$, we construct a collection of Cohen--Macaulay modules with linear resolutions where the associated sheaf is the diagonal. Through this work, we see that the resolutions constructed by Favero--Huang from homotopy path algebras and those constructed by Hanlon--Hicks--Lazarev can be viewed as two dual methods to construct resolutions of the diagonal starting from a compatible $\mathbb{Z}^n$-stratification.

papers.title: Disentangling Disk and Broad-Line Region Continuum Emission in a Sample of Active Galactic Nuclei
papers.abstract: Recent continuum reverberation-mapping measurements of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) indicate that the inter-band time lags are significantly larger than those predicted by the light travel times across the standard thin model. In addition, the observed $u$-band excess suggests the presence of diffuse continuum (DC) radiation originating in the broad-line region (BLR). Spectroscopically, the Balmer and Paschen jumps in DC emission are unique indicators to quantify the contributions of the BLR to the observed continuum. Here, we study the DC contributions of 31 AGNs, whose spectra are obtained with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and with X-shooter on the Very Large Telescope (VLT). In each spectrum, at least one of the Balmer and Paschen jumps is covered. For each object, we performed radiative transfer calculations using Cloudy within the Locally Optimally-emitting Clouds (LOC) model to construct source-specific DC spectral templates. We quantified the DC contribution by incorporating these templates as continuum components in spectral decomposition. The average ratio of the DC to total (i.e., disk+DC) continua is ~33% just below the Balmer jump (~3625 \AA). The Balmer jump provides a stronger constraint on the DC component than the Paschen jump. Simulations based on mock spectra further demonstrate that an unsuitable template can introduce systematic, wavelength-dependent biases to the inferred DC fraction. Our results underscore the importance of employing appropriate DC templates in the spectral decomposition to infer the substantial DC contribution. Upcoming time-resolved spectra will enable more detailed modelling and tighter constraints on the disk and BLR.

papers.title: Disk 2-point functions for conformal loop ensemble: a derivation from the SLE loop CFT
papers.abstract: We give a derivation of the bulk two-point functions of two-dimensional critical loop models in the disk based on conformal loop ensembles (CLE) and the conformal field theory of SLE loop measures developed by Baverez--Jego. Combining local Ward identities with the spectral resolution of the SLE-loop CFT, we express the two-point functions as contour integrals involving known CLE three-point structure constants and Virasoro conformal blocks. With a suitable choice of contour, these integrals are absolutely convergent and provide a unified representation of a broad class of correlation functions, valid for both irrational and rational central charges. For irrational central charges, evaluating these integrals by residues determines the discrete closed-channel spectrum and yields expansions that agree with the analytic bootstrap predictions of Downing--Jacobsen--Nivesvivat--Ribault--Saleur.

authors.name: Xin Sun
authors.institution: China Automotive Technology and Research Center

papers.title: Acoustic Markers of Engagement in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Their Caregivers
papers.abstract: Characterizing user engagement is essential for developing effective human-computer interaction (HCI) applications, particularly for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Because home-based HCI naturally involves caregivers as conversational facilitators, analyzing both child and caregiver vocalizations can provide critical insights into characterizing interaction dynamics. Using a dataset of home-based socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions, this work demonstrates how child and caregiver vocalization patterns can model engagement in HCI contexts. We employed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with child and caregiver acoustic data to identify acoustic features that significantly differentiated engagement from disengagement. The results demonstrated that children and caregivers share three significant acoustic markers of engagement: mean Alpha Ratio (AlphaRatio), mean Harmonics-to-Noise Ratio (HNR), and mean Spectral Slope 500-1500 (SlopeV500-1500). This reflects cleaner and smoother vocalizations during engagement across both groups. Furthermore, we evaluated a State x Group interaction model to compare the magnitudes of standardized state-dependent differences between children and caregivers. The results indicated that children exhibit significantly greater state-related variation than caregivers in three acoustic features: AlphaRatio, HNR, and SlopeV500-1500.

papers.title: Accelerating Muon with Spectral Residual Correction
papers.abstract: Muon constructs matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum. A common route to accelerating Muon is to modify the gradient or momentum before this transformation. We explore a complementary direction: refining the parameter step while retaining Muon's momentum recursion. Derived from the parameter subproblem of the ADMM-Inspired Momentum framework, AIMuon uses the gradient--momentum residual to correct the tentative spectral step. The residual undergoes a separate matrix-sign transformation, while spectral--nuclear duality determines the relative weighting of the momentum and residual directions. In practice, both directions are approximated with Newton--Schulz iterations and their combination is rescaled to match Muon's update magnitude. We establish a stochastic stationarity bound for the corresponding exact iteration. On GPT-2-small, GPT-2-medium, and Qwen3-0.6B, AIMuon reaches Muon's final validation loss with 8.98\%, 10.05\%, and 6.49\% fewer optimization steps, respectively, while achieving lower final validation loss than Muon, Muon-Nesterov, and MONA.

papers.title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.

papers.title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach
papers.abstract: Firms routinely conduct randomized experiments, creating archives that could improve treatment-effect estimation in new experiments. However, past experiments evaluate related but different interventions, so their estimates may be biased for the current target. We study when and how borrowing from multiple auxiliary experiments can reduce the mean squared error (MSE) of a single treatment-effect estimate. In the oracle case, when biases and variances are known, borrowing from even one biased experiment strictly reduces MSE. In practice, we propose three shrinkage estimators and characterize their asymptotic MSE as the number of auxiliary experiments grows. Our analysis shows that average auxiliary bias and cross-study bias dispersion affect the relative performance of these estimators. As expected, smaller average bias magnitude generally improves performance. Surprisingly, bias dispersion can both benefit and harm our first estimator, the general plug-in estimator. On one hand, a more dispersed bias allows flexibility in cancelling the bias. On the other hand, the bias cancellation is imperfect as we only have an estimate of the bias, leading to overfitting. Motivated by this tradeoff, we propose a pooled plug-in estimator that restricts study-specific reweighting to limit this overfitting. However, both plug-in estimators can perform poorly when average bias is large. To address this, we develop a fixed-weight estimator with a hypothesis-testing gate that borrows only when the aggregate auxiliary mean is not significantly different from the target mean. Simulations illustrate the relative strengths of these estimators across bias environments and the relevance of the limiting analysis for finite collections of experiments. We also provide managerial guidance on which shrinkage estimator to use based on average bias and bias dispersion.

authors.name: Qianxi Zhang
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

papers.title: ESSI: Computationally Efficient Semantic Search for Sparse Autoencoder Concepts
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose diffusion model activations into interpretable features, but steering a model with them requires identifying which features map to a given semantic concept, if any.
