For low-cost lasers, coherence lengths are unfortunately very poorly tabulated, and the issue is confounded by multimode emission phenomena generating structured changes in fringe visibility that can be confusing to the uninitiated.[3]

In this article, we describe an easy-to-implement characterization technique for measuring the coherence lengths of laser pointers in the presence of multimode behavior. The experiment was conducted by undergraduates and master’s students as part of independent research projects at San José State University, and we have found it to be an excellent means of teaching students about the properties of optical interference, laser beam alignment, hardware communication, signal processing, and data analysis. In this respect, the report complements instructional laboratory reports discussing coherence length measurements and optical interferometers using other kinds of lasers.[9, 3, 30, 2, 15, 16, 8] However, we go beyond previous works by reporting larger optical path differences than previous works and by reporting on an interferometer design based on a noncollinear arrangement of overlapping beams imaged onto a CMOS array as the experiment is being conducted. The design simplifies alignment and allows the practitioner to simultaneously achieve phase-resolved measurements.

The design simplifies alignment and allows the practitioner to simultaneously achieve phase-resolved measurements.

Scientific applications of the study include measurements of coherence length properties of several commonly available commercial devices for which coherence length information had not previously been made available. We focused on green laser pointers, and within this category there appears to be no clear “winner” between diode lasers and DPSS lasers in terms of coherence length. In some cases diode laser coherence lengths are shorter than comparably priced DPSS lasers, and in other cases they are significantly longer. Nearly universally, however, coherence lengths of diode-based and DPSS laser pointers alike tend to be quite a bit longer than one might naively expect, often extending tens of centimeters. The results open possibilities for developing new kinds of low-cost optical interferometry devices including, perhaps especially, those those requiring large optical-path-difference absolute values but not necessarily requiring the ability to accommodate large optical-path-length variations in time.

papers.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
papers.abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.

papers.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
papers.abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.

papers.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.

papers.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
papers.abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

papers.title: On a potential type II singular model of the Navier Stokes equations
papers.abstract: It is shown that a particular class of partial type I or type II functions are not singularity models for the three dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with or without smooth, compactly supported forces. This extends part of the results for the axially symmetric case to the full three dimension case. Some connections to the recent literature are also discussed.

papers.title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($\sigma=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

papers.title: Nonholonomic Event-Triggered Source Seeking
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an event-triggered source seeking control (ET-SSC) strategy for autonomous vehicles modeled as nonholonomic unicycles. The key feature of the proposed design is the separation between the continuous probing motion required for gradient extraction and the event-triggered update of the source-seeking correction. This separation enables aperiodic computation and transmission of the correction while the periodic probing signals remain continuously active. The triggering mechanism acts on a low-pass-filtered gradient estimate, obtained by high-pass (washout) filtering, demodulation, and low-pass filtering of the measured signal, and combines a relative and an absolute threshold. Stability is proved with a time-periodic Lyapunov function constructed along the exponentially stable periodic solution of the filtered closed loop, establishing practical exponential convergence of the vehicle to a neighborhood of the unknown source. The guaranteed minimum dwell time is strictly positive and independent of the probing frequency, which excludes Zeno behavior. Unlike available Lie-bracket analyses of the forward-velocity design, the proposed averaging-based analysis accommodates anisotropic quadratic source fields with distinct spatial curvatures. The resulting ET-SSC framework therefore provides a resource-aware implementation in which the source-seeking correction is updated aperiodically while the information-generating probing motion remains continuous.

papers.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
papers.abstract: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.

papers.title: Early Assessment Submission and Subsequent Course Outcome: A Day-30 Landmark Observational Analysis of OULAD with Explicit Weighting Diagnostics
papers.abstract: We examined the association between submission of an assessment by day 30 and final course outcome in the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). To avoid classifying students who withdrew during the exposure window as comparable non-submitters, the main analysis was restricted to students enrolled at a day-30 landmark. In the CCC/2014J course presentation, 1,820 students remained after exclusions for missing covariates and unsupported exposure categories; 1,624 had submitted at least one non-banked assessment by day 30. The difference in favorable final outcome rates (Pass or Distinction) was 0.3743. A normalized inverse-probability-weighted contrast was 0.3861 (95% full-refit bootstrap interval 0.3242 to 0.4447). The overlap-weighted contrast was 0.3261 (0.2667 to 0.3870), describing a different weighted population. The weights were unstable in the smaller comparison group, and measured covariates remained imbalanced under inverse-probability weighting. We independently reconstructed the cohort and estimates from the official UCI archive, examined eligibility and missing-data exclusions, and repeated descriptive analyses in three other course presentations. Those comparisons also showed positive associations, but their confidence intervals cannot account for unmeasured differences between the groups. The study identifies a reproducible association among selected learners, not the effect of requiring or encouraging earlier submissions.

papers.title: Interfacial Transition Waves and Domain Wall Self-Pinning in Bi-stable Mechanical Metamaterial
papers.abstract: The understanding of transition waves in mechanical metamaterials currently derives from architectures fitting one of three archetypes as distinguished by the stability and order parameter: multi-stable with scalar or vector order parameter, and bi-stable with scalar order parameter. However, a fourth archetype is conspicuously absent: bi-stable with vector order parameter. Completing the tetrad, in this article, we numerically examine the transformation dynamics unique to bi-stable mechanical metamaterials with vector order parameter. We report two types of interfacial transition waves, whose propagation is restricted to the narrow region of configurational boundaries (e.g., domain walls). We show that the wave speed may depend on its polarization. In addition, we reveal an approach to regulate the severity of discreteness effects, which elevates discreteness as an intrinsic, tunable mechanism for controlling the wave speed -- including pinning/de-pinning of the domain wall -- without altering the metamaterial architecture. The results support applications in, e.g., reconfigurable mechanical circuits and complex domain patterning, and motivate further investigation of metamaterials with unconventional transition processes.

papers.title: Differential Transmutations and First-Passage Expansions for Monomial Brownian Boundaries
The Strong AJ Conjecture for Hyperbolic Prime Knots is False
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a knot in $S^3$. The strong AJ conjecture relates two of its invariants. The first is the minimal-order annihilator $\widehat A$ of the $n$th colored Jones polynomial $J(n)$. The second is the two-variable $A$-polynomial of Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen. The conjecture says that after specialization $\varepsilon^*(\widehat A)\asymp A$. Zhang gave the first family of composite-knot counterexamples. For $8_{11}$ the specialization of $\widehat A$ carries an extra trefoil factor $L+M^6$. We prove this by verifying L\^e's $\widehat P=\widehat A$ conjecture. Zhang's corrected formulation of the AJ conjecture agrees with L\^e's weak AJ conjecture, which we prove for $8_{11}$. Li, Li, and Sun have since reported counterexamples of the weak AJ conjecture among non-hyperbolic prime knots. This work was AI assisted, and parts of it have been formalized in Lean.

papers.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

papers.title: A simple approach to ends of manifolds and the Freudenthal compactification
papers.abstract: In this note we give an alternative definition of the Freudenthal end-compactification of a non-compact manifold by defining ends to be the filters of open subsets with compact boundaries that have a base of connected subsets. We start by defining these notions and proving that the resulting compactification is equivalent to the Freudenthal compactification. In particular, we explicitly discuss the equivalence between our definitions and those from two different approaches: maximal binding families and inverse limits. After that, we give an example of a non-metrizable manifold, showing how these new definitions make it easier to identify ends and understand the topology of the end-compactification. We also prove a well-known metrization theorem, showing an application of our definition. Finally, we also give an alternative proof of the topological characterization of the Freudenthal compactification.

papers.title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
papers.abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

papers.title: Who Should Verify? Reviewer Selection with Partial Information and Outcome Audits
papers.abstract: Selecting an AI reviewer requires evidence about what it does after reading a draft. On a fixed batch of items, a team can keep the original answers or adopt one reviewer's answers throughout. We ask how much it costs to certify that the chosen procedure falls at most a specified number of correct answers short of the best available procedure, for every completion of the unobserved evidence. When all reviews are available and only verified answer keys cost money, we give an exact stopping rule and an integer program for the cheapest certificate in hindsight. When reviews and keys both have prices, a polynomial-time algorithm using the completed record approximates the minimum certificate cost within a factor logarithmic in the number of procedures. This dependence is tight to leading order unless P equals NP. Finding a certificate can be much more expensive. We exhibit a two-procedure family with $n$ unresolved items where one purchase suffices in hindsight but the exact minimax expected search cost is $(n+1)/2$. For two binary procedures under a known independent and identically distributed item law, five counts suffice to compute an optimal search policy. We replay reviews on 2,000 MMLU questions, 896 numerical reports, and 48 Singapore electricity forecast reports. With reviews available, a targeted audit used 6.9% fewer keys on MMLU and 1.2% fewer on numerical reports than a fixed order selected on development data. Compared with selection by stand-alone accuracy, the chosen procedures gained 2.94 percentage points on held-out MMLU questions and zero on numerical reports. On electricity reports, five checks certified a tie across all 48, yet each procedure was correct only eight times.

papers.title: Cross-Linguistic Distinctive-Feature Constraints on Segmental Triphones: Evidence for Contrastive Dispersion
papers.abstract: Natural speech reflects articulatory and perceptual constraints, yet how these pressures shape consecutive segment transitions across languages remains underexplored. We analyze adjacent distinctive-feature distances in token-weighted segmental triphones across 17 Universal Dependencies corpora spanning nine language families, transcribed into IPA and mapped to 24 PanPhon features using Hamming and cosine metrics. Natural sequences exhibit an intermediate-distance mode (8-10 features under Hamming, except Vietnamese; 0.28-0.38 under cosine). Against an unrestricted within-word shuffled baseline, natural words reject the inventory-only null (W = 0, p < 10-4), showing higher expected distance, narrower dispersion, and lower joint triphone entropy in all 17 languages. Under a stricter within-word consonant-vowel template baseline, expected distance and dispersion are no longer separated, whereas joint entropy remains lower in 16 languages (p = 1.07x10-4). Entropy decomposition reveals higher mutual information between incoming and outgoing transitions in all 17 languages and all nine families (W = 0, p < 10-4), demonstrating sequential coupling beyond syllable-template alternation. Word-level mean-SD correlations and directional asymmetries do not replicate cross-linguistically.

papers.title: Transition-Metal Substitutions in MOF-5: A Hybrid-DFT Study of Oxygen Electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Hybrid density functional theory calculations were used to investigate the stability, electronic properties, and catalytic activity of transition-metal impurities substituting Zn sites (M\(_{\rm Zn}\)) in the MOF-5 metal-organic framework [Zn\(_4\)O(BDC)\(_3\), BDC = 1,4-benzenedicarboxylate], with M = Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu. Most substitutions introduce \(3d\) states within the MOF-5 band gap and induce localized magnetic moments. Partially occupied \(3d\) states promote orbital hybridization and charge transfer with oxygenated intermediates, activating the dopant sites toward oxygen electrocatalysis. The oxygen reduction and evolution reaction (ORR and OER) activities were evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode model. Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Fe\(_{\rm Zn}\) exhibit calculated ORR overpotentials of 0.57~V, while Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Co\(_{\rm Zn}\) yield OER overpotentials of 0.42 and 0.51~V, respectively, approaching those of benchmark precious-metal electrocatalysts. These findings identify Mn substitution as a promising strategy for achieving bifunctional ORR/OER activity in MOF-5 and establish a link between dopant electronic structure and catalytic performance to guide the design of MOF-based electrocatalysts.

papers.title: The $n!$ theorem via quaternionic rotation of Cherednik algebras
papers.abstract: We give a proof of the $n!$ theorem based on the representation theory of Cherednik algebras and an analog of the rotation of complex structures arising from an action of the quaternions.

papers.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.

papers.title: Uniqueness of $L_{p}$ Minkowski Problem in the supercritical range near the affine exponent
papers.abstract: We study the isotropic $ L_{p} $-Minkowski problem. The equation is affine invariant at the exponent $ p = -n-1 $, where all origin-centered ellipsoids with the volume of the unit ball are solutions, and it is known that the unit sphere is the only solution for $ p \in (-n-1, 1) $. We prove uniform $ C^{0} $ estimates for all solutions in the supercritical range $ p < -n-1 $. This allows us to prove a key spectral estimate of the Hilbert-Brunn-Minkowski operator on solutions. We then utilize the Rayleigh quotient method with position vectors as test functions for the operator adapted from Ivaki-Milman to prove uniqueness in the range $ p \in (-n-1- \delta_{n}, -n-1) $ for some $ \delta_{n} > 0 $.

papers.title: Energy-constrained Brownian motion
papers.abstract: For reflected Brownian motion in an interval of length $N$, we consider the first time at which the length of time since the most recent visit to the boundary reaches $M$; this random `lifetime' comes from the interpretation in which the Brownian motion has a finite energy capacity $M$, uses energy at unit rate in the interior, and gets its energy replenished up to $M$ on every visit to the boundary. We prove distributional asymptotics for the lifetime in three different regimes depending on the relative growth of $N$ and $M$; these one-dimensional results parallel results in the random walk case by Wade and Grinfeld. We also present some initial results on the multidimensional version of the problem, for one scaling regime in the case of a ball, and conjectures on the behaviour in general domains.

papers.title: Boundary remainders and optimal convergence rates for planar spectral partitions
papers.abstract: Let $S_m(\Omega)$ denote the infimum of the sum of the first Dirichlet eigenvalues over partitions of a bounded connected planar domain $\Omega$ into exactly $m$ nonempty connected open cells. We study the convergence of $|\Omega|S_m(\Omega)/m^2$ to its universal limit $c_*$. If the full topological boundary has zero area, we bound the absolute error by the area of its tubular neighborhood at scale $m^{-1/2}$, together with an $O(m^{-1/2})$ term. This yields rates $O_\Omega(m^{-1/2})$ on Lipschitz domains and $O_\Omega(m^{-\alpha/2})$ on domains with finitely many $C^{0,\alpha}$ boundary charts, $0<\alpha<1$, for all sufficiently large integers. The square and a fixed smooth domain have positive matching lower bounds of order $m^{-1/2}$. For each $\alpha\in(0,1)$, a fixed H\"older graph domain attains the order $m^{-\alpha/2}$ along a subsequence. Little H\"older domains satisfy the corresponding little-$o$ estimate, but no prescribed additional factor tending to zero works for the whole class, even with domain-dependent constants. An auxiliary energy with variable cell count gives the boundary estimate; a positive correction on the square and sparse graph constructions yield the lower bounds.

papers.title: Uniformising random greedy maximal independent sets on graphs with at most five vertices
papers.abstract: A random greedy algorithm scans the vertices of a finite graph in increasing order of independent exponential arrival times and accepts each vertex unless an accepted neighbour blocks it. We ask an inverse question: can strictly positive finite arrival rates be chosen so that the terminal inclusion-maximal independent sets are all equally likely? We call this exact property exponential greedy uniformisability (EGU). We establish the complete small-order classification: every finite simple graph on at most five vertices is EGU, with the unique exception of the five-vertex path $P_5$ up to graph isomorphism. A strict $2\times2$ probability minor provides an explicit obstruction for the exceptional graph; the positive cases are certified by graph-isomorphism reduction and exact constructive witnesses. We explain the independent-exponential-clock probability law and the formal Lean 4 verification, registered as Palomar PALOMAR-2026-11-19-000021 (version 1). The registration is a formal proof record, not a claim of novelty certification or journal peer review.
papers.intro:
Random sequential adsorption on graphs (RSA) and random greedy independent-set algorithms start from a random ordering and accept a vertex when no previously accepted neighbour forbids it [4, 2]. The result is maximal by inclusion, but generally neither maximum by cardinality nor uniformly distributed among maximal independent sets. An equal-rate exponential race gives a uniform random permutation. Here, in contrast, the rates are design parameters: we wish to control the entire terminal-set law. Unequal rates in RSA are not themselves new [3]; the question is whether they can enforce an exact uniform law over the finite set of terminal configurations.

papers.title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
papers.abstract: Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.

Unlike RGB images, depth cameras and LiDARs deliver metric 3D measurements of the body: they remove the ambiguity of depth and scale, are unaffected by illumination, and place the person in world coordinates.

However, existing point-based methods are designed around one kind of sensor. Depth-camera approaches [21, 55, 31, 8] expect dense inputs of several thousand sampled points, while LiDAR approaches [28, 45, 44, 46, 1] operate on sparse scans with only hundreds of points and recover the missing geometry by aggregating long point sequences, up to 32 frames in the latest methods. Each sensor has its own models and benchmarks, and the data are not interchangeable: after 2 cm voxelization, the median person has 2.3k points in the Azure Kinect views of HuMMan [9] but about 100 for the most distant LiDAR in FreeMotion [45]; in addition, labels come in different body models. Image-based mesh recovery, by comparison, has gained substantially from training one model across many datasets [19, 10]. We are not aware of any model that serves both sensor families with one set of weights.

To bridge this gap, we present SparseHPS (Fig. 2), a novel network that estimates human pose and shape from point clouds, frame by frame or over a stream. Its encoder is LitePT [61], a point transformer over sparse voxels that uses convolutions at the fine levels and attention at the coarse ones. Specifically, 24 learnable query tokens, one per body joint plus one for shape and one for translation, cross-attend to voxels from the two coarsest stages of the encoder, and all joint tokens share one linear head. Instead of predicting the global position directly from a token, each voxel votes for the pelvis location, weighted by the translation token. In addition, a causal memory lets each token attend to its own states in the seven previous frames; for a frame with no history, the computation reduces exactly to the single-frame model. We refer to the single-frame variant as SparseHPS-S and to the variant with memory as SparseHPS-T.

papers.title: The 1-Loop and Ohtsuki-Takata Invariants for Alternating Braids
papers.abstract: In a step towards resolving the 1-loop conjecture, Ohtsuki and Takata defined their own eponymous invariant in terms of an open knot diagram, and showed that it is equal to the adjoint Reidemeister torsion for two-bridge knots. Garoufalidis and Yoon then showed that the 1-loop invariant is equal to the Ohtsuki-Takata invariant using a technique involving a collapsed octahedral decomposition. This paper expands those techniques to relate the matrix determinants of the 1-loop and Ohtsuki-Takata invariants for the case of reduced alternating braids.

papers.title: Large Reported CHB-MIT Adaptation Gains Disappear with Pretrained Encoders and Matched Probes
papers.abstract: Dani and Liebe (2026) (DL) report that adapting the final encoder block of BIOT and CBraMod with self-supervised learning (SSL) improves CHB-MIT seizure-detection ROC-AUC by 36.2 and 29.5 points over linear probing. We investigate these results with their released code and an independent pipeline. The release loads pretrained weights for adaptation only when an otherwise unset configuration key is supplied, and its CBraMod probe reads the reconstruction head with dropout active. With pretrained initialisation and a probe on the encoder output in evaluation mode, the fixed-recipe adaptation gain on DL's split is -0.6 points for BIOT (95% interval [-3.8, +2.6]) and +0.01 for CBraMod ([-0.02, +0.04]) across five seeds. Across DL's split and five subject rotations on CHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG, with equally tuned linear probes (30 configurations, up to 500 epochs, validation-based early stopping), mean adaptation effects range from -1.1 to +5.7 ROC-AUC points over 18 comparisons (related settings and feature variants). Twelve of 18 support equivalence within +/-3 points under dependence-adjusted inference (8 of 12 rotation and 4 of 6 fixed-split comparisons); six are unresolved. After correcting rotation intervals for dependence, no positive effect has a 95% interval excluding zero. The +/-3 margin is an analysis threshold, not a clinically validated one, and smaller margins support fewer equivalences. Two fixed-probe gains near +21 points shrink under the same tuning, with smaller benefits unresolved. We also audit a CHB-MIT protocol shared by at least 14 papers. No tested configuration reproduces DL Table 1 as a whole. These findings concern the tested configurations; the encoder-level probe and subsequent checks were chosen post hoc.
papers.intro:
EEG foundation models such as BIOT (Yang et al., 2023), LaBraM (Jiang et al., 2024) and CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025a) are pretrained on large unlabelled EEG corpora and transferred to clinical tasks. Dani & Liebe (2026) (hereafter DL) propose a low-cost adaptation step between pretraining and probing: update only the final encoder block with the model’s own SSL objective on unlabelled windows of the target dataset, then train a linear probe, reporting results on CHB-MIT (Shoeb, 2009; Goldberger et al., 2000), TUAB and TUEV. Our primary analysis concerns the reported adaptation gains on CHB-MIT; Section 5 examines their data-amount and patient-count claims, quoted from their abstract, as exploratory analyses. These three claims are our reproduction targets. • C1 (headline gain). SSL adaptation (SA) improves on linear probing (LP). The largest gain in DL’s results, +36.2 ROC-AUC, is BIOT on CHB-MIT (LP 46.93, SA 83.08, DL Table 1); for CBraMod DL report LP 54.14 and SA 83.67 (+29.5). DL’s abstract states the gain as “up to 20×\times AUCPR” (BIOT 1.53 to 31.52). ROC-AUC is our primary metric, matching the validation selection criterion of the release’s main trainer (Section 2); precision–recall performance is in Section 4.3 and Appendix E.17. • C2 (data amount). “Under a fixed compute budget, peak performance requires only 20–50% of available unlabeled data.” • C3 (patient count). “Critically, when total window count is fixed, performance remains invariant to patient count.” Our primary purpose is to reproduce a published result. DL followed a CHB-MIT protocol that at least 13 other papers also use (Section 3.3).

Our audit identifies two implementation choices that materially affect the comparison. With the released defaults the adaptation step updates a randomly initialised encoder, whereas linear probing uses the pretrained weights: the SSL step loads the checkpoint only if a configuration key is set that no shipped file sets. The CBraMod probe also reads reconstruction outputs with dropout active, and the inherited CHB-MIT protocol tests on two patients (Section 3). Starting adaptation from the pretrained weights and probing the encoder output in eval mode (the encoder-level probe, Section 2) removes the large gains on DL’s CHB-MIT split: the SA gain is −0.6-0.6 for BIOT and +0.01+0.01 for CBraMod (intervals in Table 1). Under a revised protocol with five subject rotations on CHB-MIT and Siena and the fixed probe recipe, gains of the reported size are rejected and the CBraMod gain is equivalent to zero within ±3\pm 3. Equal-budget probe tuning reduces the raw-linear BIOT gains of +1.9 to +9.2 seen under the fixed training recipe. The expanded search covers 18 related comparisons (Section 4.3; Tables 14 and 15).

EEG foundation-model benchmarks compare many models and adaptation strategies across many datasets under one harmonised pipeline (Xiong et al., 2025; Kastrati et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026); they ask which model transfers best, and run every model inside their own pipeline. We instead audit the implementation underlying one published adaptation method, running the authors’ released code at a fixed commit and changing one setting at a time, and make no ranking of models. Data-leakage studies show that EEG test sets sharing subjects with training sets inflate accuracy, including for seizures (Brookshire et al., 2024; Shafiezadeh et al., 2023), part of a wider pattern in machine-learning-based science (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023). The inherited CHB-MIT protocol is not of this kind: its test patients are not in training, and its problems are a two-patient test set, a boundary-based label rule and duplicated test windows (Section 3.3). Random-weight and noise-input controls test whether gains require pretrained representations or EEG-specific adaptation data; such controls are standard in epidemiology (Lipsitch et al., 2010) and have been proposed for clinical EEG foundation-model benchmarks (Zare, 2026). We apply both: a probe on randomly initialised weights next to every adapted arm (Saxe et al., 2011), and SSL adaptation on Gaussian noise, which alone can shape useful features (Baradad Jurjo et al., 2021). Variance that a single split hides (Bouthillier et al., 2021) motivates the subject rotations and the corrected intervals (Nadeau & Bengio, 2003); event-level scoring follows SzCORE (Dan et al., 2025).

EEG foundation-model benchmarks compare many models and adaptation strategies across many datasets under one harmonised pipeline (Xiong et al., 2025; Kastrati et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026); they ask which model transfers best, and run every model inside their own pipeline. papers.title: Sparse IRSs in Acylindrically Hyperbolic Groups that Surject Onto $\mathbb{Z}$
papers.abstract: For a non-elementary acylindrically hyperbolic group $\Gamma$ that surjects onto the integers, we construct an invariant random subgroup $\Lambda$ of $\Gamma$ for which the expected word-length of the shortest non-trivial element of $\Lambda$ is infinite. We refer to these as ``sparse" IRSs. The construction employs properties of renewal processes on $\mathbb{Z}$ as well as work of Dahmani, Guirardel, and Osin (arxiv:1111.7048v5) on the freeness of normal closures of certain elements in non-elementary acylindrically hyperbolic groups. We contrast this with the case of property (T) groups which cannot possess such IRSs. As an application, we answer a question posed in (arxiv:1612.09510v1) by constructing IRSs of $\mathrm{Isom}^+(\mathbb{H}^n)$ which have infinite expected injectivity radius, something which is impossible for higher-rank geometries due to work by Abert, Bergeron, et al. (arxiv:1210.2961v4)

An invariant random subgroup (IRS) of a topological group GG is a probability distribution on the set of closed subgroups of GG which is invariant under the action of conjugation. These objects were first introduced as such in the paper [3] for countable groups. But they found significant geometric application in [1], where they were used to establish certain asymptotics on Betti numbers of lattices in semisimple Lie groups in terms of their covolume. In that same paper it was shown, as a corollary of the Stück-Zimmer Theorem [15], that any non-atomic ergodic IRS of a center-free higher-rank simple Lie group GG is a so-called ‘lattice IRS.’ If XX is the symmetric space for GG and M=Γ\XM=\Gamma\backslash X is a finite-volume GG-manifold, then the corresponding lattice IRS of GG is obtained by picking a base frame uniformly at random on MM. This determines a random conjugate of Γ\Gamma, and the law of this random conjugate is invariant under conjugation by elements of GG, so this is an IRS of GG..

papers.title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
papers.abstract: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. The protocol charges decoy false alarms, unnecessary actions and endorsed developer assertions, counts invalid outputs as misses, folds newly automatable findings back into P1 with discovery credit, and fixes safety bounds and a break-even cost gate in advance. On a synthetic credit-scorecard harness, five scripted reference policies show why this matters: naive case accuracy (4/6) and pooled detection (3/5) tie four flawed policies, whereas the protocol separates all five and credits only the reference policy with detection beyond P1. One fold-back round raises a P1-parroting policy's naive scores without any change to the policy. A regression matrix of sixteen mutants covers nine ways in which earlier versions of the evaluation passed misleadingly. No LLM agent has been evaluated yet; we specify a falsifiable pilot.
papers.intro:
Banks validate the quantitative models behind credit and risk decisions through effective challenge: critical, independent analysis by people with the competence and standing to change how a model is used [1, 2, 3]. Validators reconcile specifications with implementations, probe boundaries, test outcome analyses and write findings. LLM agents can read submissions, call tools and draft findings, and agentic systems for model-risk tasks are already being built [4]. Plausible prose is not assurance, however, and indirect prompt injection turns developer-supplied material into an untrusted input [5, 6].

In April 2026, SR 26-2 replaced most of SR 11-7 [1, 2]. It excludes generative and agentic AI from its model scope and leaves controls for such tools to banks’ own risk management practices, while the models being validated stay in scope [2]. In the EU, creditworthiness assessment is a high-risk AI use [7]. An AI-enabled validation workflow, rather than the model under validation, is therefore an engineering object that banks must govern themselves, and it is our subject.

papers.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
papers.abstract: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

This paper reports that measurement. Four coding agents ran with their permission prompts off, inside a container that could reach only the vendor’s API and a local mock service. I deposited every design choice before the first run [3]. The hidden tests are my own checks of each task, written from the task text and frozen by hash before any run, and kept where the agent could not read them. Three results matter most.

1. Under the rules file, one agent reported the task complete while it failed most of my hidden tests. Its own tests passed. It had added a requirement the task did not ask for. In 11 of its 36 steps, Codex CLI reported the task complete with all tests passing, while fewer than half of my hidden tests passed. Its score on my tests fell from 99.0% without the file to 67.7% with it. The other three agents, with the same file and the same tests, moved by less than 2.5 points. 2. My main measure found no bugs for the file to fix. The checkers flagged 31 spots in the code the agents wrote. I read each one without knowing which arm it came from, and all 31 were false alarms. With or without the file, every agent wrote zero real bugs of the kind I checked for, so this test could not show the file helping. On bugs the file made no difference I could see. That is not proof it has no effect, only that this test could not tell. 3. The agents rarely tried to cross the lines I built. I built four: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Three agents met them. A gate stood in front of the mock service to block forbidden requests. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind it at the three HTTP boundaries, and only the neutral-file arm ran without it. In 5 of 90 steps behind the gate, an agent tried to cross, 3 without the file and 2 with it. All 5 were OpenCode with DeepSeek, and the gate blocked every request, 11 in all. Where there was no gate, 4 of 60 runs with the neutral file crossed, and none of the 30 package runs without the file or with the rules file did. One result hints that behaviour moved with the file. Without the file, OpenCode used an access token it found in the repository in all 5 runs. With the file, the token reached the service in none of 5, and its one try was blocked by the gate. Five runs are too few to prove it. The next study will test it.

papers.title: Combinatorial relative orientability for toric and tropical geometry
papers.abstract: Many problems in enumerative geometry are solved by computing the degree of the top Chern class of a suitable vector bundle. Results from $\mathbb{A}^1$-homotopy theory allow to answer enumerative questions over arbitrary fields, replacing the top Chern class by the Euler class in Chow-Witt groups. For its degree to be well-defined, one needs the vector bundle to be relatively oriented. Another way to solve enumerative problems is to translate them to tropical geometry, where they become combinatorial problems. In this paper, we give a combinatorial description of relative orientability for vector bundles over smooth proper toric varieties. We show that it behaves well under tropicalization, establishing a tropical version of relative orientability, which will allow to the use of tropical geometry to answer enumerative questions over arbitrary fields. As a demonstration, we prove a quadratically enriched version of the Bernstein-Khovanskii-Kushnirenko theorem via tropical geometry. Lastly, we define the notion of $k$-phase structures on tropical hypersurfaces, generalizing the real case.

papers.title: Gumbel Substitution: Removing Sampler Drift from RL Without Trusting the Sampler
papers.abstract: When RL rollouts come from untrusted samplers on arbitrary hardware, precision and checkpoint lag, the sampling distribution $q$ differs from the trainer's policy $p$, and training on the sampler's tokens adds a drift term equal to supervised fine-tuning toward $q$. Published corrections (TIS, MIS, IcePop, score centering, GSPO, CISPO) all need $q(y)$, which a permissionless sampler reports and can misreport. We introduce Gumbel substitution. The coordinator fixes public Gumbel noise for every token position, bit-identical across GPUs, and the sampler draws $y=\arg\max(\ell^q+G)$. The trainer recomputes $v^*=\arg\max(\ell^p+G)$, the token its own policy would have drawn with the same noise, and scores $v^*$ in the sampler's context. For a sampler that follows the protocol, $v^*$ is an exact sample from $p$ given the prefix, so the drift vanishes in expectation for any $q$, without sampler-reported probabilities. We measure the residual left by the deployed heads, bound the one added by admission gates, and state what an adaptive sampler can still do. The same comparison gives a per-token match rate that admits and pays samplers. In the lab, on a 9B model with the same head on both sides, the expected drift of uncorrected training is at least 170 to 4,800 times that of substitution. On a 2B model under strong mismatch, uncorrected training collapses while substitution stays stable, comparable to MIS with score centering given the true $q$. On a permissionless network, a 9B model was trained for 158 optimizer steps on 15.75B tokens from heterogeneous samplers, with no skipped step and 1.21% of tokens substituted; it improved on all eight held-out benchmarks.

Rollout generation dominates the compute of RL for language models: about 4.5×4.5\times the training FLOPs in INTELLECT-2 [1], and 80 to 84% of the GPUs in recent large runs, which report inference-to-training ratios of 3.9:1 to 5.4:1 [2] and 4,096 inference chips out of 4,864 [3]. Moving it onto a permissionless network of independent GPUs would cut its cost, and recent work has made this practical: TOPLOC [12] makes untrusted inference verifiable, and INTELLECT-2 [1] trained a 32B model asynchronously on rollouts from untrusted machines. One problem remains open, and it is the one that destabilizes training. On such a network, samplers choose their hardware, their precision and the checkpoint they sample from, and the trainer accepts their tokens without trusting them. We deployed the method on Reliquary, subnet 81 of Bittensor, an open network in which a coordinator (the subnet’s validator) pays anyone for compute it can verify; the samplers are independent operators paid per verified token.

papers.title: Passivity Correction of the Thermistor Model in Bolometric Power Sensors and Its Dependence on Bead Temperature
papers.abstract: This paper closes a series of works on thermistor bolometric power sensors, coaxial and waveguide, by treating what the two have in common. The per-state transformation m introduced in the waveguide work, which corrects the thermistor impedances of the model in each bridge state so that the two-port of the mount is passive, is analyzed on the eleven sensors of the preceding papers: the corrections are a few tenths of a percent in the coaxial mounts and one to two percent in the waveguide mounts, follow one pattern within each family, and the hottest state is the one whose efficiency departs most from the others. The transformation is tested by an independent measurement: the substituted powers of the three states, read with the manufacturer's procedure against a leveled source whose reflection is obtained from the closure of three Apollonius circles, give efficiency ratios of 0.999 +/- 0.016 and 0.997 +/- 0.008 (k = 2), which contain the values at the passivity floor (0.996, 0.998) and exclude those of the first pass (0.941, 1.023). Three sensors were swept in the bridge resistance, 23 and 31 states, and a fourth is treated apart: the correction reduces to one constant per state, the parallel resistance of the bead, represented by a law with one term scaling with the bridge resistance and one exponential in the bead temperature, with one thermal coefficient per family. The same property explains why the cross-ratio of four measured reflection coefficients, invariant under any state-independent two-port, departs from that of the four bridge resistances.

In the course of the investigation of thermistor bolometric power sensors, once an equivalent model and the physical conditions that determine its parameters had been established, with results consistent with the available calorimetric certificates both for the coaxial mounts (478A, 8478B) [1] and for the K486 waveguide mounts and one specimen of the R486 [2], all the sensors examined—regardless of their characteristics and of the differences in their physical construction—were found to share one problem: the passivity of the scattering matrix implied by the model. We recall that the basic model, which can be found in either of the reference documents, consists of a thermistor represented by its impedance Zth,iZ_{\mathrm{th},i}, where ii denotes the state in which the reflection coefficient of the sensor Γi\Gamma_{i} is measured, i=2i=2 being the central state recommended by the manufacturer for the operation of the sensor, and of a scattering matrix SS common to all the states, which represents the physical connection between the thermistor and the sensor port (Fig. 1).

The efficiency of a bolometer mount has been obtained from impedance data since the work of Kerns [3], Beatty and Reggia [4] and Engen [5, 6], and the microcalorimeter [7] remains the primary standard against which such determinations are judged, in coaxial line [8] and in waveguide [9, 10, 11, 12], with the direct-comparison transfer [13, 14] and the key comparisons of calibration factor [15] as the link to the working standards; thermoelectric and bolometric standards have been compared in [16]. The thermistor itself has been modeled as a nonlinear element by Kazemipour and Ziadé [17, 18], and the two preceding works of this series [1, 2] determine the calibration factor from the reflection coefficients of three bridge states with a physically constrained model of the bead. Kazemipour and Ziadé report a capacitance of the bare thermistor, measured in a test fixture, that depends on the bias resistance; what none of these works describes is how the bead changes within its mount from one bridge state to the next, as a function of its temperature and under the passivity of the mount, nor tests that change by substituted power; the present paper is about that change, and it uses the microcalorimeter literature only as the reference the final verification is compared with.

papers.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.

papers.title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication over Tor using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
papers.abstract: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.
papers.intro:
Achieving private and anonymous communication is an ongoing challenge. Specifically regarding voice communication, despite end-to-end encryption that is commonly used, there is significant exposure of metadata, i.e., further information attached to the encrypted data[1]. Furthermore, besides metadata, quantum computing puts asymmetric encryption itself at risk: With quantum-algorithms, conventional RSA and ECC public-key cryptography could be attacked through Shor’s algorithm, significantly reducing its computational hardness[2]. While quantum-computing at this scale is not yet practicably available, confidential data should be resistant to future threats by design[3]. Moreover, centralized infrastructure puts providers of services at risk of being targeted by cyberattacks[4].

papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
